# Energy: how rooftop solar spreads

The Bass model is the standard description of how a new technology spreads: some households adopt because of advertising and subsidies (the *innovation* coefficient `p`), most because people they know have adopted (the *imitation* coefficient `q`). This tutorial runs the [Bass diffusion model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/bass_diffusion.html) from the zoo, compares it with the Bass equation and asks how much the structure of a social network slows adoption down.

Start your own project from it with `modelly zoo copy bass_diffusion my_solar` (the same command in bash and PowerShell).

## Build and run

Five thousand households; a step is a tenth of a year. With `mixing="well-mixed"` every household sees the adoption share of the whole population, as in Bass’s original model.

```ipython3
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from modelly.zoo.bass_diffusion.model import BassDiffusion, BassScenario, bass_curve

scenario = BassScenario(rng=3, households=5000, innovation=0.03, imitation=0.38)
model = BassDiffusion(scenario)
model.run()
frame = model.datacollector.get_model_vars_dataframe()
frame.iloc[::40]
```

|  | time | adoption |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.0 | 0.0000 |
| 40 | 4.0 | 0.2370 |
| 80 | 8.0 | 0.6456 |
| 120 | 12.0 | 0.9054 |
| 160 | 16.0 | 0.9812 |
| 200 | 20.0 | 0.9948 |

## Plot: the S-curve against the Bass equation

```ipython3
years = frame["time"].to_numpy()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.plot(years, frame["adoption"], label="agent-based, well mixed")
ax.plot(years, bass_curve(years, 0.03, 0.38), "k--", label="Bass equation")
ax.set_xlabel("years")
ax.set_ylabel("share of households adopted")
ax.legend(frameon=False);
```

![../../_images/83c5cb606ad9876f5f5dda2b2f7d17710e079d3639f4a7fe165fffe4fbed5e0a.png](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/_images/83c5cb606ad9876f5f5dda2b2f7d17710e079d3639f4a7fe165fffe4fbed5e0a.png)

The yearly number of new adopters peaks at `t* = ln(q / p) / (p + q)`:

```ipython3
new = np.diff(frame["adoption"].to_numpy()) / scenario.dt
print(f"peak of the simulated adoption rate: {years[1:][np.argmax(new)]:.1f} years")
print(f"Bass prediction:                     {np.log(0.38 / 0.03) / 0.41:.1f} years")
```

```myst-ansi
peak of the simulated adoption rate: 6.6 years
Bass prediction:                     6.2 years
```

## Analysis: does the network matter?

On a random network each household sees only its neighbours. With few neighbours, clusters of non-adopters see fewer adopters than the population average, and imitation is slower.

```ipython3
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
for degree in (2, 4, 10, 50):
    network = BassDiffusion(BassScenario(rng=3, mixing="network", degree=degree))
    network.run()
    curve = network.datacollector.get_model_vars_dataframe()
    half = curve["time"][curve["adoption"] >= 0.5].iloc[0]
    ax.plot(curve["time"], curve["adoption"], label=f"{degree} neighbours: half in {half:.1f} y")
ax.plot(years, bass_curve(years, 0.03, 0.38), "k--", lw=1, label="Bass equation")
ax.set_xlabel("years")
ax.set_ylabel("share adopted")
ax.legend(frameon=False);
```

![../../_images/e70ab76195c26f851a2f35e0b23ee05bc8e89d07b21b4a5cc143830c31ff2b9c.png](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/_images/e70ab76195c26f851a2f35e0b23ee05bc8e89d07b21b4a5cc143830c31ff2b9c.png)

## Going further

- Read a real social network with `modelly.space.networks.read_edge_list`.
- Make `innovation` depend on a subsidy that starts in a given year.
- Calibrate `p` and `q` on an adoption series by least squares on `bass_curve`.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/using_modelly_in_your_project.md -->

# Using Modelly in your project

This guide takes you from an empty folder to a reproducible, measured agent-based model that lives in its own repository, uses Modelly as a dependency, and runs as a script, in a notebook, or as a batch of replications. Every snippet is complete; copy them in order.

## 1. Install Modelly as a dependency

Modelly needs Python 3.12 or newer. From an empty project folder:

```bash
mkdir epidemic && cd epidemic
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install modelly-abm
```

The distribution is `modelly-abm` and the import is `modelly`. Pin the version you tested against (`modelly-abm==1.3.3`), or declare it in your own `pyproject.toml`:

```toml
[project]
name = "epidemic"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.12"
dependencies = [
  "modelly-abm>=1.3",
  "pandas",
]

[project.optional-dependencies]
viz = ["modelly-abm[viz]>=1.3"]
```

Then `pip install -e .` (or `pip install -e ".[viz]"` for the browser UI).

On Linux (glibc and musl, x86-64 and ARM64), macOS (Intel and Apple silicon) and Windows (x86-64 and ARM64), on regular and free-threaded CPython, `pip install modelly-abm` installs a wheel with Modelly’s compiled modules. Elsewhere it installs the pure Python package, which gives the same results more slowly, and building from the source distribution compiles the modules when a C compiler is available (on Windows, MSVC through setuptools). Check which one you have:

```python
import modelly.core.rng

print(modelly.core.rng.NATIVE)  # True: randint, choice, shuffle and sample run in C
```

The results are the same either way, seed for seed; only the speed differs.

## 2. Lay out the project

One model per package, with the three Modelly pieces in three files:

```text
epidemic/
├── pyproject.toml
├── epidemic/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   ├── scenario.py      # the inputs: parameters and the seed
│   ├── agents.py        # what one agent does
│   └── model.py         # the world: space, population, step, reporters
├── scripts/
│   └── run.py           # one run, prints a result
├── notebooks/
└── tests/
    └── test_model.py
```

The separation is not cosmetic. The scenario is what you vary between runs, the agents are what you reason about, and the model is what you measure. Keeping them apart keeps each file short.

## 3. Write the scenario

`epidemic/scenario.py`. Every parameter has a type and a default, and the seed is part of it:

```python
from modelly.scenarios import Scenario

class EpidemicScenario(Scenario):
    """Everything that can vary between runs."""

    n: int = 500
    width: int = 30
    height: int = 30
    infection_chance: float = 0.3
    recovery_time: int = 10
    initially_infected: int = 5
```

A scenario instance is one run: `EpidemicScenario(n=2000, rng=42)`. The `rng` argument seeds both random number generators the model exposes (`model.random`, a stdlib `Random`, and `model.rng`, a numpy `Generator`), so the same scenario always gives the same run.

## 4. Write the agents

`epidemic/agents.py`. Agents move on a grid and infect their cellmates. The two attributes the model will aggregate every step are declared as `Column`s, so the model can read them for the whole population as numpy arrays; the agent still uses them as plain attributes.

```python
from modelly import Column
from modelly.space import CellAgent

SUSCEPTIBLE, INFECTED, RECOVERED = 0, 1, 2

class Person(CellAgent):
    """Moves to a neighbouring cell, infects cellmates, recovers after a while."""

    state = Column(int, default=SUSCEPTIBLE)
    days_infected = Column(int, default=0)

    def __init__(self, model, cell, infected=False):
        super().__init__(model)
        self.cell = cell
        if infected:
            self.state = INFECTED

    def step(self):
        self.cell = self.cell.neighborhood.select_random_cell()
        if self.state != INFECTED:
            return
        for other in self.cell.agents:
            if other.state == SUSCEPTIBLE and (
                self.random.random() < self.scenario.infection_chance
            ):
                other.state = INFECTED
        self.days_infected += 1
        if self.days_infected >= self.scenario.recovery_time:
            self.state = RECOVERED
```

Rules of thumb:

- `self.random` and `self.rng` are the model’s seeded generators. Never import `random` or call `np.random` directly, or your runs stop being reproducible.
- `self.scenario` is the model’s scenario; read parameters from it instead of copying them.
- Use a `Column` for an attribute the *model* aggregates, filters or records every step. Keep a scratch value that only the agent reads as a plain attribute: a column read costs about 20 ns more per access and `+= 1` about 60 ns, nothing for a few accesses but it adds up in a tight loop.

## 5. Write the model

`epidemic/model.py`. The model owns the space, creates the population, defines the step order, and exposes the quantities you want to measure.

```python
import numpy as np

from modelly import Model
from modelly.data.collector import DataCollector
from modelly.space import OrthogonalMooreGrid

from epidemic.agents import INFECTED, RECOVERED, SUSCEPTIBLE, Person
from epidemic.scenario import EpidemicScenario

class Epidemic(Model):
    def __init__(self, scenario: EpidemicScenario = EpidemicScenario):
        super().__init__(scenario=scenario)
        self.grid = OrthogonalMooreGrid(
            (scenario.width, scenario.height), torus=True, random=self.random
        )
        cells = self.random.choices(self.grid.all_cells.cells, k=scenario.n)
        infected = [i < scenario.initially_infected for i in range(scenario.n)]
        Person.create_agents(self, scenario.n, cells, infected=infected)

        self.datacollector = DataCollector(
            model_reporters={
                "susceptible": lambda m: m.count(SUSCEPTIBLE),
                "infected": lambda m: m.count(INFECTED),
                "recovered": lambda m: m.count(RECOVERED),
            },
            agent_reporters={"state": "state"},
        )
        self.datacollector.collect(self)

    def count(self, state: int) -> int:
        """How many people are in ``state``: one numpy comparison, no loop."""
        return int((self.columns[Person].state == state).sum())

    def step(self):
        self.agents.shuffle_do("step")
        self.datacollector.collect(self)
        self.running = self.count(INFECTED) > 0
```

What each line buys you:

- `create_agents(model, n, cells, infected=infected)`: a sequence of length `n` is spread one value per agent, anything else is broadcast. One call creates the whole population.
- `self.columns[Person].state` is a numpy view of every person’s state; `count` is a vectorised reporter. With 10,000 agents it costs microseconds instead of a millisecond.
- `agent_reporters={"state": "state"}` records a column straight from the array.
- `self.running` is the stop condition that `run_model()` honours.

## 6. Run it

`scripts/run.py`:

```python
from epidemic.model import Epidemic
from epidemic.scenario import EpidemicScenario

model = Epidemic(EpidemicScenario(n=1000, rng=7))
model.run_for(60)  # 60 ticks; or model.run_model() until running is False

frame = model.datacollector.get_model_vars_dataframe()
print(frame.tail())
frame.plot(title="SIR").get_figure().savefig("sir.png")
```

`run_for(duration)` advances model time by `duration`; `run_until(t)` runs to an absolute time; `step()` is one tick. All three go through the same event scheduler, so a model that also schedules events (`self.schedule_event(fn, after=3.5)`) mixes ticks and events correctly.

## 7. Look at the data

```python
model_vars = model.datacollector.get_model_vars_dataframe()  # one row per tick
agent_vars = (
    model.datacollector.get_agent_vars_dataframe()
)  # one row per agent per tick
share_infected = agent_vars["state"].eq(1).groupby("Step").mean()
```

For a snapshot of the whole population right now, without going through the collector:

```python
table = model.columns[Person]
table.to_dataframe()  # indexed by unique_id, one column per Column
table.where(table.state == 1)  # the infected, as an AgentSet
table.days_infected[table.state == 1].mean()
```

## 8. Replicate and sweep

A scenario can spawn independent, seeded replications:

```python
import pandas as pd

from epidemic.model import Epidemic
from epidemic.scenario import EpidemicScenario

runs = []
for chance in (0.1, 0.2, 0.3):
    base = EpidemicScenario(infection_chance=chance, rng=1)
    for scenario in base.spawn_replications(20):
        model = Epidemic(scenario)
        model.run_model()
        runs.append(
            {
                "chance": chance,
                "peak": model.datacollector.get_model_vars_dataframe()[
                    "infected"
                ].max(),
            }
        )

print(pd.DataFrame(runs).groupby("chance")["peak"].describe())
```

Each replication has its own seed derived from the base scenario, so the sweep is reproducible end to end. Runs are independent, so they parallelise without any change to the model:

```python
from modelly.scenarios import RunConfiguration, run_scenarios

scenarios = [
    s
    for chance in (0.1, 0.2, 0.3)
    for s in EpidemicScenario(infection_chance=chance, rng=1).spawn_replications(20)
]
store = run_scenarios(scenarios, RunConfiguration(Epidemic, until=120), workers=8)
```

For a plain factorial design, `run_grid` is the shortest path: it builds every combination times the replicates, gives each run its own seed, runs them in parallel and returns a DataFrame in design order, identical whatever the number of workers.

```python
from modelly import run_grid

def peak(task):
    scenario = EpidemicScenario(infection_chance=task["chance"], rng=task["seed"])
    model = Epidemic(scenario)
    model.run_model()
    return {"peak": model.datacollector.get_model_vars_dataframe()["infected"].max()}

if (
    __name__ == "__main__"
):  # needed on macOS and Windows, where workers re-import the script
    results = run_grid(peak, {"chance": [0.1, 0.2, 0.3]}, replicates=20, seed=1)
    print(results.groupby("chance")["peak"].describe())
```

On Linux the workers are forked, so a function defined in a notebook works too. `MODELLY_WORKERS` sets the pool size; `workers=1` runs inline.

## 9. Test it

`tests/test_model.py`. Seeds are part of the API, so tests can assert exact numbers:

```python
from epidemic.model import Epidemic
from epidemic.scenario import EpidemicScenario

def test_same_seed_same_run():
    a = Epidemic(EpidemicScenario(n=200, rng=3))
    b = Epidemic(EpidemicScenario(n=200, rng=3))
    a.run_for(20)
    b.run_for(20)
    assert a.count(1) == b.count(1)

def test_epidemic_ends():
    model = Epidemic(EpidemicScenario(n=200, recovery_time=3, rng=3))
    model.run_model()
    assert model.count(1) == 0
    assert model.time > 0
```

## 10. Make it fast

- Put the population-wide work on columns and numpy (`count` above); keep interactions in `step`.
- Move whole-population phases out of the per-agent loop with the column helpers: `table.days_infected[table.state == 1] += 1`, `table.remove_where(mask)`, `table.do_where(table.draw(p), "method")`. `draw` uses the model’s seeded generator.
- Use `model.agents.shuffle_do("step")` rather than your own loop: it shuffles once and skips agents removed earlier in the same tick.
- `cell.neighborhood` is cached per cell; call it freely.
- If identical individuals face identical probabilities (an insect’s stage, age and sex), keep them as counts in a `CohortTable`: survival becomes `cohorts.thin(s)`, one binomial draw per row instead of one draw per individual, with the same law. The stage-structured playbook runs hundreds of times faster this way.
- A column attribute read inside `step` costs about 27 ns against 6 ns for a plain attribute; keep scratch values that only the agent reads as plain attributes.
- Record with attribute names (`"state"`) rather than lambdas when you can; they are gathered in C.
- Profile before optimising: `python -m cProfile -s tottime scripts/run.py | head -30`. In a healthy model, the top entries are your agents’ own methods.

The numbers behind these recommendations are in [performance.md](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/performance.html).

## 11. Visualise it (optional)

With `modelly[viz]` installed:

```python
from modelly.viz import SolaraViz, make_space_component, make_plot_component

from epidemic.model import Epidemic

page = SolaraViz(
    Epidemic(),
    components=[
        make_space_component(
            lambda a: {"color": ["tab:blue", "tab:red", "tab:green"][a.state]}
        ),
        make_plot_component(["susceptible", "infected", "recovered"]),
    ],
    name="Epidemic",
)
```

```bash
solara run app.py
```

# Starting a project

`modelly new` writes a model project that is seeded, tested and linted from its first commit: the parameters and their seed in one place, a test that the same seed gives the same data, and lint settings that catch reproducibility bugs and O(N²) loops as you write them.

```bash
modelly new forest-fire                      # the grid template, in ./forest-fire
modelly new epidemic --template network      # another template
modelly new --list-templates                 # what each template models
python -m modelly new forest-fire            # the same, without the modelly script on PATH
```

The commands are the same on Windows, macOS and Linux. The folder must not exist yet, or be empty: `modelly new` never overwrites a file, and exits with status 2 without writing anything when the folder has something in it.

## What you get

```text
forest-fire/
├── pyproject.toml           depends on modelly-abm; [tool.modelly.lint] and pytest settings
├── README.md                how to set up, run, test, lint and profile; an ODD outline
├── .gitignore
├── forest_fire/
│   ├── __init__.py          exports ForestFireModel, ForestFireScenario and SEED
│   ├── scenario.py          the parameters, their defaults, and the default seed
│   ├── agents.py            the agent class
│   └── model.py             the model: builds the world from a scenario, steps it
└── tests/
    └── test_determinism.py  same seed, same data; another seed, another run
```

The project name becomes the package name (`forest-fire` gives `forest_fire`) and the class names (`ForestFireModel`, `ForestFireScenario`). The project contains no shell scripts: every command in its README is `python -m ...`, which runs the same everywhere.

Template

The model

Uses

grid (default)

traders on a torus grid give wealth to cellmates; inequality (Gini) emerges

OrthogonalMooreGrid, CellAgent, a Column

network

an infection spreads over a random contact network (SIR)

Network from networkx (the network extra), a Column per state

continuous

correlated random walkers in a wrapping space; their alignment is recorded

ContinuousSpace, ContinuousSpaceAgent

cohort

colonies whose individuals are counted by age class, not one object each

CohortTable with binomial survival and births

geo

news spreads among residents who walk a town of square districts, in metres

GeoSpace, GeoAgent, a Column (the geo extra)

llm

citizens ask a language model what they now think of a proposal, after talking to a few others

LLMAgent, decide_all, a Client with an offline FakeProvider

plugin

not a model: a package that extends Modelly, here with a stratified design sampler

a modelly.samplers entry point, modelly-abm>=X.Y,<2 declared (see [Plugins](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/plugins.html))

The `geo` template builds its districts in code, so it runs offline; `districts()` in `model.py` is the one function to replace with `geopandas.read_file(...)` for a real town. The `llm` template asks a local function (`local_responder` in `model.py`) instead of a language model, so its test runs offline and costs nothing; pass `client=Client(AnthropicProvider(...))` or another provider to the model to ask a real one (see [Language-model agents](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/llm_agents.html) for keys, caching, replay and budgets).

## The seed

`scenario.py` holds every parameter of a run and the default seed:

```python
SEED = 42  # the default seed: pass rng=... for another, reproducible, run

class ForestFireScenario(Scenario):
    n: int = 100
    width: int = 10
    height: int = 10

    def __init__(self, *, rng=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(rng=SEED if rng is None else rng, **kwargs)
```

`ForestFireModel()` runs the default scenario with `SEED`, so even the first run reproduces. `ForestFireModel(ForestFireScenario(rng=7, n=500))` changes the seed and a parameter; every draw in the model comes from `self.random` and `self.rng`, which the scenario seeds.

## Set up, test, lint, profile

```bash
cd forest-fire
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows PowerShell: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
python -m pytest                   # the determinism test
python -m modelly lint forest_fire # no findings in a fresh project
python -m modelly profile forest_fire.model:ForestFireModel --steps 50
```

The determinism test runs the model twice from one seed and compares everything its `DataCollector` recorded; it also checks that another seed gives another run, so a seed that is accidentally ignored fails the test. Keep it passing as the model grows: it is the cheapest guard against a draw from the global `random` module or a loop over a set.

`[tool.modelly.lint]` in `pyproject.toml` selects every rule and relaxes the O(N²) warnings in `tests/`; see [Checking a model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/lint.html) for the rules, `--fix` and `# noqa`. The profiler is described in [Profiling a model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/profile.html).

## The README and the ODD protocol

The generated README ends with the outline of the ODD protocol (Overview, Design concepts, Details), the usual way to describe an agent-based model in a paper: purpose and patterns; entities, state variables and scales; process overview and scheduling; design concepts; initialization; input data; submodels. Fill it in as the model takes shape, and it becomes the model description of the paper.

## Long project names

The templates are formatted for names of ordinary length. With a long project name some lines of the generated code pass the usual 88 characters; run your formatter once (`ruff format .`) after creating the project.

# Best Practices

Here are some general principles that have proven helpful for developing models.

## Model Layout

A model should be contained in a folder named with lower-case letters and underscores, such as `wolf_sheep`. Within that directory:

- `Readme.md` describes the model, how to use it, and any other details.
- `model.py` should contain the model class.
- `agents.py` should contain the agent class(es).
- `app.py` should contain the Solara-based visualization code (optional).

You can add more files as needed, for example:

- `run.py` could contain the code to run the model.
- `analysis.py` could contain any analysis code.

Input data can be stored in a `data` directory, output data in an `output`, processed results in a `results` directory, images in an `images` directory, etc.

All our [examples](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples.html) follow this layout.

## Randomization

If your model involves some random choice, you can use the built-in `random` property that many Modelly objects have, including `Model`, `Agent`, and `AgentSet`. This works exactly like the built-in `random` library.

```python
class AwesomeModel(Model):
  # ...

  def cool_method(self):
    interesting_number = self.random.random()
    print(interesting_number)

class AwesomeAgent(Agent):
  # ...
  def __init__(self, model, ...):
    super().__init__(model)
    # ...

  def my_method(self):
    random_number = self.random.randint(0, 100)
```

`Agent.random` is just a convenient shorthand in the Agent class to `self.model.random`. If you create your own `AgentSet` instances, you have to pass `random` explicitly. Typically, you can simply do, in a Model instance, `my_agentset = AgentSet([], random=self.random)`. This ensures that `my_agentset` uses the same random number generator as the rest of the model.

Models also expose `self.rng`, a NumPy `Generator`, which is useful for vectorized random draws.

When a model object is created without a seed, its random number generators are seeded from fresh operating system entropy, so every run differs. The seed determines the sequence of random numbers; if you instantiate a model with the same seed, you will get the same results. To allow you to set the seed, make sure your model has an `rng` argument in its `__init__` and passes it on to `super().__init__()`.

```python
class AwesomeModel(Model):

  def __init__(self, rng=None):
    super().__init__(rng=rng)
    ...

  def cool_method(self):
    interesting_number = self.random.random()
    print(interesting_number)

>>> model0 = AwesomeModel(rng=0)
>>> model1 = AwesomeModel(rng=0)
>>> model0.random.random() == model1.random.random()
True
```


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/migrating_from_mesa.md -->

# Migrating from Mesa

Modelly’s authoring model will feel familiar if you have written a Mesa model: a `Model` subclass owns the world, `Agent` subclasses hold behaviour, a `DataCollector` records. The differences are where Mesa accumulated several generations of API (schedulers, two grid systems, `batch_run`) and Modelly keeps one. This page maps every Mesa construct to its Modelly equivalent, for Mesa 2.x and Mesa 3.x code alike.

Start with the codemod. It rewrites the mechanical parts (imports, agent constructors, a few model attributes) and prints a report of every line that needs a decision, each pointing to a section below:

```bash
python -m modelly.migrate path/to/your/model/          # dry run: shows the diff and the report
python -m modelly.migrate path/to/your/model/ --write  # applies the rewrites
```

Then work through the report top to bottom. A typical Mesa 3 model is done after the imports; a Mesa 2 model needs the scheduler and grid sections.

## Imports

Mesa

Modelly

import mesa

import modelly

from mesa import Agent, Model, DataCollector

from modelly import Agent, Model, DataCollector

mesa.agent, mesa.model

modelly.core.agent, modelly.core.model

mesa.datacollection

modelly.data.collector

mesa.discrete_space (3.2+), mesa.experimental.cell_space (3.0, 3.1)

modelly.space

mesa.space (MultiGrid, SingleGrid, NetworkGrid, ContinuousSpace)

modelly.space, see [Grids](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/migrating_from_mesa.html#grids-and-positions)

mesa.time (schedulers)

nothing to import, see [Activation](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/migrating_from_mesa.html#activation-and-schedulers)

mesa.batchrunner.batch_run

modelly.scenarios, see [Batch runs](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/migrating_from_mesa.html#batch-runs)

mesa.visualization

modelly.viz (same component names)

mesa.experimental.devs (ABMSimulator, DEVSimulator)

methods on Model, see [Events](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/migrating_from_mesa.html#events-and-simulators)

mesa.experimental.continuous_space

modelly.space.continuous

mesa.experimental.signals, mesa.experimental.meta_agents

modelly.time.signals, modelly.behaviour.meta_agents

mesa.experimental.scenarios

modelly.scenarios

mesa.experimental.data_collection

modelly.data.recorders

The codemod does all of these, for import statements and for dotted names in code (`mesa.discrete_space.CellAgent` becomes `modelly.space.CellAgent`). A Mesa module with no Modelly equivalent is reported, not silently rewritten: the property-layer modules (`mesa.space.property_layer`, `mesa.discrete_space.property_layer`; use `grid.create_property_layer`, see [Grids](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/migrating_from_mesa.html#grids-and-positions)) and every other `mesa.experimental.*` module, such as `mesa.experimental.devs` (see [Events](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/migrating_from_mesa.html#events-and-simulators)).

## Agents

**Constructor.** Mesa 2 agents took an id; Modelly assigns `unique_id` itself, starting at 1:

```python
# Mesa 2
class Sheep(mesa.Agent):
    def __init__(self, unique_id, model, energy):
        super().__init__(unique_id, model)

# Modelly (and Mesa 3)
class Sheep(Agent):
    def __init__(self, model, energy):
        super().__init__(model)
```

`model.next_id()` no longer exists; delete those calls. The codemod rewrites the `super()` call and flags the constructor signature so you remove the parameter from the callers too.

**Random numbers.** `self.random` and `self.model.random` work as in Mesa, and `self.rng` is a seeded numpy `Generator`. Never use the `random` module or `np.random` directly.

**Creating many agents.** `Sheep.create_agents(model, n, energy=energies)` creates `n` agents in one call; a sequence of length `n` gives one value per agent, anything else is broadcast.

## Activation and schedulers

Mesa 2 schedulers are gone (Mesa 3 removed them as well). Activation is a method call on an `AgentSet`, and `model.agents` is always up to date, so there is no `schedule.add`:

Mesa 2

Modelly

self.schedule = RandomActivation(self)

delete

self.schedule.add(agent)

delete; agents register themselves

self.schedule.step()

self.agents.shuffle_do("step")

BaseScheduler (insertion order)

self.agents.do("step")

SimultaneousActivation

self.agents.do("step"); self.agents.do("advance")

StagedActivation(stage_list=["a", "b"])

self.agents.do("a"); self.agents.do("b")

RandomActivationByType

self.agents_by_type[Sheep].shuffle_do("step"), one line per type

self.schedule.steps

self.time

self.schedule.get_agent_count()

len(self.agents)

self.schedule.agents

self.agents

self.schedule.remove(agent)

agent.remove()

Mesa 3’s `self.agents.shuffle_do("step")`, `select`, `groupby`, `agg`, `get` and `set` exist with the same signatures.

## Grids and positions

Modelly has one grid system, the cell space (`modelly.space`), which Mesa 3 ships as `mesa.discrete_space`. Mesa 2’s `mesa.space.MultiGrid` and `SingleGrid` translate as follows. An agent that lives on a grid subclasses `CellAgent` and has a `cell` instead of a `pos`.

Mesa 2 (mesa.space)

Modelly

MultiGrid(width, height, torus)

OrthogonalMooreGrid((width, height), torus=torus, random=self.random)

SingleGrid(width, height, torus)

same, with capacity=1

Von Neumann neighbourhoods (moore=False)

OrthogonalVonNeumannGrid(...)

HexGrid

HexGrid((width, height), ...)

NetworkGrid(G)

Network(G, random=self.random)

grid.place_agent(agent, pos)

agent.cell = grid[pos]

grid.move_agent(agent, pos)

agent.cell = grid[pos]

grid.move_to_empty(agent)

agent.cell = grid.select_random_empty_cell()

grid.remove_agent(agent)

agent.cell = None (or agent.remove() to leave the model)

agent.pos

agent.cell.coordinate

grid.get_neighbors(pos, moore=True, include_center=False, radius=1)

agent.cell.neighborhood.agents (radius 1) or agent.cell.get_neighborhood(radius=r, include_center=...).agents

grid.get_neighborhood(pos, ...)

agent.cell.get_neighborhood(radius=r) (cells)

grid.get_cell_list_contents([pos])

grid[pos].agents

grid.is_cell_empty(pos)

grid[pos].is_empty

grid.empties

grid.empties

PropertyLayer

Moving along the grid: `agent.move_relative((dx, dy))`, or `Grid2DMovingAgent` with `agent.move("north")`.

`ContinuousSpace` lives under `modelly.space.continuous`; agents subclass `ContinuousSpaceAgent`, keep their position in a shared numpy array, and query with `get_neighbors_in_radius` and `get_nearest_neighbors`.

## Model

Mesa

Modelly

Model(seed=42)

Parameters belong in a `Scenario` subclass (typed defaults plus the seed) rather than in the model’s `__init__` signature; see [Using Modelly in your project](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/using_modelly_in_your_project.html).

## Data collection

`DataCollector` keeps Mesa’s API: `model_reporters`, `agent_reporters`, `agenttype_reporters`, `tables`, `collect(model)`, `get_model_vars_dataframe()`, `get_agent_vars_dataframe()`, `get_agenttype_vars_dataframe(type)`, `get_table_dataframe(name)`. Attribute-name reporters (`{"energy": "energy"}`) are the fast path. Declaring an attribute as a `Column` makes `model.columns[Sheep].energy` a numpy view, which is the Modelly way to write a vectorised model reporter.

## Batch runs

Mesa’s `batch_run(Model, parameters, iterations, max_steps, ...)` becomes scenarios and a runner:

```python
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor

from modelly.scenarios import RunConfiguration, run_scenarios

scenarios = [
    s
    for density in (0.6, 0.7, 0.8)
    for s in MyScenario(density=density, rng=1).spawn_replications(10)
]
config = RunConfiguration(MyModel, until=100)

with ProcessPoolExecutor() as pool:
    store = run_scenarios(scenarios, config, executor=pool)
```

Each replication has its own seed derived from the base scenario, so the sweep is reproducible. For a quick loop, `for scenario in base.spawn_replications(n): model = MyModel(scenario)`. For a plain list of runs or a factorial grid with one seed per run, `modelly.run_batch` and `modelly.run_grid` (in `modelly.batch`) run them over processes; see [Batch](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/batch.html).

## Events and simulators

`ABMSimulator`, `DEVSimulator` and `mesa.experimental.devs` do not exist. The model schedules directly: `self.schedule_event(fn, at=t)` or `after=dt`, `self.schedule_recurring(fn, Schedule(interval=2.0))`, and `run_for` / `run_until` advance time through the same event list that drives `step`.

## Visualization

`SolaraViz`, `SpaceRenderer`, `make_space_component`, `make_plot_component`, `Slider` and the portrayal style classes keep their Mesa 3 names and signatures under `modelly.viz`. Mesa 2’s `ModularServer` and the JavaScript modules have no equivalent; rewrite those visualisations with `SolaraViz` (tutorial 6).

## Checklist

1. Run the codemod, read the report.
1. Replace schedulers with `AgentSet` calls; delete `schedule.add`.
1. Move grid code to cells: `agent.cell`, `cell.neighborhood`, `grid.select_random_empty_cell()`.
1. Move parameters into a `Scenario`; pass `rng` instead of `seed`.
1. Run your tests with `-W error`; Modelly raises instead of warning for removed APIs.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/netlogo.md -->

# From NetLogo

`python -m modelly.netlogo` (or `modelly netlogo`) translates a NetLogo model, a `.nlogo` file, into a Python module you can run, test and lint like any Modelly model. It reads a well-defined subset of NetLogo, listed below. Anything outside that subset stays in the output as a `# NETLOGO` comment, and the report lists it with its line number. Nothing is dropped without being listed.

```bash
python -m modelly.netlogo fire.nlogo -o fire.py      # translate a model to a file
python -m modelly.netlogo model.nlogo                # print the Python on stdout
python -m modelly.netlogo --example wolf_sheep -o wolf_sheep.py   # a bundled model
python -m modelly.netlogo --example fire --show      # print the bundled NetLogo source
```

```python
from fire import FireModel, FireScenario

model = FireModel(FireScenario(rng=1, density=62))
while model.running:
    model.step()
print(model.burned_trees / model.initial_trees)
print(model.datacollector.get_model_vars_dataframe().tail())
```

The translated model’s `setup` runs when the model is created, and `step()` runs `go` once. `stop` in `go` sets `model.running = False`. The sliders and switches are fields of the generated `Scenario`, along with the world’s size, so `FireScenario(density=62, max_pxcor=50)` changes a run without editing the code. Every random draw goes through the model’s seeded generator (`self.random`), including the order of each `ask`, so a seed fixes the whole run. The output passes `modelly lint` and ruff.

Exit status: **0** every line was translated (lines that only change the view may have been dropped), **1** some lines were not translated (the output marks them and stderr lists them), **2** a usage error (no input, a file that cannot be read, an unknown `--example`).

## What a translation looks like

The NetLogo procedures become methods of the model class. A procedure that a turtle or a patch runs takes that agent as its argument. Each `ask` block becomes a nested function, run once per agent by `self.ask(agents, function)`:

```text
to go                                          def go(self):
  if not any? patches with [ pcolor = red ]        if not len([patch for patch in self.patches if patch.pcolor == RED]) > 0:
    [ stop ]                                           self.running = False
  ask patches with [ pcolor = red ] [                  return
    ask neighbors4 with [ pcolor = green ]
      [ ignite ]                                   def ask_1(patch_3):
    set pcolor red - 3.5                               def ask_2(patch_5):
  ]                                                        self.ignite(patch_5)
  tick                                                 self.ask([patch_4 for patch_4 in self.neighbors4(patch_3) if patch_4.pcolor == GREEN], ask_2)
end                                                    patch_3.pcolor = RED - 3.5

                                                   self.ask([patch_2 for patch_2 in self.patches if patch_2.pcolor == RED], ask_1)
                                                   self.tick()
```

## The subset

NetLogo

Modelly

globals [ ... ]

model attributes, set to 0 at the start and by clear-all

sliders and switches (interface tab)

fields of the generated Scenario, copied to model attributes

the view (GRAPHICS-WINDOW)

the min_pxcor … max_pycor and wrap fields of the Scenario

patches, patches-own [ ... ]

a Patch agent per cell of an OrthogonalMooreGrid

turtles, turtles-own [ ... ]

Turtle agents (CellAgent)

breed [ wolves wolf ], wolves-own [ ... ]

a subclass of the turtle class per breed

to name [inputs] ... end, to-report

methods of the model

setup, go

run by __init__ and step

clear-all (ca), reset-ticks, tick, ticks

self.clear_all(), self.reset_ticks(), self.tick(), self.ticks

ask agents [ ... ]

self.ask(agents, function): each agent in a new random order, dead turtles skipped

agents with [ ... ]

a list comprehension

set, let

an assignment to the agent, the model or a local (nonlocal when needed)

if, ifelse, repeat

if, if/else (or a conditional expression), for _ in range(n)

create-turtles, create-<breed>, hatch, hatch-<breed>, sprout, sprout-<breed>

self.create, self.hatch, self.sprout, then the block for each new turtle

die, stop

turtle.die() then return; return (and running = False in go)

fd/forward, bk/back, rt/right, lt/left, setxy, move-to

methods of the turtle

neighbors, neighbors4, patch-here, turtles-here, <breed>-here

lists of agents

one-of, count, any?, nobody

self.one_of, len, len(...) > 0, None

random, random-float, random-xcor, random-ycor, random-pxcor, random-pycor

draws from self.random

self, myself, not, and, or, xor, = != < > <= >=, + - * / mod ^, abs, sqrt

the Python equivalents

pxcor, pycor, pcolor, xcor, ycor, heading, color, who

attributes of the patch or turtle

red, green, brown, …

the color numbers of modelly.netlogo.colors (red - 3.5 works)

set-default-shape, hide-turtle, pen-down, print, show, …

dropped (display only), and listed in the report

The code tab’s comments are skipped. A turtle reads and sets the variables of the patch under it by name, as in NetLogo: `set pcolor brown` in a sheep’s code is `turtle.patch.pcolor = BROWN`. A NetLogo name that would hide a Python keyword or an attribute of the runtime gets a trailing underscore (a slider called `width` is `width_`); `-` becomes `_` and `?` is dropped (`grass?` is `grass`).

## Semantics

- **Turtles are patch-centred.** A turtle stands on the cell of a patch. `fd n` moves `round(n)` patches along the heading, the heading rounded to the nearest multiple of 45 degrees (one of the eight neighbours); in a world that does not wrap, the turtle stops at the edge. `setxy x y` moves to the patch nearest to the point and raises `ValueError` outside a world that does not wrap. `xcor` and `ycor` are the patch’s coordinates. Models whose behaviour depends on sub-patch positions (flocking, continuous distances) need a human.
- **Agent sets are lists.** `ask` takes a snapshot, shuffles it with the model’s generator, and skips turtles that died since, as NetLogo does.
- **`die` ends the turtle’s code.** The procedure returns; a procedure that may kill its turtle is followed, in its caller, by a check that returns when the turtle is dead.
- **A procedure runs as the kind of agent that first calls it** (the observer when nothing calls it). Calling it from another kind of agent is reported.
- **Switches** are stored as `0` (on) and `1` (off) in a `.nlogo` file; a slider whose bounds, step and value are whole numbers is an `int` field, any other a `float`.
- **The view** is read from the `GRAPHICS-WINDOW` block of the interface tab (the patch coordinates and the two wrap flags); without one the world is NetLogo’s default, patches -16 to 16, wrapping.
- **Data.** A `DataCollector` records `ticks`, every global and the size of every breed (and of all turtles) at `reset-ticks` and at every `tick`, where NetLogo updates its plots.

## The report

Each line the translation could not make is printed on stderr, as `file:line: reason: source`, and kept in the output as a comment at the place it was:

```text
$ python -m modelly.netlogo spiral.nlogo -o spiral.py
spiral.nlogo:2: not translated: unknown command 'layout-circle': layout-circle turtles 5
```

```python
    def setup(self):
        """NetLogo ``to setup``, run by the observer."""
        # NETLOGO line 2, not translated (unknown command 'layout-circle'): layout-circle turtles 5
```

The module’s docstring says how many lines are left. Search for `NETLOGO`, write the Python for each, and run the model’s test. A command the translator does not know makes it skip the rest of that line (and any block the line opens), so one unknown primitive costs one line, not the procedure.

## The bundled models

Two models ship with the translator, in `modelly/netlogo/models/`, and both translate with no line left over:

- **`fire.nlogo`**: a fire spreads from the forest’s left edge to the trees on the four sides of each burning tree. The share of trees burned jumps from a few percent to almost all near a density of 59%, the site-percolation threshold of the square lattice. On a 101 x 101 forest, averaged over five seeds, the translated model burns 8% of the trees at a density of 50%, 15% at 55%, 56% at 59%, 89% at 63% and 97% at 70% (`tests/netlogo/test_translate.py` checks the transition with three seeds).
- **`wolf_sheep.nlogo`**: sheep eat grass that regrows after a countdown, wolves eat sheep, and both reproduce and starve; the populations oscillate. The test runs it for 100 ticks with the default sliders, checks that both populations stay alive and that a seed reproduces the run.

Both sources were written for Modelly, inspired by Wilensky’s NetLogo models library Wolf Sheep Predation (1997) and Fire (1997); sources written from the published model descriptions, not copied. (Wilensky, U. 1997. NetLogo Wolf Sheep Predation model and NetLogo Fire model. Center for Connected Learning and Computer-Based Modeling, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL.) The models library code is under a non-commercial licence and is not included.

## Limits

- Not supported: links, `of`, `list` and other list primitives, `while`, `foreach`, `map`, anonymous procedures, `distance`, `in-radius`, `face`, `patch-at`, `set breed`, `stop` inside a reporter, extensions, string primitives, choosers and input boxes (reported as interface widgets). Each one is reported where it appears.
- Positions are whole patches (see Semantics): models that rely on fractional turtle positions translate and run, but do not behave like the original.
- `patches` is a list of every patch, so `ask patches with [...]` visits every patch once per call, as in NetLogo. A large world is slower than NetLogo’s compiled engine; for speed, move a translated phase to the model as columns (see [Vectorised phases](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/vectorised_phases.html)).
- The translator checks the names it reads against the declarations, but it does not type-check: a NetLogo program that NetLogo itself rejects may still translate.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/r_and_julia.md -->

# From R and Julia

Modelly writes its results as Parquet files, an open columnar format that R, Julia, DuckDB, Spark and most data tools read directly, and it can be driven from R through [reticulate](https://rstudio.github.io/reticulate/) and from Julia through [PythonCall](https://juliapy.github.io/PythonCall.jl/). This page shows both directions: the results in R or Julia, and a model run from R or Julia.

The Python snippets on this page run in Modelly’s test suite (`tests/test_r_julia_guide.py`), which also runs the SQL of the R and Julia snippets through DuckDB’s Python package and makes the same calls into Modelly that the reticulate and PythonCall snippets make. The R and Julia code itself is not run in CI.

## Writing the results

In Python, with `pip install "modelly-abm[experiments]"` (pyarrow and DuckDB):

```python
from pathlib import Path

import duckdb

from modelly.examples.basic.boltzmann_wealth_model.model import BoltzmannWealth
from modelly.experiments import Experiment, ScenarioSpace, designs

# One run: the DataCollector's model and agent reporters, one Parquet file each.
model = BoltzmannWealth()
for _ in range(20):
    model.step()
model.datacollector.to_parquet("out/model.parquet")  # time, Gini
model.datacollector.to_parquet(
    "out/agents.parquet", kind="agent"
)  # Step, AgentID, Wealth

# A sweep: one Parquet file per run, with its parameters, seed and step on every row.
experiment = Experiment(
    model=BoltzmannWealth,
    space=ScenarioSpace(n=(50, 100), width=10, height=10),
    design=designs.latin_hypercube(4),
    replicates=2,
    steps=10,
    outputs=["gini"],
    store="runs/boltzmann",
    seed=42,
)
experiment.run(executor="serial")

# Optionally, one DuckDB database file holding every run as a table.
Path("results.duckdb").unlink(missing_ok=True)
with duckdb.connect("results.duckdb") as con:
    con.sql(
        "CREATE TABLE runs AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet('runs/boltzmann/run-*.parquet')"
    )
```

Each run file of the store has the columns `run_id`, `point`, `replicate`, `seed`, the scenario parameters (`n`, `width`, `height`), `step` and the outputs (`gini`); see [Experiments and sweeps](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/experiments.html). Parquet is the format to share: any reader of any version opens it. A DuckDB database file is opened only by a DuckDB of a compatible storage version, so use the same DuckDB release in Python and in R or Julia, or share the Parquet files.

## Reading the results in R

The [arrow](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/r/) package reads one file into a data frame; the [duckdb](https://duckdb.org/docs/api/r) package queries many files with SQL without loading them first.

```r
library(arrow)
model <- read_parquet("out/model.parquet")
agents <- read_parquet("out/agents.parquet")
summary(model$Gini)

library(DBI)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT n, avg(gini) AS gini FROM read_parquet('runs/boltzmann/run-*.parquet') WHERE step = 10 GROUP BY n ORDER BY n")
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)

# The database file written above
con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb(), dbdir = "results.duckdb", read_only = TRUE)
dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT replicate, count(*) AS rows FROM runs GROUP BY replicate ORDER BY replicate")
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

`arrow::open_dataset("runs/boltzmann")` with dplyr verbs is the other way to work on a whole store lazily.

## Reading the results in Julia

[Parquet2.jl](https://expandingman.gitlab.io/Parquet2.jl/) reads a file as a Tables.jl table; [DuckDB.jl](https://duckdb.org/docs/api/julia) queries many with SQL.

```julia
using DataFrames, Parquet2
model = DataFrame(Parquet2.Dataset("out/model.parquet"))
agents = DataFrame(Parquet2.Dataset("out/agents.parquet"))

using DuckDB
con = DBInterface.connect(DuckDB.DB)
gini = DataFrame(DBInterface.execute(con, "SELECT n, avg(gini) AS gini FROM read_parquet('runs/boltzmann/run-*.parquet') WHERE step = 10 GROUP BY n ORDER BY n"))
DBInterface.close!(con)

con = DBInterface.connect(DuckDB.DB, "results.duckdb")
rows = DataFrame(DBInterface.execute(con, "SELECT replicate, count(*) AS rows FROM runs GROUP BY replicate ORDER BY replicate"))
DBInterface.close!(con)
```

## Gridded results: netCDF

A model that records a grid every step (a property layer, a heat map) exports it as an `xarray.Dataset` with a `time` dimension (`pip install "modelly-abm[xarray]"`), which xarray writes as netCDF, the format of gridded data in climate and ecology:

```python
import numpy as np

from modelly import DataCollector, Model

class Warming(Model):
    """A 4 x 4 grid that warms at random each step."""

    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(rng=1)
        self.heat = np.zeros((4, 4))
        self.datacollector = DataCollector(model_reporters={"heat": "heat"})

    def step(self):
        self.heat = self.heat + self.rng.random((4, 4))
        self.datacollector.collect(self)

model = Warming()
model.run_for(3)
grid = model.datacollector.to_xarray(dims={"heat": ("x", "y")})  # heat: (time, x, y)
grid.to_netcdf("out/heat.nc")
```

R reads it with `stars::read_ncdf("out/heat.nc")` or `ncdf4::nc_open("out/heat.nc")`; Julia with `NCDatasets.NCDataset("out/heat.nc")["heat"]`.

## The R package

The `modelly` R package (in `r/modelly` of the repository) runs, inspects and calibrates Modelly models from R without writing any Python. Results come back as data frames.

```r
install.packages("reticulate")
remotes::install_github("RemiPelloux/Modelly", subdir = "r/modelly")
modelly::install_modelly()  # once: a Python environment "r-modelly" with modelly-abm

library(modelly)
target <- paste0(modelly_tutorial(), ":Epidemic")  # the SIR model of the calibration guide
modelly_parameters(target)                          # name, type and default of each
run <- modelly_run(target, beta = 0.4, gamma = 0.1, seed = 99, steps = 40)
plot(run$step, run$infected, type = "l")

fit <- modelly_calibrate(
  target,
  priors = list(beta = prior_uniform(0.05, 1), gamma = prior_uniform(0.02, 0.5)),
  observed = list(infected = run$infected[-1]),
  steps = 40, particles = 100, generations = 6, seed = 2027
)
fit        # the posterior summary: beta 0.423 (0.332 to 0.553), gamma 0.098 (0.067 to 0.139)
plot(fit)  # a histogram of each parameter's particles
fit$particles; fit$trace
```

That is the [calibration guide](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/calibration.html)’s SIR tutorial, end to end from R. It gives the posterior the guide shows for Python, number for number, because the same seed drives the same runs. Any model works as a target: `"path/to/model.py:MyModel"` or `"package.module:MyModel"`. Scenario parameters are passed by name. Whole numbers need no `L`: the package converts a value to an integer when the scenario field is an `int`. `modelly_model(target, ...)` returns the model object itself, for stepping it from R (`model$step()`).

The package is a thin layer over `modelly.bindings`, a Python module of plain functions that the Julia package uses too. Calibration runs serially, because an R session embedding Python has no script for worker processes to re-import. `R CMD check` passes with no note, and the package’s tests run the tutorial and check that the posterior’s intervals contain the true values. The release workflow runs `R CMD check` on Linux, macOS and Windows before every release.

## Running Modelly from R (reticulate)

Install Modelly in a Python environment and point reticulate at it; every Modelly class and function is then callable from R. R numbers are doubles: pass whole numbers with an `L` (`42L`), because a seed or a count must be a Python `int`.

```r
library(reticulate)
use_virtualenv("~/my-study/.venv", required = TRUE)  # or use_condaenv(), use_python()

boltzmann <- import("modelly.examples.basic.boltzmann_wealth_model.model")
scenario <- boltzmann$BoltzmannScenario(rng = 42L, n = 100L)
model <- boltzmann$BoltzmannWealth(scenario = scenario)
for (i in 1:20) model$step()

gini <- model$datacollector$get_model_vars_dataframe()  # an R data.frame
plot(gini$Gini, type = "l")
model$datacollector$to_parquet("out/from_r.parquet")

# A sweep, from R
experiments <- import("modelly.experiments")
experiment <- experiments$Experiment(
  model = boltzmann$BoltzmannWealth,
  space = experiments$ScenarioSpace(n = tuple(50L, 100L), width = 10L, height = 10L),
  design = experiments$designs$latin_hypercube(4L),
  replicates = 2L, steps = 10L, outputs = list("gini"),
  store = "runs/from_r", seed = 42L
)
experiment$run(executor = "serial")
```

Your own model works the same way: `import_from_path("model", path = "my_model")` imports a `model.py` from a folder of your project.

## The Julia package

`Modelly.jl` (in `julia/Modelly.jl` of the repository) does from Julia what the R package does from R, on the same `modelly.bindings`, and gives agent columns as arrays without a copy:

```julia
using Pkg; Pkg.add(url = "https://github.com/RemiPelloux/Modelly", subdir = "julia/Modelly.jl")
using Modelly

target = Modelly.tutorial() * ":Epidemic"
run = simulate(target; seed = 99, steps = 40, beta = 0.4, gamma = 0.1)   # a DataFrame
fit = calibrate(target;
    priors = (beta = prior_uniform(0.05, 1.0), gamma = prior_uniform(0.02, 0.5)),
    observed = (infected = run.infected[2:end],), steps = 40, seed = 2027)
fit.summary   # beta 0.423, gamma 0.098: the posterior of Python and R

m = model("modelly.examples.basic.boltzmann_wealth_model.model:BoltzmannWealth"; seed = 1)
wealth = column(m, "MoneyAgent", "wealth")   # shares memory with the agents
wealth[1] = 99                               # the first agent's wealth is now 99
```

Give priors as a NamedTuple or a vector of pairs: the draws follow the priors’ order, so a `Dict`, which has none, gives a valid posterior that differs from the one Python and R give for the same seed. `column` wraps the model’s numpy array with `PyArray`, so reading and writing it costs no copy; it is valid until agents of that class are added or removed. The first `using Modelly` installs Python and modelly-abm through CondaPkg; set `JULIA_CONDAPKG_BACKEND=Null` and `JULIA_PYTHONCALL_EXE` to use an environment you have. Its tests (the tutorial’s posterior to the last digit, a column written without a copy) pass with the latest stable Julia on Linux, macOS and Windows in the release workflow.

## Running Modelly from Julia (PythonCall)

PythonCall manages its own Python by default; to use the environment Modelly is installed in, set two variables before `using PythonCall`.

```julia
ENV["JULIA_CONDAPKG_BACKEND"] = "Null"
ENV["JULIA_PYTHONCALL_EXE"] = expanduser("~/my-study/.venv/bin/python")  # Windows: .venv\Scripts\python.exe
using PythonCall, DataFrames

boltzmann = pyimport("modelly.examples.basic.boltzmann_wealth_model.model")
scenario = boltzmann.BoltzmannScenario(rng=42, n=100)
model = boltzmann.BoltzmannWealth(scenario=scenario)
for _ in 1:20
    model.step()
end

gini = DataFrame(PyPandasDataFrame(model.datacollector.get_model_vars_dataframe()))
model.datacollector.to_parquet("out/from_julia.parquet")
```

Julia integers convert to Python `int` and Julia floats to Python `float`, so no suffix is needed. Keyword arguments are written as in Python.

## Reproducibility across languages

The seed, not the language, fixes a run: the same scenario and seed give the same results whether the model is started from Python, R or Julia, because every draw happens in Modelly’s generators. Record the seed and the Modelly version next to the results; [Reproducible studies](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/provenance.html) does that for you with `modelly run` and `modelly bundle`.

# Premiers pas

*Cette page est une traduction de la [page anglaise](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/getting_started.html) ; les corrections sont les bienvenues.*

Modelly est un framework modulaire pour construire, analyser et visualiser des modèles à base d’agents.

Les **modèles à base d’agents** sont des simulations informatiques où plusieurs entités (les agents) agissent et interagissent les unes avec les autres selon le comportement qui leur a été programmé. Les agents peuvent représenter des cellules vivantes, des animaux, des êtres humains, voire des organisations entières ou des entités abstraites. Parfois, on comprend comment se comportent les composants individuels d’un système et l’on veut voir quels comportements et quels effets émergent, à l’échelle du système, de leurs interactions. D’autres fois, on a une bonne idée du comportement global du système et l’on cherche quels comportements individuels l’expliquent. Ou bien on veut savoir comment amener des agents à coopérer ou à se concurrencer le plus efficacement possible. Ou l’on veut simplement construire un joli jouet avec de petits points colorés qui se déplacent.

## Vue d’ensemble

Pour avoir une idée générale des fonctionnalités et de la structure de Modelly, commencez ici :

- [Vue d’ensemble de la bibliothèque MODELLY](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/overview.html) : découvrez les concepts et composants essentiels de Modelly.

## Tutoriels

Pour apprendre pas à pas à construire des modèles à base d’agents avec Modelly, suivez ces tutoriels :

- [Créer votre premier modèle](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/0_first_model.html) : apprenez à créer votre premier modèle Modelly.
- [AgentSet](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/1_agentset.html) : apprenez à gérer plus efficacement les agents avec l’AgentSet de Modelly.
- [Activation des agents](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/2_agent_activation.html) : découvrez différentes façons d’activer les agents avec `do`, `shuffle_do` et `map`, qui couvrent les activations aléatoire, séquentielle, simultanée, par étapes, par type et conditionnelle.
- [Planification d’événements](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/3_event_scheduling.html) : apprenez à planifier des événements et à gérer le temps dans votre modèle Modelly.
- [Ajouter un espace](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/4_adding_space.html) : apprenez à ajouter un espace à votre modèle Modelly et à comprendre l’architecture des espaces de Modelly.
- [Collecter des données](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/5_collecting_data.html) : apprenez à collecter des données au niveau du modèle et des agents avec le DataCollector de Modelly.
- [Visualisation de base](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/6_visualization_basic.html) : apprenez à construire un tableau de bord interactif avec le module de visualisation de Modelly.
- [Visualisation dynamique des agents](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/7_visualization_dynamic_agents.html) : apprenez à représenter dynamiquement vos agents dans votre tableau de bord interactif.
- [Visualisation avec SpaceRenderer](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/8_visualization_rendering_with_space_renderer.html) : apprenez à tirer pleinement parti de SpaceRenderer pour enrichir vos visualisations.
- [Visualisation des couches de propriétés](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/9_visualization_property_layer_visualization.html) : apprenez à visualiser les couches de propriétés dans Modelly.
- [Composants de visualisation personnalisés](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/10_visualization_custom.html) : apprenez à ajouter des composants visuels personnalisés à votre tableau de bord interactif.
- [Simulation à événements discrets](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/11_discrete_event_simulation.html) : apprenez à construire un modèle purement événementiel avec `schedule_event` et à le valider par la théorie des files d’attente.
- [Modèles hybrides ABM-DEVS](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/12_hybrid_abm_devs.html) : apprenez à combiner l’activation des agents par `step()` et des événements planifiés dans un modèle épidémique spatial.

## Votre propre projet

- [Utiliser Modelly dans votre projet](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/using_modelly_in_your_project.html) : d’un dossier vide à un modèle reproductible et mesuré, dans son propre dépôt.
- [Démarrer un projet](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/new_project.html) : `modelly new` écrit un projet initialisé avec une graine, testé et vérifié dès son premier commit.
- [Bonnes pratiques Modelly](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/best-practices.html) : un tour d’horizon des conseils et des recommandations pour utiliser Modelly.

## Cours et tutoriels par domaine

- [Cours](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/course/index.html) : douze séances qui mènent une classe d’un premier modèle à une étude validée et reproductible qui lui est propre.
- [Tutoriels par domaine](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/domains/index.html) : un tutoriel par discipline, chacun construit sur un modèle du zoo.

## Venir d’un autre outil

- [Migrer depuis Mesa](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/migrating_from_mesa.html) : une correspondance construction par construction et un codemod, `python -m modelly.migrate`, qui réécrit les parties mécaniques et signale le reste.

- [Depuis R et Julia](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/r_and_julia.html) : lisez les résultats Parquet de Modelly depuis R et Julia, et pilotez un modèle depuis R.

Vous les trouverez [ici](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples.html).

Bonne modélisation avec Modelly, et n’hésitez pas à nous contacter !

# Primeros pasos

*Esta página es una traducción de la [página en inglés](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/getting_started.html); las correcciones son bienvenidas.*

Modelly es un framework modular para construir, analizar y visualizar modelos basados en agentes.

Los **modelos basados en agentes** son simulaciones por ordenador en las que varias entidades (los agentes) actúan e interactúan entre sí según el comportamiento que se les ha programado. Los agentes pueden representar células vivas, animales, personas, e incluso organizaciones enteras o entidades abstractas. A veces entendemos cómo se comportan los componentes individuales de un sistema y queremos ver qué comportamientos y efectos surgen, a nivel del sistema, de su interacción. Otras veces tenemos una buena idea de cómo se comporta el sistema en su conjunto y queremos averiguar qué comportamientos individuales lo explican. O queremos ver cómo conseguir que los agentes cooperen o compitan de la forma más eficaz. O simplemente queremos construir un juguete vistoso con puntitos de colores que se mueven.

## Visión general

Si quiere hacerse una idea general de las funcionalidades y la estructura de Modelly, empiece aquí:

- [Visión general de la biblioteca MODELLY](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/overview.html): conozca los conceptos y componentes fundamentales de Modelly.

- [Programación de eventos](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/3_event_scheduling.html): aprenda a programar eventos y a gestionar el tiempo en su modelo de Modelly.
- [Añadir un espacio](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/4_adding_space.html): aprenda a añadir un espacio a su modelo de Modelly y a entender la arquitectura de espacios de Modelly.
- [Recoger datos](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/5_collecting_data.html): aprenda a recoger datos a nivel del modelo y de los agentes con el DataCollector de Modelly.

- [Visualización de capas de propiedades](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/9_visualization_property_layer_visualization.html): aprenda a visualizar capas de propiedades en Modelly.

- [Modelos híbridos ABM-DEVS](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/12_hybrid_abm_devs.html): aprenda a combinar la activación de agentes basada en `step()` con eventos programados en un modelo epidémico espacial.

# Primeiros passos

*Esta página é uma tradução da [página em inglês](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/getting_started.html); correções são bem-vindas.*

Modelly é um framework modular para construir, analisar e visualizar modelos baseados em agentes.

**Modelos baseados em agentes** são simulações computacionais com várias entidades (os agentes) que agem e interagem entre si de acordo com o comportamento programado. Os agentes podem representar células vivas, animais, pessoas e até organizações inteiras ou entidades abstratas. Às vezes, entendemos como os componentes individuais de um sistema se comportam e queremos ver que comportamentos e efeitos surgem, no nível do sistema, da interação entre eles. Outras vezes, temos uma boa ideia de como o sistema se comporta como um todo e queremos descobrir que comportamentos individuais o explicam. Ou queremos ver como fazer os agentes cooperarem ou competirem da forma mais eficaz. Ou simplesmente queremos construir um brinquedo divertido com pontinhos coloridos se movendo.

Se quiser ter uma ideia geral dos recursos e da estrutura do Modelly, comece aqui:

# 入门

*本页译自[英文页面](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/getting_started.html)，欢迎指正。*

Modelly 是一个用于构建、分析和可视化基于智能体的模型的模块化框架。

**基于智能体的模型**是一类计算机模拟：多个实体（即智能体）按照为其编写的行为相互作用。智能体可以代表活细胞、动物、个人，甚至整个组织或抽象实体。有时，我们了解系统中各个组成部分的行为，想看看它们的相互作用会在系统层面涌现出怎样的行为和效应。有时，我们对系统的整体行为已有很好的认识，想找出能够解释它的个体行为。又或者，我们想知道如何让智能体最有效地合作或竞争。也可能，我们只是想做一个有许多彩色小点四处移动的有趣玩具。

## 概览

如果想大致了解 Modelly 的功能和结构，请从这里开始：

- [MODELLY 库概览](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/overview.html)：了解 Modelly 的核心概念和组成部分。

# Modelly Core Examples

This repository contains a curated set of classic agent-based models implemented using Modelly. These core examples are maintained by the Modelly development team and serve as both demonstrations of Modelly’s capabilities and starting points for your own models.

## Overview

The examples are categorized into three groups:

1. **Basic Examples** - Simpler models that use only stable Modelly features; ideal for beginners
1. **Advanced Examples** - More complex models that demonstrate additional concepts
1. **Behaviour Examples** - Models built on the behaviour building blocks (`modelly.behaviour`): meta-agents and continuous states

## Basic Examples

The basic examples are relatively simple and use only the core building blocks: agents, spaces, scenarios, data collection and the browser visualization. They are good starting points for learning how to use Modelly.

### [Boltzmann Wealth Model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/basic/boltzmann_wealth_model.html)

Completed code to go along with the [tutorial](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/tutorials/0_first_model.html) on making a simple model of how a highly-skewed wealth distribution can emerge from simple rules.

### [Boids Flockers Model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/basic/boid_flockers.html)

[Boids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boids)-style flocking model, demonstrating the use of agents moving through a continuous space following direction vectors.

### [Conway’s Game of Life](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/basic/conways_game_of_life.html)

Implementation of [Conway’s Game of Life](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conway%27s_Game_of_Life), a cellular automata where simple rules can give rise to complex patterns.

### [Schelling Segregation Model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/basic/schelling.html)

Modelly implementation of the classic [Schelling segregation](http://nifty.stanford.edu/2014/mccown-schelling-model-segregation/) model.

### [Virus on a Network Model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/basic/virus_on_network.html)

This model is based on the NetLogo [Virus on a Network](https://ccl.northwestern.edu/netlogo/models/VirusonaNetwork) model.

## Advanced Examples

The advanced examples are more complex. They are good starting points for learning how to build more complex models.

### [Epstein Civil Violence Model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/advanced/epstein_civil_violence.html)

Joshua Epstein’s [model](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.092080199) of how a decentralized uprising can be suppressed or reach a critical mass of support.

### [Demographic Prisoner’s Dilemma on a Grid](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/advanced/pd_grid.html)

Grid-based demographic prisoner’s dilemma model, demonstrating how simple rules can lead to the emergence of widespread cooperation – and how a model activation regime can change its outcome.

### [Sugarscape Model with Traders](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/advanced/sugarscape_g1mt.html)

This is Epstein & Axtell’s Sugarscape model with Traders, a detailed description is in

Chapter four of *Growing Artificial Societies: Social Science from the Bottom Up (1996)*.

The model shows how emergent price equilibrium can happen via decentralized dynamics.

### [Wolf-Sheep Predation Model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/advanced/wolf_sheep.html)

Implementation of an ecological model of predation and reproduction, based on the NetLogo [Wolf Sheep Predation](http://ccl.northwestern.edu/netlogo/models/WolfSheepPredation) model.

## Behaviour Examples

These examples use `modelly.behaviour` (meta-agents, continuous states and thresholds) and `modelly.time.signals`. Those packages follow semantic versioning like the rest of Modelly; the tram model still lives in the `experimental/` example folder.

### [Alliance Formation Model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/advanced/alliance_formation.html)

Demonstrates `modelly.behaviour.meta_agents`: agents form alliances through a game-theoretic process, and the resulting alliances become meta-agents that can themselves form higher-level alliances.

### [Tram Route Model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/behaviour/tram_model.html)

Demonstrates continuous states and thresholds: a tram accelerates, coasts, brakes and dwells its way along a route, with every transition solved for analytically and scheduled on the event queue rather than polled for on each tick.

## Spatial Examples

These examples use the geospatial space (`modelly.space.geo`, the `geo` extra) and the dynamic and multilayer networks (`modelly.space.networks`). Their data are generated, so they run offline.

### [Commuting City](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/spatial/commuting_city.html)

Residents from a synthetic population commute across city zones on a street network, choosing workplaces by a gravity rule and routing around congestion.

### [Layered Epidemic](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/spatial/layered_epidemic.html)

An age-structured SIR epidemic on household, school and work layers, with school closure as a change of one layer’s weight.

## Language-Model Agent Examples

This example uses `modelly.llm`. It runs offline with a fake provider and replays from a bundled response cache, so it needs no API key.

### [Opinions of Persona Agents](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/examples/llm/llm_opinions.html)

Two hundred citizens with personas debate a protected bike lane on a small network; each decision goes through the reproducible `modelly.llm` client.
