The palettes are plain tuples of hex strings, so they work with Altair as well.

## One portrayal for every backend

An agent portrayal is a function that returns an `AgentPortrayalStyle` (`color`, `size`, `marker`, `alpha`, `zorder`, `edgecolors`, `linewidths`, `tooltip`, `filled`). The same function drives the Matplotlib and Altair backends of `SpaceRenderer`, the space views of `SolaraViz`, Modelly Studio, the figures below and the animations: the style classes, their defaults and the conversion of the older portrayal dicts live in one module, `modelly.viz.render.portrayal`.

When you have no portrayal yet, `ClassColours()` gives each agent class its own colour from a palette:

```python
from modelly.viz.render.portrayal import ClassColours

portrayal = ClassColours()  # Okabe-Ito
portrayal = ClassColours(palette=PALETTES["tol_bright"], size=20)
```

## A figure of the space

```python
from modelly.viz.mpl.figure import space_figure

with styles.paper("nature", columns=1):
    fig = space_figure(
        model, agent_portrayal=None, figsize=styles.figure_size("nature")
    )
    fig.savefig("space.pdf")
```

`space_figure` draws the model’s space (`model.grid`, else `model.space`) and agents with `SpaceRenderer` on a new figure: grids, hexagonal grids, networks, continuous spaces and Voronoi grids.

## Animations

```python
from modelly.examples import WolfSheep
from modelly.viz.animation import AnimationOptions, frames_from_run, save_animation

model = WolfSheep()
save_animation(frames_from_run(model, steps=200), "wolf_sheep.gif")
save_animation(
    frames_from_run(WolfSheep(), steps=200, every=2),
    "wolf_sheep.mp4",
    AnimationOptions(fps=24, figsize=(6, 6), dpi=120),
)
```

The frames are models: `frames_from_run(model, steps, every=1)` steps the model and yields it at the start and after every `every` steps; `frames_from_timeline(recorder)` yields the model at each checkpoint of a [time travel](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/timetravel.html) recording, so a run recorded once can be animated afterwards:

```python
from modelly.timetravel import Recorder
from modelly.viz.animation import frames_from_timeline

with Recorder(model, every=5) as recorder:
    model.run_for(500)
save_animation(frames_from_timeline(recorder), "run.gif")
```

`save_animation(models, path, options=None, agent_portrayal=None)` draws each frame with `space_figure` and returns the number of frames written. The suffix picks the format:

Format

Needs

Notes

.gif

Pillow, installed with Matplotlib

loops by default (AnimationOptions(loop=False) plays once); identical consecutive frames are merged

.mp4

the video extra: pip install "modelly-abm[video]"

H.264 through imageio-ffmpeg, which ships an ffmpeg binary for Windows, macOS and Linux: nothing to install system-wide

Frames are padded with white to a multiple of 16 pixels, which video codecs need. `fps`, `figsize` and `dpi` set the frame rate and the frame size (`figsize` times `dpi` pixels).

The API is in [Viz](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/viz.html).


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.md -->

# Modelly Studio

Modelly Studio is a browser app for one model: run it, change its parameters, scrub back through the run, and see the space, the plots, the agents, the profiler and the linter side by side. It works with any Modelly model, with no code to write: the parameter panel comes from the model’s `Scenario`, the space view from the same drawing code `SolaraViz` uses.

```bash
pip install "modelly-abm[viz]"
modelly studio path/to/model.py:MyModel
```

The command serves the app on `http://127.0.0.1:8765` and opens it in the default browser, on Windows, macOS and Linux alike. Stop it with Ctrl+C.

![Studio running the Wolf-Sheep example](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/_images/model.png)

A short tour of Studio: stepping Wolf-Sheep, scrubbing back, the WebGL map, an ensemble.

## Starting Studio

```bash
modelly studio modelly/examples/advanced/wolf_sheep/model.py:WolfSheep
modelly studio modelly.examples.advanced.wolf_sheep.model:WolfSheep --seed 7
modelly studio model.py:Epidemic --port 8800 --no-browser
modelly studio model.py:Epidemic --portrayal app.py:agent_portrayal
python -m modelly.studio model.py:Epidemic          # the same, without the umbrella command
```

The target is a file and a class, or a dotted module and a class, as for [`modelly profile`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/profile.html). A file inside a package (folders with `__init__.py`) is imported under its package name, so checkpoints of the model load again later; a loose file is imported under its own name with its folder on `sys.path`, so `from agents import Sheep` next to it works.

Option

Meaning

--port N

port to serve on (default 8765); 0 picks a free one

--host ADDRESS

address to listen on (default 127.0.0.1, this computer only)

--no-browser

do not open the default browser

--seed N

seed of the first run (default 42)

--portrayal FILE.py:FUNCTION

how agents are drawn: a function returning an AgentPortrayalStyle

--every N

steps between two timeline checkpoints (default 1)

--profile-steps N

how many of the last steps the profiler panel sums (default 50)

--memory-budget MIB

mebibytes the timeline’s checkpoints may take (default 256)

--results DIR

an experiment’s results store, for the [Experiments tab](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html#experiments)

--observations FILE.csv

observations to assimilate, for the [Assimilation tab](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html#ensembles-and-data-assimilation)

--analysis FILE.py:FUNCTION

posteriors and sensitivity results, for the [Analysis tab](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html#calibration-and-sensitivity)

--hub NAME

open a model of the [hub](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/hub.html) by name instead of a target

--language CODE

the labels in fr, es, pt or zh (see [Accessibility and languages](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/accessibility.html))

--classroom DIR

a folder shared by a class: the instructor shares parameters, students submit runs (see below)

--no-code

only the tabs for people who do not write code (see [Studio for everyone](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html#studio-for-everyone))

Exit status: 0 when the server stopped normally, 1 when the model raised while being built, 2 for a bad command line or a target that cannot be found. The model is built once before the server starts, so these errors show in the terminal.

The bundled examples’ `app.py` files define portrayals Studio can reuse, for example `--portrayal modelly/examples/advanced/wolf_sheep/app.py:wolf_sheep_portrayal`. Without one, each agent class gets its own colour from the colour-blind-safe Okabe-Ito palette.

## Studio for everyone

Studio can be used by someone who never writes Python: a policy analyst comparing interventions, a teacher, a student.

```bash
modelly hub install age_seir                   # once (a zoo model needs nothing installed)
modelly studio --hub age_seir --no-code        # open it by its hub name, without the code tabs
```

`--no-code` keeps the views (Model, Map), the Experiments tab and three tabs made for this. The Profiler, Lint, Log and Agents tabs are left out.

- **Compare**: pick an output (a model reporter), a parameter, and the values to try (`0.02, 0.035, 0.05`). Studio runs every value on the same replicate seeds (common random numbers, as `modelly.decide` does; see [Decisions](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/decide.html)). It shows each scenario’s mean with its 95% interval, the paired difference from the first value, and how often each scenario had the lowest value.
- **Card**: the [model card](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/model_cards.html): what the model is for, what it must not be used for, its validation and its limits.
- **Builder**: a model from a form, for teaching. Name the model and its agents, choose how many and the grid size, and pick behaviours: walk to a random neighbouring cell, give wealth to a cellmate, catch an infection from a cellmate, recover. The tab shows the code of one ordinary `model.py` and downloads it. Every combination of behaviours writes code that runs and that `modelly lint` passes (`tests/studio/test_studio_everyone.py`). `modelly.new.builder.build_code(ModelSpec(...))` does the same from Python.

**Classroom.** With `--classroom DIR`, a folder every student’s Studio can reach (a shared drive, or one machine serving the class), the Classroom tab shares the instructor’s parameter values (new sessions start from them) and lets each student submit their run: name, values, seed, steps and the final value of every model reporter. Everyone sees the table of the class’s runs, to compare them.

The Export panel’s **Report (HTML)** and **Report (PDF)** write a report to hand to someone who will not open Studio. The HTML report is one self-contained file. It holds:

- the parameters and the seed;
- a figure of every model reporter over the run;
- the scenarios compared, when there are some;
- the model card;
- the run’s manifest: the Modelly and Python versions, the model, the sha256 of its source and the steps run.

The PDF holds the same, one figure per page.

## The panels

**Run** (sidebar): Step, Run N steps, Play and Pause, Reset, and the pause between two steps while playing. Play waits for each step to be drawn before taking the next one. An exception raised by the model stops the run and shows under the buttons; the traceback is in the log.

**Parameters** (sidebar): one input per field of the model’s `Scenario`, and per keyword argument with a default of its constructor:

Field

Input

bool

checkbox

Literal[...] or an Enum

select

float between 0 and 1

slider

other int and float

number field

str

text field

anything else (tuple, dict, None)

shown, not editable

and the seed. With “Restart the run when a value changes” (on by default) a change rebuilds the model at step 0; turn it off to keep the change for Reset, or for Replay from here.

**Timeline**: a slider over every step of the run so far. Moving it shows the model at that step in every view, the live run going on untouched; Back to live returns to the latest step.

**Model**: the space (orthogonal and hexagonal grids, networks, continuous space and Voronoi grids, drawn by `SpaceRenderer`) and a plot of the `DataCollector`’s numeric model reporters. A model without a space or a collector says so instead. Above 10 000 agents and network edges, redrawing with Matplotlib at every step would stall the page, so the space view points to the Map tab instead.

**Map**: the space drawn by WebGL in the browser, for models with 100 000 agents or edges and more (see [the map](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html#the-map-large-models-in-webgl)).

**Agents**: the first 100 agents by `unique_id`, one column per attribute (the values `modelly.timetravel.agent_state` reads: plain attributes, columns and the cell or position), filtered by class.

**Profiler**: [`modelly profile`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/profile.html) over the last 50 steps: the costliest operations, microseconds per agent and the hints. Every step Studio takes is profiled; one session profiles at a time, since the profiler patches classes for the whole process.

![The profiler panel after 40 Wolf-Sheep steps](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/_images/profiler.png)

**Lint**: [`modelly lint`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/lint.html) on the model’s file. Each finding is a button; clicking it shows the rule’s `--explain` text. Check again re-reads the file after you edit it.

![The lint panel explaining MDL001](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/_images/lint.png)

**Log**: what happened in the run: new runs and their values, replays, errors, and why a model could not be checkpointed.

**Ensemble**, **Assimilation**, **Experiments** and **Analysis**: replicates and filters, a results store, posteriors and sensitivity results, in the sections below.

**Export** (sidebar): the space view and the reporters plot as PNG or SVG, the collected model data as CSV (and Parquet when `pyarrow` is installed), a checkpoint of the state shown (load it with `Model.load`), and a GIF of the run’s space view (at most 120 frames, sampled evenly). For the live run, two files that let someone else get the same run: the session as a Python script ([below](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html#recording-a-session-as-a-script)) and a [`modelly bundle`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/provenance.html) zip.

## Scrubbing and replaying

![Scrubbed back to step 7 of a Boltzmann run](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/_images/timeline.png)

Studio records each run with a [`modelly.timetravel.Recorder`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/timetravel.html), one checkpoint per step by default (`--every`). Scrubbing restores the checkpoint at or before the step and replays on to it, so the state shown is the one the run had at that step, bit for bit.

To try another future from a step: scrub to it, change parameters (with “Restart the run” off), and click Replay from here. The scrubbed-to state becomes the live run, with the changed Scenario values set on its scenario and, when the seed changed, both generators reseeded. What [the time travel guide](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/timetravel.html#replay-with-a-changed-scenario) says holds: code that reads `self.scenario.<name>` sees the new value from the next step on, but values the model copied out of the scenario when it was built keep their old ones, and constructor arguments (not on the scenario) are not applied, which the log says.

### Models that cannot be checkpointed

A model that holds a lambda (a `DataCollector` reporter, say), a generator or a class made at run time cannot be pickled, so it cannot be checkpointed. Studio then replays instead: scrubbing rebuilds the run from its start with the same parameters and seed and runs it on to the step. Seeded runs are reproducible, so the state is the same; it only takes longer on long runs. The log names what could not be saved, and the timeline says “scrubbing replays the run”. Of the bundled examples, Epstein civil violence, the prisoner’s dilemma grid, Sugarscape, the tram model and alliance formation replay; the others restore checkpoints. Making their reporters module-level functions (see [checkpoints](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/checkpoints.html)) makes scrubbing instant.

## Recording a session as a script

Export → **Session script** downloads a Python file that rebuilds the live run: it builds the model with the values and seed of the last Reset (or of the first run), takes the steps the run took, and, for each Replay from here, applies the changed Scenario values and the new seed at the step the replay started from. Running it ends with the model in the state Studio showed, bit for bit:

```bash
python wolfsheep_session_step40.py      # "WolfSheep at step 40"
```

```python
from wolfsheep_session_step40 import replay

model = replay()  # the live run's model, to inspect or run on
```

What the script holds, and what it does not:

- Scrubbing alone does not change the live run, so it is not in the script. A replay cuts the run at the step it starts from: the steps that had been taken after it are not replayed.
- The script loads the model the way Studio did, from the same target (a file path or a dotted module), so it runs wherever that target resolves: next to the model, or with the package installed.
- A parameter that is a constructor argument rather than a Scenario field is applied by Reset, not by Replay from here (see [above](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html#scrubbing-and-replaying)); the script does the same.
- Steps are counted from the model’s time, which each step advances by one.

The test suite checks the guarantee on six bundled examples, checkpointed and replayed ones alike: after a new run, steps, a scrub back, a replay with a changed seed and more steps, the script’s model has the same time, agents and attributes, generator states, collected data and scenario as Studio’s live model.

## Bundles

Export → **Bundle** reruns the live run with [`modelly run`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/provenance.html)’s recorder (the same target, values, seed and step count) and packs it as a `modelly bundle` zip: the manifest, the outputs, the model’s code, the seeds, the lock file and the Zenodo metadata. `modelly verify manifest.json` on the unpacked zip reruns it and compares the outputs. A manifest records one run built from its parameters and stepped on, so after Replay from here the bundle is refused (the log says why) and the session script is the file to share.

## Ensembles and data assimilation

**Ensemble** runs new replicates of the parameter panel’s values, each with a seed spawned from the panel’s seed (as `Scenario.spawn_replications` hands them out), and draws the mean, the median and the 5 to 95 % band of every numeric model reporter across them, step by step. The bands are the long-format frame of [`modelly.stream.Ensemble.band`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/assimilation.html) (`time`, `quantity`, `mean`, `q0.05`, `q0.5`, `q0.95`), and download as CSV. The replicates are stepped in place, so models that cannot be checkpointed work too.

**Assimilation** needs observations: `--observations observed.csv`, a CSV file with a `time` column and one column per observed model reporter (an empty field is a quantity not observed at that time). Choose a filter and run it over every observation:

- the **particle filter** weights the replicates by how well they match each observation and resamples them when the effective sample size falls below the threshold. The dashboard shows the filtered bands with the observations on top, the effective sample size over time (dots where it resampled) and every replicate’s weight at every observation, read before resampling, as a heat map;
- the **ensemble Kalman filter** adjusts model attributes (the live model’s float attributes are offered), each starting uniform within the chosen spread of its live value. The dashboard shows the bands and each parameter’s ensemble mean and standard deviation over time.

Both run synchronously when the button is pressed: keep the ensemble small (the default is 20 replicates) on slow models. The [assimilation guide](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/assimilation.html) explains the filters; resampling copies replicates through checkpoints, so the particle filter needs a model that can be checkpointed.

## Experiments

`--results runs/epidemic` opens an [experiment’s](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/experiments.html) results store in the Experiments tab: one row per finished run, with its parameters and its outputs at its last step. Each parameter gets a filter (a range slider for numbers with many values, a multiple select otherwise); the tab plots the chosen output against the chosen parameter (every run, and the mean per value) and the selected runs step by step, and downloads the selection as CSV. From Python the same queries are `modelly.studio.browser.ExperimentBrowser`.

## Calibration and sensitivity

`--analysis analysis.py:results` names a function that returns what the Analysis tab shows: a [calibration](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/calibration.html) `Posterior`, a [sensitivity](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/sensitivity.html) result (Morris, Sobol, PAWN, one at a time), or a list or a dict of them (the keys name them). For a posterior the tab draws its marginals, pairs and fits (`Posterior.plot`) and its summary with highest-density intervals; for a sensitivity result, the method’s plot and the ranked table.

```python
# analysis.py
from modelly.sensitivity import morris

from model import Epidemic
from study import calibration, space  # your own calibration and ScenarioSpace

def results():
    return {"fit": calibration.run(), "screen": morris(Epidemic, space, "infected")}
```

The function runs once, when the tab first opens. From Python, append `(name, result)` to `session.analyses` before showing `StudioApp(session)`.

## The map: large models in WebGL

The Map tab draws the shown model’s space in the browser with WebGL: agents as points, a network’s nodes and edges, a [`GeoSpace`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/geospatial.html)’s region outlines. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom, double-click to fit. Each step sends the scene as flat binary arrays and the GPU draws it, so a model with 100 000 agents or a network with 100 000 edges stays interactive where Matplotlib would take seconds per frame. Agents take their portrayal’s colour up to 20 000 agents, their class’s colour above that.

It degrades step by step: without WebGL (an old GPU driver, a locked-down browser) the same scene is drawn with Canvas 2D, slower; the “Canvas 2D instead of WebGL” checkbox forces that; and the Model tab keeps the Matplotlib view with the portrayal’s full styling. The renderer is a few hundred lines of JavaScript shipped inside Modelly (`modelly/studio/map.vue`); it loads nothing from a CDN.

## Browsers

Studio’s browser checks run locally before a release, headless with Playwright on Linux, in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit (the engine of Safari): the page loads with no file from outside the computer, the run controls work, and the map draws 100 000 agents and a 100 000-edge network in WebGL, then the 100 000 agents in Canvas 2D. Microsoft Edge is built on Chromium, so the Chromium run covers its engine; Safari itself (macOS) is not run. The suite is opt-in, one browser at a time, so the normal test run stays fast:

```bash
MODELLY_BROWSER=chromium pytest tests/studio/test_studio_browsers.py
MODELLY_BROWSER=firefox pytest tests/studio/test_studio_browsers.py
MODELLY_BROWSER=webkit pytest tests/studio/test_studio_browsers.py
```

Playwright’s WebKit for Linux is an Ubuntu build: on another distribution it may miss a few shared libraries (ICU 74, libxml2, flite, libjxl 0.8). `MODELLY_BROWSER_EXECUTABLE` points the suite at a browser binary of your own, such as a copy of Playwright’s `MiniBrowser` wrapper whose `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` adds a folder holding those libraries.

## Platforms and network

Studio is a Solara app served by uvicorn on your computer and drawn in your browser: there is nothing OS-specific in it, and paths are handled with `pathlib`. By default it listens on `127.0.0.1` only, so nothing outside your computer can reach it; `--host 0.0.0.0` shares it on your network, with no authentication, so use that on a network you trust only.

Studio’s own code makes no network request, and Solara’s telemetry is turned off. The browser asks only the Studio server for files. Solara’s page needs about 10 MB of front-end files (its Vuetify app, RequireJS, Font Awesome and their fonts), which the server takes from a cache folder (`share/solara/cdn` in the environment): a file not cached yet is downloaded from cdn.jsdelivr.net the first time the page asks for it, and `modelly studio` says so when it starts. To run offline, fill the cache once while online:

```bash
python -m modelly.studio.assets            # what is cached, what is missing
python -m modelly.studio.assets --fetch    # download the missing files
```

The cache folder can also be copied to a machine without internet access that has the same Solara version (`SOLARA_ASSETS_PROXY_CACHE_DIR` points Solara at another folder). The `solara-assets` package that used to ship these files lags behind Solara’s releases (1.58 against 1.64 at the time of writing), so Studio does not rely on it. What remains online: nothing at run time once the cache is filled; the cache itself has to be filled once, per Solara version.

## Architecture

Studio is a [Solara](https://solara.dev) app, decided for 1.3 over a separate front end: it reuses the visualisation code of `modelly.viz` (the portrayal styles, `SpaceRenderer` and its Matplotlib backend) rather than duplicating it in JavaScript, runs on Windows, macOS and Linux with nothing to build, and keeps the model in the same Python process as the panels, so the profiler, the linter and the recorder see the real objects.

Module

Role

modelly.studio.session

StudioSession: one tab’s run, with no widget (the tests drive it directly)

modelly.studio.timeline

the checkpoint recorder, or the replay timeline

modelly.studio.params

the parameter panel’s fields, from the Scenario

modelly.studio.data

series, agent table, figures and export files

modelly.studio.recording

modelly.studio.exports

the session script and the modelly bundle of the live run

modelly.studio.ensembles

replicates of the panel’s values and their bands

Each browser tab gets its own session. `StudioApp(session)` renders headless with `solara.render`, which is how the test suite opens every bundled example in Studio.

The screenshots on this page were taken headless, with Playwright driving Chromium against `modelly studio`; the video was recorded the same way, by `tools/studio/record_tour.py`.

The API is in [Studio](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/studio.html).

# Modelly in the browser

`modelly export-web` turns a model into a static web page that runs it in the reader’s browser: no installation, no Python on their machine, no server code. Python, Modelly and the model run in the tab with [Pyodide](https://pyodide.org/), CPython compiled to WebAssembly. Put the folder on GitHub Pages, in your docs, or on any static host, and share the link. The [gallery](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/gallery.html) embeds three such pages.

```bash
modelly export-web model.py:Epidemic --out site/
python -m http.server --directory site 8000     # then open http://localhost:8000
```

Browsers do not run the page from `file://` (it starts a Web Worker and fetches files), so open it through a web server, even locally.

## What the page does

The page has the same parameter panel as [Studio](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html), built from the model’s `Scenario` and its constructor’s keyword arguments: sliders for fractions, number and text fields, selects for `Literal` and `Enum` fields, checkboxes for booleans, and the seed. Reset builds the model, Step and Run advance it, Stop interrupts a run. The model runs in a Web Worker, a few steps at a time (about 50 ms of work per slice), so the page stays responsive during long runs and Stop takes effect after the current slice. Two views show the run: the agents in space (grid cells, continuous positions or network nodes, coloured by class or by a numeric attribute) and the numeric model reporters of the `DataCollector` over time.

`?lazy=1` at the end of the page’s URL waits for a click on Start before downloading anything, which is what an embedded page should do.

## What the export writes

```text
site/
  index.html app.js draw.js worker.js style.css   the page
  modelly.json                                     what to load and run
  wheels/modelly_abm-<version>-py3-none-any.whl    Modelly, pure Python
  model.zip                                        the model's code (not for an example
                                                   or a zoo model, which the wheel holds)
```

Pyodide itself comes from its official CDN (`cdn.jsdelivr.net/pyodide`) at the version `modelly.web.PYODIDE_VERSION` pins (314.0.7, Python 3.14); `--pyodide-url` points the page at another copy, such as a self-hosted one.

The export first runs the model for `--steps` steps (default 100) in a fresh Python process, to check it builds and runs, and to see which third-party packages it imports. The page loads exactly those from Pyodide, plus numpy and pandas, and nothing they merely list as dependencies: a network model loads networkx and scipy but not matplotlib. `--package NAME` adds a package the check run did not reach, `--skip-package NAME` drops one.

The shipped wheel holds Modelly without the parts a browser model does not import: the command-line tools, the Solara visualisation, the examples other than the exported one, and the C sources. Its compiled modules are replaced by their pure-Python twins, which give the same results (see [Determinism](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/determinism.html)).

Option

Meaning

--out DIR

the site folder (default site/)

--steps N

the check run’s length and the page’s default run length

--seed S

the check run’s seed and the page’s default seed

--title T

the page title (default: the class name)

--wheel PATH

ship this Modelly wheel instead, such as the WebAssembly one below

--pyodide-url URL

where the page loads Pyodide from

--package NAME, --skip-package NAME

edit the list of Pyodide packages

The same from Python:

```python
from pathlib import Path

from modelly.web import WebExport, export_web

export_web(WebExport("model.py:Epidemic", Path("site"), steps=50))
```

## Compiled modules in WebAssembly

The five C modules of `modelly/_native` (`fastrng`, `fastloop`, `fastcell`, `fastset` and, since 1.4, `fastevents`) also build for WebAssembly with Emscripten, through `pyodide build`:

```bash
pip install pyodide-build                       # with Python 3.14, Pyodide 314's version
pyodide xbuildenv install 314.0.7
pyodide xbuildenv install-emscripten
bash scripts/build-wasm-wheel.sh                # writes dist/wasm/modelly_abm-...-wasm32.whl
modelly export-web model.py:Epidemic --out site/ --wheel dist/wasm/modelly_abm-*.whl
```

The page footer says which version runs: “pure Python” or “compiled: fastrng, fastloop, fastcell, fastset”. The compiled wheel is the whole package (it is not trimmed), about 1.1 MB against about 770 KB for the pure one, and the browser checks run every example with both.

## What runs in the browser

Every example of `modelly/examples` and every zoo model runs from its static export in a headless Chromium, with the pure wheel and with the compiled one (`tests/web/test_browser.py`, opt-in with `MODELLY_BROWSER_TESTS=1`; `scripts/release-checks.sh browser` runs it before a release). That includes the language-model example (its replay client answers offline; in Pyodide the calls go one at a time, since threads cannot start) and the geospatial commuting city (geopandas, shapely and pyproj come from Pyodide).

What does not work in a browser tab: anything that starts threads or processes (parallel `run_batch` and experiment executors, the threaded LLM client falls back to one call at a time), network access other than `fetch` (a live LLM provider, OpenStreetMap downloads), and packages Pyodide does not build. The page reports a package it cannot find in its footer; the model then fails on the import with a normal traceback in the status line.

## First load

Most of a first visit is Pyodide itself and the two packages every model needs: the WebAssembly interpreter (3.4 MB compressed), its standard library (2.5 MB), numpy (3.0 MB) and pandas (4.2 MB), about 13.5 MB from the CDN. The site adds 0.5 MB (the pure wheel) or 0.85 MB (the compiled one). A model that uses scipy (the grid models’ neighbour sums, the continuous and network spaces’ KD-trees) adds 14 MB more.

Measured with `tools/web/measure_load.py`: a cold first visit (fresh browser context, HTTP cache off) in headless Chromium 1248 on Linux, the site served from localhost and Pyodide from `cdn.jsdelivr.net`, the clock running from navigation to the model built and drawn at step 0. The machine (16 cores) was shared with other jobs, which slows the WebAssembly start-up; three runs per row, median shown (the pure-wheel rows measured on v1.4.2; reports in `paper/data/browser_load/`).

Site

Transferred

No throttling

50 Mbit/s, 40 ms

DevTools “Fast 4G”

Age-structured SEIR (zoo), pure wheel

14.3 MB

4.4 s

7.0 s

20.0 s

Age-structured SEIR (zoo), compiled wheel

14.4 MB

22.4 s

Forest fire (zoo, needs scipy), pure wheel

28.3 MB

5.4 s

10.1 s

35.0 s

“Fast 4G” is Chrome DevTools’ preset: 9 Mbit/s down at 90% efficiency (about 1 MB/s), 165 ms round trip. At that speed the transfer alone takes 14 s, so no export can start in under 10 s there; on a 50 Mbit/s line a zoo model without scipy is ready in 8 s.

Later visits read Pyodide and the packages from the browser cache and start in a few seconds. `tools/web/measure_load.py SITE_DIR --profile fast-4g` measures a site the same way.

# Plugins

A separate package can add spaces, executors, samplers, collectors, Studio views and lint rules to Modelly without any change to Modelly itself. It declares them as [entry points](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/entry-points/) in its `pyproject.toml`, and Modelly finds them once the package is installed.

```bash
modelly new hexworld --template plugin   # a plugin package, tested, for Modelly 1.x
modelly plugins --check                  # what is installed, for which Modelly, and does it load
```

## Plugin API v1

The entry-point groups below, `Plugin`, `discover`, `load_all` and `PluginError` are the plugin API, version 1 (`modelly.plugins.API_VERSION`). They are **stable and frozen for the 1.x line**: no group is renamed or removed and the loading rules below do not change before 2.0, which carries them over unchanged or with a migration path. A plugin written for 1.5 keeps working in every later 1.x release.

## Entry-point groups

Group

What the entry point names

modelly.spaces

a space class (a grid, a mesh, a geographic space)

modelly.executors

an executor that runs batches of model runs (processes, a cluster)

modelly.samplers

a sampler of parameter designs (Sobol, Latin hypercube, Halton)

modelly.collectors

a data collector or a reporter factory

modelly.studio_views

a view for Modelly Studio

modelly.lint_rules

a rule for modelly lint

modelly.hub_sources

an extra hub index: a URL or path, or a function returning one or several

The groups are listed in `modelly.plugins.GROUPS`. What each kind of object must provide is set by the feature that uses it; the discovery mechanism below is the same for all.

## What Modelly does with each group

Group

Read by

The entry point names

modelly.executors

Experiment.run(executor=name), modelly experiment

an Executor subclass (or a factory taking the executor’s options)

modelly.samplers

[design] kind = "name" in an experiment file; modelly.experiments.designs.design_factory(name)

a factory n -> Design, as designs.latin_hypercube

modelly.lint_rules

modelly lint (and the Studio lint panel)

an object with rule, a modelly.lint.Rule with a code of its own, and check(tree), yielding the (line, column) of each hit in the parsed module

modelly.hub_sources

modelly hub search, info and install, after the public index

a URL or path string, or a function returning one or a list

modelly.studio_views

modelly studio: one more tab, named after the entry point

a Solara component taking the Studio state, as the built-in views

modelly.spaces

your model, through discover("modelly.spaces")[name].load()

a space class

modelly.collectors

your model, through discover("modelly.collectors")[name].load()

a reporter or a reporter factory for DataCollector

No Modelly feature picks a space or a collector by name (a model constructs its space and its reporters itself), so those two groups are read by models, not by Modelly. A lint rule that reuses a built-in code, or a view or rule that fails to load, is skipped with a `RuntimeWarning`; the others still run.

## An example plugin

[`examples/plugins/modelly-example-plugin`](https://github.com/RemiPelloux/Modelly/tree/main/examples/plugins/modelly-example-plugin) is a complete third-party package with one entry point in every group: a ring of cells, a uniform random sampler, a share-of-agents reporter, an executor, the lint rule `EXP001` (`print()` in model code), a Studio tab showing the scenario and a hub source (an empty private index). `pip install -e` it next to Modelly to try it; `tests/test_example_plugin.py` checks each entry point the way Modelly reads it.

## Declaring a plugin

```toml
# pyproject.toml of the package "modelly-hexworld"
[project.entry-points."modelly.spaces"]
hexworld = "hexworld.space:HexWorld"

[project.entry-points."modelly.samplers"]
halton = "hexworld.sampling:halton"
```

After `pip install modelly-hexworld` (or `pip install -e .` while you develop it) the entry points are visible to every Python process using that environment.

### Which Modelly a plugin supports

A plugin declares the Modelly versions it works with as an ordinary dependency, with a lower bound on the minor version it was written for and an upper bound below the next major:

```toml
[project]
dependencies = ["modelly-abm>=1.5,<2"]
```

Modelly reads that requirement from the installed metadata (`Plugin.requires`, here `">=1.5,<2"`). When the running version is outside it, `Plugin.compatible` is false and `load()` raises `PluginError` without importing the plugin’s code, so a plugin built for another version is skipped with a warning by the feature that reads it instead of failing inside it. A plugin that does not mention `modelly-abm` loads as before (`requires` is None); `modelly plugins` marks it as declaring no version.

### Starting from the template

`modelly new hexworld --template plugin` writes a package with one entry point (a stratified design sampler under `modelly.samplers`), the declaration above for the running minor version, and tests that check the entry point and that the same seed gives the same points. Replace the sampler with your extension, or add modules and entry points next to it.

### Checking what is installed

```text
$ modelly plugins --check
Modelly 1.5.0, plugin API v1
modelly.spaces: 1
  ring            modelly-example-plugin      modelly-abm>=1.4,<2     ok
modelly.executors: 1
  in_order        modelly-example-plugin      modelly-abm>=1.4,<2     ok
...
```

Without `--check` nothing is imported; with it every plugin is loaded, and the command exits with 1 when one is incompatible or fails to import.

## Finding and loading plugins

```python
from modelly.plugins import discover, load_all

spaces = discover("modelly.spaces")  # {"hexworld": Plugin(...)}; nothing imported yet
HexWorld = spaces["hexworld"].load()  # imported now, then cached

loaded, errors = load_all("modelly.samplers")  # every plugin of the group
for name, error in errors.items():
    print(f"{name} did not load: {error}")
```

- **Lazy.** `discover(group)` reads the installed metadata only; a plugin’s module is imported the first time `load()` is called on it, so a slow or heavy plugin costs nothing until it is used. The scan of the installed metadata is kept for the session and redone when `sys.path` or one of its folders changes; `modelly.plugins.clear_cache()` forces it, for example after installing a plugin into a running process.
- **Isolated.** A plugin that fails to import raises `PluginError` (an `ImportError`) that names the plugin, its entry point and its distribution, with the original error as its cause. It never stops other plugins from being found or loaded; `load_all` returns the failures apart from the objects.
- **Deterministic.** Plugins come back sorted by name. When two installed distributions declare the same name in a group, the first distribution in alphabetical order wins and a `RuntimeWarning` names both.

Any group name works with `discover`, so a feature can define its own group with the same helper.

## Testing a plugin

A test does not need to build or install a package: a folder on `sys.path` that holds a `<name>-<version>.dist-info` directory with a `METADATA` file and an `entry_points.txt` is an installed distribution as far as `importlib.metadata` is concerned. `tests/test_plugins.py` does exactly that with pytest’s `tmp_path` and `monkeypatch.syspath_prepend`.

```text
fake-site/
  fakeplug-1.0.dist-info/
    METADATA            Metadata-Version: 2.1 / Name: fakeplug / Version: 1.0
    entry_points.txt    [modelly.spaces]
                        ring = fake_modelly_plugin:Ring
  fake_modelly_plugin.py
```

The API is on the [plugins API page](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/plugins.html).

# Installing on a locked-down Windows machine

A work or university laptop often has no administrator rights, a proxy, and sometimes no direct internet access. Modelly installs and runs without any of them: it needs no administrator rights, no compiler (the wheels include the compiled modules, for x64 and ARM64) and no service, and Studio listens on this computer only.

## 1. Python, without administrator rights

Use one of these; each installs for your account only.

- **The python.org installer.** Run it, tick *Install for current user only* (or leave *Install launcher for all users* unticked), and tick *Add python.exe to PATH*.
- **winget**, if your machine has it: `winget install Python.Python.3.13 --scope user`.
- **uv**, a single program in your user folder that installs Python and packages:

```powershell
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c "irm https://astral.sh/uv/install.ps1 | iex"
uv python install 3.13
```

- **The Microsoft Store** Python, where the Store is allowed.

Check it works: `py --version` (the launcher) or `python --version`.

## 2. A virtual environment and Modelly

```powershell
py -3.13 -m venv $HOME\modelly-env
& $HOME\modelly-env\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install "modelly-abm[viz,experiments]"
& $HOME\modelly-env\Scripts\python.exe -m modelly --version
```

Calling the environment’s `python.exe` by its path, as above, needs no activation script. If you prefer to activate it and PowerShell refuses to run `Activate.ps1` (“running scripts is disabled”), allow scripts for this window only, which needs no rights:

```powershell
Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope Process -ExecutionPolicy Bypass
& $HOME\modelly-env\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```

With uv instead: `uv venv $HOME\modelly-env --python 3.13`, then `uv pip install --python $HOME\modelly-env "modelly-abm[viz,experiments]"`.

## 3. Behind a proxy

pip reads the proxy from the environment, and uses the certificates Windows trusts (so a company’s own certificate authority works without extra steps on pip 24.2 or later):

```powershell
$env:HTTPS_PROXY = "http://proxy.example.org:8080"
python -m pip install "modelly-abm[viz,experiments]"
```

If pip still reports a certificate error, ask your IT department for the company’s root certificate as a `.pem` file and point pip at it: `python -m pip config set global.cert C:\path\company-root.pem`.

## 4. Without internet access

Download the wheels on a machine that has access, with the same Python version and architecture, then carry the folder over:

```powershell
# on the connected machine
python -m pip download "modelly-abm[viz,experiments]" -d modelly-wheels --platform win_amd64 --python-version 3.13 --only-binary=:all:
# on the offline machine
python -m pip install --no-index --find-links modelly-wheels "modelly-abm[viz,experiments]"
```

Use `--platform win_arm64` for an ARM laptop. Studio loads its page’s JavaScript and fonts from a cache; fill it once on the connected machine, `python -m modelly.studio.assets --fetch`, and copy the cache folder it prints, or run that command on the offline machine while it is briefly online ([Studio](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html#platforms-and-network)).

## 5. Running Studio

```powershell
python -m modelly studio path\to\model.py:MyModel
```

Studio listens on `127.0.0.1`, this computer only, so Windows Defender Firewall does not ask for an exception and no administrator is needed. The browser opens on `http://127.0.0.1:8765`; if port 8765 is taken, pass `--port 0` for a free one.

## The R and Julia packages

Both need no administrator rights either. R installs packages into your user library when the system one is not writable (R asks once to create it). `modelly::install_modelly()` creates a Python environment in your user folder. `Modelly.jl`’s first `using Modelly` installs Python and Modelly into Julia’s depot, also in your user folder (see [From R and Julia](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/r_and_julia.html)).


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/event_ordering.md -->

# Event ordering

What runs first when several things are due at the same time. Modelly orders every event, the model’s steps included, by three keys, in this order:

1. **Time.** An earlier event runs first.
1. **Priority.** At the same time, the lower priority value runs first: `Priority.HIGH` (1), then `Priority.DEFAULT` (5), then `Priority.LOW` (10). A model’s `step` is scheduled at `Priority.HIGH`.
1. **Insertion order.** At the same time and priority, the event scheduled first runs first.

```python
from modelly import Model
from modelly.time import Priority

class Clock(Model):
    def step(self):
        print("step", self.time)

    def default(self):
        print("default", self.time)

    def high(self):
        print("high", self.time)

model = Clock(rng=1)
model.schedule_event(model.default, at=2)
model.schedule_event(model.high, at=2, priority=Priority.HIGH)
model.run_for(3)
```

Events hold their function by a weak reference, so schedule a method or a module-level function, not a lambda that nothing else keeps.

At time 2 this runs `high` (HIGH, scheduled before the step at time 2 was), then `step` (HIGH, scheduled when the step at time 1 ran), then `default`. The step at time 2 is scheduled when the step at time 1 runs, so an event scheduled at HIGH priority before then runs before it, and one scheduled at HIGH priority after it runs after it.

This is the rule Modelly 2.0 keeps (epic H4 of its [roadmap](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/2.0.0.html)): no model’s order changes in 2.0, so there is nothing to warn about (see [Deprecations](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/deprecations.html)). `tests/test_event_ordering.py` checks each rule.

The order is the same in the compiled and the pure-Python schedulers, after a checkpoint is loaded, and on every platform, since it uses no wall-clock time and no object identity.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/accessibility.md -->

# Accessibility and languages

Modelly Studio and this documentation aim at [WCAG 2.2](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/) level AA: usable with a keyboard and a screen reader, readable at 200% zoom, with text contrast of at least 4.5:1, and in more than one language.

## How it is checked

`scripts/release-checks.sh a11y` runs [axe-core](https://github.com/dequelabs/axe-core), the standard automated WCAG checker, in Chromium. It checks every rule tagged WCAG 2.0, 2.1 and 2.2, levels A and AA, on:

- the home page, the getting-started page and its French translation;
- a zoo page, the Studio, Decisions and What’s new guides, and the course;
- Studio itself, in English, in French in no-code mode, and in Arabic (right to left), after a step has run, so the plots are drawn.

Any violation fails the stage, and the stage runs before every release. An automated checker finds only part of the accessibility problems a person meets: it cannot judge whether a screen reader’s reading order makes sense or whether a task can be finished with the keyboard alone. Those passes need people who use these tools; please [report](https://github.com/RemiPelloux/Modelly/issues) anything that gets in your way.

## What Studio does

- **Zoom.** The page can be zoomed and scaled (Solara’s page template turned that off).
- **Names.** Every slider is named after its field and every icon button after its icon. Every plot has alternative text from its panel’s title, so a screen reader says what each control and figure is.
- **Contrast and focus.** Field labels and the app bar meet 4.5:1. The keyboard focus is a visible 3-pixel ring in Okabe-Ito blue.
- **Colour.** Agents and series use the Okabe-Ito palette, which stays distinct for the common forms of colour blindness, by default.
- **Language.** `modelly studio model.py:Model --language fr` shows every label in French; `es`, `pt` and `zh` are also shipped. The page declares its language to screen readers. Arabic, Hebrew, Persian and Urdu turn the page right to left; their catalogs are not written yet, so their labels are in English.

The layer lives in `modelly/templates/index.html.j2`, which Solara finds before its own page template, and `modelly/studio/a11y.py`.

# Geospatial models

`modelly.space.geo` starts a model from real maps: census zones as polygons, land cover as a raster, streets as a routable network, and a synthetic population drawn from census tables.

```bash
pip install "modelly-abm[geo]"         # GeoPandas, Shapely, pyproj, rasterio
pip install "modelly-abm[geo,osm]"     # and OSMnx, to download OpenStreetMap streets
```

GeoPandas, Shapely, pyproj and rasterio ship wheels for Windows, macOS and Linux that bundle GDAL and PROJ, so nothing has to be installed on the system. Importing `modelly.space.geo` without them raises an `ImportError` that names the extra. Writing GeoParquet also needs `pyarrow`.

## One coordinate reference system, set at the space

A `GeoSpace` works in one projected CRS, so that distances are in metres (or feet), not degrees. The CRS is chosen once, when the space is created:

- `GeoSpace(regions, crs="EPSG:2154")` uses the CRS you name and reprojects `regions`;
- `GeoSpace(regions)` uses the CRS of `regions`, or, when that is geographic (latitude and longitude, such as EPSG:4326), the UTM zone that covers them.

Everything that comes in later can carry its own CRS and is reprojected: `GeoAgent(space, model, point, crs="EPSG:4326")`, `space.move_to(agent, point, crs=...)`, `space.project(geometry, crs=...)` and `space.project_points(xy, crs=...)`.

```python
import geopandas as gpd

from modelly import Model
from modelly.space.geo import GeoAgent, GeoSpace

zones = gpd.read_file("zones.gpkg").set_index("zone_id")  # any CRS

class Resident(GeoAgent):
    pass

model = Model(rng=42)
space = GeoSpace(zones, random=model.random)
home = space.random_points("Z042", 1, model.rng)[0]
resident = Resident(space, model, home)
resident.region  # "Z042"
resident.move_to((2.35, 48.85), crs="EPSG:4326")  # a longitude and latitude
```

## Agents as points, polygons as regions

`GeoSpace` is a `ContinuousSpace`: every agent’s position is a row of one numpy array (`space.agent_positions`), and the continuous space’s KD-tree queries work in metres: `get_agents_in_radius`, `neighbors_within(radius)` (every agent’s neighbours in one call) and `get_k_nearest_agents`. The regions are the rows of `space.regions`, a GeoDataFrame indexed by region label, with one STRtree over their polygons.

Question

Call

Which region is this point in?

space.region_of(point); space.regions_of(xy) for many

Which agents are in region r?

space.agents_in_region(r); space.region_counts() for all

Which agents are inside this polygon, or within 500 m of this line?

space.agents_within(geometry), space.agents_within(geometry, distance=500)

Which regions border r?

space.region_neighbors(r) (queen), kind="rook" for a shared edge

Which regions are within 2 km of r?

space.region_neighbors(r, distance=2000)

Region adjacency as a matrix

space.contiguity("queen"), a scipy CSR matrix

Region membership of the agents is computed for the whole population at once and cached until an agent moves.

## Export

`space.to_geodataframe()` gives one point per agent with its `unique_id`, its `region` and any attributes you name; `space.to_geodataframe("regions")` gives the regions with an `n_agents` column. `space.to_file(path)` writes either one, chosen by suffix: `.parquet` for GeoParquet, `.geojson` for GeoJSON (in WGS 84, as the format requires). Both open in QGIS and in GeoPandas.

```python
space.to_file("residents.parquet", attributes=("age", "income"))
space.to_file("zones.geojson", what="regions")
```

## Rasters as property layers

A `RasterLayer` holds one band with its affine transform, CRS and nodata value. Its `values` are shaped like an orthogonal grid, `(width, height)`, with `y` increasing northward, so the band can be a grid’s property layer: the grid and the raster then share one array.

```python
from modelly.space.geo import RasterLayer

land = RasterLayer.from_file("landcover.tif")
grid = land.to_grid("cover", random=model.random)  # an OrthogonalMooreGrid
grid[(10, 4)].cover  # the pixel under cell (10, 4)
land.sample_agents(space)  # the value under every GeoAgent, nan outside or on nodata
land.to_file("landcover-after.tif")  # writes the band back as a GeoTIFF
```

`land.sample(xy, crs=...)` samples at any points, reprojecting them if needed; `land.reproject("EPSG:3035")` warps the band into another CRS.

## Road networks and routing

A `RoadNetwork` wraps any NetworkX graph whose nodes have `x` and `y` coordinates, the OSMnx convention, and gives every node a cell of a `Network` space (`roads.space`), so agents can also stand on intersections as `CellAgent`s. Edges without a `length` get the straight-line length.

```python
from modelly.space.geo import RoadNetwork, download_osm

roads = RoadNetwork(graph, random=model.random)  # graph.graph["crs"] is honoured
roads.add_travel_times(speed=13.9)  # length / speed, unless an edge has its own speed
path = roads.shortest_path(home, work, weight="travel_time")  # nodes or points
minutes = roads.travel_time(home, work) / 60
# scipy, many sources at once
matrix = roads.distance_matrix(origins, weight="travel_time")
near = roads.agents_within(space, origin, 1000)  # agents within 1 km along the streets

# needs the osm extra and a connection
lyon = download_osm("Lyon, France", random=model.random)
```

`download_osm` downloads; cache the graph (`osmnx.save_graphml`) instead of calling it on every run. After changing edge attributes yourself, call `roads.invalidate()` so the next `distance_matrix` is rebuilt.

## Synthetic populations

Census tables give, per region, the number of people in each level of each attribute, not the joint table. `ipf(seed, marginals)` fits a joint table to the marginals by iterative proportional fitting, keeping the seed’s zeros; `synthesize_population` does it per region and returns one row per person:

```python
from modelly.population import synthesize_population

people = synthesize_population(
    {"age": ["0-17", "18-64", "65+"], "car": [True, False]},
    {"Z042": {"age": [210, 600, 190], "car": [700, 300]}, ...},
    model.rng,
)
for zone, group in people.groupby("region"):
    for point, age in zip(space.random_points(zone, len(group), model.rng), group.age):
        Resident(space, model, point).age = age
```

Each region gets exactly its total and its first attribute’s counts; the other marginals are met to within the rounding (the fitted table is rounded to whole people at random, from `model.rng`, so a seed gives the same people). The full toolkit, with households, homes, schools, workplaces and contact networks, is `modelly.population`: see [Synthetic populations](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/population.html). The two functions above are the same in both places.

## Real-data samples

`modelly.space.geo.samples` bundles three small extracts of Burlington, Vermont, so that models and tests on real data run offline. None holds personal data.

Call

Returns

Source and licence

sample_roads()

a RoadNetwork of the drivable streets of downtown: 255 junctions, one-way streets kept

OpenStreetMap, ODbL 1.0, © OpenStreetMap contributors

sample_landcover()

a RasterLayer of 120 x 120 ESA WorldCover 2021 pixels (10 m) over the Intervale

ESA WorldCover, CC BY 4.0, © ESA WorldCover project 2021

sample_neighbourhoods()

the 41 census tracts of Chittenden County as a GeoDataFrame

U.S. Census Bureau, public domain

The files are in `modelly/space/geo/data`, with their sources, retrieval dates, changes and checksums in `NOTICE.md` there. The OpenStreetMap extract is a derived database under the ODbL: a database you make from it must be offered under the ODbL as well. To fetch the full sources, check their SHA-256 and cut the extracts again (the same commands in bash and PowerShell):

```text
python scripts/geo_data.py download data/raw    fetch and verify the full sources
python scripts/geo_data.py verify data/raw      verify sources already downloaded
python scripts/geo_data.py build data/raw       rebuild the bundled extracts (geo extra)
```

The full sources are the Census Bureau’s 2023 tract boundaries of Vermont (112 KB), the WorldCover tile N42W075 (65 MB) and an Overpass query of the streets pinned to 2026-10-01. The query’s checksum is over its elements, sorted, so the server’s own timestamp in the reply does not change it.

## Zoo models on real data

Three zoo models run on the samples by default and take your own data through their scenario:

- [Traffic assignment](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/road_traffic.html) (`road_traffic`): random trips routed by shortest path over the OpenStreetMap streets; flows match the exact edge betweenness. `RoadTrafficScenario(roads=RoadNetwork(graph))` runs it on another street graph.
- [Habitat selection](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/habitat_selection.html) (`habitat_selection`): animals disperse over the WorldCover raster and settle in proportion to habitat preference. `HabitatScenario(cover=RasterLayer.from_file(path).values)` runs it on another raster.
- [Schelling on real neighbourhoods](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/schelling_regions.html) (`schelling_regions`): two groups move between census tracts, neighbours by contiguity. `SchellingRegionsScenario(adjacency=GeoSpace(regions).contiguity())` runs it on other regions.

## Checkpoints

`GeoSpace`, `RasterLayer` and `RoadNetwork` are saved by `model.save` and restored by `Model.load` like any other part of the model (see [Checkpoints](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/checkpoints.html)). The STRtree, the contiguity matrices, the cached region membership and the routing matrices are not saved but rebuilt on first use. A raster attached to a grid stays shared with it after a load.

## Example

[Commuting City](https://github.com/RemiPelloux/Modelly/tree/main/modelly/examples/spatial/commuting_city) puts it together on generated data: zones of a synthetic city, residents from a synthetic population, workplaces by a gravity rule over travel times, and congested routing on a street lattice. The [API reference](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/geo.html) lists every class and function.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/population.md -->

# Synthetic populations

`modelly.population` builds a starting population from aggregate tables: people with their attributes, grouped into households, living at points of their region, going to schools and workplaces, and linked by a contact network. Every step adds columns to one pandas DataFrame with one row per person, so the result creates one agent per row, fills the columns of a column-backed agent set, or summarises into the inputs of a cohort model.

The toolkit needs only numpy and pandas. `locate_households` takes a `GeoSpace`, which needs the `geo` extra (`pip install "modelly-abm[geo]"`); everything else works on plain coordinates.

Step

Call

Adds

People from marginal tables

synthesize_population (IPF, then trs rounding)

region and one column per attribute

Or whole records from a sample

anneal (simulated annealing)

the rows of the sample to copy

Check the fit

marginal_errors

a table of target and synthetic counts

Households

assign_households

household

Homes

locate_households

x, y

Schools and workplaces

assign_places

school, work (or any name)

Contacts

contact_network

a MultilayerNetwork

## People from census marginals

Census tables give, per region, the number of people at each level of each attribute (age band, sex, household size) but not the joint table. `ipf(seed, marginals)` fits a joint table to the marginals by iterative proportional fitting; its seed can be a cross-tabulation of a microsample, so the fit keeps the sample’s associations (and its zeros). `trs` turns the fitted table into whole people: it keeps the floor of every cell and draws the people left over in proportion to the fractional parts (truncate, replicate, sample; Lovelace and Ballas 2013). `synthesize_population` does both, region by region:

```python
import numpy as np

from modelly import Model
from modelly.population import marginal_errors, synthesize_population

categories = {"age": ["0-17", "18-64", "65+"], "sex": ["f", "m"]}
marginals = {
    "T01": {"age": [210, 600, 190], "sex": [508, 492]},
    "T02": {"age": [90, 330, 80], "sex": [251, 249]},
}
model = Model(rng=42)
people = synthesize_population(categories, marginals, model.rng)
errors = marginal_errors(people, marginals, categories)
```

Every region gets exactly its total and its first attribute’s counts. The other marginals are met to within the rounding: each count is off by less than the number of levels of the first attribute, and `marginal_errors` shows by how much. The people are drawn from `model.rng`, so a seed gives the same population.

`modelly.space.geo.ipf` and `modelly.space.geo.synthesize_population` are the same functions; they keep working through 1.x with a deprecation warning and go in 2.0 (see [Deprecations](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/deprecations.html)).

## Whole households by combinatorial optimisation

IPF fits a table of people; it cannot keep the members of a household together. The combinatorial-optimisation approach (Williamson, Birkin and Rees 1998) does: choose as many records as the region has households from a sample of household records, with replacement, so that their totals match the region’s tables. `anneal` searches by simulated annealing: it swaps one chosen record for another, keeps every swap that lowers the total absolute error, and keeps a swap that raises it by `d` with probability `exp(-d / T)`, the temperature `T` falling at every swap.

```python
import pandas as pd

from modelly.population import Annealing, anneal, total_absolute_error

# One row per sample household: its members per age band and a one-hot of its size.
sample = pd.read_csv("household_sample.csv")
targets = {"children": 210, "adults": 600, "seniors": 190, "size_1": 120, "size_2": 140}
chosen = anneal(sample, targets, Annealing(size=430), model.rng)
total_absolute_error(sample, chosen, targets)
households = sample.iloc[chosen].reset_index(drop=True)
```

`Annealing` also sets the number of swaps tried (`iterations`, default 20,000), the starting temperature (in people) and the cooling factor per swap. The sample is yours: a public-use microdata sample, a survey, or a sample you make up. Modelly ships none.

## Households

`assign_households` groups the people of each region into households of the sizes in a household-size table. It rounds the table to whole households with `trs`, grows or shrinks random households one member at a time until they hold exactly the region’s people, gives every household a head among the people who can head one, and spreads the others over the remaining places at random. The people, and so the marginals, do not change.

```python
from modelly.population import HouseholdSpec, assign_households

sizes = [0.28, 0.34, 0.16, 0.14, 0.08]  # shares of households of 1 to 5 people
spec = HouseholdSpec({"T01": sizes, "T02": sizes}, heads=["18-64", "65+"])
people = assign_households(people, spec, model.rng)
```

A region that needs more heads than it has adults is an error, not a silent fix.

## Homes, schools and workplaces

`locate_households` puts each household at a random point of its region; all its members share it. `assign_places` then sends the people who attend a kind of place to the nearest place with room, in random order, never farther than `max_distance` (in the coordinates’ units, metres for a `GeoSpace`). People with no place within reach get `-1`. The places are a DataFrame with `x`, `y` and `capacity`; a person’s place is `places.iloc[person.school]`.

```python
import pandas as pd

from modelly.population import PlaceSpec, assign_places, locate_households
from modelly.space.geo import GeoSpace

space = GeoSpace(tracts, random=model.random)  # tracts indexed like the marginals
people = locate_households(people, space, model.rng)
centres = tracts.to_crs(space.crs).geometry.centroid
schools = pd.DataFrame({"x": centres.x, "y": centres.y, "capacity": 600})
people = assign_places(
    people, schools, PlaceSpec("school", ["0-17"], max_distance=10_000), model.rng
)
people = assign_places(people, workplaces, PlaceSpec("work", ["18-64"]), model.rng)
```

## Contact networks

`contact_network` links the people who share a place, one layer per kind of place, in a `MultilayerNetwork` (see [Networks](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/networks.html)): everybody in a household knows everybody else in it; the pupils of a school are split at random into classes and the workers of a workplace into teams, each a clique. Node `i` is row `i` of `people`. The default layers are household (weight 1), school (0.5, classes of 25) and work (0.25, teams of 10); `ContactLayers` changes them.

```python
from modelly.population import ContactLayers, contact_network
from modelly.space.networks import contact_matrix

network = contact_network(people, model.rng)
groups = pd.Categorical(people.age, categories=categories["age"]).codes
contacts = contact_matrix(network, groups)  # mean contacts between age groups
pressure = network.adjacency() @ infected  # for a network epidemic
```

The [layered epidemic example](https://github.com/RemiPelloux/Modelly/tree/main/modelly/examples/spatial/layered_epidemic) runs an epidemic on a network of the same three layers.

## Starting the age-structured SEIR model

The [age-structured SEIR](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/age_seir.html) zoo model runs on a synthetic population through `scenario_from_population`, which counts the age groups and measures the contact matrix on the network. Its default scenario does not change.

```python
from modelly.zoo.age_seir.model import AgeSEIR, scenario_from_population

scenario = scenario_from_population(people, network, ("0-17", "18-64", "65+"), rng=5)
seir = AgeSEIR(scenario)
seir.run()
seir.attack_rate(), seir.final_size()
```

`tests/population/test_sample_region.py` builds a population of about 20,000 people for the 41 census tracts of Chittenden County, Vermont (the bundled boundaries, see [Geospatial models](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/geospatial.html#real-data-samples)) from illustrative tables, checks that it reproduces every marginal within the rounding tolerance, that households, schools and workplaces respect their sizes, capacities and distances, and that the SEIR model started from it follows its final-size relation.

## Privacy

Everything here works from aggregate tables, and the people it makes are synthetic: no row is a real person, and Modelly bundles no personal data and no microdata. The marginals in the tests and on this page are made up. Aggregates of very small areas can still disclose people: use published, disclosure-controlled tables, keep any microdata sample under the terms it was released with, and do not publish a synthetic population fitted to unpublished small counts.

# Networks: dynamic and multilayer

Contact structures change over time and have several layers at once: the same people meet at home, at school and at work. `modelly.space.networks` models both, on numpy and scipy only. For a static network whose nodes are cells that agents move between, use the `Network` cell space; the structures here are for who-meets-whom.

Nodes are any hashable labels, or a count `n` for labels `0 .. n-1`. Every node has a row, in the order nodes were added, so the adjacency is a sparse matrix whose rows line up with per-node numpy arrays: an infection state, an agent column.

## Temporal networks

A `TemporalNetwork` edge is active on `start <= time < end`:

```python
import math

from modelly import Model
from modelly.space.networks import TemporalNetwork

model = Model(rng=1)
contacts = TemporalNetwork(clock=model)  # queries follow model.time
contacts.add_edge("ann", "bob", (0, 8))  # meet during the first eight steps
contacts.add_edge("bob", "cy", (3, math.inf), weight=2.0)  # from step three on
contacts.neighbors("bob")  # at model.time
```

The network keeps the pending activations and expirations in two heaps, so moving time forward touches only the edges that change: O(changed edges), not O(edges). Without a clock, call `contacts.advance_to(time)`, which returns the number of edges switched. Moving time backward replays every edge from the start. Neighbour queries (`neighbors`, `weighted_neighbors`, `degree`, `has_edge`) cost O(degree); `adjacency()` is the active network as a CSR matrix, rebuilt only after a change. Edge-list files with `start` and `end` columns load with `read_temporal_edge_list`.

## Multilayer networks

```python
from modelly.space.networks import MultilayerNetwork

network = MultilayerNetwork(n_people, {"household": 1.0, "school": 0.5, "work": 0.25})
network.add_edge(0, 1, "household")
network.add_edges(classmates, "school")

network.neighbors(4, "school")  # one layer
network.neighbors(4)  # any layer
# {node: layer weight x edge weight}
network.weighted_neighbors(4, ["household", "work"])
pressure = network.adjacency() @ infected  # all layers, weighted, one sparse product
# close the schools: the edges stay, the weight is zero
network.add_layer("school", 0.0)
```

Adding or removing an edge costs O(1). Each layer’s matrix is cached and rebuilt, from that layer’s edges only, the first time `adjacency` is called after the layer changed.

## Contact matrices

`contact_matrix(network, groups)` gives `C[a, b]`, the mean contact weight a member of group `a` has with members of group `b`, from the network’s (weighted) adjacency, optionally for some layers only. `age_groups(ages, [18, 65])` turns ages into groups: children, adults, seniors. For an undirected network `N[a] C[a, b] = N[b] C[b, a]`.

```python
from modelly.space.networks import age_groups, contact_matrix

groups = age_groups(ages, [5, 18, 30, 50, 65])
household = contact_matrix(network, groups, layer="household")
everything = contact_matrix(network, groups)
```

## Import and export

From

Call

NetworkX graph

from_networkx(graph, layer_attribute="layer", weight="weight")

igraph graph (if igraph is installed)

from_igraph(graph, layer_attribute="layer")

CSV source,target[,layer][,weight]

read_edge_list(path); write_edge_list(network, path)

CSV source,target,start[,end][,weight]

read_temporal_edge_list(path, clock=model)

CSV files are read and written as UTF-8 on every platform. Node labels read from a file are strings.

## Network statistics as reporters

`degree_distribution`, `degrees`, `mean_degree`, `clustering`, `average_clustering`, `component_sizes` and `largest_component` take a `MultilayerNetwork`, a `TemporalNetwork`, a `Network` space, a NetworkX or igraph graph, or a scipy sparse matrix. They read the structure as a simple undirected graph and cost a few sparse products, so they are cheap enough to collect every step. On simple undirected graphs they equal NetworkX’s `degree_histogram`, `clustering`, `average_clustering` and connected component sizes (the tests check it).

`network_reporter(attribute, statistic)` makes a `DataCollector` model reporter that, unlike a lambda, can be checkpointed:

```python
from modelly import DataCollector
from modelly.space.networks import largest_component, mean_degree, network_reporter

model.datacollector = DataCollector(
    {
        "mean_contacts": network_reporter("network", mean_degree),
        "giant": network_reporter("network", largest_component),
    }
)
```

## Checkpoints

Both network types are plain Python data and are saved and loaded with the model; a temporal network’s clock is restored as the loaded model. Cached matrices are rebuilt when needed.

## Example

[Layered Epidemic](https://github.com/RemiPelloux/Modelly/tree/main/modelly/examples/spatial/layered_epidemic) runs an age-structured SIR epidemic on household, school and work layers and closes the schools when prevalence crosses a threshold. The [API reference](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/networks.html) lists every class and function.
