# Decisions

`modelly.decide` turns model runs into a comparison that a decision can rest on. It compares strategies with intervals, costs them against what they achieve, tests them across many possible futures, and searches a policy’s parameters. Every result comes from a seed, so the same study rerun gives the same tables.

```python
from modelly.decide import Strategy, compare, cost_effectiveness, model_runner

run = model_runner(AgeSEIR, {"deaths": deaths}, scenario=SEIRScenario)
study = compare(
    run,
    [Strategy("nobody"), Strategy("seniors", {"vaccinated": (0, 0, 10_000)})],
    replicates=20,
    seed=7,
)
study.rank("deaths")  # best first, with intervals and how often each was best
study.difference("deaths")  # each strategy minus the first, paired by replicate
```

## Comparing strategies

A `Strategy` is a name, the parameters it sets and its cost: a number, or a function of one run’s outputs. `compare(run, strategies, replicates=..., seed=...)` runs each strategy `replicates` times. `run(params, seed)` builds and runs the model and returns its outputs; `model_runner(model_class, outputs, scenario=...)` writes that function for you.

Replicate `r` of every strategy gets the same seed: **common random numbers**. When the strategies consume the random numbers the same way, they face the same chance events (the same first infections, the same unlucky contacts), the difference between two strategies in one replicate is close to the effect of the strategy alone, and `difference(output)`, the interval of those paired differences, is much narrower than the two separate intervals. When a strategy changes the order of the draws, the pairing buys little: measure it with `modelly.explain.treatment_effect`, which reports the variance reduction (see [Causes and explanations](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/explain.html#treatment-effects-and-common-random-numbers)). `summary(output)` gives each strategy’s mean and Student-t interval (95% by default, `confidence=` to change it). `rank(output, lower_is_better=True)` orders the strategies and adds `best_share`: the share of replicates in which each was the best, an estimate of the probability that it is the right choice.

The runs are independent, so `workers=` spreads them over processes: `compare`, `robust` and `optimise` take it (default 1, one run after another; `None` uses every core). The results come back in the order the loop gives, with the same seeds, so they are identical whatever `workers` is. `run` is sent to each worker; a closure such as `model_runner`’s needs Linux, where workers are forked. `optimise` runs one trial’s replicates in parallel and its trials in turn, since each trial depends on the ones before.

## A worked example: who gets the vaccine?

`modelly.decide.vaccination` is the study of this section. In the [age-structured SEIR model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/age_seir.html) (100,000 people in three age groups), 10,000 doses can be given before the epidemic to children, to adults, to seniors, or to nobody. The outputs are the infections and the deaths, each group’s infections times an illustrative fatality ratio (0.01%, 0.2%, 3%). The cost is 20 per dose plus 150 per infection for care.

```python
from modelly.decide import cost_effectiveness, net_benefit
from modelly.decide.vaccination import vaccination_study

study = vaccination_study(replicates=20, seed=7)
study.rank("deaths")
cost_effectiveness(study, "deaths_averted")
net_benefit(study, "deaths_averted", wtp=100_000)
```

Strategy

Deaths (95% interval)

Deaths averted vs nobody

Cost

242.0 (241.0 to 243.1)

180.0 (178.3 to 181.8)

Vaccinating the children is the cheapest choice, cheaper than giving no doses at all, because children drive transmission and every infection they would have passed on costs care. Vaccinating the seniors averts the most deaths, at 9,942 per extra death averted over vaccinating the children. Seniors were the best choice in every replicate (`best_share` 1.0), and the intervals of the deaths averted are under four deaths wide. Here the pairing is not what makes them narrow: vaccinating adds a cohort row, which reorders the draws, so the arms are close to independent (variance ratio about 0.8); 100,000 people make each run’s result precise on its own. Run again with the same seed, the study gives the same tables (`tests/decide/test_decide.py`). The fatality ratios and costs are illustrative: the model’s card, at the end of [its page](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/age_seir.html), says what it must not be used for.

## Cost-effectiveness

`cost_effectiveness(comparison, effect)` places the strategies by mean cost and mean effect. A strategy is **dominated** when another costs no more and achieves at least as much, and **extendedly dominated** when a mix of two others would buy more effect for the same money. The remaining strategies form the efficient frontier. Each has an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio (`icer`) over the previous one: the price of one more unit of effect. `net_benefit(comparison, effect, wtp)` sets a willingness to pay per unit of effect and ranks `wtp * effect - cost` per replicate, with intervals.

## Robust decisions

When the world’s parameters are uncertain, a strategy tuned to one best guess can fail elsewhere. `robust` runs every strategy in every future:

```python
from modelly.decide import robust, sample_futures

futures = sample_futures({"beta": (0.025, 0.05), "recovery": (0.15, 0.3)}, 30, seed=1)
result = robust(run, strategies, futures, "deaths", replicates=5, threshold=300)
result.summary()  # mean, worst, max_regret, mean_regret, satisficing; minimax regret first
```

`sample_futures` draws futures by Latin hypercube sampling from ranges. Within a future every strategy gets the same seeds. The **regret** of a strategy in a future is how much worse it does than the best strategy there. `summary()` ranks by the largest regret (minimax regret), the usual criterion when the futures cannot be given probabilities. With a `threshold` it also reports the share of futures in which each strategy meets it.

## Optimising an intervention

`optimise(run, space, objective, trials=50, seed=0)` searches a policy’s parameters with Optuna’s TPE sampler (`pip install "modelly-abm[decide]"`). `space` maps names to ranges or lists of choices. Every proposal is evaluated on the same replicate seeds, and the sampler is seeded, so the same call gives the same trials and the same optimum:

```python
from modelly.decide import optimise

best = optimise(
    run,
    {"vaccinated_seniors": (0, 20_000)},
    lambda out: out["deaths"],
    trials=40,
    seed=2,
)
best.params, best.value, best.trials
```

## What these numbers are not

A comparison is only as good as its model: intervals cover the model’s chance, not its assumptions. Read the [model card](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/model_cards.html) before presenting a ranking, show the intervals with it, and say what was left out. The tables above never forecast what will happen; they say which strategy does best in the model, and by how much.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/explain.md -->

# Causes and explanations

`modelly.explain` says why an outcome happened, not only that it did. It covers:

- the effect of an intervention, with an interval;
- the agents an outcome depends on;
- what a recorded run would have done with one change;
- how much each parameter moved an emulator’s prediction.

```python
from modelly.explain import attribute, counterfactual, shapley, treatment_effect

effect = treatment_effect(
    run, control={}, treated={"imitation": 0.40}, output="adoption"
)
effect.mean, effect.low, effect.high, effect.variance_reduction
```

## Treatment effects and common random numbers

`treatment_effect(run, control, treated, output, replicates=30, seed=0)` runs both arms `replicates` times. Replicate `r` of both arms gets the same seed: **common random numbers**. The two runs of a pair then see the same chance events, so their difference is the effect of the treatment plus far less noise. The `Effect` holds the mean difference and its interval. By default it also measures what the pairing bought. The treated arm is run again on independent seeds, and `variance_reduction` is the variance of the unpaired difference divided by that of the paired one: how many times fewer runs the pairing needs for the same precision. `workers=` runs the replicates over processes with identical results, as in [Decisions](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/decide.html#comparing-strategies); `attribute` takes it too.

On the [Bass diffusion zoo model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/bass_diffusion.html), raising imitation from 0.38 to 0.40 adds about 2.05 percentage points of adoption after 60 steps (1.92 to 2.18 for 30 pairs with `seed=0`). Common random numbers reduce the variance of that estimate 24 to 62 times over ten seeds of the study (median 42); for a larger change, to 0.45, 10 to 19 times. The ratio is itself an estimate from 30 pairs, hence the spread. Every household draws one number per step whatever the parameters, so the pairs stay aligned until their adoptions differ.

The pairing only helps while the two arms consume the random numbers the same way. In the [age-structured SEIR model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/age_seir.html), vaccinating a group adds a cohort row, which changes the order of the binomial draws from the first step. The two arms are then effectively independent, and the measured ratio is 0.6 to 1.3 over ten seeds, no gain. On the [hospital epidemic](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/hospital_epidemic.html), the contact response changes when people are infected, and the gain is 1.9 times on the peak occupancy. `variance_reduction` measures this for your model rather than assuming it. To keep the pairing, write interventions that leave the number and order of the draws unchanged: a per-agent [random stream](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/determinism.html) helps.

## Attribution: which agents mattered

`attribute(build, candidates, output, steps=..., seeds=...)` reruns the model once per candidate agent, intervening on that agent at the start, and records how far the outcome moves from the baseline on the same seed:

```python
from modelly.explain import attribute

def immunise(model, agent):
    agent.state = State.RESISTANT

found = attribute(
    lambda seed: VirusOnNetwork(num_nodes=60, initial_outbreak_size=1, rng=seed),
    lambda model: list(model.agents),
    lambda model: sum(a.state != State.SUSCEPTIBLE for a in model.agents),
    steps=40,
    seeds=[1],
    intervene=immunise,
)
found.top(3)  # unique ids, largest effect first
```

The default intervention removes the agent. Effects are kept by unique id and averaged over the seeds, with intervals. In a sixty-person outbreak on a contact network with one index case, immunising the index case moves the outbreak by 45 to 51 infections, depending on the seed. The next agent moves it by 4 to 10. Attribution ranks the index case first for every seed tested (`tests/explain/test_explain.py`).

## Counterfactuals on a recorded run

A run that has already happened can be asked “what if”. `counterfactual` continues it from a recorded step (see [Time travel](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/timetravel.html)) twice: as it was, and with a change applied:

```python
from modelly.timetravel import Recorder

with Recorder(model, every=1) as recorder:
    model.run_for(30)

effect = counterfactual(recorder, 3, cure_everyone, 30, ever_infected, branches=8)
```

With one branch, both continuations draw exactly the numbers of the recorded run, so the difference is the change’s effect in that run. With `branches=n`, pair `i` is reseeded from the run’s own seed, the same seed for both members of the pair, and the result has an interval.

## Shapley values on an emulator

`shapley(predict, point, background, names)` splits an [emulator](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/emulators.html)’s prediction at `point`, minus its mean over a background sample, between the parameters. It computes the values exactly, by enumerating every subset of parameters (`2**d` evaluations, up to 16 parameters); the values add up to the difference:

```python
from modelly.explain import shapley

emulator = GaussianEmulator.from_results(results, space, ["attack"])
predict = emulator.select("attack").predict_unit
shapley(predict, point_in_unit_cube, background_units, names=list(space.dimensions))
```

An emulator makes each of the `2**d` evaluations cheap, so the explanation costs no model runs.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/assimilation.md -->

# Live data and data assimilation

A digital twin is a model that keeps up with the system it stands for: every time new data arrives, the model’s picture of the present is corrected, and its forecast starts again from there. `modelly.stream` (provisional, new in 1.4) does this for agent-based models in three parts:

- **sources** hand out observations as they arrive: a table in memory, a growing CSV file, an HTTP endpoint, an MQTT or a Kafka topic;
- an **observation operator** reads the same quantities from a model;
- an **ensemble** of replicates runs in lock step, and a **filter** keeps it close to the observations: a particle filter weights and resamples whole runs, an ensemble Kalman filter adjusts continuous parameters.

This page is a nowcasting tutorial. A synthetic “truth” run plays the world; we observe its daily case counts with noise and ask the filters what is happening now (the number currently infected, which nobody observes), what will happen next, and what the contact rate is. The code runs as is, top to bottom; the test suite runs it too (`tests/stream/test_assimilation_tutorial.py`).

## A small epidemic

```python
import math

import numpy as np

from modelly import Agent, Model
from modelly.scenarios import Scenario

class TownScenario(Scenario):
    people: int = 1000
    seeded: int = 10  # infected on day 0
    beta: float = 0.3  # infections per infected person and day, in a susceptible town
    recovery: float = 0.15  # chance of recovering each day

class Person(Agent):
    def __init__(self, model, infected):
        super().__init__(model)
        self.infected = infected
        self.recovered = False

class Town(Model):
    def __init__(self, scenario):
        super().__init__(scenario=scenario)
        self.beta = scenario.beta  # an attribute, so a filter can adjust it
        self.new_cases = 0
        for i in range(scenario.people):
            Person(self, infected=i < scenario.seeded)

    def step(self):
        people = list(self.agents)
        chance = 1 - math.exp(-self.beta * self.prevalence / len(people))
        draw = self.random.random
        self.new_cases = 0
        for person in people:
            if person.infected:
                if draw() < self.scenario.recovery:
                    person.infected, person.recovered = False, True
            elif not person.recovered and draw() < chance:
                person.infected = True
                self.new_cases += 1

    @property
    def prevalence(self):
        return sum(person.infected for person in self.agents)
```

The contact rate lives on the model as `self.beta`, read at every step: that is what lets a filter set it on a running replicate.

## The truth and its observations

The truth is one run with `beta = 0.45`. Each day we record the new cases plus Gaussian noise of standard deviation 3, and keep the true prevalence aside to score the filters later.

```python
DAYS = 50
NOISE = 3.0

truth = Town(TownScenario(rng=1, beta=0.45))
noise = np.random.default_rng(99)
records, true_prevalence = [], []
for day in range(1, DAYS + 1):
    truth.step()
    records.append({"time": day, "cases": truth.new_cases + noise.normal(0, NOISE)})
    true_prevalence.append(truth.prevalence)
```

```python
from modelly.stream import ObservationOperator, ReplaySource

observe = ObservationOperator(cases=lambda model: model.new_cases)
infected = ObservationOperator(infected=lambda model: model.prevalence)
```

`ReplaySource(records)` replays the table; in a live twin the same loop polls a `CSVSource` that a data pipeline appends to, an `HTTPSource`, or a broker (see [Live sources](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/assimilation.html#live-sources)). `observe` maps a model to what the world reports; `infected` reads what we want to know but never see.

## An ensemble

An `Ensemble` builds `n` replicates of one scenario, each with a seed spawned from the scenario’s (replicate `i` has the seed `Scenario.spawn_replications(n)[i]` would give it). We do not know the contact rate, so each replicate draws its own from a prior: anything between 0.2 and 0.8.

```python
from modelly.stream import Ensemble

REPLICATES = 40
prior = {"beta": lambda rng: rng.uniform(0.2, 0.8)}

filtered = Ensemble(Town, TownScenario(rng=2), REPLICATES, prior=prior)
free = Ensemble(Town, TownScenario(rng=2), REPLICATES, prior=prior)
```

`free` is the same ensemble left alone: it shows what the model knows without the data.

## Particle filter

The particle filter (Gordon, Salmond & Smith 1993) treats each replicate as a particle. At each observation it runs the replicates to the observation’s time, weights each by the likelihood of the observation (`ObservationOperator.log_likelihood`, Gaussian errors of standard deviation `sd`), and when the weights become too uneven it resamples: replicates with little weight are dropped and the likely ones duplicated. The test of unevenness is the effective sample size (ESS) `1 / sum(w**2)`; the filter resamples when it falls below `threshold * n` (half the ensemble by default), with systematic resampling (Douc & Cappé 2005). A duplicate is a checkpoint copy of the whole model, agents and events included, reseeded so that it goes its own way from the next draw on.

```python
from modelly.stream import ParticleFilter

pf = ParticleFilter(filtered, observe, sd=NOISE)

errors_filtered, errors_free = [], []
for observation in ReplaySource(records).poll():
    pf.assimilate(observation)
    free.advance(observation.time)
    now = true_prevalence[int(observation.time) - 1]
    errors_filtered.append(pf.estimate(infected)["infected"] - now)
    errors_free.append(free.values(infected).mean() - now)

def rmse(errors):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(np.square(errors))))

rmse_filtered, rmse_free = rmse(errors_filtered), rmse(errors_free)
```

`pf.estimate(infected)` is the weighted mean of the hidden prevalence across replicates: the nowcast. Over the 50 days its root mean square error is about 5 people for the filtered ensemble (`rmse_filtered`) against about 69 for the free one (`rmse_free`): the free replicates, with contact rates spread over the prior, peak at different times and heights, while the filter keeps the runs whose case counts agree with the data. `pf.history` has one row per observation (time, ESS, whether it resampled, and the log evidence `log p(y_t | y_<t)`, whose sum estimates the log marginal likelihood of the data); `pf.resamplings` counts the resamplings.

The replicates that survive also carry a contact rate (0.47 here):

```python
pf_beta = float(np.average([model.beta for model in filtered], weights=pf.weights))
```

A particle filter learns a fixed parameter only by keeping the replicates that drew a good one: after many resamplings few distinct values remain. The ensemble Kalman filter below is the tool for parameters.

## Bands now and ahead

`band` and `forecast` give the spread of any operator across the (weighted) replicates as a plain DataFrame, one row per time and quantity, with the mean and the quantiles you ask for (5%, 50% and 95% by default). This is what a plot, a report or Studio’s live view reads.

```python
now = pf.band(infected)
ahead = pf.forecast(DAYS + 14, infected, quantiles=(0.05, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.95))
```

```text
    time  quantity       mean  q0.05  q0.25  q0.5  q0.75  q0.95
0   50.0  infected  14.6    9.0   12.0  14.0   16.3   20.9
1   51.0  infected  12.6    8.0   10.0  13.0   14.0   19.0
...
14  64.0  infected   2.0    0.0    1.0   2.0    3.0    4.9
```

The forecast runs checkpoint copies of the replicates; the ensemble itself stays at day 50, ready for tomorrow’s observation. Weighted quantiles place each replicate’s weight at the midpoint of its step in the cumulative weights and interpolate (the Hazen definition when the weights are equal).

## Ensemble Kalman filter for the contact rate

The ensemble Kalman filter (Evensen 1994, 2003) treats the parameters as part of the state (state/parameter augmentation). At each observation it runs the replicates on, then shifts each replicate’s parameters by the Kalman gain estimated from the ensemble, `cov(beta, cases)` over `var(cases) + sd**2`, times the gap between a perturbed observation and what that replicate predicted. The perturbations (Burgers, van Leeuwen & Evensen 1998) keep the ensemble’s spread right; they come from a generator derived from the scenario’s seed, so the filter is deterministic.

```python
from modelly.stream import EnsembleKalmanFilter

ensemble = Ensemble(Town, TownScenario(rng=3), REPLICATES, prior=prior)
enkf = EnsembleKalmanFilter(
    ensemble,
    observe,
    sd=2 * NOISE,
    parameters=["beta"],
    bounds={"beta": (0.0, 2.0)},
)
enkf.run(ReplaySource(records))
beta_estimate = enkf.estimate()["beta"]
```

The estimate ends at 0.451 against the true 0.45, with a spread of 0.03 across replicates; `enkf.history` shows the mean and spread of `beta` after each observation. Two things are worth knowing:

- The filter adjusts attributes, not agents: an agent-based state (who is infected) is not a vector it can shift, so replicates whose epidemic is ahead or behind the truth push the parameter the wrong way for a while. A larger `sd` than the measurement noise, here twice it, makes the filter trust each observation less and absorbs that.
- `bounds` clips each parameter after every update, so a contact rate never goes negative.

## Reproducibility

For a seed, every result above is bit-identical from run to run, with the compiled core or the pure-Python one (`MODELLY_PURE_PYTHON=1`). The ensemble’s seeds are spawned from the scenario’s without changing it, the prior draws, resampling uniforms and Kalman perturbations come from seed sequences derived from it in domains of their own, and duplicate `slot` of the `g`-th resampling is reseeded from the key `(g, slot)`. The test suite checks this (`tests/stream/test_particle.py`). Replicates run one after the other in this process, in index order; parallel stepping would move models between processes at every observation and is not done.

Models with per-agent random streams (`agent_streams = True`) resample correctly, but a duplicate’s agents keep the streams of the agents they were copied from: only `model.random` and `model.rng` are reseeded.

## Live sources

Every source has `poll(until=None)`, which hands out the observations not seen yet, in time order, each once; a filter’s `run(source)` assimilates them. For a broker, install the extra and point the source at a topic whose messages are JSON records with a `time` field:

```python
# Not run here: it needs a broker.
from modelly.stream import KafkaSource, MQTTSource

# pip install "modelly-abm[mqtt]"
cases = MQTTSource("town/cases", host="broker.example.org")

# or: pip install "modelly-abm[kafka]"
cases = KafkaSource(
    "town-cases",
    config={"bootstrap.servers": "broker.example.org:9092", "group.id": "twin"},
)

def every_morning():
    pf.run(cases)  # yesterday's messages
    return pf.forecast(pf.ensemble.time + 14, infected)  # the next two weeks
```

Call `every_morning` from whatever schedules your jobs and publish the frame it returns; `close()` on a source releases its connection. `client=` and `consumer=` take a client you configured yourself (authentication, TLS), or a stand-in in tests. The code of this section needs a broker, so the test suite does not run it.

## References

- Gordon, N. J., Salmond, D. J. & Smith, A. F. M. (1993). Novel approach to nonlinear/non-Gaussian Bayesian state estimation. *IEE Proceedings F*, 140(2), 107-113.
- Douc, R. & Cappé, O. (2005). Comparison of resampling schemes for particle filtering. *Proceedings of the 4th International Symposium on Image and Signal Processing and Analysis*, 64-69.
- Evensen, G. (1994). Sequential data assimilation with a nonlinear quasi-geostrophic model using Monte Carlo methods to forecast error statistics. *Journal of Geophysical Research*, 99(C5), 10143-10162.
- Burgers, G., van Leeuwen, P. J. & Evensen, G. (1998). Analysis scheme in the ensemble Kalman filter. *Monthly Weather Review*, 126(6), 1719-1724.
- Evensen, G. (2003). The Ensemble Kalman Filter: theoretical formulation and practical implementation. *Ocean Dynamics*, 53(4), 343-367.

# Publishing a reproducible study

Four commands take a model from one run on your machine to an archive a reviewer can rerun with a single command. `modelly run` writes the outputs and a manifest that records everything that produced them; `modelly verify` reruns a manifest and compares; `modelly bundle` packs a run into one zip; `modelly odd` writes the skeleton of the model’s ODD protocol description. All four work the same on Windows, macOS and Linux, need no network, and use `git` only when it is installed.

```bash
modelly run model.py:Epidemic --scenario scenario.toml --steps 365 --out runs/
modelly verify runs/manifest.json          # outputs match
modelly bundle runs/ --out epidemic-study.zip
modelly odd model.py:Epidemic > ODD.md
```

## For authors

### Run and record

```bash
modelly run model.py:Epidemic --scenario scenario.toml --steps 365 --out runs/
```

The target is a file and a class (`path/to/model.py:Epidemic`) or a dotted module (`package.module:Epidemic`), as for [the profiler](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/profile.html). The scenario file is a flat TOML table; a `seed` key is the seed, every other key is a parameter. Parameters the model’s constructor takes by name go to it, the others to its `Scenario`.

```toml
seed = 42
beta = 0.3
gamma = 0.1
```

`--param key=value` adds or overrides a parameter, `--seed` overrides the seed, and `--input data.csv` (repeatable) records the hash of a data file the model reads. Without any seed a seed is drawn and recorded, so even that run can be repeated.

The run folder then holds one file per table the model’s `DataCollector` holds and `manifest.json`:

File

Content

model.parquet

model reporters, one row per collection

agents.parquet

agent reporters, with Step and AgentID

agents_<Class>.parquet

agent-type reporters

table_<name>.parquet

each DataCollector table

manifest.json

the record described below

Parquet needs `pyarrow`; without it, and for a table Parquet cannot hold (mixed objects), the file is UTF-8 CSV. The manifest says which.

### What the manifest records

The manifest is JSON with a `format` field, `modelly-manifest/1`. A reader accepts any manifest of its major version and refuses others with a clear error. Every path in it is relative to the manifest’s folder and written with forward slashes; every hash is `sha256:<hex>` over the file’s bytes.

Field

Content

target

the model class and where it was loaded from (file or module)

code

the code root (the model file’s folder), a hash of each model source file the run imported, one hash over all of them, and, inside a git working tree, the commit, whether the tree is dirty and a hash of the uncommitted diff

environment

Modelly’s version and build (compiled, pure or partial, with the state of each compiled core), Python version and implementation, platform, the installed versions of Modelly’s dependencies, and every installed package (packages)

scenario

the scenario file and its hash, the parameters given, and every value the model’s scenario held

run, seeds

the step count, the seed and the seed sequence it expanded to

inputs

each --input file and its hash

outputs

each table: file, format, hash, rows and columns

timing

wall-clock and CPU seconds of building and running the model

Cite the manifest, or its hash, next to every number in the paper it produced.

### Bundle for an archive

```bash
modelly bundle runs/ --out epidemic-study.zip
```

Entry

Content

manifest.json

the manifest, its paths rewritten for the archive

outputs

the recorded tables

llm-responses.jsonl.gz

the language-model replies of the run, when its model has a modelly.llm.Client

code/

the model’s source files

inputs/

the --input files and the scenario file

requirements.lock

name==version of every package installed at run time (pip install -r)

seeds.json

the seed, its seed sequence and the step count

.zenodo.json

Zenodo deposit metadata

CITATION.cff

a citation stub for the study that cites Modelly

Entries are sorted, stored uncompressed and carry a fixed date and mode, so the same run gives a byte-identical archive on any machine: the archive’s hash identifies the study. Bundling refuses a run whose outputs, code or recorded replies changed since `modelly run`.

A model that calls a language model through `modelly.llm` (a `Client` among its attributes, `self.llm` by convention) gets its replies recorded: `modelly run` exports every reply its clients hold to `llm-responses.jsonl.gz`, sorted by key, and the manifest names the file, its hash and the number of replies (`llm_cache`). The bundle packs the file, and `modelly verify` reruns the model with every client answering from it, read-only, whatever provider and cache the model builds: the study verifies with no network and no API key, and a call the record does not hold stops the rerun with `CacheMiss` instead of reaching the provider.

`.zenodo.json` and `CITATION.cff` hold `TODO` where only you know the answer: the title, the creators, the licence. Fill them in, then upload the zip to [Zenodo](https://zenodo.org/), which reads `.zenodo.json` and gives the deposit a DOI.

### Describe the model: ODD

```bash
modelly odd model.py:Epidemic > ODD.md
```

The [ODD protocol](https://doi.org/10.18564/jasss.4259) (Overview, Design concepts, Details) is the usual way to describe an agent-based model in a paper. `modelly odd` builds the model without running it and writes the seven elements, filled from the code where the code can say:

Element

Filled from

1. Purpose and patterns

the model class’s docstring

2. Entities, state variables and scales

each agent class, its Column declarations (Agent.column_specs()), its attributes and initial count; the model’s scalar attributes; its spaces and their dimensions

3. Process overview and scheduling

the statements of step() in order, and the agent methods it calls through do, shuffle_do or map

4. Design concepts

the eleven concepts; Observation lists the DataCollector reporters

5. Initialization

the scenario’s parameters, defaults and values, and the initial population

6. Input data

left to you

7. Submodels

each agent method, scheduled ones first, with its docstring

Every place that needs a human holds a `TODO` marker. `--scenario`, `--param` and `--seed` build the model as `modelly run` does.

## For reviewers

Unpack the archive, install the lock file in a fresh environment, and verify:

```bash
python -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.lock
.venv/bin/modelly verify manifest.json
```

On Windows the scripts are in `.venv\Scripts\` instead of `.venv/bin/`.

`modelly verify` reruns the model with the recorded parameters, seed and step count, then compares every output table with the recorded one, column by column and row by row. It prints `outputs match`, or the first difference:

```text
outputs differ: table 'model', column 'Gini', row 12: expected 0.4312, got 0.4415
```

The row is the 0-based position in the table. Before the rerun it checks the code files, the input files and the Modelly and Python versions against the record and prints what differs as notes on stderr; a note alone does not fail the check.

Numeric columns are compared with `numpy.isclose`; both tolerances are 0 by default, so the values must be identical. A study run on another processor or operating system may differ in the last bits of some floating-point results; `--rtol 1e-12` (or `--atol`) accepts that, and a report should say which tolerance it used.

Exit code

modelly verify

0

outputs match

1

an output differs (the first difference is printed)

2

bad command line, unreadable or unsupported manifest, or the model cannot be loaded

3

the model raised during the rerun (traceback on stderr)

`modelly run` and `modelly odd` exit 0 on success, 2 for a target or scenario that cannot be used and 3 when the model raises; `modelly bundle` exits 0 or 2.

## For journals

A submission that ships the bundle lets the editor check three things without reading code:

- the archive’s hash matches the one cited in the paper (the bundle is byte-deterministic);
- `modelly verify manifest.json` prints `outputs match` in a fresh environment built from `requirements.lock`;
- `ODD.md` and `CITATION.cff` are complete (no `TODO` left).

Rerunning needs neither the authors’ machine nor a network connection.

## Limits

- The code root is the folder of the model file. Source files outside it that the model imports (an installed package) are identified by `environment.packages`, not by hash.
- Hashes are over bytes: a checkout that converts line endings (git’s `autocrlf` on Windows) changes the hash of the source files, and `verify` notes it. The outputs are compared by value, so the check itself still passes.
- Parameters given as Python tuples are stored as JSON lists.
- A model that reads data files is rerun with the paths in its parameters; keep those paths relative to where the study is run, and record the files with `--input`.

From Python, the same steps are `modelly.provenance.run_study`, `verify`, `bundle` and `odd_markdown` ([API](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/provenance.html)).


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/model_cards.md -->

# Model cards

A model card is a short, standard description that goes with a model. It says what the model is for, what it must not be used for, which data it rests on, how it was validated, its known limits and the people decisions taken with it could affect. Every [zoo model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/index.html) has one, shown at the end of its page. `modelly card` writes one for your model, checks it, and keeps track of whether its validation still holds.

```bash
modelly card new model.py:Epidemic -o card.toml   # a skeleton from the code
modelly card stamp card.toml                      # run the validation tests; stamp on success
modelly card check card.toml                      # complete, and validated on this source?
modelly card show card.toml                       # as Markdown, for a README or a paper
```

## What a card holds

The card is a `card.toml` file next to the model:

```toml
schema = 1
name = "epidemic"
title = "Household epidemic"
model = "model.py:Epidemic"
summary = "An SIR epidemic in households, for comparing school closures."

intended_use = ["Comparing closure policies in relative terms, on stated contact rates."]
out_of_scope = ["Forecasting case counts: nothing is calibrated to a real outbreak."]
data = ["Household sizes from the 2021 census table bundled in data/households.csv."]
limits = ["Homogeneous mixing outside households; no age structure."]
ethics = ["Closure decisions affect children and parents unequally; show intervals."]
references = ["Ball, F. et al. (1997). Epidemics with two levels of mixing. Ann. Appl. Prob."]
sources = []

[[validation]]
check = "final size against the household final-size relation, three seeds"
test = "tests/test_validation.py::test_final_size"
```

Section

What goes in it

intended_use

the questions the model is built to answer, and for whom

out_of_scope

uses it is not fit for, and why

data

the data behind the defaults and inputs, or that there is none

validation

each check: the claim, and the pytest target that checks it

limits

assumptions, and the regimes where results stop being trustworthy

ethics

who could be affected by decisions taken with it, and how

references

the papers the model and its validation come from

sources

globs of the files the validation depends on; empty means the model’s module

`modelly card new` fills what the code tells (the name, the model target, a summary from the class docstring) and leaves a `TODO` in every section only you can write. A card with a `TODO`, an empty section or no validation test is incomplete.

## Stale validation

`modelly card stamp card.toml` runs the card’s validation tests with pytest, from the current folder (`--root` to choose another). When they pass, it writes a `[validated]` table: a digest of the model’s source files, the Modelly version and the date. When they fail, it prints pytest’s output and leaves the card as it was.

```toml
[validated]
source = "sha256:6a004228a934a9d59400cb7b31af0b0c140936de7e90e92b47c76c84d4f7f834"
modelly = "1.5.0"
date = "2026-11-03"
```

`modelly card check` recomputes the digest. If the model changed since the stamp, the card is **stale**: its validation passed on code that is no longer there, and the check fails until the tests are run again. The digest reads the files with LF line endings, so a Windows checkout gives the digest written on Linux or macOS. By default it covers the model class’s module; list more files in `sources` (`["src/epidemic/*.py"]`, relative to the card) when the model spans several.

`modelly card check --zoo` checks every zoo card. The test suite does the same, so a change to a zoo model fails the tests until its card is stamped again.

## In a project

Put `modelly card check` in your tests or your pre-commit configuration, next to `modelly lint`:

```yaml
- repo: https://github.com/RemiPelloux/Modelly
  rev: v1.5.0
  hooks:
    - id: modelly-lint
    - id: modelly-card-check
```

`modelly card show` prints the card as Markdown for a README, a supplement or the [provenance bundle](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/provenance.html) of a study. From Python:

```python
from modelly.card import card_markdown, problems, read_card

card = read_card("card.toml")
problems(card, ".")  # [] when complete and validated on this source
print(card_markdown(card))
```


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/hub.md -->

# The model hub

The hub is where Modelly models are published, found, installed and cited. It is a static index (`index.json`) in the public repository [RemiPelloux/modelly-hub](https://github.com/RemiPelloux/modelly-hub), served on GitHub Pages and changed by pull request after automatic checks. There is no server and no account: the index is a file, and the models’ archives live on Zenodo, which gives each one a DOI.

```bash
modelly hub search malaria                 # models matching every word, best first
modelly hub info within_host               # what it is for, its limits, how to cite it
modelly hub install within_host outbreak/  # a zoo model into a folder
modelly hub install seir_plus              # a package, into this environment
```

## Finding and installing

`modelly hub search` reads the public index and lists the models whose name, keywords, title, field or summary contain every word, best match first; `--field ecology` narrows the list. `modelly hub info NAME` shows the summary, the intended and out-of-scope uses from the [model card](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/model_cards.html), the Modelly versions the model supports and its DOI.

`modelly hub install NAME` first checks that the model supports the running Modelly. A zoo model is part of Modelly, so installing it writes its module and README into a folder, as `modelly zoo copy` does. A package is installed with pip into the running environment: from its archive when the entry has one, downloaded and checked against the sha256 the index records (and against its Sigstore signature, when the entry is signed and the `sigstore` package is installed) before pip sees it; otherwise from PyPI by its pinned requirement.

The index read last is cached, so search and info work offline. `MODELLY_HUB` (paths or URLs separated by `:`, or `;` on Windows) replaces the public index, for a private one or a local file; a package can add indexes through the `modelly.hub_sources` [plugin group](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/plugins.html).

## What an entry holds

```json
{
  "name": "within_host",
  "title": "Within-host and between-host epidemic",
  "field": "epidemiology",
  "summary": "Hosts infect each other; each infection is a viral ODE inside its host.",
  "version": "1.5.0",
  "kind": "zoo",
  "target": "modelly.zoo.within_host.model:WithinHost",
  "modelly": ">=1.5,<2",
  "source": {"requirement": "modelly-abm>=1.5,<2"},
  "card": {"intended_use": ["..."], "validation": ["..."], "validated": {"source": "sha256:..."}},
  "doi": "10.5281/zenodo.1234567",
  "signature": {"url": "...", "sha256": "...", "identity": "...", "issuer": "..."}
}
```

`kind` is `zoo` for a model shipped inside Modelly and `package` for one installed from an archive or PyPI; `source` says where its code is, with a `url` and its `sha256` for an archive. The card is the model’s card, validation stamp included.

## Publishing a model

A project is ready for the hub when it has:

- a `[tool.modelly.hub]` table in `pyproject.toml` with the model’s `target` (`package.module:Class`) and `field`;
- a [model card](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/model_cards.html) that is complete and validated on the current source (`modelly card stamp card.toml`);
- a wheel in `dist/` (`python -m build`).

```bash
modelly hub publish .                                  # hub-entry.json, nothing sent
modelly hub publish . --zenodo --sign you@example.org  # shows what would be sent and run
ZENODO_TOKEN=... modelly hub publish . --zenodo --no-dry-run              # the sandbox
ZENODO_TOKEN=... modelly hub publish . --zenodo --production --no-dry-run # a real DOI
```

Publishing is a dry run unless `--no-dry-run` is given: it writes `hub-entry.json` and prints every request it would send to Zenodo and the signing command it would run. With `--no-dry-run`, `--zenodo` creates a Zenodo deposition, uploads the wheel (and its signature), sets the metadata and publishes it, then records the DOI and the file’s URL and hash in the entry; the token comes from `ZENODO_TOKEN` and is never written anywhere. The sandbox (sandbox.zenodo.org) is the default, so a first publication can be tried without minting a real DOI; `--production` uses zenodo.org. `--sign IDENTITY` signs the wheel with Sigstore’s keyless signing, which opens a browser to log in as that identity; it needs `pip install sigstore`.

Then open a pull request adding the entry to `index.json` in [modelly-hub](https://github.com/RemiPelloux/modelly-hub). The repository’s checks run `modelly hub check` on the index: the schema, unique names, a Modelly specifier that parses, a complete card with a validation stamp, and the hash of every file the entry points to.

## Checking an index

```bash
modelly hub check index.json    # exit 1 and one line per problem
modelly hub zoo-index           # the index of the zoo models, as the hub lists them
```

From Python:

```python
from modelly.hub import install, load, search

hub = load()
for entry in search(hub, "epidemic", field="epidemiology"):
    print(entry.name, entry.summary)
install(hub.get("within_host"), "outbreak/")
```

# Performance and scale

How fast Modelly runs, how to make a model faster, and how to run it on more than one core without losing its results. Start with the audit to see where the time goes, then pick the step that fits your model.

- [Performance audit](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/performance.html) 
 how the core data structures were measured, what changed, and what is still on the table.
- [Vectorised step phases](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/vectorised_phases.html) 
 keep agents as objects and move the bulk of a step into arrays.
- [GPU arrays](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/gpu.html) 
 run column phases, cohort tables and cell-space operators on a GPU with one setting, and the same random numbers.
- [From laptop to cluster](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/distributed.html) 
 split one model across processes or machines, each worker holding one part of the space.
- [Determinism and platforms](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/determinism.html) 
 the same model, scenario and seed give the same run on Windows, macOS and Linux.

# Performance audit

This page records how Modelly’s core data structures were audited, what was measured, what changed, and what is still on the table. Numbers come from the benchmark configurations in `benchmarks/configurations.py` (“large” sizes) and from micro-benchmarks run on the same machine, best of several alternating before/after runs, measured in CPU time.

## The question

Modelly keeps one Python object per agent and stores collections of them in dictionaries: `AgentSet` was a `weakref.WeakKeyDictionary`, the model registry is a plain `dict`, and a cell holds a `list` of the agents standing on it. Is that the right shape, and where does the time go?

The short answer: the shapes are right for the operations a simulation performs (ordered membership, O(1) removal, stable shuffles), but four things around them were costing far more than the containers themselves. Those were fixed. The one structural change with a large constant factor (columnar agent state) is a roadmap item, not a patch.

## What the profile showed

Profiling the four benchmark models at their “large” configuration put the framework’s own overhead in five places, in order of cost:

1. **Empty-cell search on dense grids.** `Grid.select_random_empty_cell` tried 50 random cells, then fell back to `np.argwhere` over the whole grid, on every call. On a 99% full grid that is 14 µs per call, and a Schelling model at that density spends most of its step there.
1. **Per-agent data collection.** `DataCollector` built one closure call per reporter per agent, read `agent.model.time` through the observable descriptor for every agent, and called `deepcopy` on `None` and numpy scalars. About 390 ns per agent per step.
1. **Double-built views.** Every `select`, `shuffle`, `sort` and `groupby` on `model.agents` built a strong-reference set and then rebuilt it as a weak one. Counting fully grown grass in Wolf-Sheep built a 10,000-entry weak dictionary to call `len()` on it: 2.2 ms of a 17 ms step.
1. **`WeakKeyDictionary` overhead.** Its pure-Python wrapper and iteration guard made construction, membership and iteration about twice the cost of a dict keyed on `weakref.ref` objects.
1. **Unconditional property-layer writes.** Every agent move wrote the `empty` layer twice through a numpy scalar index, even when the cell’s emptiness had not changed.

Two defects came out of the same pass:

- `Cell.get_neighborhood` was decorated with `functools.cache` on a method, which is one global cache keyed on the cell. Discarding a grid left all its cells alive (10,000 cells after building and dropping fifteen 100x100 grids), and `connect()` on any cell cleared every cell’s cache in the process.
- `Grid.__init__` registered each grid’s private cell class in the global `copyreg` dispatch table, so a discarded grid stayed reachable from it.

## Columnar agent state

`modelly.core.columns` adds the one structural change with a large constant factor, as an opt-in. A `Column` declared on an agent class stores that attribute in a numpy array owned by the model (one table per concrete class, rows in insertion order, swap-remove on removal, the same scheme the continuous space uses for positions). The agent reads and writes its own row through a descriptor; the model reads everyone through `model.columns[Cls].<name>`, a zero-copy view.

Measured on the Boltzmann model with 10,000 agents, CPU time:

Boltzmann shuffle_do("step"), object loop

22.3 ms

21.0 ms

within noise

The last two rows are the trade-off. A column attribute is a plain `property` installed on the class (the interpreter inlines property getters, which it never does for a custom descriptor) that reads the agent’s row through a `memoryview`, so a read returns a Python `int`, `float` or `bool` rather than building a numpy scalar, and arithmetic on it is Python arithmetic. That took a read from 79 ns to 27 ns and `+= 1` from 171 ns to 72 ns (CPython 3.15), and a Boltzmann exchange step over 5,000 column agents from 5.0 ms to 3.1 ms, against 1.6 ms with plain attributes. Dtypes a `memoryview` cannot index (strings, objects, complex, datetimes) keep numpy indexing, and a write a `memoryview` rejects (a float into an int column) falls back to numpy’s own assignment, so values and errors are unchanged. A column is still not the place for a scratch value read in a tight loop. `where` is bounded by building the `AgentSet` from 10,000 objects, not by the mask.

Recording a column with `DataCollector` is a straight slice of the table when the reporters are all columns of one class and the collected agents are that class’s whole population; rows are then in table order rather than registration order (identical until an agent is removed).

## Continuous space

`get_agents_in_radius` compares one point against every position, so a model where every agent asks for its neighbours is O(n²) per step. `ContinuousSpace.neighbors_within(radius)` builds one `scipy.spatial.cKDTree` from the positions as they are now and queries it for the whole population in a single call; on a torus the tree is periodic. A model uses it once per step and gives every agent the same snapshot of positions (a simultaneous update).

Boids, per step

Per-agent scans

One tree per step

400 agents

12.1 ms

8.1 ms

2,000 agents

98.2 ms

41.7 ms

10,000 agents

about 2.5 s (extrapolated)

227 ms

What remains per agent is its own numpy arithmetic on a handful of neighbours.

## Agent lifecycle

Models with high birth and death rates (an insect population, an epidemic with recovery and reinfection) spend much of their step creating and removing agents, so the framework’s share of such a model is the lifecycle path. Measured as a bare `Agent(model)` followed by `agent.remove()`, and as the notebook agent below inside its real model:

Birth + death

Mesa 2.3

Modelly, first audit

Modelly now

bare agent, bare model

372 ns

861 ns

421 ns

agent in model.agents (liveness check)

35 ns

160 ns

35 ns

What changed, in order: the `emit` decorator’s wrapper checks for listeners inline and calls `notify` only when someone can hear; `remove()` uses `try/except` instead of a `contextlib.suppress` context manager (about 300 ns); the strong registry is a `dict` subclass, so membership, length and the registry writes run in C; `Agent.__init__` and `Agent.remove` inline the registration when the model keeps the default `register_agent` and `deregister_agent` (a flag computed per class, with a test that an override is still honoured); the cooperative `super().__init__()` is skipped for plain subclasses; the listener test is four attribute reads with no dict lookups. A three-day bisect at 2,800 agents on the medfly model below puts the current path at 11.4 ms against 11.7 ms for a stripped-down path with none of Modelly’s features and 11.2 ms for Mesa 2.3: the lifecycle is at parity.

### FastRandom

A quarter to a third of an agent-based model’s time is the standard library’s `random`, whose `randint`, `choice`, `shuffle` and `sample` are Python loops calling `_randbelow` per draw. `modelly.FastRandom` reimplements the four with the rejection loop written inline, making the same `getrandbits` calls in the same order, so a seed gives exactly the same numbers as `random.Random` (tested across seeds, sizes and both `sample` code paths). `model.random` is a `FastRandom`. On CPython 3.15, against a standard library that has itself become cheaper, per call:

Draw

Faster than random.Random by

How

randint(6, 11)

3 to 4%

type(x) is int (specialised by the interpreter) instead of two operator.index calls; bit length from a 4,096-entry table instead of int.bit_length()

choice

11 to 12%

the same table

sample(list of 3,000, 3)

20 to 26%

the table, and the Sequence ABC check skipped for list, tuple and range

shuffle(3,000)

15 to 27%

lists over 64 elements are walked in runs of constant bit length, so the inner loop has no lookup at all

Every change makes the same `getrandbits` calls in the same order; a test shuffles every length from 0 to 139 and lengths around each power of two and compares with the standard library element for element, and then compares the next draw.

**The compiled core.** Pure Python had nothing left to remove: what remained of a draw was the Python function call around a C call. `modelly/_native/fastrng.c` implements `randint`, `choice`, `shuffle`, `sample` and `_randbelow` in C as “fastcall” methods (the cheapest call CPython has). The type extends `_random.Random` and generates words from the same Mersenne Twister state the base class uses, so `random()`, `gauss`, `getrandbits`, `seed` and `getstate` from the standard library and the compiled methods consume one stream exactly as `random.Random` does; the stdlib’s `sample` set-size rule and both of its code paths are reproduced draw for draw. Anything outside the fast paths (ranges of 2³² or more, non-int arguments, sequences that are not lists or tuples, `counts=`) goes to the standard library’s own code, which reads the same state. At import a self-test compares a mixed sequence of draws with `random.Random`; on any mismatch, without a compiler, or with `MODELLY_PURE_PYTHON=1`, `FastRandom` is the pure-Python `PyFastRandom` above. Per call:

Draw

random.Random

PyFastRandom

compiled FastRandom

randint(6, 11)

193 ns

185 ns

59 ns

choice(list of 3,000)

190 ns

168 ns

72 ns

shuffle(3,000), per element

206 ns

156 ns

38 ns

Assembly would not beat this: generating a word is 2 to 3 ns of C that compilers already turn into near-optimal code, and the rest is the interpreter’s call, which no language can avoid. Platform wheels carry the compiled modules (Linux glibc and musl on x86-64 and ARM64, macOS, Windows x86-64 and ARM64, the GIL and the free-threaded interpreters); other platforms install the pure wheel.

A second compiled module, `modelly/_native/fastloop.c`, runs `do` and `shuffle_do` on the model’s agent registries and the breadth-first walk behind `Cell.get_neighborhood`. Each loop has an identical pure-Python twin in `modelly/_native/loops.py`, used when the module is not built or `MODELLY_PURE_PYTHON=1` is set; `tests/native` checks the two against each other.

A third, `modelly/_native/fastcell.c`, is the setter of `CellAgent.cell`: add to the new cell (capacity check, `CellFullException`), remove from the old one (`AgentMissingException` chained from the `ValueError`), and write `empty` only on a transition, through the normal attribute protocol so a grid’s property-layer `empty` still updates. It runs `Cell.add_agent` and `remove_agent` inline only when the cell’s type resolves them to `Cell`’s own (checked per type, revalidated on CPython’s type version tag, so an override or a later patch is called instead), and reads the `_agents` and `capacity` slots at their offsets. Its twin is `py_set_cell` in `modelly/_native/cells.py`. A first version that used plain attribute lookups was no faster than Python 3.15’s specialised bytecode; the slot reads are what made the difference.

Measured on Python 3.15, one pinned core (`nice taskset -c 5`) of a shared 16-core laptop at load 3 to 4, CPU time, base (`main`) and new alternating in separate processes, identical results checked every round:

### Compiled `select` and `agg`

A fourth module, `modelly/_native/fastset.c`, runs the loops behind `AgentSet.select`, `get` and `agg`, and the two loops every weak `AgentSet` view is made of. `keep_if` gains least: the cost is the call of the filter, and Python 3.15 calls a Python function from its own bytecode about as cheaply as C can. The playbooks barely use `select` or `agg` (they are written with column phases), so they show no change: every Modelly variant, size `large`, `main` and this branch alternating in fresh pinned interpreters for 6 rounds, had a median ratio between 0.89 and 1.02 with every interquartile range containing 1.0, and the same results bit for bit on three seeds, compiled and pure.

### Compiled event heap

Every scheduled event (and every step, which is an event of the default schedule) went through `heapq` on `Event` objects, so each push and pop called `Event.__lt__`, a Python method, about log2(n) times. A fifth module, `modelly/_native/fastevents.c`, holds the event list’s heap: `EventHeap` runs `heapq`’s own sift steps, in the same order, on entries that carry the event’s time, priority and unique id, read once when it is pushed and compared as C numbers. That gives exactly what `Event.__lt__` gives for an `Event` whose time is a float, a numpy `float64` or an int of magnitude at most 2^53 (all exact as doubles); a subclass of `Event`, a `Fraction` time or a larger int is compared by calling `<` on the events, as `heapq` does. The twin, `PyEventHeap` in `modelly/_native/events.py`, is the previous list with `heapq`; `tests/native/test_event_heap.py` runs both on random schedules (ties, numpy times, huge ints, fractions, NaN, subclasses, cancellations, compactions) and checks every pop and the whole heap array after every operation. Both pickle through `EventList` as the events in heap order, the format of 1.3, so a checkpoint written with the compiled heap resumes under `MODELLY_PURE_PYTHON=1` and the reverse (`tests/native/test_event_heap_pickle.py`, wolf-sheep resumed bit for bit). The keys are read at push: an event’s time and priority must not change while it is on a list, which they never could without breaking the heap.

Two changes around it, both in Python and both in the twin too: time advance asks the heap for the next event *if it is due* (`pop_due`) instead of popping the first future event and pushing it back, and `schedule_event` builds one weak reference to the callback instead of two (a `WeakMethod` costs about 0.5 µs); the event still refuses a callback that dies with the call.

Measured locally against the 1.3.3 release (built from its tag with the same compiler and dependencies), both sides in that environment’s interpreter, CPU time in fresh interpreters, the two alternating, pinned with `taskset -c 3` on a shared 16-core laptop, every round’s results hashed and compared (identical in every round):

Wolf-sheep schedules one regrowth event per patch eaten (several hundred a step); the rest of its step is the agents’ own Python, so the event list is a small share of it and the gain is 5%: measurable (every one of 15 rounds faster), not large. The predator-prey playbook regrows its grass as a column and schedules no event but the step, so it has nothing for the heap to speed up (see the release comparison below).

### Compiled column gather

A `DataCollector` attribute reporter, `AgentSet.get` and `agg` read one attribute per agent through `operator.attrgetter`. For a `Column` attribute that calls its Python getter from C, a frame per agent, unless the collected agents are exactly one class’s whole table (then the column is sliced). `fastset.attr_values` now runs the getter’s three reads itself, `agent._column_table._views[position][agent._column_row]`, for any agent whose class’s attribute is a Column property (the getter carries its position), caching each class’s position (revalidated on the class’s version tag) and its table’s view; any error runs the getter, which raises what it raises (`ColumnMissingError` for a removed agent). Plain attributes are read as before. The collector uses it one attribute at a time, mixed reporter sets included; the rows are identical (`tests/native/test_column_gather.py`, every dtype, interleaved classes, overridden and replaced properties, grown tables).

### Profile-guided optimisation

`benchmarks/pgo.py` builds the compiled modules twice from the same source: once with the build’s flags (-O3), once with GCC 16’s profile-guided optimisation (-fprofile-generate, a training run of every Modelly playbook at size small, the 17 core operations and an event-heavy schedule, `benchmarks/pgo_training.py`, then -fprofile-use), and times every Modelly playbook variant at size large in the two, paired as `modelly bench --against` does (7 rounds, pinned to core 3, results identical in every round, measured locally). The medians fall on both sides of 1 (0.993 to 1.003) and the interquartile ranges are within 1.5% of it, two of them entirely below 1 by at most 0.7% and one entirely above it by at most 0.5%: no playbook is measurably faster. What the compiled modules do per call is a handful of C operations around interpreter calls, and the branches a profile could reorder are already the predictable ones. The build does not use a profile, and `hatch_build.py` has no PGO option. Clang (which needs `llvm-profdata merge` between the two steps) and MSVC (`/GL` with `/LTCG:PGINSTRUMENT` and `/LTCG:PGOPTIMIZE`) were not tried: this machine has no MSVC, and the measurement above gives no reason to expect a different answer.

No variant is slower by the guard’s criterion; the largest median, Sugarscape’s 1.004, has its whole interquartile range within 1%. The playbooks are written with column phases and schedule no event but the step, so the event heap and the column gather have nothing to speed up in them; predator-prey in particular regrows its grass as a column, so it is not faster (the event-heavy wolf-sheep example above is). An earlier session that ran the checkout in a development interpreter with pyarrow installed measured the grid epidemic 2 to 4% slower; split into build and run, the difference was all in the run’s garbage collection, and with both sides in one interpreter it is 0.99 (20 rounds, IQR 0.96 to 1.03). That is why `--against` now runs both sides in the release environment’s interpreter.

The performance guard (`python -m modelly.dev perf`, 17 core operations, measured locally) finds no operation slower than 1.3.3: medians from 0.983 (creating and removing agents with columns) to 1.028 (creating and removing plain agents, IQR 0.994 to 1.034); the two neighbourhood walks read 1.016 and 1.019 with lower quartiles of 1.002 and 1.004, under the guard’s 3% threshold and on code this release does not change; `schedule+run event` reads 0.993, since its 500 events at distinct times make every heap comparison a single step.

Measured on Linux only: Windows and macOS could not be measured on this machine, so the claim “no playbook slower than 1.3.3” holds for Linux x86-64 and is untested elsewhere.

### Memory-mapped columns

`modelly.core.storage` decides where a table’s columns live. `InMemory` is the default and what 1.3 did. `MemoryMapped(directory)` keeps every numeric column in a `numpy.memmap` file in a fresh folder under `directory`; the operating system pages rows in and out, so a table can hold more rows than fit in memory, and a column that doubles is grown by extending its file, without copying the rows already written. Opt in with `model.columns.storage = MemoryMapped(...)` before the first agent of a class is created, or `CohortTable(rng, storage=MemoryMapped(...), ...)`. The folder is deleted by `close()`, at the end of a `with` block, or when the storage is garbage-collected. Object columns cannot be mapped and stay in memory. A checkpoint (or any pickle) carries the rows, not the file names, and loading it copies them into a new folder under the same directory; since a checkpoint is built in memory, saving and loading one needs as much memory as its columns. `tests/core/test_storage.py` checks that a memory-mapped run holds the same rows as an in-memory one (agents growing past several doublings, and a cohort table of three million rows on disk), that checkpoints resume bit for bit in a new folder, and that the folder goes.

A row of a `ColumnTable` belongs to an `Agent` object, which stays in memory (225 bytes with its registry entries, “Memory per agent” below, before its row attributes), so a hundred million agents need over 22 GB for the objects alone, whatever the columns’ storage. A hundred million rows do fit as a `CohortTable`, rows without objects. `benchmarks/large_columns.py` builds one (count, stage, age, patch and a float trait per row, 19 bytes) and runs a stage-structured life cycle on it: binomial thinning by stage, ageing, stage transitions and offspring draws.

The run, measured locally on v1.4.2 (one JSON per run in `paper/data/large_columns/`): 100 million rows (2.55 GB of columns at the table’s capacity of 2^27 rows), three steps, each in its own systemd scope with a hard limit and no swap (`systemd-run --user --scope -p MemoryMax=... -p MemorySwapMax=0`); “cgroup peak” is the scope’s `memory.peak`, which counts the mapped file pages it holds as well as anonymous memory. Results identical across the runs that finished (3,815,571,746 individuals, the same offspring count).

A hundred million rows run well inside 16 GB either way; the file-backed table costs 10 to 15% per step here (the page cache sat on a fast SSD and the whole file fit in memory). Under a limit smaller than the run needs in memory, the memory-mapped table finishes and the in-memory one is killed. The temporaries of a step (a 100-million-element survival array and the binomial draws, 800 MB each) stay in memory whatever the storage. A table whose columns exceed the machine’s memory follows the same path, at the disk’s speed.

### Free-threaded CPython

All four modules load on free-threaded CPython (wheels for 3.14t and 3.15t; tested on 3.15t) and declare `Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED`, so importing Modelly leaves the GIL off; before 1.3 they refused to load and the pure twins ran instead. What each one does to be safe:

- `fastrng`: every draw holds the generator’s per-object critical section, the lock `_random.Random`’s own methods take, so a draw from C and a `random()` from the standard library never interleave on one state. A list being shuffled, sampled or chosen from is locked with it. Draws from one generator shared by threads are atomic (tested: the threads together draw exactly the serial sequence, in some order), but which thread gets which number depends on scheduling: give each thread its own model, or its own generator.
- `fastloop`: list items are read as new references; a cell’s `connections` dict is walked inside its critical section.
- `fastcell`: the per-type layout cache is per thread; `bind()` and its readers share one `PyMutex`; slots are read through `getattr` and `list.remove` runs itself, since both take the object’s lock.
- `fastset`: list items are read as new references; weak-reference keys are snapshotted with `PyDict_Keys`, which locks the dict.

GIL builds compile the same code with the locks as empty blocks (`modelly/_native/ftcompat.h`); paired micro-benchmarks of `shuffle`, `randint`, `choice`, `sample`, the cell move, `do` and the neighbourhood walk against `main` were within noise (medians 0.92 to 0.98). On CPython 3.15t (Linux x86-64) the whole suite passes with the compiled modules, and `tests/native/test_threads.py` (four threads; shared draws, independent replicates on threads equal to serial runs, agents moved across a shared grid, `select` and `agg` while another thread adds and removes agents) passed 25 repeated runs at ten times its default rounds. ThreadSanitizer was not run: it needs an instrumented interpreter.

`fastevents` (1.4) holds the heap’s critical section in every method and declares `Py_MOD_GIL_NOT_USED`; the column gather in `fastset` reads items as new references and type version tags with relaxed loads. Both were built and tested on the GIL interpreter only: the machine they were written on has no free-threaded CPython, so the 3.15t build of these two is untested.

No reduction was kept in 1.3 so far. `__slots__` for the framework attributes (`model`, `unique_id`) was measured and gives nothing on Python 3.13 and later: an instance without slots already stores its attributes inline at 8 bytes each, exactly what a slot costs (88 bytes for a two-attribute object either way, 112 with three more attributes in a subclass), while it would forbid a subclass from relying on `Agent.__dict__` semantics. The two registry entries are the next target; a more compact registry must keep iteration order, membership in C and the removal semantics, so it is a design change rather than a patch.

### No regression from release to release

Every release is benchmarked against the previous published one before it is tagged: the previous wheel from PyPI against the new wheel built by the release workflow (same toolchain), installed with identical dependencies, on one machine. Three measurements, each in paired, alternating runs so that load and frequency drift hit both versions alike:

- **Core operations** (17, including Column reads, agent removal with columns, cell moves and neighbourhood walks): two persistent processes pinned to one core, short bursts in ABBA order, over several sessions with the starting version swapped; a numpy-only control must read 1.00.
- **The playbooks** (13 Modelly variants): the same seeds in two persistent processes, ABBA, CPU time of the steps, results compared seed by seed.
- **A research notebook** (a 576-season factorial at 1/30 scale): its seasons in chunks alternating between the two versions, records compared chunk by chunk.

1.3.1 against 1.2.0 (median ratio of CPU time, 1.3.1 / 1.2.0; below 1 is faster):

Between releases, a pre-commit hook (`python -m modelly.dev install-hooks`) refuses any commit that makes one of 17 core operations more than 3% slower than the last release, in about ten seconds; CONTRIBUTING.md describes it.

1.3.0 had two small regressions that this check found after its release: a Column read was about 2.5% slower (the getter kept the column’s name for a clearer error) and, on regular builds, the neighbourhood walk and the cell move paid for free-threading safety they do not need. 1.3.1 removes both; the free-threaded builds keep their safe paths.

### How we evaluate against other frameworks

Micro-benchmarks say where time goes; whether a framework is faster for a researcher is decided on a real model. The method we use, and recommend for any comparison:

1. **Same model, same seeds.** Take a research notebook written for the other framework and migrate it with `python -m modelly.migrate`, changing nothing but the framework API. Seed both from the same value so the random streams match.
1. **Prove equivalence before timing.** Run both to completion and compare every output table by checksum. Only bit-identical outputs make the timings comparable; a migration that changes the activation order or the random stream is a different model.
1. **Time CPU, pinned, alternating.** Wall-clock on a shared machine swings by 2x; CPU time of the experiment cell, in-process, pinned to one core, with the two frameworks alternating for at least three rounds, is stable to a few percent. Keep every round, not only the best.
1. **Profile both and compare shares.** The profiler inflates call-heavy code, so compare each function’s share of its own run, and attribute the remainder by bisection: swap one piece for a minimal stand-in and measure again.

Applied to a medfly population model written for Mesa 2.3 (21 cells, a 576-season factorial experiment, bit-identical output CSVs), the comparison went through two stages.

**Stage one: the model’s own code.** The profile put 68% of the time in the notebook’s model code, 25% in `random` and 7% in Modelly. Three changes to the model, identical in both notebooks and preserving the random stream (an early exit in the fruit status update placed after its random draw, `len(self.slots) < capacity` instead of two property hops, and re-filtering the free-fruit pool only on days when fruits were removed) cut the experiment cell by 3x on both frameworks: Modelly 30 s to 9.4 s, Mesa 26 s to 7.8 s, same checksums.

A third round of model-code changes, again identical on both sides and stream-preserving (an incremental rot score per fruit instead of a daily loop over its slots, an inlined capacity test in the egg-laying loop, `FastRandom` seeding on the Modelly side), took the experiment cell from 14.1 s to 11.2 s on Modelly and from 13.3 s to 11.0 s on Mesa, same checksums. Dispatching the 576 independent seasons of the factorial to a forked process pool, records reassembled in the original order so the CSV is identical, brings the cell to 1.3 to 1.6 s of wall-clock on eight workers: the largest practical gain on this workload, and the one that needs no re-validation of the model.

**Stage two: the framework.** Whole-cell rounds swing by up to 2x on a shared machine, so the comparison moved to a finer instrument: two persistent processes, one per framework, pinned to the same core, running the 576 seasons in 48 chunks with the order alternating, each chunk’s records hashed and compared (no mismatch in any run). Measured that way, the gap before this round was 2.1%, and none of it was in the model’s arithmetic:

1. **The random draws.** `FastRandom.randint` had become 4% *slower* than the standard library on CPython 3.15, which now inlines Python-to-Python calls well; the `operator.index` calls were the difference. The table above lists the fixes; this was the largest item.
1. **Agent birth and death.** One model flag (`_quiet`: default registry and nobody listening) replaces four attribute reads, and one class flag (`_extra_hooks`: columns or datasets) replaces two. The flag only ever turns false (on `observe`, `observe_class`, a batch, a suppress, or an overridden `register_agent`), so a stale value can only send an agent down the slower, still correct path. Creation went from 295 ns to 225 ns at the notebook’s live population, against 281 ns for Mesa.
1. **The garbage collector.** About 11% of the run on both frameworks. Collecting identical garbage costs the same on both (78 to 83 ms per 240,000 objects); what differs is where collections fall relative to season boundaries, which depends on allocation counts. With the collection threshold set equally on both sides, Modelly is ahead at four of five values and behind at one. We report the default threshold. `gc.freeze()` after the imports would have given Modelly another 2.4%; applied to both sides it gives nothing, so it is a process setting rather than an engine property, and Modelly does not do it.

A model written agent by agent runs at Mesa’s speed: 6% faster with the compiled generator, about 2% slower with the standard library’s.

Models that spend most of their time in framework calls gain more from the same treatment. Two public playbooks without a Mesa 2 grid, migrated from Mesa 2.3 by the codemod and the steps it reports (`benchmarks/migrated_mesa2/`), run at 0.21 (insects) and 0.37 (Boltzmann wealth) of Mesa 2.3’s CPU time, bit-identical. Five Mesa 3.5 playbooks migrated by the codemod alone (`benchmarks/migrated_mesa3/`) run at 0.44 (Boltzmann wealth), 0.53 (insects), 0.73 (grid epidemic), 0.85 (network) and 0.91 (Schelling) of Mesa 3.5’s CPU time (measured on v1.4.2). They are not bit-identical, since Modelly derives `model.random` from the seed differently, but over 100 seeds 24 of their 26 statistics are equivalent within half a standard deviation and no test is significant after a Holm correction. Flocking (Mesa’s legacy `ContinuousSpace`) and predator-prey and Sugarscape (Mesa 3.5’s `PropertyLayer`) do not migrate by the codemod alone. Timings and agreement: `paper/data/migrated.json`, ten alternating rounds, pinned.

Measured and rejected on this workload: a `shuffle` that draws its random words in one call (it reproduces the permutation but leaves the stream in a different place for the next draw, and is 3x slower); a cheaper `Model` construction (it is 18 µs; 576 of them are 10 ms).

### The playbooks: same model, each framework’s own idiom

The migration above answers “what does identical code cost”. The second question is what each framework lets a modeller write. `benchmarks/playbooks/` holds eight models, each implemented for Mesa 2.3 with per-agent methods on `MultiGrid`, `SingleGrid`, `ContinuousSpace` and `NetworkGrid`, for the current Mesa 3.5 with its cell spaces (`OrthogonalMooreGrid`, `CellAgent`, `Network`), its experimental continuous space and `AgentSet.shuffle_do`, as in Mesa’s own examples, and for Modelly with `Column` state, `CellIndex` (integer rows for the cells of any discrete space plus their sparse adjacency), `Occupancy` / `claim`, `pairs_within` / `move_all`, `ColumnTable.thin` and the `DataCollector` column reporters. The rules for a fair comparison, enforced by the runner:

1. Same model: same rules, same phase order (synchronous, or one agent at a time in a random order), same parameters, same graph and initial positions where seeds can be shared; the Mesa side uses numpy where a Mesa modeller would.
1. Agreement in distribution, checked: every implementation runs the same seeds and each summary statistic is compared with the Mesa reference by Welch’s t-test (flagged below 0.01). The implementations draw their random numbers in different orders, so the outputs differ run by run and must agree in law; `vectorised_phases.md` states why each vectorised phase has the law of its per-agent loop.
1. Determinism, checked: the first seed runs twice per implementation. (This check caught the Mesa side being unseeded when the seed was passed positionally: Mesa 2.3 reads it from the keyword arguments in `Model.__new__`.)
1. CPU time of a fresh interpreter per run, build and steps timed separately, pinned to one core, implementations alternating over ten rounds, every round reported.

The Mesa 3.5 implementations agree with Mesa 2.3’s: over 100 paired seeds all 40 summary statistics are equivalent within half a standard deviation, and no test falls below 5% (`paper/data/agreement_small_baselines_summary.json`, which also holds the mesa-frames variants); flocking, the network and the insects draw the same numbers in the same order and reproduce Mesa 2.3 run for run. Where a phase searches cells one agent at a time (Sugarscape’s foragers), every implementation uses the same single-pass loop. Median CPU seconds of the steps at the large size, all variants in one session, ten rounds, pinned to a performance core (CPU 2, performance governor, turbo disabled, so the core runs at its fixed 1.9 GHz base frequency; every per-round ratio is within 19% of its median, and a second session agrees with this one within 4% on every ratio, `paper/data/playbooks_session1/`). Measured on v1.4.2’s code. Absolute seconds are longer than with turbo; the ratios are the point. “Mesa 3.5 + numpy” (`mesa3np_model.py`, three playbooks) is the hand-vectorised Mesa baseline: a `mesa.Model` that holds the population as numpy arrays over Mesa’s grid and property layers, with no `Agent` objects:
