The “cell lists” column is the same model with Mesa’s data structure, every cell holding the list of its agents, so movement and predation stay per-agent loops: 1.5 to 2.4x over Mesa 2.3 on the epidemic and predator-prey (1.3 to 14x over Mesa 2.3 and 1.3 to 11x over Mesa 3.5 across its four playbooks). The gap opens when the cell becomes a column of rows: the random walk is one `random_neighbor` call over the grid’s CSR adjacency, the exposure count a `bincount`, the predation a vectorised matching with the law of the shuffled sequential rule. Construction is reported separately (a 180x180 Moore grid builds in 0.11 s, a 30,000-node network in 0.4 s, against milliseconds for Mesa 2.3’s lazy structures, and about the same for Mesa 3.5’s cell spaces); the build+run speed-ups over Mesa 2.3 in the results are correspondingly lower (20x, 5.2x, 32x, 10x, 5.3x, 224x, 9.1x, 5.9x, 4.0x). Mesa 3.5 is itself faster than Mesa 2.3 on five playbooks (1.3x to 3.1x), about as fast on Sugarscape (1.03x) and flocking (1.00x; both use `mesa.space.ContinuousSpace`, which runs it 1.6x faster than Mesa 3.5’s experimental continuous space) and slower on predator-prey (0.91x). On flocking, part of Modelly’s gain is the neighbour search: Mesa 3.5 with one periodic `scipy.spatial.cKDTree` per step (`flocking/mesa3kd_model.py`, 9.20 s, the same statistics as Mesa 3.5 on 110 seeds, `paper/data/flocking_kdtree.json`) runs 2.7x faster than Mesa 3.5’s own search, and Modelly’s columns are 12x faster again. mesa-frames (development branch, commit `ef92326`, polars 2.0 on one thread) is 2.1x to 6.1x faster than Mesa 2.3 on three of its four playbooks and slower on Sugarscape (0.70x); Modelly columns are 3.0x to 9.6x faster than mesa-frames. One thread is mesa-frames’ better setting on the cores a run would get: pinned to the four performance cores, four polars threads are slower than one on all four workloads, five alternating rounds (grid epidemic 1.98 s against 1.69 s, Schelling 3.41 s against 2.86 s, Boltzmann wealth 2.14 s against 1.82 s, Sugarscape 5.46 s against 3.78 s; `paper/data/frames_threads_pinned.json`). With all 16 threads, unpinned, single runs were slower on three workloads and 1.4x faster on Schelling (2.05 s against 2.84 s; `paper/data/frames_threads.json`).

The hand-vectorised Mesa 3.5 baseline is faster than Modelly’s columns: 4.5x on the epidemic, 1.8x on Schelling, 2.7x on Boltzmann wealth; the gap shrinks with the population on the epidemic and Schelling’s model (1.6x and 1.0x at ten times the timed size, `paper/scripts/sizes.py`). It is the same arithmetic without the agents: Modelly keeps an `Agent` per individual, with its identity, its `step()` and the agent-set API, and that bookkeeping is the difference. It agrees with Mesa 2.3 in distribution (`paper/data/agreement_small_mesa3np_summary.json`; one statistic, Schelling’s segregation index, differs by 0.24 sd, p = 0.045 after Holm).

The last three playbooks have phases that are sequential by nature, and each still has an exact array form (`vectorised_phases.md`, §7 to §9). Schelling’s unhappy residents move one at a time to random empty cells; since every move takes one empty cell and frees one, the pool of empty cells keeps its size, and all the moves become one sort over slots drawn up front. In the Boltzmann exchange, who gives in the random order is the least fixed point of a monotone map over the drawn order and partners, reached in a few array passes; the `DataCollector` slices the wealth column instead of visiting agents. In Sugarscape the foragers’ choices depend on the cells taken before their turn, so the walk to the first free cell stays a loop, but everything it reads (the visible cells, their sugar, the head of each forager’s ranking) is one array pass, and eating and starving move after the loop without changing the law. Rankings are not sorted up front: the loop takes a forager’s head when it is free and sorts the ranking only when that cell is not free at its turn (under a third of the turns). That gives the same runs, bit for bit, as sorting every ranking, and is 2.5x faster (median of 5 paired runs, range 1.9 to 2.6x, thread CPU time, large size, a loaded machine). Schelling’s “cell lists” variant is far ahead of Mesa 2.3 (14x) because its happiness count, three quarters of Mesa’s run, is an array pass even there; Mesa’s move to a random empty cell already runs in constant expected time. Sugarscape’s is not (1.3x): it runs the same single-pass search as both Mesa versions. (An earlier Mesa 2.3 Sugarscape built a whole-grid mask per forager with `select_cells`; the cached neighbourhood gives the same runs, bit for bit, 4 to 5x faster, and is what Mesa’s own example does.)

The insect playbook is a stage-structured population under sterile releases, an original model with the dynamics of the medfly workload (thousands of eggs a day, stage-specific mortality, density-dependent larval survival). Agent creation is at parity, so the individual-level gap is the per-agent loop only (5.7x over Mesa 2.3, 3.2x over Mesa 3.5). The cohort variant represents every insect in the same (stage, age, sex) class as one row and thins it with a binomial draw; it has the same law as the individual model (the agreement table shows it) and runs in 11 ms. Absolute times vary by up to 2x between sessions on a shared machine; the ratios much less.

## GPU backend

The `modelly-gpu` variant of the grid epidemic (`benchmarks/playbooks/grid_epidemic/modelly_gpu.py`) is the column variant `modelly` with its step on CuPy: the same agents and grid, the columns as a `DeviceTable`, the adjacency as a `DeviceCellIndex`, the draws from a `PhiloxStream` ([GPU arrays](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/gpu.html)). Measured by `benchmarks/playbooks/gpu_speedup.py` at 10 million agents on a 1000 x 1000 torus (ten agents per cell; the playbook’s density would need 16 million Python cell objects), 60 steps, seed 1. Raw numbers: `benchmarks/playbooks/results/gpu_speedup.json` (the same file as `paper/data/gpu_speedup.json`), measured on v1.4.2’s code.

**Machine.** A laptop: Intel Core Ultra 7 356H, 30 GB, and an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5050 Laptop GPU (8 GB, driver 615.78, CUDA runtime 13.2 from the `cupy-cuda13x` 14.2.0 wheel); numpy 2.5.4. Shared with other jobs: every run was started through a guard that lets one heavy job run at a time, but the load from lighter work was not controlled and the CPU frequency was not pinned.

**Method.** A fresh interpreter per run, the two variants alternating; the wall clock around the 60 steps with the device synchronised before each reading (a GPU’s time is not the process’s CPU time); the build (agents, grid, upload) timed apart. One untimed GPU run first fills CuPy’s kernel cache.

About 350 ms per step on one CPU core against 10 ms on the GPU. The building is the same Python work for both (10 million `Person` agents) and dominates a 60-step run: build plus steps is 1.6 to 1.8x faster on the GPU. The comparison is with one CPU core: a sweep can run one replicate per core instead, which narrows the GPU’s lead in throughput (not measured). The 10x target of the 1.4.0 roadmap is met on this mid-range laptop GPU for the steps; it is not a claim about construction, which the GPU does not touch.

**Equality.** `gpu_speedup.py --equality` ran `modelly-gpu` with the same seed on numpy (56.1 s: the numpy fallback computes Philox numbers with array operations) and on CuPy (0.72 s, 78x faster): the infected series of the 60 steps is identical and so is the SHA-256 of the final `state`, `days` and `row` columns of all 10 million agents. The test suite checks the same on every backend that loads (`tests/gpu`), JAX with 64-bit types included. Against the CPU column variant, which draws from `model.rng`, the agreement is in distribution, as for every playbook variant.

**Where the GPU does not pay.** At the playbook’s own large size (20,000 agents) the steps take 0.14 to 0.16 s on CuPy against 0.08 to 0.14 s for the CPU column variant (3 seeds each): kernel launches and synchronisations cost more than the arithmetic. The insect cohorts on a `DeviceCohortTable` take 1.52 to 1.53 s for 120 days against 7 to 8 ms for the host `CohortTable` (3 seeds): the table has fewer than two hundred rows. Both variants run on CuPy because the roadmap asks that they do, and give the numpy run’s integers there; neither is a reason to use a GPU. Apple Metal (JAX) was not measured: no Apple GPU was available.

## Caches

Two results are now reused instead of recomputed:

- `DataCollector.get_agent_vars_dataframe` keeps the frame it last built and the number of steps it covered; a later call converts only the new steps and appends them. A dashboard that reads the frame every tick pays for one tick of rows instead of the whole history.
- `ContinuousSpace.neighbors_within` keys its lists on the radius, the population size and a hash of the position array, so repeated queries within a step cost a hash of the positions (tens of microseconds for 10,000 agents) instead of a tree build, and any position change, including a direct write to the array, invalidates it.

Measured on the same machine; each would have bought a few percent at the cost of complexity or of a different random stream for the same seed.

The remaining per-agent framework cost in the grid models is about 0.6 µs of a 1.4 µs agent-step (the cell move, the neighbourhood lookup, the shuffle and the membership check); the rest is the agent’s own logic. Going meaningfully faster from here means the columnar state on the roadmap, not more micro-tuning.

## Behaviour notes

- Seeded runs that call `select_random_empty_cell` on a dense grid draw from the index instead of from repeated random tries, so the sequence of chosen cells differs from earlier versions for the same seed. Runs are still fully reproducible for a given seed.
- Iterating an `AgentSet` walks a snapshot: adding or removing agents while iterating no longer raises, and `do`/`shuffle_do`/`map` still skip agents removed earlier in the same pass.
- `select_random` and `select` on `model.agents` now return a weak `AgentSet` like every other view (previously `select_random` leaked a strong-reference set).

## What is next

These are the changes with the largest remaining upside. Each is a project, not a patch.

1. **Vectorised movement on grids** is in: a cell-row column plus `CellIndex.random_neighbor` moves a whole population in one call, and `Occupancy` / `claim` answer the per-cell questions a step still has. What remains is a visualisation path for agents that keep their cell as a column rather than in the cell’s list.
1. **Shared-memory replications.** `workers=` runs replications in processes that each hold a full model; a shared column store would let a sweep over one large model fan out without copying it.
1. **Compiled hot loops.** The neighbourhood lookup and `do` / `shuffle_do` on the model’s registries now run in `modelly/_native/fastloop.c`, the cell move in `modelly/_native/fastcell.c` (7 to 14% on the cell-list playbooks), and `select`, `agg` and the weak views in `modelly/_native/fastset.c`. What remains per agent is the random-neighbour lookup around the draw and the property-layer `empty` setter.

## How to re-run

```bash
python benchmarks/global_benchmark.py        # the four reference models, saves timings_N.pickle
python benchmarks/compare_timings.py a.pickle b.pickle
python benchmarks/playbooks/compare.py --core 5   # the eight playbooks against Mesa 2.3
```

`modelly bench` runs the Modelly variants of the playbooks on every operating system without shell tools, keeps a history and reports regressions. Run it from the repository root (or point `--playbooks` at the directory):

```bash
modelly bench --label v1.2.0                       # record a named baseline (size large, 3 rounds)
modelly bench --baseline v1.2.0                    # compare; exit 1 on a regression above 10%
modelly bench --size small --rounds 5 --only grid_epidemic --only schelling:modelly
modelly bench --history ~/bench/modelly.jsonl --core 3 --threshold 0.05
MESA_PYTHON=.venv-mesa2/bin/python modelly bench   # the Mesa variants too
modelly bench --against 1.3.3 --rounds 7 --core 3  # this checkout against a release, paired
```

`--against VERSION` (or `release`, the last tag) builds that release from its tag in this repository with the performance guard’s builder (same compiler, same numpy, pandas, scipy and networkx, cached in `.modelly-bench/`), then runs every Modelly variant once per side per round, the side order swapped every round, with the same seed. Both sides run in the release environment’s interpreter, the checkout’s with the checkout first on `PYTHONPATH`, so both import the same third-party packages: run from a development environment that has pyarrow installed, the checkout imported it and the release did not, which added about 10,000 objects for the garbage collector and moved where its collections fall (the grid epidemic’s 60 steps spend more time collecting than computing). The two runs must give identical results; the report gives each variant’s median per-round CPU ratio and its interquartile range, and exits 1 when a variant’s median is above 1 + `--threshold` and even its lower quartile is above 1 (the performance guard’s criterion), or when results differ. Nothing goes to the history.

Each variant runs in a fresh interpreter; the order of the variants alternates from one round to the next. Runs are pinned to one core through `psutil` (`pip install modelly-abm[bench]`) on Linux and Windows; macOS has no CPU affinity API, and the report says the runs were not pinned. Every invocation appends one JSON line to the history file (`.modelly-bench/history.jsonl` by default): the Modelly version, which compiled modules were active, Python, platform, pinning, and every round’s CPU seconds per variant. The baseline is the entry named by `--baseline` (a `--label`, or an index such as `0` or `-2`), else the latest entry at the same size.

# Vectorised step phases: when a loop over agents is an array operation

Modelly keeps agents as objects and moves the bulk of a step into arrays: `Column` state, `ColumnTable.draw` / `do_where` / `remove_where` / `thin`, `CellIndex` and `Occupancy` / `claim` for any discrete space, `pairs_within` / `move_all` for continuous space. A model written this way runs a different *program* from the per-agent loop, so it has to be the same *model*. This page states when it is, and how the claim is checked in the benchmark playbooks.

The setting throughout: a step phase in which every agent `i` draws its own randomness and updates its own state from a snapshot of the model taken at the start of the phase (synchronous update). Random-activation models whose agents read state that other agents wrote earlier in the same phase are a different model, and most playbooks are written synchronously on both frameworks for that reason. Sections 7 to 9 are the exceptions: three sequential, randomly ordered phases (Schelling moves, Boltzmann giving, Sugarscape foraging) whose law an array program still reproduces exactly.

## 1. Independent draws commute with order (the Bernoulli phase)

**Claim.** Let agent `i` perform action `A_i` with probability `p_i`, the draws independent, and let `A_i` read only the start-of-phase snapshot and write only agent `i`’s own state. Then the per-agent loop in any order, shuffled or not, and the vectorised form

```python
mask = table.draw(p)  # one Bernoulli vector, p a scalar or one p_i per row
table.do_where(mask, "A")  # or remove_where(mask), or a column write
```

produce the same joint distribution of the end-of-phase state.

**Why.** The end state is a deterministic function of the snapshot and the vector of outcomes `(X_1, …, X_n)`, since no action reads another’s write. In both programs the `X_i` are independent Bernoulli(`p_i`) variables: the loop draws them one at a time from one generator, the vector form draws them in one call. Same distribution of the inputs to the same function gives the same distribution of the output. Order of evaluation, and therefore the shuffle, plays no role. A loop that short-circuits (for instance, stops testing cellmates after the first success) still draws each `X_i` from the stated law.

Used by: every `draw` / `do_where` / `remove_where` phase in the playbooks (deaths, reproduction, recovery, resistance, laying).

## 2. Contact aggregation (exposure to k independent sources)

**Claim.** A susceptible agent that has `k` infected contacts, each infecting it independently with probability `β`, becomes infected with probability

```default
p(k) = 1 - (1 - β)^k
```

and, given the start-of-phase configuration, the infections of different susceptibles are independent.

**Why.** It escapes all `k` attempts with probability `(1-β)^k`. Each pair (source, target) has its own coin and no coin is shared between two targets, so conditional on the configuration the targets’ outcomes are independent. With §1 this makes the whole infection phase one draw with `p = 1 - (1-β)**k`.

`k` itself is an array: for same-cell contact it is `index.counts(rows, infected)[rows]`, a `bincount`; for contact along the connections of any discrete space it is `index.neighbor_sum(infected_per_cell)`, one sparse matrix-vector product over the CSR adjacency that `CellIndex` builds once from the cells’ `connections`. Used by: `grid_epidemic`, `network_contagion`.

## 3. Uniform tie-breaking by a random permutation

**Claim.** When at most one agent per cell may take a resource (“the first sheep in the shuffled order eats the grass”), the winner is uniformly distributed among the cell’s candidates. Permuting the candidate rows with `rng.permutation` and keeping the first occurrence of each cell (`np.unique(rows[order], return_index=True)`) picks the winner with the same law, independently across cells.

**Why.** A uniform random permutation restricted to the candidates of one cell is a uniform permutation of them, so its first element is uniform; the restrictions to different cells are independent given the cell membership. Used by: `predator_prey` grazing.

## 4. Movement as a column, occupancy from a sort

An agent whose cell is a column of cell rows moves by assignment: `table.row = index.random_neighbor(table.row, rng)` moves every agent to a uniformly chosen neighbouring cell, the same law as “pick a random cell of my neighbourhood” one agent at a time (§1 with the move as the action, since no move reads another agent’s move). No cell keeps a list of its agents. When a phase needs the cellmates, `Occupancy(table.row, n_cells)` sorts the rows once and answers “who is in cell c” and “a random member of cell c” from the sorted order, O(n log n) per step instead of a list update per move.

Agents placed this way are in no cell’s agent list, so declare them to the index for the space and the visualisation: `index.track(model, Person, column="row")`. `space.agents` then lists them after the cell-list agents, and the renderers place each one at `index.cells[agent.row]`.

**Claim (claim with retry).** Let claimants act in a uniformly random order and each take a uniformly random member of its cell not yet taken. Then in every cell exactly min(claimants, members) are taken, the taken members form a uniform random subset of the cell’s members, and the served claimants a uniform random subset of its claimants. `claim(occupancy, cells, rng)` draws for every unserved claimant a uniformly random member of its cell, rejects draws of taken members, resolves collisions in favour of a uniformly random priority, and repeats while a claimant still has a free member; it produces a matching with the same law.

**Why.** Both procedures treat the members of a cell symmetrically and the claimants of a cell symmetrically, so the law of the matching is invariant under relabelling either side; the only such law on injections of a fixed size is the uniform one, and the size is min(claimants, members) in both since each stops only when no claimant has a free member. The rejection step keeps every draw uniform over the free members, so no round biases the outcome. Used by: `predator_prey`, wolves eating sheep.

## 5. Cohort compression (super-individuals) by binomial thinning

**Claim.** Consider `n` individuals in the same state whose next state depends only on that shared state, on model-level quantities fixed for the phase, and on an independent draw each. Represent them as one cohort with `count = n`. Then:

- survival with probability `s`: `count ~ Binomial(n, s)` has the law of the number of individual survivors, because a sum of `n` independent Bernoulli(`s`) variables is Binomial(`n`, `s`) (`ColumnTable.thin`);
- a binary attribute drawn at a transition (sex at emergence, fertile mating): the split `(Binomial(n, q), n - Binomial(n, q))` has the law of the counts of the two individual outcomes;
- an event each member triggers independently with probability `q`, each producing a fixed number `c` of offspring in a common state: the offspring count `c · Binomial(n, q)` has the law of the individual-level total, and the offspring form one new cohort because they share one state.

By induction over phases and days, the vector of per-state counts of the cohort model has the same distribution as that of the individual model, for any history. What is lost is only individual identity, which the individual model never used.

**Scope.** Cohorts must stay homogeneous: every member must face the same probabilities at every phase. Stage durations that are fixed numbers of days, daily survival that depends on stage and on a model-level density, and fecundity that depends on stage and age in stage all keep a cohort homogeneous. A per-individual continuous trait (body size, position) breaks it unless the cohorts are keyed on that trait too. `modelly.CohortTable` implements the three operations: `thin(s)`, `split(p, where, **changes)` and `draw(p, where)`, plus `merge()` to keep one row per state. Used by: `insect_cohorts`, variant `modelly-cohorts`, against the individual-level `modelly` and `mesa` variants.

## 6. Neighbour search in continuous space

Not a distributional claim but a cost one. For `n` agents and a query radius `r`, `ContinuousSpace.neighbors_within(r)` and `pairs_within(space, r)` build one KD-tree (`O(n log n)`) and answer every query from it; asking each agent in turn with a scan of all positions costs `O(n²)`. The two return the same neighbour relation (points at distance exactly `r` aside), as the `flocking` playbook shows: both implementations compute identical headings to machine precision from the same initial state.

## 7. Moves to random empty cells, one at a time

**Claim.** Let `m` movers, in a uniformly random order, each move to a uniformly random empty cell of a space with capacity one, the cell it leaves becoming empty. Put the `E` cells empty at the start in a pool, give every mover an independent uniform slot in `0 … E-1`, and process the movers in their order: a mover takes the cell in its slot and leaves its old cell there. This has the same law, and it vectorises: sort the movers by slot, keeping their order within a slot; the first in each slot takes the pool’s cell, every later one takes the old cell of the mover before it in that slot.

**Why.** Each move takes one empty cell and frees one, so the number of empty cells is `E` at every turn, and the pool, slot for slot, is exactly the set of cells empty at that turn (a mover’s own cell is occupied by itself until it leaves, so it is never in the pool when it draws). A uniform slot is therefore a uniform empty cell, independently of the past, which is the sequential rule. Because the pool size never changes, the slots can all be drawn up front. `SingleGrid.move_to_empty` in Mesa and `select_random_empty_cell` (the empty-cell index) in Modelly draw uniformly among the empty cells too. Used by: `schelling`, variant `modelly`.

## 8. Giving in a random order (the Boltzmann exchange)

**Claim.** Agents act once each in a uniformly random order; an agent holding a coin at its turn gives one to a uniformly random agent. Draw the order `turn` and every agent’s partner up front. Agent `i` gives if and only if it starts with a coin or some giver `k` with `turn[k] < turn[i]` chose it as partner. The set of givers is the least fixed point of `G ↦ rich ∪ {i : some k ∈ G with turn[k] < turn[i] has partner[k] = i}`, reached by iterating from `G = rich`; the new wealth is `w - [i ∈ G] + #{k ∈ G : partner[k] = i}`.

**Why.** An agent’s wealth at its turn is its starting wealth plus the coins it received from earlier givers; it cannot have given yet. So whether `i` gives depends only on the givers before it, and induction over the turns shows the sequential givers satisfy the fixed-point equation and are contained in every set that does, which is the least fixed point. Drawing a partner for an agent that does not give changes nothing, since that draw is never used. The map is monotone, so the iteration only adds givers and stops after a few rounds (a chain of agents that start empty and pass a coin on in increasing turn order). Used by: `boltzmann_wealth`.

## 9. Foraging in a random order with fixed sugar

**Claim.** In the Sugarscape movement rule, foragers act in a uniformly random order; each moves to the free visible cell with the most sugar if it holds more than its own (nearest first, then uniformly at random), eats all the sugar of its cell and starves when its store reaches zero. Rank, for every forager and from the start-of-step sugar, the visible cells richer than its own by (sugar, distance, an independent uniform key); walk the foragers in a random order, each taking the first free cell of its ranking; then eat, burn and starve as column operations. This has the same law.

**Why.** During the phase, sugar changes only where a forager eats: at a cell it occupies, which no other forager can choose, so every forager sees the start-of-step sugar of every free cell. A forager that starves frees a cell holding no sugar, which is never richer than another forager’s own cell, so deferring the deaths changes no choice. What remains sequential is occupancy (who took or freed which cell before this turn), which the loop tracks; the random key picks uniformly among the free cells tied on sugar and distance. No ranking needs a full sort: a forager takes the head of its ranking (its minimum, found for all foragers at once) unless that cell is not free at its turn, and only then is its ranking sorted and walked; the order, and so every choice, is the one the full sort gives. Used by: `sugarscape`, variant `modelly`.

## How the playbooks check the claims

`benchmarks/playbooks/compare.py` runs every implementation of a playbook on the same list of seeds and compares each summary statistic against the Mesa reference with Welch’s t-test; a p-value below 0.01 is flagged in the results. It also runs the first seed twice per implementation to confirm determinism. The distributions, not the samples, are what the theorems above say must match: the implementations draw their random numbers in different orders and from different generators, so their outputs differ run by run and agree in law. Timing a migrated model that matches the random stream bit for bit is a separate method, described in [performance.md](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/performance.html).


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/gpu.md -->

# GPU arrays

`modelly.gpu` runs the array side of a model (column phases, cohort tables and the operators of a cell space) on a GPU, with one setting, and draws the same random numbers there as on the CPU. The agents stay Python objects on the host; their columns are copied to the device, the step phases run there, and the results come back when the agents need them.

Backend

Where it runs

Install

numpy

the CPU, always; the fallback of every GPU path

nothing

cupy

NVIDIA GPUs through CUDA, Linux and Windows

pip install "modelly-abm[gpu]" (CuPy wheels bundle the CUDA runtime; only the driver is needed)

jax

CPU everywhere; CUDA on Linux and Windows; Metal on macOS where jax-metal supports it

pip install "modelly-abm[diff]", plus "jax[cuda13]" for NVIDIA or jax-metal for Apple GPUs

Metal has not been tested in Modelly’s own runs: the JAX path uses only operations every JAX backend has, but no Apple GPU was available to check it.

## One setting

```python
from modelly.gpu import get_backend

backend = get_backend("cupy")  # or "jax", "numpy", "auto" (a GPU backend if one loads)
```

`get_backend()` without a name reads the `MODELLY_BACKEND` environment variable (numpy when it is unset), so the same script runs on a laptop and on a GPU machine:

```bash
MODELLY_BACKEND=cupy python run.py
```

A backend that cannot load (no CuPy, no device) falls back to numpy with a `BackendFallbackWarning`; `get_backend(name, strict=True)` raises instead. `import modelly` and the numpy backend import neither CuPy nor JAX, and nothing in the CPU column code changed: a model that does not ask for a GPU runs exactly as before.

## A column phase on the GPU

The `modelly-gpu` variant of the grid epidemic playbook (`benchmarks/playbooks/grid_epidemic/modelly_gpu.py`) is the column variant with its step on the device:

```python
from modelly.gpu import DeviceCellIndex, DeviceTable, PhiloxStream, get_backend

backend = get_backend()
stream = PhiloxStream(seed, stream=0, backend=backend)
cells = DeviceCellIndex(model.index, backend)  # the grid's adjacency, once
people = DeviceTable.from_columns(model.columns[Person], stream)

def step():
    xp = people.xp  # numpy, cupy or jax.numpy
    rows = cells.random_neighbor(people.row, stream)  # a random walk on the grid
    people.row = rows
    infected = people.state == I
    exposure = cells.counts(rows, infected)[rows]  # infected cellmates
    catches = (people.state == S) & people.draw(infect[exposure])
    people.state = xp.where(catches, I, people.state)

people.write_to(model.columns[Person])  # back to the agents
```

Updates are functional: `people.state = ...` replaces the column, because JAX arrays cannot be written in place. The population is fixed while the columns are on the device; add and remove agents on the host table and copy again.

## The same numbers on every device

`PhiloxStream(seed, stream)` is a counter-based generator: Philox4x32-10 (Salmon et al., 2011) keyed by the seed. Element `i` of draw number `c` is computed from the counter `(i // k, sub, c, stream)` alone, with no state carried from one number to the next, so a GPU computes the same number for agent `i` as the CPU, whatever the order, the batch or the device. The implementation is checked against the published Random123 known-answer vectors, and numpy, the CuPy kernels and JAX are checked against each other bit for bit (`tests/gpu/test_philox.py`, `test_streams.py`). Numpy’s own `numpy.random.Philox` is the 4x64 variant, so its streams are different numbers.

Draw

Construction

Same on every backend

uniform, float64

((w0 >> 5) * 2**26 + (w1 >> 6)) / 2**53, numpy’s construction

yes (JAX: with jax_enable_x64)

uniform, float32

(w >> 8) / 2**24

yes

integers in [0, high)

high * w >> 32, bias below high / 2**32

yes

Bernoulli(p)

uniform < p

yes, for the same p

Binomial(n, p)

inversion below a mean of 10, BTRS (Hörmann 1993) above

inversion: yes; BTRS: see below

Both binomial samplers are exact: their variates have the Binomial law (tested by chi-square against the probability mass function). The inversion decides with `+ - * /` and comparisons only, which IEEE 754 makes identical everywhere. BTRS takes logarithms, whose last bit may differ between numpy, CUDA and XLA; a different bit changes a variate only when a uniform falls within one rounding error of the acceptance bound, so the results are the same in practice (they were in every test and every playbook run) and the same law always.

Without `jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)`, JAX has no 64-bit types: its floats are float32 and its integers int32, so its uniforms are the float32 ones and its runs differ from numpy’s float64 runs (in the same law). Integers drawn by `bits` and `integers` are the same in both modes.

## Exactness against the CPU

What “equal” means for each kind of state:

State

GPU against the numpy run of the same code

integer columns (states, counts, cell rows, days)

bit for bit

integer sums (counts, neighbor_sum of integers, totals_by)

bit for bit

float sums (counts with float weights, neighbor_sum of floats)

within a few ulps: additions in another order

float elementwise arithmetic

bit for bit for + - * /; exp, log, pow within one ulp

A phase whose integer outcome depends on a transcendental function (the grid epidemic’s `1 - (1 - beta) ** k`) can tabulate it once on the host, as the playbook does, so the comparison that decides a draw is the same on every device. The comparison with the CPU column variant (`modelly`), which draws from `model.rng`, is in distribution, like every other playbook variant.

## Populations larger than the GPU

`plan_memory(rows, bytes_per_row, backend)` sizes batches to half the free device memory (or a `budget`), and `run_batched(plan, phase, columns, backend)` copies each batch of host rows in, runs the phase and copies the outputs back. A phase that draws by position (`draw.random(n, start=start)`) gives the same numbers whatever the batch size, so a batched run equals the run in one batch bit for bit. Only phases whose rows do not read one another batch exactly; a reduction over rows (counts per cell) is the sum of per-batch reductions, which the caller adds.

## Speed

Measured on a laptop RTX 5050 (8 GB): the grid epidemic’s 60 steps at 10 million agents run 34x faster on CuPy than the CPU column variant; see [Performance](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/performance.html#gpu-backend) for the conditions and the other numbers. What does not get faster:

- **Small tables.** A cohort table has fewer than two hundred rows; on a GPU each operation is a kernel launch of a few microseconds plus a device synchronisation for every data-dependent size, so `insect_cohorts` runs slower on CuPy than on numpy. Use the GPU from about a hundred thousand rows.
- **JAX and changing shapes.** JAX compiles every operation for every new array shape. A `DeviceCohortTable` changes length every day, so on JAX each step recompiles; the binomial sampler pads its input to a power of two to bound that, but the cohort playbook still takes about a second per step on JAX’s CPU backend. Fixed-size column phases (a population that does not change size) compile once.
- **The numpy fallback** draws Philox numbers with array operations, about 50 ns per number, several times slower than `model.rng`. It is the reference the GPU runs are checked against, not a fast CPU path: keep the `ColumnTable` code for CPU runs.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/distributed.md -->

# From laptop to cluster

`modelly.distributed` (provisional, new in 1.4) splits one model across processes or machines: each worker holds the agents of one part of the space, and the workers exchange the agents at their borders. For the same seed a split run gives the same results as one process, byte for byte: the same reporter values at every step and, at the end, every agent in the same place with the same attributes and random streams.

```python
from modelly.distributed import Cluster, partition
from modelly.examples.distributed.grid_epidemic import EpidemicScenario, GridEpidemic

scenario = EpidemicScenario(rng=42, width=200, height=200, people=50_000)

with Cluster(backend="dask", workers=4) as cluster:
    model = cluster.build(GridEpidemic, scenario, partition=partition.grid_blocks(2, 2))
    model.run_for(100)
    cluster.collect().to_parquet("runs/epidemic.parquet")
```

The same model runs in one process as any Modelly model does (`GridEpidemic(scenario)`, `model.run_for(100)`). Splitting it is a choice of backend and partition, not a rewrite.

## What a model must do to be split

Only models written to a contract can be split. Most of it is what a synchronous model does anyway; the build and the run refuse, with the reason, the breaches they can see.

1. **Declare the split.** A class attribute `partitionable = Partitionable(space=..., phases=..., reporters=...)` names the model attribute that holds the space, the phases of one step and the reporters. The model’s `step` runs the phases: `self.partitionable.step(self)`.
1. **Use per-agent streams.** `agent_streams = True` on the class, and every draw in a phase from the agent’s own `self.random` or `self.rng`. A phase that draws from `model.random` or `model.rng` (directly, or through a space or cell collection seeded with them, such as `cell.neighborhood.select_random_cell()`) is refused at the step it happens.
1. **Phases are synchronous and local.** A phase is one method every agent runs. It reads other agents only within its `radius` (Chebyshev cells on a grid, hops on a network, distance in a continuous space), writes only the agent running it, and does not depend on the order in which agents run or neighbours are listed. The usual pattern is a phase that decides `next_state` from the neighbours’ `state`, then a phase that copies `next_state` to `state`.
1. **Moves happen in moving phases.** A phase declared with `moves=True` may change the agent’s cell or position; after it, agents standing on another partition’s ground migrate there, with their random streams. Moves into cells with a capacity are refused: who gets a free cell would depend on the order of the moves.
1. **Agents hold plain data.** Attributes are numbers, strings, arrays, tuples and the like, not references to agents, cells or the model (keep a stream key or a coordinate instead). Agent classes are defined at module level, so they can be sent to another process.
1. **Every agent has a place in the partitioned space**, and the model schedules no events of its own. Agents with `Column` state are not supported yet.
1. **Stream keys do not depend on the partition.** An agent’s streams are seeded from the model’s seed and its `stream_key()`, `unique_id` by default. By default every worker builds the whole initial population in the single-process order and keeps its part, so `unique_id` is the same everywhere. A model that builds only its own part (below), or creates agents during the run, overrides `stream_key()` with a key of its own; the build refuses different populations keyed on `unique_id`, and a phase that creates such agents is refused.

The breaches the checks cannot see (reading past the radius, depending on the order of neighbours, writing to another agent) change the results. `check_independence` finds them: it runs the model in one process and split, and raises at the first output that differs.

```python
from modelly.distributed import check_independence, partition

check_independence(
    GridEpidemic,
    scenario,
    [partition.grid_blocks(2, 2), partition.grid_blocks(4, 4)],
    steps=20,
)
```

Run it on a small scenario before a long split run.

## A model, in full

The grid epidemic of `modelly.examples.distributed.grid_epidemic`, shortened:

```python
from modelly import Model
from modelly.distributed import Partitionable, Phase, Sum
from modelly.distributed.building import owns
from modelly.space import OrthogonalMooreGrid
from modelly.space.cells.agents import CellAgent

S, I, R = 0, 1, 2

class Person(CellAgent):
    def __init__(self, model, cell, state, key):
        super().__init__(model)
        self.key, self.cell, self.days = key, cell, 0
        self.state = self.next_state = state

    def stream_key(self):
        return self.key  # the index in the creation order, whoever builds the person

    def move(self):
        self.cell = self.random.choice(self.cell.neighborhood.cells)

    def expose(self):  # reads the people in its own cell and the eight around it
        if self.state == S:
            around = [self.cell, *self.cell.neighborhood.cells]
            k = sum(other.state == I for cell in around for other in cell.agents)
            if k and self.random.random() < 1 - (1 - self.model.scenario.beta) ** k:
                self.next_state = I
        elif self.state == I:
            self.days += 1
            if self.days >= self.model.scenario.recovery:
                self.next_state = R

    def advance(self):
        self.state = self.next_state

def infected(model):
    return sum(1 for agent in model.agents if agent.state == I)

class GridEpidemic(Model):
    agent_streams = True
    partitionable = Partitionable(
        space="grid",
        phases=(Phase("move", moves=True), Phase("expose", radius=1), Phase("advance")),
        reporters={"I": Sum(infected)},
    )

    def __init__(self, scenario):
        super().__init__(scenario=scenario)
        s = self.scenario
        self.grid = OrthogonalMooreGrid(
            (s.width, s.height), torus=True, random=self.random
        )
        cells = list(self.grid.all_cells)
        for key, pick in enumerate(self.rng.integers(0, len(cells), s.people).tolist()):
            if owns(self, cells[pick].coordinate):
                Person(self, cells[pick], I if key < s.infected else S, key)

    def step(self):
        self.partitionable.step(self)
```

The model’s own generator is used while building (every worker draws the same numbers there); during a step only the people’s streams are.

## Partitions

Space

Partition

Halo

A 2-D grid (torus or not; tested on OrthogonalMooreGrid)

partition.grid_blocks(rows, cols): rectangles of nearly equal size, the larger first

cells within radius (Chebyshev) of the block

A Network

partition.graph(parts, imbalance=0.03): nodes ordered by breadth-first search from a far node of each component, cut into equal runs, then refined by greedy boundary moves (k-way Fiduccia-Mattheyses) within the imbalance

nodes within radius hops

A ContinuousSpace

partition.kd(parts): recursive bisection of the domain along its longest side at the population quantile (a k-d tree)

agents within radius of the box, wrapping on a torus

Every partitioner is deterministic and pure numpy, so all workers compute the same layout. The graph partitioner is not METIS: on a 30 by 30 lattice cut in four it cuts about twice the edges of the best split, and far fewer than a random one. A layout answers `owner`, `owners`, `halo` and `neighbours` (`GraphLayout.cut()` and `sizes()` measure a graph split).

## What happens in a step

For each phase, in order:

1. if the phase’s radius is above zero, each worker sends copies of its agents within the radius of a neighbour (ghosts) to that neighbour, which places them in its copy of the space;
1. every worker runs the phase on its own agents; the run checks that the model’s generators did not move and that no agent keyed on `unique_id` was created;
1. ghosts are removed;
1. after a moving phase, agents now on another partition’s ground are sent there with their streams and registered, by sender and then in the sender’s order.

Then every worker computes its part of each reporter and the parts are reduced. `Sum`, `Min` and `Max` are exact on integers; a float `Sum` adds the parts with `math.fsum`, but each part is rounded before, so use integer reporters where byte identity matters.

## Building only your own part

By default each worker builds the whole initial population, then drops the agents of other partitions: simple, and always correct, but every worker holds the whole population while it builds. `owns(model, location)` (in `modelly.distributed.building`) lets the model’s `__init__` build only the agents its worker owns, as the example above does: it is always `True` in one process, so the model builds the same agents there. The agents need stream keys of their own. `kd` splits cannot answer `owns`, since their boxes come from the built positions. Each worker still holds the whole space (every cell of the grid, every node of the network).

## Backends

Backend

Use

How it runs

"local"

tests, debugging, check_independence

every partition in this process, one after the other

"mpi"

clusters, the fastest exchange

one partition per MPI rank; launch the script with mpirun -n <partitions> python run.py

"dask"

a laptop or a Dask cluster, no MPI needed

one Dask actor per partition (a local cluster of one-thread processes, or address= / client=)

"ray"

a Ray cluster

one Ray actor per partition; ray.init arguments as options

Under MPI every rank runs the same script, and every `DistributedModel` method is collective: call it on every rank, never inside `if cluster.is_root:`. All ranks get the same results; write files from the root only:

```python
with Cluster(backend="mpi") as cluster:  # mpirun -n 4 python run.py
    model = cluster.build(GridEpidemic, scenario, partition.grid_blocks(2, 2))
    model.run_for(365)
    frame = cluster.collect()
    if cluster.is_root:
        frame.to_parquet("runs/epidemic.parquet")
```

An error on one rank is raised on every rank, so a failed run stops instead of waiting forever. With Dask and Ray the ghosts and migrants travel through the process that called `build`, a round trip per exchange: fine for a few workers, slower than MPI for many. Install with `pip install "modelly-abm[distributed]"` (mpi4py, which needs an MPI library: Open MPI or MPICH on Linux and macOS, MS-MPI on Windows), `"modelly-abm[dask]"` or `"modelly-abm[ray]"`.

## Outputs and checkpoints

- `model.collect()` (or `cluster.collect()`): a pandas frame, one row per step and one for the build, with `time` and every reporter.
- `model.snapshot(("state", "days"))`: every agent by stream key with its location and the attributes named, equal to `modelly.distributed.snapshot(single_process_model, ...)`.
- `model.states()`: the full state of every agent, for exact comparisons.
- `model.checkpoint("runs/ckpt")` writes `part-00000.ckpt` … one file per partition (a core checkpoint of its model, plus its layout) and `index.json` (the model class, the partitions, the time, the reporter rows so far and each file’s SHA-256). `cluster.restore("runs/ckpt")` continues the run draw for draw, on any backend with the same number of workers; a file that no longer matches its digest is refused. Like every checkpoint, the files are pickles: only restore checkpoints you made or trust.

## Scaling, measured

`benchmarks/distributed/weak_scaling.py` measures weak scaling on the grid epidemic: every worker owns a block of the same size with the same number of people, so perfect scaling keeps the time per step constant, and the efficiency is `T(1) / T(K)`.

Next to each split run of K workers the script times K independent copies of one block’s model running at the same time with no communication at all, and keeps the slowest. That separates what the machine gives (`T_copies(1) / T_copies(K)`) from what the split run keeps of it (`T_copies(K) / T(K)`, the protocol’s efficiency).

Measured on one laptop (Intel Core Ultra 7 356H, 16 cores of three kinds, Linux, Python 3.15, Open MPI 5.0, mpi4py 4.1) shared with other jobs: the load average before each run is in the table. Wall-clock seconds per step after a warm-up step, the build excluded; the raw numbers, with every copy’s time, are in `benchmarks/distributed/results/` (measured on v1.4.2’s code; the same files as `paper/data/weak_*.json`).

What this shows, and what it does not:

- **This laptop is not a cluster.** K copies of the same model with no communication already slow down to 9-25% of one copy at 8 to 16 processes (cores of different speeds, a shared memory bus, a lower all-core clock, other jobs). No split run can do better than that here.
- **The protocol keeps 42-56% of the machine with 10,000 people per worker** from four workers on **and 74-87% with 40,000**: the exchange grows with a block’s border, the work with its area, so larger blocks scale better. A step of this model costs about 1.5 microseconds per person, so the border traffic weighs heavily at small blocks; a model with more work per agent hides it better.
- **Dask pays a round trip through the coordinator** for every exchange (eight per step here): it is the backend that runs everywhere without MPI, not the fast one.
- **The 1.4 target, at least 70% weak scaling efficiency from 1 to 64 workers, is not measured.** It needs 64 cores of a cluster with a fast interconnect; one 16-core laptop cannot show it. Measured here, the split run’s own efficiency against the machine’s (the protocol column) is the part the code controls.

## Limits in 1.4

- Agents with `Column` state, models with events of their own and moves into cells with a capacity are refused.
- Each worker holds the whole space, and by default the whole initial population at build time (see `owns` above).
- Partitions are fixed at build: there is no load balancing while the run goes on.
- One worker runs one partition, and a restore needs the same number of partitions.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/determinism.md -->

# Determinism and platforms

The same model, scenario and seed give the same run on Windows, macOS and Linux, with the compiled modules or in pure Python, straight through or resumed from a checkpoint. This page says what that promise covers, how the test suite checks it, and the few outputs that are compared with a tolerance.

## What is promised

- **Same seed, same run.** All randomness comes from `model.random` and `model.rng`, both seeded from the scenario. Two runs with the same seed in two processes are identical.
- **Compiled and pure Python agree.** Every C function in `modelly/_native` has a Python twin that gives identical results; `MODELLY_PURE_PYTHON=1` selects the twins.
- **A resumed run is the same run.** A model saved at step *k* with `model.save` and loaded with `Model.load` finishes exactly as the run that never stopped.
- **Every platform gives the same bytes**, with the exceptions listed below.

## How the suite checks it

`tests/determinism/` runs every bundled example (`modelly/examples/**`, including the spatial and language-model examples) for a fixed number of steps from seed 42, then takes a SHA-256 digest of:

- the tables its `DataCollector` holds (model variables, and agent variables if any);
- the final state of the model and of every agent (the same snapshot time travel compares: public scalars, columns, cell or position) and a digest of both generators’ state.

The digest is taken over canonical bytes, never over `repr` or text with platform line endings: JSON with sorted keys and no whitespace, floats written exactly (`float.hex`), agents written by `unique_id`, sets and graphs sorted. The suite then checks that:

1. a pure-Python interpreter (`MODELLY_PURE_PYTHON=1`) and a compiled one give the same exact digest for every example;
1. a run saved at mid-run, loaded and finished gives the same exact digest as a straight run;
1. every example reproduces the golden digest recorded in `tests/determinism/golden.json`;
1. the reference models of [split runs](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/distributed.html) (`modelly.examples.distributed`: a grid epidemic, a network SIR model and walkers in continuous space, which are golden examples too) give the single-process outputs when split from the golden seed: the grid into 1, 2, 4 and 16 blocks, the network into 2, 4 and 16 parts, the plane into 2, 4 and 16 boxes. Every reporter row and every agent’s attributes, location and random streams must be equal byte for byte (`check_independence`), so a split run on any platform gives the golden run. Under `mpirun`, `tests/distributed/test_mpi.py` checks the same on 2 and 4 MPI ranks.

Before a release, `scripts/release-checks.sh` runs the distributed tests under Open MPI and makes, unpacks and verifies three `modelly bundle`s in a fresh interpreter, on Linux. The `build`, `mpi` and `platforms` workflows run the same checks on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows (MS-MPI there, 2 ranks), and check 3 then compares the three platforms through the golden file; they are manual-only, so a release says which platforms its checks covered.

## Outputs compared with a tolerance

IEEE 754 makes `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `sqrt` correctly rounded, so they give the same bits on every platform. The transcendental functions (`exp`, `log`, `pow` with a non-integer exponent, `arctan2`) and BLAS reductions (`numpy.linalg.norm`) are not: each platform’s maths library and numpy’s SIMD kernels may differ in the last bit. Examples whose recorded floats pass through them are compared at **10 significant digits** in the golden check (`float_digits` in `golden.json`):

Example

Why

alliance_formation

initial power and position from normal draws (the sampler’s tails use log and exp)

boid_flockers

headings from arctan2, distances from linalg.norm

epstein_civil_violence

arrest probability from exp

sugarscape_g1mt

welfare from pow, trade price from exp and log

commuting_city

destination choice from exp, congestion from pow

layered_epidemic

infection probability from exp

`commuting_city` is also compared on the platform that wrote `golden.json` only: its projections and geometry come from the PROJ and GEOS libraries bundled inside the pyproj and shapely wheels, and those builds differ between platforms by more than the last digits. On every other platform its golden check is skipped with that reason; checks 1 and 2 still run everywhere.

Models coupled with [`modelly.couple`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/coupling.html) have two more such outputs: the decay of a field (`exp`) and the error norm `solve_ivp` uses to choose its steps.

Every other example is compared bit for bit. Checks 1 and 2 are always exact: they run on one machine, where the maths library is the same. A last-bit difference can only change a discrete decision if a random draw falls exactly on it, which is negligible over the short golden runs; integers, counts and generator states are never rounded.

Digests also depend on the versions of the libraries that build the model: numpy keeps its `Generator` streams stable, but a networkx release that changed a graph generator would change `virus_on_network`. When that happens the golden file is regenerated on purpose.

## Updating the golden digests

A deliberate change to an example or to the framework that changes results needs new digests:

```bash
python -m modelly.dev golden            # check: prints what differs, exit 1
python -m modelly.dev golden --update   # rewrite tests/determinism/golden.json
python -m modelly.dev golden --json     # this build's exact digests, to compare two machines
```

Commit the new `golden.json` with the change and say in the commit why results changed.

## Examples that cannot be checkpointed yet

Two examples refuse `model.save`, and the suite checks that they still do, so the entry goes as soon as they can be saved:

- `alliance_formation`: meta-agent classes are created at run time, and pickle cannot find them by name;
- `tram_model`: `ContinuousState` rates and `Threshold` callbacks are closures.

## Writing a deterministic model

- Draw every random number from `self.random` or `self.rng`, never from `random` or `numpy.random`; pass `seed=self.random` to library generators such as networkx.
- Do not iterate over a `set` of agents or strings whose order matters; sort by `unique_id`.
- Use module-level functions, not lambdas, for reporters and scheduled callbacks, so the model can be checkpointed.
- Open text files with `encoding="utf-8"`, and write files you hash with `newline="\n"`.

`modelly lint` finds most of these (see [Checking a model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/lint.html)).

## Streams of each agent’s own

By default every agent draws from the model’s two generators, so what one agent draws depends on how many numbers the agents before it drew. A model can give each agent generators of its own instead (provisional, new in 1.4):

```python
class Epidemic(Model):
    agent_streams = True  # agent.random and agent.rng are the agent's own
```

Each agent’s seed is derived from the model’s seed and the agent’s `stream_key()`, its `unique_id` unless overridden. An agent then draws the same numbers whatever the activation order and however many agents there are, and checkpoints and pickles continue every stream. This is what a run split across processes needs, since an agent takes its stream with it. Override `stream_key()` when the creation order itself could change, for example to key agents on an identifier read from data. The model’s own `self.random` and `self.rng`, and the bulk draws of columns and cohorts, still use the model’s generators. Turning the flag on changes the numbers a model draws, so results differ from a run without it for the same seed.

# Core

`modelly.core` holds the model, agents, agent sets, columns, the random source and the exceptions. `modelly.Model`, `modelly.Agent`, `modelly.Column` and `modelly.FastRandom` are the same objects as `modelly.core.Model`, `modelly.core.Agent` and so on.

Module

Contents

modelly.core.model

Model

modelly.core.registry

the agent registries the model inherits (agents, agents_by_type, agent_types)

modelly.core.agent

Agent

modelly.core.agentset

AgentSet, AbstractAgentSet, GroupBy

modelly.core.columns, modelly.core.column_access

Column and the column tables

modelly.core.rng

FastRandom, PyFastRandom

modelly.core.checkpoint

the checkpoint file format behind Model.save and Model.load

modelly.core.exceptions

the exceptions raised by Modelly

## Model

`Model` takes its agent registries from `modelly.core.registry`, its scheduling methods from `modelly.time.schedule` and its signals from `modelly.time.signals`; all of them are listed below.

The model class for Modelly framework.

Core Objects: Model

#### `class Model(*args: Any, rng: RNGLike | SeedLike | None = None, scenario: S | type[S] = <class 'modelly.scenarios.scenario.Scenario'>, **kwargs: Any)`

Base class for models in the Modelly ABM library.

This class serves as a foundational structure for creating agent-based models. It includes the basic attributes and methods necessary for initializing and running a simulation model.

**Type Parameters:**

A: The agent type used in this model S: The scenario type used in this model

**Variables:**

- **running** – A boolean indicating if the model should continue running.
- **time** – the current simulation time.
- **random** – a seeded python.random number generator.
- **rng** – a seeded numpy.random.Generator
- **scenario** – the scenario instance containing model parameters

Notes

Model.agents returns the AgentSet containing all agents registered with the model. Changing the content of the AgentSet directly can result in strange behavior. If you want change the composition of this AgentSet, ensure you operate on a copy.

Create a new model.

Overload this method with the actual code to initialize the model. Always start with super().__init__() to initialize the model object properly.

**Parameters:**

- **args** – arguments to pass onto super
- **rng** – Seed for the random number generator. Accepts any value accepted by numpy.random.default_rng(). Ignored if a Scenario instance is passed; used to instantiate the scenario when a Scenario class is passed.
- **scenario** – A Scenario instance or subclass to use for this model. If a class is passed it is instantiated with rng. If an instance is passed, rng must not be set.
- **kwargs** – keyword arguments to pass onto super

Notes

Pass either rng or a Scenario instance, not both. Passing rng alongside a Scenario class is valid — rng is forwarded to the class constructor.

#### `property scenario: S`

Return scenario instance.

#### `run_model() → None`

Run the model until the end condition is reached.

Overload as needed.

#### `step() → None`

A single step. Fill in here.

#### `save(path: str | Path, *, compress: bool = False) → None`

Save the whole model to one checkpoint file.

The file holds the agents, spaces, columns, scheduled events, data collected so far and the exact state of `random` and `rng`, so `Model.load` resumes the run draw for draw.

**Parameters:**

- **path** – The file to write.
- **compress** – Gzip the payload (smaller, slower).

**Raises:**

[**CheckpointError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.exceptions.CheckpointError) – If a callback the model holds, such as an event callback or a reporter, is a lambda or nested function.

#### `classmethod load(path: str | Path) → Self`

Load a model saved with `save`.

Warning

A checkpoint is a pickle: loading one runs code chosen by whoever wrote it. Only load files you created or otherwise trust.

**Parameters:**

**path** – The checkpoint file.

**Returns:**

The saved model, an instance of the class it was saved from.

**Raises:**

[**CheckpointError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.exceptions.CheckpointError) – If the file is not a checkpoint, was written by another Modelly or Python release, or holds no `cls`.

#### `checkpoint_every(interval: float, path_pattern: str, *, compress: bool = False) → CheckpointWriter`

Save a checkpoint every `interval` time units.

**Parameters:**

- **interval** – Time between checkpoints; the first is `interval` from now.
- **path_pattern** – The file name, formatted with `time`, e.g. `"run-{time:04.0f}.ckpt"`.
- **compress** – Gzip each checkpoint.

**Returns:**

The writer; call its `stop()` to end the checkpoints.

#### `property agent_types: list[type]`

Return a list of all unique agent types registered with the model.

#### `property agents: _HardKeyAgentSet[A]`

Provides a _HardKeyAgentSet of all agents in the model, combining agents from all types.

**Returns:**

The agent set containing all agents with strong references.

**Return type:**

_HardKeyAgentSet

Warning

This returns the actual internal _HardKeyAgentSet used by Modelly for agent registration and tracking. It uses strong references to prevent premature garbage collection and reduce performance overhead caused by weak reference management.

**Do not modify this AgentSet directly** (e.g., by adding or removing agents manually). Direct modifications can break the model’s agent tracking system and cause unexpected behavior. Instead:

- Use `Agent()` to create new agents (automatically registers them)
- Use `agent.remove()` to remove agents (automatically deregisters them)
- For read-only operations or transformations, work on a copy: `model.agents.copy()`

Notes

This is Modelly’s core agent registration system. All agents created via `Agent.__init__` are automatically registered here.

#### `property agents_by_type: dict[type[A], _HardKeyAgentSet[A]]`

A dictionary where keys are agent types and values are the corresponding _HardKeyAgentSets.

**Returns:**

Dictionary mapping agent types to their AgentSets.

**Return type:**

[dict](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)[[type](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#type)[A], _HardKeyAgentSet[A]]

Warning

Each AgentSet in this dictionary is a _HardKeyAgentSet with strong references, forming part of Modelly’s core agent registration system.

**Do not modify these AgentSets directly**. Direct modifications can break agent tracking and cause unexpected behavior. Instead:

- Use `Agent()` to create new agents (automatically registers them)
- Use `agent.remove()` to remove agents (automatically deregisters them)
- For read-only operations, work on copies: `model.agents_by_type[AgentType].copy()`

Notes

This is part of Modelly’s core agent registration system. All agents are automatically registered in the appropriate type-specific AgentSet when created via `Agent.__init__`.

#### `batch()`

Note

#### `class Agent(model: M, *args, **kwargs)`

Base class for a model agent in Modelly.

**Variables:**

- **unique_id** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – A unique identifier for this agent.

Notes

Agents must be hashable to be used in an AgentSet. In Python 3, defining __eq__ without __hash__ makes an object unhashable, which will break AgentSet usage. unique_id is unique relative to a model instance and starts from 1

**Parameters:**

- **args** – Passed on to super.
- **kwargs** – Passed on to super.

to make proper use of python’s super, in each class remove the arguments and keyword arguments you need and pass on the rest to super

#### `classmethod column_specs() → dict[str, Column]`

The `Column` declarations of this class (name to column), in table order.

On the class, a column attribute is the fast property that reads the agent’s row; this returns the declarations themselves (dtype, default).

#### `remove() → None`

Remove and delete the agent from the model.

#### `step() → None`

A single step of the agent.

#### `classmethod create_agents(model: Model, n: int, *args, **kwargs) → AgentSet[T]`

Create N agents.

**Parameters:**

- **model** – the model to which the agents belong
- **args** – arguments to pass onto agent instances each arg is either a single object or a sequence of length n
- **n** – the number of agents to create
- **kwargs** – keyword arguments to pass onto agent instances each keyword arg is either a single object or a sequence of length n

**Returns:**

AgentSet containing the agents created.

Warning

A list, tuple, ndarray, or pandas Series argument is treated as one value per agent and must have length n; a length mismatch raises ValueError. This is especially easy to hit with coordinate tuples: create_agents(model, 2, pos=(10, 20)) does NOT give both agents pos=(10, 20); it gives agent 0 pos=10 and agent 1 pos=20, since the tuple’s length (2) matches n (2).

To assign the same sequence value to every agent, broadcast it explicitly as a length-n list of that value, e.g.: create_agents(model, 2, pos=[(10, 20)] * 2)

**Raises:**

[**ValueError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#ValueError) – If a sequence argument’s length does not match n.

#### `classmethod from_dataframe(model: Model, df: pd.DataFrame, **kwargs) → AgentSet[T]`

Create agents from a pandas DataFrame.

Each row of the DataFrame represents one agent. The DataFrame columns are mapped to the agent’s constructor as keyword arguments. Additional keyword arguments (**kwargs) can be used to set constant attributes for all agents.

**Parameters:**

- **model** – The model instance.
- **df** – The pandas DataFrame. Each row represents an agent.
- ****kwargs** – Constant values to pass to every agent’s constructor. Only non-sequence data is allowed in kwargs to avoid ambiguity with DataFrame columns.

**Returns:**

AgentSet containing the agents created.

Note

If you need to pass variable data or sequences, add them as columns to the DataFrame before calling this method.

## Agent sets

`AgentSet` takes its selection methods (`select`, `select_random`) from `modelly.core.agentset.selection` and its attribute methods (`get`, `set`, `agg`) from `modelly.core.agentset.attributes`; they are listed under `AgentSet`.

AgentSet: the weak-reference ordered set every view is made of.

#### `class AgentSet(agents: Iterable[A], random: Random | None = None)`

Bases: [`AbstractAgentSet`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.agentset.abstract.AbstractAgentSet), [`Generic`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Generic)

A collection class that represents an ordered set of agents using weak references.

This implementation uses weak references to agents, allowing for efficient management of agent lifecycles without preventing garbage collection.

**Variables:**

**random** (*Random*) – The random number generator for this agent set.

Notes

The AgentSet maintains weak references to agents, which means that agents not referenced elsewhere in the program may be automatically removed from the AgentSet. This is the default implementation for most use cases where automatic cleanup is desired.

Internally the set is a plain `dict` keyed on `weakref.ref` objects (a `weakref.ref` hashes and compares like its referent while that is alive), which is about twice as fast as `weakref.WeakKeyDictionary` for construction, membership and iteration because it skips that class’s pure-Python wrapper and iteration guard. Each ref carries a callback that drops the entry when its agent is garbage collected. All bulk operations walk a snapshot of the keys, never the live dict, so a callback or user code mutating the set mid-iteration is always safe.

Initialize the AgentSet with weak references to agents.

**Parameters:**

- **agents** (*Iterable**[*[*Agent*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.agent.Agent)*]*) – An iterable of Agent objects to be included in the set.
- **random** (*Random** | **None*) – The random number generator for this agent set.

#### `to_list() → list[A]`

**Return type:**

Notes

#### `select(filter_func: Callable[[A], bool] | None = None, at_most: int | float = inf, inplace: bool = False, agent_type: type[A] | None = None) → AbstractAgentSet[A]`

Select a subset of agents from the AbstractAgentSet based on a filter function and/or quantity limit.

**Parameters:**

- **filter_func** (*Callable**[**[*[*Agent*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.agent.Agent)*]**, *[*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*]**, **optional*) – A function that takes an Agent and returns True if the agent should be included in the result. Defaults to None, meaning no filtering is applied.
- **at_most** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)* | *[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*, **optional*) – The maximum amount of agents to select. Defaults to infinity. - If an integer, at most the first number of matching agents are selected. - If a float between 0 and 1, at most that fraction of original the agents are selected.
- **inplace** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*, **optional*) – If True, modifies the current AbstractAgentSet; otherwise, returns a new AbstractAgentSet. Defaults to False.
- **agent_type** ([*type*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#type)*[*[*Agent*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.agent.Agent)*]**, **optional*) – The class type of the agents to select. Defaults to None, meaning no type filtering is applied.

**Returns:**

A new AbstractAgentSet containing the selected agents, unless inplace is True, in which case the current AbstractAgentSet is updated.

**Return type:**

[AbstractAgentSet](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.agentset.abstract.AbstractAgentSet)

**Raises:**

- [**TypeError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#TypeError) – If at_most is not an integer or float, or is a boolean.
- [**ValueError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#ValueError) – If at_most is a negative integer, or a float not in the range (0.0, 1.0].

Notes

- at_most just return the first n or fraction of agents. To take a random sample, shuffle() beforehand.
- at_most is an upper limit. When specifying other criteria, the number of agents returned can be smaller.

#### `select_random(n: int | float = 1, *, weights: str | Callable[[A], float] | Sequence[float] | None = None, replace: bool = False, inplace: bool = False) → AbstractAgentSet[A]`

Select a random or weighted sample of agents from the AbstractAgentSet.

**Parameters:**

- **n** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)* | *[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*, **optional*) – The number or fraction of agents to select. Defaults to 1. - If an integer >= 1, the number of agents to select. - If a float in (0, 1], the fraction of agents to select.
- **weights** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)* | **Callable**[**[*[*Agent*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.agent.Agent)*]**, *[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*] **| **Sequence**[*[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*] **| **None**, **optional*) – Weights for selection. - If a str: uses the specified agent attribute name. - If a Callable: calls the function on each agent to compute its weight. - If a Sequence: a sequence of numerical weights of the same length as the AgentSet. - If None: uniform random selection. Defaults to None.
- **replace** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*, **optional*) – Whether to sample with replacement. Defaults to False.
- **inplace** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*, **optional*) – If True, modifies the current AbstractAgentSet; otherwise, returns a new AbstractAgentSet. Defaults to False.

**Returns:**

A new or updated AbstractAgentSet containing the sampled agents.

- [**TypeError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#TypeError) – If n or weights is of an unsupported type.

#### `set(attr_name: str, value: Any) → AgentSet[A]`

Set a specified attribute for the agents in the AgentSet.

The behavior is derived from `value` (the same value-based rule pandas uses for column assignment):

- A `list`, `tuple`, `numpy.ndarray` or `pandas.Series` is treated as one value per agent and is assigned element-wise, in iteration order (the same order `get` uses), so a `get -> transform -> set` round-trip stays consistent. It must have the same length as the AgentSet; a length mismatch raises `ValueError`.
- Any other value (a scalar, a string, or any non-sequence) is broadcast: every agent receives the same value.

**Parameters:**

- **attr_name** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The name of the attribute to set.
- **value** (*Any*) – The value(s) to assign. See above for how the shape of `value` selects element-wise vs broadcast assignment.

**Returns:**

The AgentSet instance itself, after setting the attribute.

**Return type:**

[AgentSet](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.agentset.weak.AgentSet)

**Raises:**

[**ValueError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#ValueError) – If `value` is a sequence whose length does not match the number of agents in the AgentSet.

Notes

A per-agent sequence is recognized by its type (list, tuple, ndarray, Series). To assign a single sequence value to every agent, broadcast it explicitly, e.g. `[shared_list] * len(agentset)`.

#### `sort(key: Callable[[A], Any] | str, ascending: bool = False, inplace: bool = False) → AbstractAgentSet[A]`

Sort the agents in the AbstractAgentSet based on a specified attribute or custom function.

**Parameters:**

- **key** (*Callable**[**[*[*Agent*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.agent.Agent)*]**, **Any**] **| *[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – A function or attribute name based on which the agents are sorted.
- **ascending** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*, **optional*) – If True, the agents are sorted in ascending order. Defaults to False.
- **inplace** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)*, **optional*) – If True, sorts the agents in the current set; otherwise, returns a new sorted AgentSet. Defaults to False.

**Returns:**

A sorted set. Returns the current set if inplace is True.

The interface and shared algorithms of every agent set.

#### `class AbstractAgentSet`

Bases: `SelectionMixin`, `AttributeMixin`, [`ABC`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/abc.html#abc.ABC), [`MutableSet`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.MutableSet), [`Generic`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Generic)

An abstract base collection class that represents an ordered set of agents within an agent-based model (ABM).

This class defines the minimal interface that all AgentSet implementations must follow. Subclasses are free to override methods with optimized implementations based on their storage mechanism (weak references vs strong references).
