## Columns

Columnar agent state: declare a `Column` on an `Agent` subclass and that attribute lives in a model-owned numpy array, readable per agent and as a whole.

Columnar agent state: attributes stored in model-owned numpy arrays.

Declare a `Column` on an `Agent` subclass and that attribute lives in one numpy array per agent class instead of in each instance’s `__dict__`. The agent keeps working as an object (`agent.wealth` reads and writes its own row) while the model gets a zero-copy view of every agent’s value at once:

```default
class MoneyAgent(Agent):
    wealth = Column(int, default=1)

table = model.columns[MoneyAgent]
table.wealth.mean()                    # numpy, no Python loop
table.wealth[table.wealth > 10] -= 1   # bulk update, in place
rich = table.where(table.wealth > 10)  # an AgentSet
```

Rows are in insertion order; removing an agent moves the last row into the freed slot, so a view is valid until the next add or remove. Use columns for the attributes you aggregate, filter, record or update in bulk; a plain attribute is still the cheapest thing to read inside `step`. Each column is a fast property on the class (`modelly.core.column_access`).

#### `class Column(dtype: Any = <class 'float'>, default: Any = 0)`

Descriptor declaring an agent attribute stored in a model-owned array.

**Parameters:**

- **dtype** – numpy dtype of the column.
- **default** – value every new agent starts with.

Declare a column with its dtype and the default each new agent gets.

#### `class ColumnTable(specs: dict[str, Column], random: Random, rng: Generator, storage: InMemory = InMemory())`

The arrays of one agent class, one row per live agent.

Attribute access (`table.wealth`) and item access (`table["wealth"]`) return a view of the live rows. `table.unique_id` is always present.

Allocate one array per column plus the unique_id column, in `storage`.

#### `property columns: list[str]`

Column names, `unique_id` first.

#### `property agents: list[Agent]`

The agents in row order (a copy of the list).

#### `where(mask: ndarray) → AgentSet`

Return the agents whose row is True in `mask` as an AgentSet.

#### `draw(p: float | ndarray) → ndarray`

One Bernoulli draw per agent from the model’s seeded numpy generator.

`p` is a probability or one probability per row. The “reproduce with probability p” phase of a step is `table.do_where(table.draw(p), "spawn")`.

#### `do_where(mask: ndarray, method: str, *args, **kwargs) → int`

Call `method` on every agent whose row is True in `mask`; return how many.

The agents are snapshotted first, so the method may add or remove agents.

#### `remove_where(mask: ndarray) → int`

Remove every agent whose row is True in `mask`; return how many.

The “die” phase of a step: `table.remove_where(table.energy < 0)`. Each agent goes through `agent.remove()`, so spaces and datasets are updated.

#### `thin(name: str, survival: float | ndarray) → ndarray`

Replace the counts in column `name` by Binomial(count, survival) draws.

For a row of `count` identical individuals, each surviving independently with probability `survival`, the number left is Binomial(count, survival) (a sum of Bernoulli draws), so one draw per cohort has the individual model’s law. Returns the live-rows view of the column after the draw.

#### `to_dataframe() → DataFrame`

Copy the live rows into a DataFrame indexed by `unique_id`.

#### `add(agent: Agent) → int`

Append a row for `agent` (with the column defaults) and return it.

#### `remove(agent: Agent) → None`

Free `agent`’s row by moving the last row into it.

Per-agent access: on the class, each column is a property that reads the agent’s row through a `memoryview` (see `Agent.column_specs()` for the declarations).

Fast per-agent access to `Column` attributes.

A `Column` declared on an agent class is replaced on that class by a plain `property`: the interpreter inlines property getters, which a custom descriptor never gets. The getter reads the agent’s row through a `memoryview` of the column’s array, which returns a Python `int`, `float` or `bool` instead of building a numpy scalar, so the value is cheaper to read and much cheaper to do arithmetic on. Dtypes a `memoryview` cannot index (strings, objects, complex, datetimes) keep the numpy array.

Measured on CPython 3.15, one access inside a step:

plain attribute read 6 ns += 1 13 ns Column, descriptor read 79 ns += 1 171 ns Column, this module read 27 ns += 1 72 ns

#### `fast_view(array: ndarray) → Any`

A `memoryview` of `array` when it indexes to Python scalars, else `array`.

#### `column_property(name: str, position: int, column: Column) → property`

The property installed for column `name`, at `position` in the class’s specs.

#### `collect_column_specs(cls: type) → dict[str, Column]`

The columns of `cls`: inherited ones first, in MRO order, then its own.

Agent classes already processed keep their declarations in `_column_specs` (their attributes are properties by then); other bases, such as plain mixins, are scanned for `Column` instances.

#### `install_column_properties(cls: type, specs: dict[str, Column]) → None`

Replace every column of `cls` by its fast property.

## Random numbers

`model.random` is a `FastRandom`: a `random.Random` that gives exactly the standard library’s numbers for a seed, faster. When the compiled core is built for the interpreter (platform wheels for Linux and macOS, or `bash scripts/build-native.sh` in a checkout), `randint`, `choice`, `shuffle`, `sample` and `_randbelow` run in C on CPython’s own Mersenne Twister state; otherwise `FastRandom` is `PyFastRandom`, the pure-Python version. `modelly.core.rng.NATIVE` says which one is in use, and `MODELLY_PURE_PYTHON=1` forces the Python one.

A faster `random.Random` with the standard library’s exact streams.

`FastRandom` is a compiled core (`modelly._native.fastrng`, C on CPython’s own Mersenne Twister state) when it is built for this interpreter and passes a stream self-test at import, and the pure-Python `PyFastRandom` otherwise. `MODELLY_PURE_PYTHON=1` forces the Python version. Both give, for a seed, exactly the numbers `random.Random` gives.

`random.Random` implements `randint`, `choice`, `shuffle` and `sample` in Python, and each draw goes through `_randbelow` as a separate method call plus argument validation. In an agent-based model those four calls run millions of times per experiment. `FastRandom` reimplements them with the rejection loop written inline, making the same `getrandbits` calls in the same order, so for a given seed it produces exactly the same numbers as `random.Random`; a run seeded with either is reproducible with the other.

#### `class PyFastRandom(x=None)`

`random.Random` with the hot draws inlined in Python; identical streams.

The fallback for `FastRandom` where the compiled core is unavailable. Both versions pickle to the same state, so a pickle written with one loads into the other and continues the same stream.

Initialize an instance.

Optional argument x controls seeding, as for Random.seed().

#### `randint(a: int, b: int) → int`

Return a random integer in [a, b], like `random.randint`.

#### `choice(seq: Sequence[Any]) → Any`

Return a random element of `seq`, like `random.choice`.

#### `shuffle(x: MutableSequence[Any]) → None`

Shuffle `x` in place, like `random.shuffle` (same stream).

#### `sample(population: Sequence[Any], k: int, *, counts=None) → list`

Return `k` unique elements of `population`, like `random.sample`.

#### `class FastRandom(x=None)`

`random.Random` with its hot draws in C; identical streams.

`randint`, `choice`, `shuffle`, `sample` and `_randbelow` run in C on the same Mersenne Twister state as the rest of `random.Random`.

Initialize an instance.

Optional argument x controls seeding, as for Random.seed().

## Checkpoints

`Model.save`, `Model.load` and `Model.checkpoint_every` (listed under `Model`) write and read this format; see [Checkpoints](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/checkpoints.html).

Model checkpoints: save a run to one file and resume it bit for bit.

A checkpoint is a short text header followed by a pickle of the model:

```default
MODELLY-CHECKPOINT
{"format": 2, "modelly": "1.3.0", "python": "3.13", "compression": "gzip"}
<pickle, compressed or not>
```

The header is read without unpickling anything, so a file from another format, Modelly release or Python version is refused with a clear error before any of its bytes run.

Security: the payload is a pickle, and unpickling runs code chosen by whoever wrote the file. Only load checkpoints you created or otherwise trust.

#### `save_model(model: Model, path: str | Path, *, compress: bool = False) → None`

Write `model` to `path` as a checkpoint (see `Model.save()`).

The bytes go to a sibling temporary file first and `os.replace` moves it into place (atomic on every platform), so a reader never sees half a checkpoint.

#### `load_model(path: str | Path) → Model`

Read a checkpoint written by [`save_model()`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.checkpoint.save_model) (see `Model.load()`).

#### `class CheckpointWriter(model: Model, interval: float, path_pattern: str, compress: bool)`

Save the model every `interval` time units (see `Model.checkpoint_every()`).

Each save is a one-off LOW priority event that schedules the next one before writing, so the checkpoint itself holds the following save and a resumed run keeps checkpointing.

Schedule the first save `interval` time units from now.

#### `write() → None`

Schedule the next save, then save to `path_pattern.format(time=...)`.

#### `stop() → None`

Cancel the next save.

# Space

`modelly.space` holds the discrete cell spaces (grids, networks, Voronoi meshes), continuous space, property layers and the integer cell index. The names most models need are exported by the package itself: `from modelly.space import OrthogonalMooreGrid, CellAgent`.

Module

Contents

modelly.space.cells

Cell, CellCollection, the cell agents, CellIndex, Occupancy

modelly.space.base

DiscreteSpace, the base of every discrete space

modelly.space.grid

Grid, OrthogonalMooreGrid, OrthogonalVonNeumannGrid, HexGrid, property layers

modelly.space.network

Network

modelly.space.voronoi, modelly.space.delaunay

VoronoiGrid and the triangulation behind it

modelly.space.continuous

ContinuousSpace, ContinuousSpaceAgent, vectorised helpers

## Cells

`Cell` takes its neighbourhood methods (`neighborhood`, `get_neighborhood`) from `modelly.space.cells.neighborhood`; they are listed under `Cell`.

Cells are positions in space that can have properties and contain agents.

A cell represents a location that can: - Have properties (like temperature or resources) - Track and limit the agents it contains - Connect to neighboring cells - Provide neighborhood information

Cells form the foundation of the cell space system, enabling rich spatial environments where both location properties and agent behaviors matter. They’re useful for modeling things like varying terrain, infrastructure capacity, or environmental conditions.

#### `class Cell(coordinate: tuple[int, ...], position: ndarray | None = None, capacity: int | None = None, random: Random | None = None)`

The cell represents a position in a discrete space.

**Variables:**

- **coordinate** (*Coordinate*) – the logical position(or index) of the cell in the discrete space
- **position** (*np.ndarray** | **None*) – the physical position of the cell in the discrete space
- **agents** (*List**[*[*Agent*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.agent.Agent)*]*) – the agents occupying the cell
- **capacity** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – the maximum number of agents that can simultaneously occupy the cell
- **random** (*Random*) – the random number generator

Notes

Neighborhoods are cached per cell, keyed on `(radius, include_center)`. The cache belongs to the cell (not to the class), so discarding a space frees its cells, and changing one cell’s connections only invalidates that cell’s own neighborhoods.

Initialise the cell.

**Parameters:**

- **coordinate** – coordinates of the cell
- **position** – physical coordinates of the cell
- **capacity** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – the capacity of the cell. If None, the capacity is infinite
- **random** (*Random*) – the random number generator to use

#### `property position: ndarray`

**Returns:**

**Return type:**

np.ndarray

Returns a CellCollection of all neighboring cells for the given radius.

**Parameters:**

- **include_center** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – include the center of the neighborhood

**Returns:**

a CellCollection of all neighboring cells

#### `property neighborhood: CellCollection[Cell]`

Returns the direct neighborhood of the cell.

This is equivalent to cell.get_neighborhood(radius=1)

Collection class for managing and querying groups of cells.

The CellCollection class provides a consistent interface for operating on multiple cells, supporting: - Filtering and selecting cells based on conditions - Random cell and agent selection - Access to contained agents - Group operations

This is useful for implementing area effects, zones, or any operation that needs to work with multiple cells as a unit. The collection handles efficient iteration and agent access across cells. The class is used throughout the cell space implementation to represent neighborhoods, selections, and other cell groupings.

#### `class CellCollection(cells: Mapping[T, list[CellAgent]] | Iterable[T], random: Random | None = None)`

An immutable collection of cells.

**Variables:**

- **cells** (*List**[*[*Cell*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.cells.cell.Cell)*]*) – The list of cells this collection represents
- **agents** (*List**[*[*CellAgent*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.cells.agents.CellAgent)*]*) – List of agents occupying the cells in this collection
- **random** (*Random*) – The random number generator

Notes

With random=None the collection takes the generator of its first cell that has one, else the model generator of its first agent. A UserWarning is issued only when there is neither; pass random=self.random from a Model or Agent to avoid it.

Initialize a CellCollection.

**Parameters:**

- **cells** – cells to add to the collection
- **random** – a seeded random number generator; None takes the cells’ or their agents’ model generator.

#### `property empties: CellCollection[T]`

The cells of this collection that hold no agent, as a new collection.

Reads the live occupancy lists directly, so it costs one truth test per cell rather than a property call per cell.

**Raises:**

- [**ValueError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#ValueError) – If at_most is a negative integer, or a float not in the range (0.0, 1.0].

## Cell agents

Agents that understand how to exist in and move through cell spaces.

Provides specialized agent classes that handle cell occupation, movement, and proper registration: - CellAgent: Mobile agents that can move between cells - FixedAgent: Immobile agents permanently fixed to cells - Grid2DMovingAgent: Agents with grid-specific movement capabilities

These classes ensure consistent agent-cell relationships and proper state management as agents move through the space. They can be used directly or as examples for creating custom cell-aware agents.

#### `class FixedCell`

Bases: [`HasCell`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.cells.agents.HasCell)

Mixin for agents that are fixed to a cell.

Once assigned to a cell, the agent cannot be moved to a different cell. The assignment is atomic: if cell.add_agent() raises (e.g. capacity reached), the agent’s _modelly_cell reference is left unchanged.

#### `property cell: Cell | None`

The cell the agent is fixed to.

## Discrete spaces

Abstract Base class for building cell-based spatial environments.

DiscreteSpace provides the core functionality needed by all cell-based spaces: - Cell creation and tracking - Agent-cell relationship management - Property Layer support - Random selection capabilities - Capacity management

This serves as the foundation for specific space implementations like grids and networks, ensuring consistent behavior and shared functionality across different space types. All concrete cell space implementations (grids, networks, etc.) inherit from this class.

#### `space_agents(space: DiscreteSpace) → Iterator[CellAgent]`

The agents in the cells’ lists, then those a CellIndex tracks by row column.

#### `class DiscreteSpace(capacity: int | None = None, cell_klass: type[T] = <class 'modelly.space.cells.cell.Cell'>, random: Random | None = None)`

Base class for all discrete spaces.

**Variables:**

- **capacity** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – The capacity of the cells in the discrete space
- **all_cells** ([*CellCollection*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.cells.collection.CellCollection)) – The cells composing the discrete space
- **random** (*Random*) – The random number generator
- **cell_klass** (*Type*) – the type of cell class
- **empties** ([*CellCollection*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.cells.collection.CellCollection)) – collection of all cells that are empty
- **property_layers** ([*dict*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **np.ndarray**]*) – property_layer of the discrete space

Notes

A UserWarning is issued if random=None. You can resolve this warning by explicitly passing a random number generator. In most cases, this will be the seeded random number generator in the model. So, you would do random=self.random in a Model or Agent instance.

Instantiate a DiscreteSpace.

**Parameters:**

- **capacity** – capacity of cells
- **cell_klass** – base class for all cells
- **random** – random number generator

#### `property agents: AgentSet`

Return an AgentSet with the agents in the space, row-placed ones included.

#### `abstractmethod find_nearest_cell(position: ndarray) → T`

Find the cell at or nearest to the given position.

#### `add_cell(cell: T)`

Add a cell to the space.

**Parameters:**

**cell** – cell to add

Note

Discrete spaces rely on caching neighborhood relations for speedups. Adding or removing cells and connections at runtime is possible. However, only the caches of cells directly affected will be cleared. So if you rely on getting neighborhoods of cells with a radius higher than 1, these might not be cleared correctly if you are adding or removing cells and connections at runtime.

Warning

Coordinate Collision: If a cell already exists at the specified coordinates (e.g., cell1), it will be overwritten silently by the new cell (cell2).

Ensure the target coordinates are vacant before calling this method.

#### `remove_cell(cell: T)`

Remove a cell from the space.

Discrete spaces rely on caching neighborhood relations for speedups. Adding or removing cells and connections at runtime is possible. However, only the caches of cells directly affected will be cleared. So if you rely on getting neighborhoods of cells with a radius higher than 1, these might not be cleared correctly if you are adding or removing cells and connections at runtime.

So if you rely on getting neighborhoods of cells with a radius higher than 1, these might not be cleared correctly if you are adding or removing cells and connections at runtime.

#### `property all_cells`

Return all cells in space.

Return all empty in spaces.

#### `select_random_empty_cell() → T`

Select a random empty cell.

Sparse spaces are answered by a few random draws. The first time the draws all fail (or when `_try_random` is False) the space builds an index of its empty cells, kept current by `cell.empty` from then on, so every later call is O(1) regardless of how full the space is.

**Raises:**

[**ValueError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#ValueError) – If the space has no empty cell.

### Grids

#### `property cells_with_capacity: CellCollection[T]`

Return all cells that have available capacity (i.e. are not full).

A cell is considered *available* if `not cell.is_full`.

This is meaningfully different from `empties`: `empties` only includes cells with **zero** agents. If a cell has `capacity=5` and currently holds 3 agents it is **not** empty, but it **is** still available. `cells_with_capacity` is therefore the correct API for models where agents share cells up to a finite limit.

For cells with `capacity=None` (unlimited), every cell is always available regardless of how many agents it holds.

**Returns:**

All cells where `len(agents) < capacity` (or all cells when capacity is None).

**Return type:**

[CellCollection](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.cells.collection.CellCollection)[T]

Example:

```default
# Place an agent in any non-full cell
agent.move_to(grid.select_random_cell_with_capacity())

# Count how many cells still have room
len(list(grid.cells_with_capacity))
```

#### `select_random_cell_with_capacity() → Cell`

Select a random cell that has remaining capacity.

**Raises:**

[**IndexError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#IndexError) – If every cell in the grid is at full capacity.

Example:

```default
# Safe placement that respects capacity limits
free_cell = grid.select_random_cell_with_capacity()
agent.move_to(free_cell)
```

Grid-based cell space implementations with different connection patterns.

Provides several grid types for organizing cells: - OrthogonalMooreGrid: 8 neighbors in 2D, (3^n)-1 in nD - OrthogonalVonNeumannGrid: 4 neighbors in 2D, 2n in nD - HexGrid: 6 neighbors in hexagonal pattern (2D only)

Each grid type supports optional wrapping (torus) and cell capacity limits. Choose based on how movement and connectivity should work in your model - Moore for unrestricted movement, Von Neumann for orthogonal-only movement, or Hex for more uniform distances.

The shared machinery (cell creation, property layers, empty-cell selection, pickling) lives in [`modelly.space.grid.base`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#module-modelly.space.grid.base); `Grid` is re-exported here so `from modelly.space.grid.grids import Grid` keeps working.

All cells where `len(agents) < capacity` (or all cells when capacity is None).

**Return type:**

[CellCollection](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.cells.collection.CellCollection)[T]

Example:

```default
# Place an agent in any non-full cell
agent.move_to(grid.select_random_cell_with_capacity())

# Count how many cells still have room
len(list(grid.cells_with_capacity))
```

#### `select_random_cell_with_capacity() → Cell`

Select a random cell that has remaining capacity.

**Raises:**

[**IndexError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#IndexError) – If every cell in the grid is at full capacity.

Example:

```default
# Safe placement that respects capacity limits
free_cell = grid.select_random_cell_with_capacity()
agent.move_to(free_cell)
```

### Property layers

Grids take `create_property_layer`, `add_property_layer` and `remove_property_layer` from this mixin.

Property layers: numpy arrays attached to a grid and exposed on its cells.

A property layer is one `np.ndarray` shaped like the grid. The grid exposes it as an attribute (`grid.sugar`) and every cell of that grid gets an accessor (`cell.sugar`) that reads and writes the array at the cell’s coordinate, so vectorised updates on the array and per-cell reads stay in sync for free.

#### `class HasPropertyLayers`

Mixin giving a grid named property layers backed by numpy arrays.

Expects the host to define `dimensions` (the array shape), `cell_klass` (a class private to the grid, since accessors are installed on it), `property_layers` and `_read_only_layers`.

#### `create_property_layer(name: str, default_value=0.0, dtype=<class 'float'>, read_only: bool = False) → ndarray`

Create a property layer array and attach it to cells.

Warning: Do not reassign grid.name directly — this will detach it from property_layers and break cell-level access. Use in-place operations.

grid.sugar[:] = 0 # correct grid.sugar = array # wrong — breaks cell access

#### `add_property_layer(name: str, array: ndarray, read_only: bool = False) → None`

Attach an existing array as a property layer. Shape must match self.dimensions.

Warning: Do not reassign grid.name directly — this will detach it from property_layers and break cell-level access. Use in-place operations.

grid.sugar[:] = 0 # correct grid.sugar = array # wrong — breaks cell access

#### `remove_property_layer(name: str) → None`

Remove a property_layer and its grid and cell attributes.

**Parameters:**

**name** – property_layer name.

### Network

Network-based cell space using arbitrary connection patterns.

Creates spaces where cells connect based on network relationships rather than spatial proximity. Built on NetworkX graphs, this enables: - Arbitrary connectivity patterns between cells - Graph-based neighborhood definitions - Logical rather than physical distances - Dynamic connectivity changes - Integration with NetworkX’s graph algorithms

Useful for modeling systems like social networks, transportation systems, or any environment where connectivity matters more than physical location.

#### `class Network(G: Any, capacity: int | None = None, random: Random | None = None, cell_klass: type[Cell] = <class 'modelly.space.cells.cell.Cell'>, layout: Mapping | Callable | None = None)`

A Networked grid.

**Parameters:**

- **random** (*Random*) – a random number generator
- **cell_klass** ([*type*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#type)*[*[*Cell*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.cells.cell.Cell)*]*) – The base Cell class to use in the Network
- **layout** – A dictionary mapping node IDs to physical positions (x, y), or a callable that generates them (e.g. nx.spring_layout). It defaults to nx.circular_layout This ensures all nodes possess physical (x, y) positions for visualization and spatial queries without introducing performance bottlenecks on large graphs

### Voronoi

Cell spaces based on Voronoi tessellation around seed points.

Creates irregular spatial divisions by building cells around seed points, where each cell contains the area closer to its seed than any other. Features: - Organic-looking spaces from point sets - Automatic neighbor determination - Area-based cell capacities - Natural regional divisions

Useful for models requiring irregular but mathematically meaningful spatial divisions, like territories, service areas, or natural regions.

#### `class VoronoiGrid(centroids_coordinates: ~collections.abc.Sequence[~collections.abc.Sequence[float]], capacity: int | ~collections.abc.Callable | None = None, random: ~random.Random | None = None, cell_klass: type[~modelly.space.cells.cell.Cell] = <class 'modelly.space.cells.cell.Cell'>)`

Bases: [`DiscreteSpace`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.base.DiscreteSpace)

Voronoi meshed GridSpace.

A Voronoi Tessellation Grid.

Given a set of points, this class creates a grid where a cell is centered in each point, its neighbors are given by Voronoi Tessellation cells neighbors and the capacity by the polygon area.

**Parameters:**

- **capacity** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)* | **Callable*) – capacity of the cells in the discrete space, or a callable computing the (int) capacity of a cell from its (float) polygon area
- **random** (*Random*) – random number generator
- **cell_klass** ([*type*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#type)*[*[*Cell*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.cells.cell.Cell)*]*) – type of cell class

## Integer cells: index, occupancy and row-placed agents

Integer rows for the cells of a discrete space, and sparse operators over them.

Every discrete space (grid, network, Voronoi mesh) is a set of cells joined by `connections`. Numbering the cells gives each one a row, and the connections become a sparse adjacency matrix. Whole-population questions then cost one numpy call each instead of one Python loop per agent:

- `counts(rows)`: how many agents, or how much of a quantity, sit in each cell;
- `neighbor_sum(values)`: for every cell, the sum of `values` over its neighbours;
- `random_neighbor(rows)`: one uniformly chosen neighbour for every row.

Agents that declare a `Column` for their cell row (`row = Column(np.intp)`, kept current with `self.row = cell.index` when they move) can combine these with `ColumnTable.draw` into a vectorised step phase. See `docs/vectorised_phases.md` for the equivalence arguments.

#### `class CellIndex(space: DiscreteSpace)`

Rows for the cells of `space` and the sparse adjacency between them.

Building the index writes `cell.index` on every cell, in the order of `space.all_cells`. For grids that order is the C order of the coordinates, so a per-cell vector reshaped to the grid’s dimensions is a property layer.

Number the cells of `space`; the adjacency is built on first use.

#### `track(model: Model, agent_class: type, column: str = 'row') → None`

Declare that `agent_class` keeps its cell as a row `column`.

Such agents are in no cell’s agent list; tracking them makes the space list them (`space.agents`) and lets the visualisation place them at `index.cells[agent.<column>]`.

#### `tracked_agents() → Iterator[Agent]`

The live agents of every tracked class, in table order.

#### `cell_of(agent: Agent) → Cell`

The cell a tracked agent occupies, from its row column.

#### `rows(cells: Iterable[Cell]) → np.ndarray`

Return the row of each cell in `cells`.

#### `counts(rows: ndarray, weights: ndarray | None = None) → ndarray`

Per-cell total of `weights` (or of ones) over the agents sitting in `rows`.

#### `property adjacency: csr_matrix`

The cell adjacency as a CSR matrix with one entry per connection.

#### `neighbor_sum(values: ndarray) → ndarray`

For every cell, the sum of `values` over its neighbouring cells.

#### `random_neighbor(rows: ndarray, rng: Generator) → ndarray`

One uniformly chosen neighbour row per entry of `rows`.

A row without neighbours is returned unchanged.

#### `to_layer(values: ndarray) → ndarray`

Reshape a per-cell vector to the grid’s dimensions (a property layer view).

Who sits in which cell, from a row column, without per-cell agent lists.

Agents that keep their cell as a `Column` of rows (see `CellIndex`) move by assigning the column; nothing else has to be updated. When a step needs to know who shares a cell, `Occupancy` sorts the rows once (O(n log n)) and answers per-cell questions from the sorted order. `claim` is the vectorised form of “each claimant takes one of the members of its cell, if any is left”: it has the law of the sequential version in which the claimants act in a uniformly random order (see docs/vectorised_phases.md).

#### `class Occupancy(rows: ndarray, n_cells: int)`

The agents of a table grouped by cell row, rebuilt from the row column.

Sort the agents (their table indices) by the cell row they occupy.

#### `counts() → ndarray`

How many agents sit in each cell.

#### `bounds(cells: ndarray) → tuple[ndarray, ndarray]`

The `[start, end)` slice of `order` holding the members of each cell.

#### `members(cell: int) → ndarray`

The table indices of the agents in `cell`.

#### `random_member(cells: ndarray, rng: Generator) → ndarray`

One uniformly chosen member of each cell in `cells`, or `NO_MATCH` if empty.

#### `claim(occupancy: Occupancy, cells: ndarray, rng: Generator) → ndarray`

For each claimant, one distinct member of its cell, or `NO_MATCH`.

`cells[k]` is the cell of claimant `k`. The matching has the law of the sequential rule “claimants act in a uniformly random order and each takes a uniformly random member of its cell not yet taken”: every cell ends up with min(claimants, members) matches, a uniform random subset of its members is taken and a uniform random subset of its claimants is served. Each round, every unserved claimant draws a member of its cell; draws of already taken members are rejected, collisions go to a random priority, and the losers draw again while their cell still has a free member.

## Continuous space

`ContinuousSpace` takes its neighbour queries (`get_agents_in_radius`, `neighbors_within`, `get_k_nearest_agents`) from `modelly.space.continuous.queries`; they are listed under `ContinuousSpace`.

A Continuous Space class.

#### `class ContinuousSpace(dimensions: ArrayLike, torus: bool = False, random: Random | None = None, n_agents: int = 100)`

Continuous space where each agent can have an arbitrary position.

Create a new continuous space.

**Parameters:**

- **dimensions** – a numpy array like object where each row specifies the minimum and maximum value of that dimension.
- **torus** – boolean for whether the space wraps around or not
- **random** – a seeded stdlib random.Random instance
- **n_agents** – the expected number of agents in the space

Internally, a numpy array is used to store the positions of all agents. This is resized if needed, but you can control the initial size explicitly by passing n_agents.

#### `property dimensions: ndarray`

The `(ndims, 2)` array of each dimension’s minimum and maximum (read-only).

#### `property agents: AgentSet[A]`

Return an AgentSet with the agents in the space.

#### `calculate_difference_vector(point: ndarray, agents=None) → ndarray`

Calculate the difference vector between the point and all agenents.

**Parameters:**

- **point** – the point to calculate the difference vector for
- **agents** – the agents to calculate the difference vector of point with. By default, all agents are considered.

#### `calculate_distances(point: ArrayLike, agents: Iterable[Agent] | None = None, **kwargs) → tuple[ndarray, list]`

Calculate the distance between the point and all agents.

**Parameters:**

- **point** – the point to calculate the difference vector for
- **agents** – the agents to calculate the difference vector of point with. By default, all agents are considered.
- **kwargs** – any additional keyword arguments are passed to scipy’s cdist, which is used only if torus is False. This allows for non-Euclidian distance measures.

#### `get_agents_in_radius(point: ArrayLike, radius: float | int = 1) → tuple[list, ndarray]`

Return the agents and their distances within a radius for the point.

#### `get_k_nearest_agents(point: ArrayLike, k: int = 1) → tuple[list, ndarray]`

Return the k nearest agents and their distances to the point.

Notes

This method returns exactly k agents, ignoring ties. In case of ties, the earlier an agent is inserted the higher it will rank.

If fewer than k agents are present in the space, all agents are returned and a UserWarning is emitted to indicate that the requested k could not be satisfied. If the space is empty or k <= 0, an empty result is returned without a warning.

#### `in_bounds(point: ArrayLike) → bool`

Check if point is inside the bounds of the space.

#### `neighbors_within(radius: float | int) → dict[Agent, list[Agent]]`

Return, for every agent, the other agents within `radius` of it.

One KD-tree is built from the positions as they are now and queried for the whole population in a single call, which is O(n log n) instead of the O(n²) of asking each agent in turn. On a torus the tree is periodic, so neighbours across the wrap are found. Use it at the start of a step for a simultaneous update: every agent then sees the same snapshot of positions.

The result is cached on the positions’ content, so asking again before any agent moves costs a hash of the position array instead of a new tree.

**Returns:**

dict mapping each agent to a list of its neighbours (itself excluded).

#### `torus_correct(point: ArrayLike) → ndarray`

Apply a torus correction to the point.

Continuous space agents.

#### `class HasPositionProtocol(*args, **kwargs)`

Bases: [`Protocol`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#typing.Protocol)

Protocol for continuous space position holders.

Bases: [`Agent`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.agent.Agent)

**Variables:**

- **space** ([*ContinuousSpace*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.continuous.space.ContinuousSpace)) – the continuous space in which the agent is located

#### `get_neighbors_in_radius(radius: float | int = 1) → tuple[list[ContinuousSpaceAgent], ndarray]`

**Parameters:**

**radius** – radius within which to look for neighbors

#### `get_nearest_neighbors(k: int = 1) → tuple[list[ContinuousSpaceAgent], ndarray]`

Get neighbors within radius.

**Parameters:**

**k** – the number of nearest neighbors to return

Whole-population operations on a continuous space.

`neighbors_within` on the space answers “who is near whom” with one KD-tree. The two helpers here complete the vectorised step: `pairs_within` returns the same neighbour relation as index pairs, ready for `np.add.at` or `bincount` aggregation, and `move_all` writes every agent’s new position in one call.

#### `pairs_within(space: ContinuousSpace, radius: float) → tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]`

Every unordered pair of agents within `radius`, as two row arrays `(i, j)`.

Rows index `space.agent_positions` and `space.active_agents`; `i < j` and each pair appears once. On a torus the tree is periodic.

#### `difference_vectors(space: ContinuousSpace, i: np.ndarray, j: np.ndarray) → np.ndarray`

The vector from agent `i` to agent `j` for each pair, torus-corrected.

#### `move_all(space: ContinuousSpace, positions: np.ndarray) → None`

Set every agent’s position at once; wraps on a torus, clips otherwise.

# Geospatial space

## GeoSpace

`GeoSpace` is a `ContinuousSpace`: it also has `get_agents_in_radius`, `neighbors_within` and `get_k_nearest_agents`, listed under [Continuous space](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#continuous-space).

A vector geospatial space: agents as points, polygons as regions, one CRS.

`GeoSpace` is a `ContinuousSpace` whose coordinates are those of a projected coordinate reference system (metres for UTM), so the continuous space’s KD-tree queries (`get_agents_in_radius`, `neighbors_within`, `get_k_nearest_agents`) measure real distances. Agent positions stay one numpy array; regions are the rows of a GeoDataFrame, indexed by an STRtree for point-in-polygon and distance lookups.

The CRS is set once, at the space. Inputs that carry another CRS (regions, points, geometries) are reprojected into it; a geographic CRS (latitude and longitude) is replaced by the UTM zone that covers the regions, since degrees are not distances.

#### `class GeoSpace(regions: GeoDataFrame | None = None, crs: Any = None, random: Random | None = None, *, bounds: Sequence[float] | None = None, n_agents: int = 100)`

Bases: [`RegionQueriesMixin`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/geo.html#modelly.space.geo.regions.RegionQueriesMixin), [`ContinuousSpace`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.continuous.space.ContinuousSpace)

Agents as points and polygons as regions, in one projected CRS.

**Variables:**

- **crs** – the space’s `pyproj.CRS`, or `None` for plain planar coordinates.
- **regions** – a GeoDataFrame of the region polygons in `crs`; its index labels the regions.

Create a geospatial space.

**Parameters:**

- **regions** – polygons that make up the study area, in any CRS; reprojected to `crs`.
- **crs** – the space’s CRS (anything `pyproj.CRS` accepts). Defaults to the CRS of `regions`, or to its UTM zone when that CRS is geographic.
- **random** – a seeded `random.Random`, usually `model.random`.
- **bounds** – `(minx, miny, maxx, maxy)` in `crs`; defaults to the regions’ bounds.
- **n_agents** – the expected number of agents, to size the position array.

#### `project(geometry: Any, crs: Any = None) → Any`

Return `geometry` in the space’s CRS.

**Parameters:**

- **geometry** – a Shapely geometry, a GeoSeries or a GeoDataFrame.
- **crs** – the CRS `geometry` is in; GeoPandas objects default to their own CRS. `None` for a Shapely geometry means it is already in the space’s CRS.

#### `project_points(xy: ndarray, crs: Any = None) → ndarray`

#### `to_geodataframe(what: str = 'agents', attributes: Sequence[str] = ()) → GeoDataFrame`

The agents (as points, with `attributes`) or the regions (with agent counts).

#### `to_file(path: str | Path, what: str = 'agents', attributes: Sequence[str] = ()) → Path`

Write `to_geodataframe(what, attributes)` as GeoParquet or GeoJSON, by suffix.

`.parquet` and `.geoparquet` write GeoParquet (needs `pyarrow`); `.geojson` and `.json` write GeoJSON in WGS 84, as the GeoJSON standard asks.

Region neighbourhoods of a `GeoSpace`: contiguity (queen, rook) and distance.

#### `class RegionQueriesMixin`

Neighbourhoods between the polygons of `regions`, built on one STRtree.

Relies on the host providing `regions` (a GeoDataFrame), and the cache slots `_region_tree_cache` and `_contiguity_cache`.

#### `contiguity(kind: str = 'queen') → csr_matrix`

The region adjacency as a symmetric CSR matrix, rows in `regions` order.

**Parameters:**

**kind** – `"queen"`: regions sharing at least one point are neighbours; `"rook"`: they must share a border of positive length.

#### `region_neighbors(label: Any, kind: str = 'queen', distance: float | None = None) → list`

Labels of the regions next to region `label`.

**Parameters:**

- **label** – the region label.
- **kind** – `"queen"` or `"rook"` contiguity, used when `distance` is `None`.
- **distance** – if given, every other region within this distance of `label`.

#### `regions_within(geometry: Any, distance: float | None = None) → list`

Labels of the regions that intersect `geometry`, or lie within `distance` of it.

Agents located at a point of a `GeoSpace`.

#### `class GeoAgent(space: GeoSpace, model: Model, position: Any = None, crs: Any = None)`

Bases: [`ContinuousSpaceAgent`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.continuous.agents.ContinuousSpaceAgent)

An agent at a point of a `GeoSpace`; its position is a row of the position array.

**Variables:**

- **space** ([*GeoSpace*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/geo.html#modelly.space.geo.space.GeoSpace)) – the space the agent is in.
- **position** (*np.ndarray*) – `(x, y)` in the space’s CRS.

Place a new agent in `space`.

**Parameters:**

- **space** – the geospatial space.
- **model** – the model the agent belongs to.
- **position** – a Shapely `Point` or `(x, y)`; defaults to the centre of the space.
- **crs** – the CRS of `position`, if not the space’s.

#### `move_to(point: Any, crs: Any = None) → None`

Move to `point` (a Shapely `Point` or `(x, y)`, in `crs`).

#### `property region: Any`

The label of the region the agent is in, or `None`.

#### `property geometry: Point`

The agent’s position as a Shapely `Point`.

## Rasters

Rasters as property layers: a GeoTIFF band aligned to a grid space.

A `RasterLayer` keeps one band in `values`, shaped like an orthogonal grid (`(width, height)`, indexed `[x, y]` with `y = 0` the southern row), so it can be attached to a grid as a property layer: `cell.<name>` and the raster share one array, and a vectorised update of the layer is a raster update. The affine `transform` maps pixel `(column, row)` of the north-up band to map coordinates in `crs`, as in rasterio.

#### `class RasterLayer(data: ndarray, transform: Any, crs: Any = None, nodata: Any = None)`

One raster band with its transform, CRS and nodata value.

**Variables:**

- **values** – the band, shape `(width, height)`, indexed `[x, y]` with `y` northward.
- **transform** – the `affine.Affine` from pixel `(column, row)` to map coordinates.
- **crs** – the `pyproj.CRS` of the map coordinates, or `None`.
- **nodata** – the value marking missing cells, or `None`.

Wrap a north-up band (rows from north to south, as rasterio reads it).

**Parameters:**

- **data** – a 2-D array, shape `(rows, columns)`.
- **transform** – an `affine.Affine`, or its six coefficients `(a, b, c, d, e, f)`.
- **crs** – anything `pyproj.CRS` accepts.
- **nodata** – the value of missing cells.

#### `property shape: tuple[int, int]`

the dimensions of a grid aligned to the raster.

**Type:**

`(width, height)`

#### `property array: ndarray`

a view of `values`.

**Type:**

The band north-up, shape `(rows, columns)`

#### `classmethod from_file(path: str | Path, band: int = 1) → RasterLayer`

Read one band of a raster file (GeoTIFF or any format rasterio reads).

#### `to_file(path: str | Path) → Path`

Write the band, with its transform, CRS and nodata value, as a GeoTIFF.

#### `cells_of(xy: ndarray, crs: Any = None) → ndarray`

Grid coordinate `(x, y)` of the cell under every point, `-1` outside.

**Parameters:**

- **xy** – an `(n, 2)` array of map coordinates.
- **crs** – the CRS of `xy` when it differs from the raster’s.

#### `sample(xy: ndarray, crs: Any = None) → ndarray`

The raster value under every point, as floats; `nan` outside or on nodata.

#### `sample_agents(space: GeoSpace) → np.ndarray`

The raster value at every agent of `space`, in `active_agents` order.

#### `cell_centers() → ndarray`

Map coordinates of every cell centre, shape `(width, height, 2)`.

#### `attach(grid: HasPropertyLayers, name: str, read_only: bool = False) → None`

Attach `values` to `grid` as property layer `name` (shared, not copied).

#### `to_grid(name: str, random: Random | None = None, **kwargs) → OrthogonalMooreGrid`

A new `OrthogonalMooreGrid` of the raster’s shape with the band as layer `name`.

Extra keyword arguments (`torus`, `capacity`, …) go to the grid.

#### `reproject(crs: Any, resampling: str = 'nearest') → RasterLayer`

A new layer warped to `crs` with rasterio (`resampling` names the method).

## Road networks

Road networks: a NetworkX graph with node coordinates as a `Network` space, and routing.

Nodes carry their coordinates as `x` and `y` attributes (the OSMnx convention) and edges a `length`; edges without one get the straight-line length between their ends. The graph is reprojected once into the network’s CRS. Agents can stand on its nodes as `CellAgent``s of ``space`, and route with NetworkX (one pair) or scipy (many sources).

#### `class RoadNetwork(graph: Any, crs: Any = None, random: Random | None = None, weight: str = 'length')`

A road graph in one projected CRS, its `Network` space and shortest paths.

**Variables:**

- **graph** – the NetworkX graph (any of Graph, DiGraph, MultiGraph, MultiDiGraph).
- **crs** – the `pyproj.CRS` of the node coordinates, or `None`.
- **space** – a `Network` space with one cell per node, at the node’s coordinates.
- **weight** – the default edge attribute for routing.

Wrap `graph`; its own CRS is `graph.graph["crs"]`, as OSMnx sets it.

**Parameters:**

- **graph** – a NetworkX graph whose nodes have `x` and `y` attributes.
- **crs** – the CRS to route in; defaults to the graph’s, or its UTM zone if geographic.
- **random** – a seeded `random.Random` for the `Network` space.
- **weight** – the default edge attribute shortest paths minimise.

#### `node_of(point: Any) → Any`

`point` itself if it is a node, else the node nearest to it (`Point` or `(x, y)`).

#### `nearest_nodes(xy: ndarray) → ndarray`

Row (position in `nodes`) of the node nearest to every point of `xy`.

#### `shortest_path(origin: Any, destination: Any, weight: str | None = None) → list`

The nodes of a shortest path; `origin` and `destination` are nodes or points.

#### `path_length(origin: Any, destination: Any, weight: str | None = None) → float`

The total `weight` of a shortest path between two nodes or points.

#### `travel_time(origin: Any, destination: Any) → float`

The shortest travel time between two nodes or points (see `add_travel_times`).

#### `add_travel_times(speed: float) → None`

Set `travel_time = length / speed` on every edge.

**Parameters:**

**speed** – in CRS units per unit of model time, for edges without a `speed` attribute of their own.

#### `distances_from(origin: Any, cutoff: float | None = None, weight: str | None = None) → dict`

Shortest `weight` from `origin` to every node reachable within `cutoff`.

#### `distance_matrix(origins: Any, weight: str | None = None) → ndarray`

Shortest `weight` from every origin (nodes or points) to every node, with scipy.

**Returns:**

an array of shape `(len(origins), len(nodes))`; unreachable nodes are `inf`.

#### `routing_matrix(weight: str | None = None) → csr_matrix`

The graph as a CSR matrix of `weight`, rows in `nodes` order.

Parallel edges keep the smallest weight; an undirected edge counts both ways.

#### `invalidate(weight: str | None = None) → None`

Forget the routing matrix of `weight` (all when `None`) after edges changed.

#### `path_geometry(path: list) → LineString`

The polyline through the coordinates of the nodes of `path`.

#### `agents_within(space: GeoSpace, origin: Any, distance: float, weight: str | None = None) → list[Agent]`

The agents of `space` whose nearest node is within network `distance` of `origin`.

#### `download_osm(place: str, network_type: str = 'drive', crs: Any = None, random: Random | None = None) → RoadNetwork`

Download the road network of `place` from OpenStreetMap (needs the `osm` extra).

Edges get OSMnx’s `speed_kph` and `travel_time` (seconds) attributes. This makes a network request: cache the result (`osmnx.save_graphml`) rather than calling it per run.

None of them holds personal data.

**Parameters:**

#### `sample_landcover() → RasterLayer`

# Networks

`modelly.space.networks` holds the temporal and multilayer networks, contact matrices, network statistics and importers. It needs only numpy and scipy; NetworkX and igraph are used only to convert from their graphs. The guide is [Networks](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/networks.html). The static network cell space, `Network`, is on the [Space](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#network) page.

Module

Contents

TemporalNetwork, TemporalEdge

modelly.space.networks.multilayer

MultilayerNetwork

modelly.space.networks.contacts

contact_matrix, age_groups

modelly.space.networks.base

## Temporal networks

Temporal networks: edges that exist during an interval of model time.

Every edge has an activation time `start` and an end time `end` and is active on `start <= time < end`. The network keeps two heaps of pending changes, so moving the clock forward with `advance_to` touches only the edges that switch on or off in between: O(changed edges x log edges). Neighbour queries read the active adjacency, O(degree). Given a `clock` (anything with a `time`, usually the model), every query first advances to `clock.time`, so the answers are always those of the current time.

Moving the clock backwards (a rewind) replays every edge from the start: O(edges).

#### `class TemporalEdge(u: int, v: int, start: float, end: float, weight: float)`

One edge with its lifetime, between node rows `u` and `v`.

Create new instance of TemporalEdge(u, v, start, end, weight)

#### `u: int`

Alias for field number 0

#### `v: int`

Alias for field number 1

#### `start: float`

Alias for field number 2

#### `end: float`

Alias for field number 3

#### `weight: float`

Alias for field number 4

#### `class TemporalNetwork(nodes: int | Iterable[Hashable] = 0, directed: bool = False, clock: Any = None)`

Edges with lifetimes, queried at the current time.

**Variables:**

- **nodes** – the node labels, in row order.
- **time** – the time the active edges correspond to.
- **clock** – an object with a `time` attribute that queries follow, or `None`.

Create an empty temporal network.

**Parameters:**

- **nodes** – a count (labels `0 .. n-1`) or the node labels; more are added by edges.
- **directed** – whether edges are one-way.
- **clock** – an object with a `time` attribute (a `Model`) queries advance to.

#### `add_edge(u: Hashable, v: Hashable, interval: tuple[float, float] = (-inf, inf), weight: float = 1.0) → int`

Add an edge active on `start <= time < end`, and return its id.

**Parameters:**

- **u** – one end (added as a node if new).
- **v** – the other end.
- **interval** – `(start, end)`; the default is always active.
- **weight** – the edge weight.

#### `remove_edge(edge_id: int) → None`

Remove an edge, active or not; pending changes for it are dropped lazily.

#### `advance_to(time: float) → int`

Make the active edges those of `time`; return how many edges changed.

#### `neighbors(node: Hashable) → list`

The nodes linked to `node` by an active edge.

#### `weighted_neighbors(node: Hashable) → dict`

Neighbour label to the summed weight of the active edges to it.

#### `degree(node: Hashable) → int`

The number of distinct active neighbours of `node`.

#### `has_edge(u: Hashable, v: Hashable) → bool`

Whether an active edge links `u` to `v`.

#### `active_edges() → Iterator[tuple[Any, Any, float]]`

`(u, v, weight)` for every active edge.

#### `number_of_active_edges() → int`

The number of active edges.

#### `adjacency() → csr_matrix`

The active adjacency (summed weights) as a CSR matrix, rows in `nodes` order.

## Multilayer networks

Multilayer networks: one set of nodes, several layers of weighted edges.

A contact network for an epidemic is the classic case: the same people are linked in a household layer, a school layer and a work layer, each with its own edges and its own weight (how much a contact on that layer counts). Queries take one layer, several, or all of them combined, with `combined weight = sum(layer weight * edge weight)`.

Edges are kept per layer in dictionaries of rows, so `add_edge` and `remove_edge` cost O(1) and `neighbors` costs O(degree). `adjacency` returns the sparse matrix for vectorised steps (`adjacency() @ infected`); it is cached per layer and rebuilt, in O(edges of that layer), on the first call after the layer changed.

#### `class MultilayerNetwork(nodes: int | Iterable[Hashable], layers: Mapping[str, float] | Iterable[str] = (), directed: bool = False)`

Nodes linked on named layers, each layer with a weight.

**Variables:**

- **nodes** – the node labels, in row order.
- **layer_weights** – layer name to its weight in combined queries.
- **directed** – whether an edge `u -> v` leaves `v -> u` absent.

Create a network over `nodes`.

**Parameters:**

- **nodes** – a count (labels `0 .. n-1`) or the node labels.
- **layers** – layer names, or a mapping of layer name to weight (default 1).
- **directed** – whether edges are one-way.

#### `property layers: list[str]`

The layer names, in the order they were added.

#### `add_layer(name: str, weight: float = 1.0) → None`

Add an empty layer, or change the weight of an existing one.

#### `add_edge(u: Hashable, v: Hashable, layer: str, weight: float = 1.0) → None`

Link `u` and `v` on `layer` (created if new); new nodes are added.

#### `add_edges(pairs: Iterable[tuple[Hashable, Hashable]], layer: str, weight: float = 1.0) → None`

Link every `(u, v)` of `pairs` on `layer` with the same `weight`.

#### `remove_edge(u: Hashable, v: Hashable, layer: str) → None`

Remove the edge between `u` and `v` on `layer`.

#### `has_edge(u: Hashable, v: Hashable, layer: str | None = None) → bool`

Whether `u` and `v` are linked on `layer`, or on any layer.

#### `neighbors(node: Hashable, layer: str | Sequence[str] | None = None) → list`

The nodes linked to `node` on the selected layers (all by default).

#### `weighted_neighbors(node: Hashable, layer: str | Sequence[str] | None = None) → dict`

Neighbour label to combined weight, `sum(layer weight * edge weight)`.

#### `degree(node: Hashable, layer: str | Sequence[str] | None = None) → int`

The number of distinct neighbours of `node` on the selected layers.

#### `edges(layer: str) → Iterator[tuple[Any, Any, float]]`

`(u, v, weight)` for every edge of `layer` (each undirected edge once).

#### `number_of_edges(layer: str | Sequence[str] | None = None) → int`

The number of edges on the selected layers, counted per layer.

#### `adjacency(layer: LayerSelection = None) → csr_matrix`

The combined weighted adjacency of the selected layers, rows in `nodes` order.

#### `to_networkx(layer: str | Sequence[str] | None = None) → Any`

A NetworkX graph of the selected layers, with the combined `weight` on edges.

## Contact matrices

Contact matrices: mean contacts between groups (age bands), for epidemic models.

#### `age_groups(ages: Sequence[float], breaks: Sequence[float]) → ndarray`

The group of every age: `0` below `breaks[0]`, `i` in `[breaks[i-1], breaks[i])`.

`age_groups(ages, [18, 65])` gives `0` for children, `1` for adults and `2` for people aged 65 and over.

#### `contact_matrix(network: Any, groups: Sequence[int], layer: str | Sequence[str] | None = None, n_groups: int | None = None) → ndarray`

Mean contacts a member of group `a` has with members of group `b`.

`C[a, b] = W(a, b) / N(a)`, where `W(a, b)` is the total weight of the edges from members of `a` to members of `b` and `N(a)` the size of group `a`; rows of empty groups are zero. For an undirected network `N(a) C[a, b] = N(b) C[b, a]`.

**Parameters:**

- **network** – a `MultilayerNetwork` or `TemporalNetwork`, or a sparse adjacency.
- **groups** – the group (`0 .. n_groups-1`) of every node, in row order.
- **layer** – for a multilayer network, the layer or layers to count (all by default), combined with their layer weights.
- **n_groups** – the number of groups; defaults to `max(groups) + 1`.

## Network statistics

Cheap network statistics for data collection: degrees, clustering, components.

Every statistic takes a graph in any of the forms a model holds: a `MultilayerNetwork` or `TemporalNetwork` (its current combined adjacency), a `Network` cell space, a NetworkX graph, an igraph graph or a scipy sparse matrix. The structure is read as a simple undirected graph (weights, edge directions and self-loops are ignored), and the work is a few sparse-matrix products, so a reporter costs milliseconds on large graphs. On simple undirected graphs the results equal NetworkX’s `degree_histogram`, `clustering`, `average_clustering` and connected component sizes.

`network_reporter` wraps a statistic as a `DataCollector` model reporter that can be checkpointed (no lambda):

```default
DataCollector({"giant": network_reporter("contacts", largest_component)})
```

#### `as_adjacency(graph: Any) → csr_matrix`

The binary, symmetric, loop-free adjacency of `graph` as a CSR matrix.

#### `degrees(graph: Any) → ndarray`

The degree of every node, in node order.

#### `degree_distribution(graph: Any) → ndarray`

`counts[k]` = number of nodes of degree `k`, as `networkx.degree_histogram`.

#### `clustering(graph: Any) → ndarray`

The local clustering coefficient of every node, as `networkx.clustering`.

#### `average_clustering(graph: Any) → float`

The mean local clustering over all nodes, as `networkx.average_clustering`.

#### `component_sizes(graph: Any) → ndarray`

The sizes of the connected components, largest first.

#### `largest_component(graph: Any) → int`

The number of nodes in the largest connected component.

#### `mean_degree(graph: Any) → float`

The mean degree.

#### `network_reporter(attribute: str, statistic: Callable[[Any], Any]) → partial`

A model reporter computing `statistic(getattr(model, attribute))`.

Unlike a lambda it can be pickled, so models that use it can be checkpointed.

**Parameters:**

- **attribute** – the model attribute holding the network.
- **statistic** – a module-level function of the network, such as `mean_degree`.

## Import and export

Networks from NetworkX, igraph and edge-list CSV files, and back to CSV.

Edge lists are CSV files with a header. Multilayer files have `source` and `target` columns and optional `layer` and `weight` columns; temporal files add `start` and an optional `end`. Files are read and written as UTF-8 on every platform; node labels read from a file are strings.

#### `from_networkx(graph: Any, layer_attribute: str | None = None, weight: str = 'weight') → MultilayerNetwork`

A `MultilayerNetwork` with the nodes and edges of a NetworkX graph.

**Parameters:**

- **graph** – any NetworkX graph; a directed graph gives a directed network.
- **layer_attribute** – the edge attribute naming each edge’s layer; without it, or for edges lacking it, edges go to layer `"default"`.
- **weight** – the edge attribute holding the weight (1 when missing).

#### `from_igraph(graph: Any, layer_attribute: str | None = None, weight: str = 'weight') → MultilayerNetwork`

A `MultilayerNetwork` from an igraph graph (igraph is optional, not a dependency).

Nodes are labelled by the vertex attribute `name` when present, else by index.

#### `read_edge_list(path: str | Path, directed: bool = False) → MultilayerNetwork`

A `MultilayerNetwork` from a CSV edge list (`source,target[,layer][,weight]`).

#### `write_edge_list(network: MultilayerNetwork, path: str | Path) → Path`

Write every edge of every layer as `source,target,layer,weight` (UTF-8 CSV).

#### `read_temporal_edge_list(path: str | Path, directed: bool = False, clock: Any = None) → TemporalNetwork`

A `TemporalNetwork` from a CSV edge list (`source,target,start[,end][,weight]`).

A missing or empty `end` means the edge never ends.

Node rows shared by the temporal and multilayer networks.

Nodes are any hashable labels; each gets an integer row, in insertion order, so the network’s adjacency is a sparse matrix whose rows line up with a per-node numpy vector (an agent column, a state array). Edges live in dictionaries keyed by rows, so adding or removing one edge costs O(1) and a neighbour query costs O(degree).

#### `class NodeRows`

Labels to rows and back, for a network over `nodes`.

#### `add_node(node: Hashable) → int`

Add `node` if it is new, and return its row.

#### `row(node: Hashable) → int`

The row of `node`.

#### `rows(nodes: Iterable[Hashable]) → ndarray`

The rows of `nodes`.

#### `csr_from_rows(rows: dict[int, dict[int, float]], n: int, scale: float = 1.0) → csr_matrix`

A CSR matrix with entry `scale * rows[i][j]` for every stored pair.

# Synthetic populations

`modelly.population` builds people, households, places and contact networks from aggregate tables. It needs numpy and pandas; `locate_households` takes a `GeoSpace` (the `geo` extra). The guide is [Synthetic populations](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/population.html).

Module

Contents

ipf, trs, synthesize_population, marginal_errors

modelly.population.annealing

anneal, Annealing, total_absolute_error

assign_households, household_sizes, HouseholdSpec

locate_households, assign_places, PlaceSpec

modelly.population.contacts

contact_network, place_groups, ContactLayers

## Fitting marginals

Synthetic populations from census-style marginals, by iterative proportional fitting.

Census tables usually give, per region, the count of people in each level of each attribute (age band, sex, household size) but not the joint table. `ipf` fits a joint table to those marginals, starting from a `seed` (a microsample cross-tabulation, or ones), `trs` rounds a fitted table to whole people (truncate, replicate, sample), and `synthesize_population` turns the fitted tables into one row per person, ready to create one agent per row. `marginal_errors` compares a synthetic population with the marginals it was drawn from.

**Reference:**

Lovelace, R. and Ballas, D. (2013). ‘Truncate, replicate, sample’: a method for creating integer weights for spatial microsimulation. Computers, Environment and Urban Systems, 41, 1-11.

#### `ipf(seed: ndarray, marginals: Sequence[Sequence[float]], tolerance: float = 1e-10, max_iterations: int = 1000) → ndarray`

Fit a table to its one-dimensional marginals by iterative proportional fitting.

**Parameters:**

- **seed** – the starting table, one axis per attribute; its zeros stay zero.
- **marginals** – the target totals along each axis, in axis order; all sum to the same total.
- **tolerance** – stop when no marginal is off by more than `tolerance` times the total.
- **max_iterations** – the most fitting rounds.

**Returns:**

the fitted table, of the shape of `seed`.

#### `synthesize_population(categories: Mapping[str, Sequence[Any]], marginals: Mapping[Any, Mapping[str, Sequence[float]]], rng: Generator, seed: ndarray | None = None) → DataFrame`

One row per synthetic person, with a `region` column and one column per attribute.

**Parameters:**

- **categories** – attribute name to its levels, for example `{"age": ["0-17", "18+"]}`.
- **marginals** – region label to, per attribute, the count of people at each level.
- **rng** – a numpy generator (`model.rng`) to round fitted counts to whole people.
- **seed** – the starting joint table (shape: one axis per attribute); defaults to ones.

**Returns:**

a DataFrame. The fitted table is rounded to whole people at random, one level of the first attribute at a time (floors, then the remainder drawn in proportion to the fractional parts). With whole-number marginals every region gets exactly its total and its first attribute’s counts; the other marginals are met in expectation, each count off by less than the number of first-attribute levels.

#### `trs(expected: ndarray, rng: Generator) → ndarray`

Whole counts with the same total: truncate, replicate, sample.

Every cell keeps the floor of its expected count; the people left over (the total’s rounding minus the floors) go to distinct cells drawn without replacement, in proportion to their fractional parts. Each count is then within one of its expected value and the total is exact for a whole-number total.

**Parameters:**

- **expected** – the fitted counts, any shape; they are flattened.
- **rng** – a numpy generator (`model.rng`).

**Returns:**

an `int64` array of the flattened shape.

#### `marginal_errors(people: DataFrame, marginals: Mapping[Any, Mapping[str, Sequence[float]]], categories: Mapping[str, Sequence[Any]]) → DataFrame`

Synthetic against target counts, one row per (region, attribute, level).

**Parameters:**

- **people** – one row per person, with a `region` column and one column per attribute.
- **marginals** – region label to, per attribute, the target count at each level.
- **categories** – attribute name to its levels, in the order of the marginals.

**Returns:**

a DataFrame with columns `region`, `attribute`, `level`, `target`, `synthetic` and `error` (`synthetic - target`).

## Combinatorial optimisation

Combinatorial optimisation: choose whole records from a sample to match census totals.

IPF fits a table of people; it cannot keep the members of a household together. The combinatorial-optimisation approach does: draw `size` records (households, each with its members’ counts) from a sample, with replacement, and swap one drawn record for another while that brings the totals closer to the targets. `anneal` does it by simulated annealing: a swap that worsens the total absolute error `TAE` by `d` is still taken with probability `exp(-d / T)`, where the temperature `T` falls geometrically, so the search can leave local optima early and settles at the end.

The sample is yours: a public-use microdata sample, a survey, or a synthetic sample. Modelly bundles no microdata.

References

Williamson, P., Birkin, M. and Rees, P. H. (1998). The estimation of population microdata by using data from small area statistics and samples of anonymised records. Environment and Planning A, 30(5), 785-816.

Harland, K., Heppenstall, A., Smith, D. and Birkin, M. (2012). Creating realistic synthetic populations at varying spatial scales: a comparative critique of population synthesis techniques. Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation, 15(1), 1.

#### `class Annealing(size: int, iterations: int = 20000, temperature: float = 1.0, cooling: float = 0.9995)`

One simulated-annealing run: how many records to draw and the cooling schedule.

**Variables:**

- **size** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – the number of records to draw (the region’s households, say).
- **iterations** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – the most swaps tried; the run stops early at a perfect fit.
- **temperature** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – the starting temperature, in units of the targets (people).
- **cooling** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – the factor applied to the temperature after every swap tried.

#### `total_absolute_error(sample: DataFrame, selection: ndarray, targets: Mapping[str, float]) → float`

`sum(|total of the selected records - target|)` over the target columns.

**Parameters:**

- **sample** – one row per record, with one numeric column per target.
- **selection** – row positions of the selected records (repeats allowed).
- **targets** – column name to its target total.

#### `anneal(sample: DataFrame, targets: Mapping[str, float], settings: Annealing, rng: Generator) → ndarray`

Row positions of `settings.size` records of `sample` whose totals fit `targets`.

**Parameters:**

- **sample** – one row per record, with one numeric column per target (for a household: its children, adults, seniors, a one-hot of its size, …).
- **targets** – column name to its target total in the region.
- **settings** – the number of records and the cooling schedule.
- **rng** – a numpy generator (`model.rng`): the start and every swap.

**Returns:**

an `intp` array of `settings.size` row positions, with repeats.

## Households

Households: synthetic people grouped by a household-size distribution, each with a head.

Census tables give, per region, how many households have one, two, three… members. `assign_households` draws that many households for the people of each region (rounded to whole households with `trs`, then grown or shrunk one member at a time until they hold exactly the region’s people), gives every household a head among the people who can head one (adults), and spreads everybody else over the remaining places at random. The people, and so their marginals, are unchanged: only a `household` column is added.

#### `class HouseholdSpec(sizes: Mapping[Any, Sequence[float]], heads: Sequence[Any], column: str = 'age')`

How to group the people of each region into households.

**Variables:**

- **sizes** ([*collections.abc.Mapping*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)*[**Any**, *[*collections.abc.Sequence*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Sequence)*[*[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*]**]*) – region label to the shares (or counts) of households with 1, 2, …, k members; only the proportions matter.
- **heads** ([*collections.abc.Sequence*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Sequence)*[**Any**]*) – the levels of `column` whose people can head a household (adults).
- **column** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the attribute `heads` refers to.

#### `household_sizes(people: int, shares: Sequence[float], rng: Generator) → ndarray`

Sizes of households that hold exactly `people` people, in random order.

**Parameters:**

- **people** – the number of people to house.
- **shares** – the shares (or counts) of households with 1, 2, …, k members.
- **rng** – a numpy generator (`model.rng`).

**Returns:**

an `int64` array of household sizes between 1 and k that sums to `people`.

#### `assign_households(people: DataFrame, spec: HouseholdSpec, rng: Generator) → DataFrame`

A copy of `people` with a `household` column: ids unique across regions.

**Parameters:**

- **people** – one row per person, with a `region` column and `spec.column`.
- **spec** – the household sizes per region and who can head a household.
- **rng** – a numpy generator (`model.rng`).

**Raises:**

[**ValueError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#ValueError) – if a region has more households than people who can head one.

## Homes and places

Homes, schools and workplaces: where synthetic people live, study and work.

`locate_households` puts every household at one random point of its region (all its members share it). `assign_places` then sends the people who attend a kind of place (pupils to schools, workers to workplaces) to the nearest place that still has room, in random order, never farther than a maximum distance: people with no place within reach get `-1`. Distances are straight lines in the coordinates’ units (metres in a projected CRS such as a `GeoSpace`’s).

#### `class PlaceSpec(name: str, members: Sequence[Any], column: str = 'age', max_distance: float = inf)`

Who attends a kind of place, and how far they may travel to it.

**Variables:**

- **name** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the column of people that receives the place (`"school"`, `"work"`).
- **members** ([*collections.abc.Sequence*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Sequence)*[**Any**]*) – the levels of `column` whose people attend.
- **column** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the attribute `members` refers to.
- **max_distance** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – nobody is sent farther than this; unlimited by default.

#### `locate_households(people: DataFrame, space: Any, rng: Generator) → DataFrame`

A copy of `people` with `x` and `y`: one random point per household.

**Parameters:**

- **people** – one row per person, with `region` and `household` columns.
- **space** – a `GeoSpace` whose regions are the people’s regions (anything with `random_points(region, n, rng)` returning an `(n, 2)` array).
- **rng** – a numpy generator (`model.rng`).

#### `assign_places(people: DataFrame, places: DataFrame, spec: PlaceSpec, rng: Generator) → DataFrame`

A copy of `people` with a `spec.name` column: the row of `places`, or `-1`.

**Parameters:**

- **people** – one row per person, with `x`, `y` and `spec.column`.
- **places** – one row per place, with `x`, `y` and `capacity` (people it takes).
- **spec** – who attends and how far they may go.
- **rng** – a numpy generator (`model.rng`): the order in which people choose.

**Returns:**

the copy; a person’s place is `places.iloc[place]`. Everybody else gets `-1`.

## Contact networks

Contact networks from places: who meets whom at home, at school and at work.

`contact_network` links the people who share a place on one layer per kind of place, in a `MultilayerNetwork` (`modelly.space.networks`): everybody in a household knows everybody else in it; pupils of a school are split at random into classes, and workers of a workplace into teams, each a clique. Node `i` is the `i`-th row of `people`, so `contact_matrix(network, groups)` gives the mean contacts between age groups for an age-structured model, and `network.adjacency() @ infected` drives a network epidemic.

#### `class ContactLayers(weights: Mapping[str, float]=<factory>, group_sizes: Mapping[str, int]=<factory>)`

The layers of a contact network and the size of the cliques on each.

**Variables:**

- **weights** ([*collections.abc.Mapping*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*]*) – layer name to its weight; each name is a column of people holding the place (household, school, workplace) of every person, `-1` for none.
- **group_sizes** ([*collections.abc.Mapping*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)*]*) – layer name to the people per clique within one place (a class, a team); a layer not listed links everybody who shares a place.

#### `contact_network(people: DataFrame, rng: Generator, layers: ContactLayers | None = None) → MultilayerNetwork`

A `MultilayerNetwork` over the rows of `people`, one layer per kind of place.

**Parameters:**

- **people** – one row per person, with one column per layer (see `ContactLayers`).
- **rng** – a numpy generator (`model.rng`) to split places into classes and teams.
- **layers** – the layers, their weights and clique sizes; household (1.0), school (0.5, classes of 25) and work (0.25, teams of 10) by default.

#### `place_groups(places: ndarray, size: int | None, rng: Generator) → list[ndarray]`

The rows that share each place, in place order, split at random into `size` groups.

**Parameters:**

- **places** – the place of every row; `-1` (no place) is left out.
- **size** – people per group within a place; `None` keeps each place whole.
- **rng** – a numpy generator, used only when `size` is given.

# Time

`modelly.time` holds the event list, events and event generators, the scheduling methods of the model, and signals (observables that notify subscribers when they change).

Module

Event, EventList, EventGenerator, Schedule, Priority
