- **names** ([*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **...**]*) – the variables’ names.
- **params** ([*collections.abc.Mapping*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **Any**]*) – passed to `rhs`.
- **atol** (*rtol**,*) – the tolerances of the integration.

#### `class Companion(model: Any, limit: MeanField)`

A model and its mean-field limit, side by side, from the same starting state.

Start the ODE from the model’s current aggregate state.

#### `advance(duration: float) → None`

Integrate the limit over `duration`; record it next to the model’s state.

Call it after each model step, with the time that step covers.

#### `gap() → float`

The largest difference between the model and its limit, over times and variables.

#### `frame() → Any`

A DataFrame with each variable twice: `<name>` (the model) and `<name>_limit`.

#### `class GapBySize(sizes: tuple[int, ...], gaps: tuple[float, ...], exponent: float)`

The mean gap at each population size, and its fitted power of the size.

#### `gap_by_size(run: Callable[[int, int], Companion], sizes: Sequence[int], seeds: Sequence[int]) → GapBySize`

`run(size, seed)` returns a finished companion; the gaps and their exponent.

The exponent is the slope of `log gap` against `log size`: about `-0.5` while the gap is sampling noise, flatter where the model departs from its limit.

# Emulate

`modelly.emulate` fits emulators to a model’s runs, chooses runs by active learning and rules out parameters by history matching. How to use it is in [Emulators](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/emulators.html).

## Emulators

What every emulator shares: named outputs, predictions on the unit cube, accuracy, data.

An emulator is fitted to `units[point, dimension]` (points of the unit cube of a `ScenarioSpace`, as designs draw them) and `values[point, output]`. `predict` returns the mean and standard deviation of every output; `select` keeps one output, and an emulator with one output and its `space` stands in for the model in `modelly.sensitivity`. [`Emulator.from_results()`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.base.Emulator.from_results) trains one on the runs of an `Experiment`.

#### `output_names(count: int, names: Sequence[str] | None = None) → list[str]`

`names` checked against `count` outputs, or `y0, y1, ...`.

#### `as_columns(values: ndarray) → ndarray`

`values` as a float array `[point, output]` (one column for a 1-d array).

#### `class Emulator`

Base class: a fit of several outputs over the unit cube.

Subclasses implement `fit`, `predict` and `_subset`.

**Variables:**

- **names** ([*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*]*) – the outputs, in column order.
- **space** ([*modelly.experiments.space.ScenarioSpace*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/experiments.html#modelly.experiments.space.ScenarioSpace)* | **None*) – the space whose unit cube the inputs are (`None` if not known).

#### `classmethod fit(units: ndarray, values: ndarray, names: Sequence[str] | None = None, **options: Any) → Emulator`

Fit to `units[point, dimension]` and `values[point, output]`.

#### `predict(units: ndarray) → tuple[ndarray, ndarray]`

The predicted mean and standard deviation, each `[point, output]`.

#### `select(name: str) → Emulator`

The emulator of one output (for the sensitivity methods).

#### `predict_unit(units: ndarray) → ndarray`

The predicted mean of the only output (the sensitivity methods call this).

#### `score(units: ndarray, values: ndarray) → dict[str, float]`

The normalised root-mean-square error of every output on test data.

The error is divided by the test values’ standard deviation: 0 is perfect, 1 is no better than predicting their mean.

#### `classmethod from_results(results: Results, space: ScenarioSpace, outputs: Mapping[str, str | Callable[[ndarray], float]] | Sequence[str], **options: Any) → Emulator`

Fit to an experiment’s runs: one point per design point, replicates averaged.

`outputs` lists recorded outputs (each run’s last value) or maps each to a statistic of its series (`"last"`, `"max"`, `"mean"`… or a function); `options` go to `fit`.

#### `unit_of(space: ScenarioSpace, params: Mapping[str, Any]) → ndarray`

The unit-cube position of `params`: the inverse of `space.point`.

A level of an integer range or a choice maps to the centre of its share.

#### `reducer(statistic: str | Callable[[ndarray], float]) → Callable[[ndarray], float]`

The function a statistic names (`"last"`, `"max"`…), or the function given.

#### `training_data(results: Results, space: ScenarioSpace, outputs: Mapping[str, str | Callable[[ndarray], float]] | Sequence[str]) → tuple[ndarray, ndarray]`

`(units, values)` of an experiment’s runs, one row per design point.

A Gaussian-process emulator: one process per output, on the unit cube.

Each output gets the Gaussian process of [`modelly.calibrate.gp`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/calibrate.html#module-modelly.calibrate.gp) (squared exponential kernel, one length scale per input, a fitted noise term), fitted with restarts by default. Besides the mean and standard deviation it gives the predictive covariance and the variance after more runs (`condition`), which the active-learning designs of [`modelly.emulate.active`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#module-modelly.emulate.active) use.

Example

```default
>>> import numpy as np
>>> units = np.linspace(0, 1, 9)[:, None]
>>> emulator = GaussianEmulator.fit(units, np.sin(6 * units[:, 0]))
>>> mean, sd = emulator.predict([[0.5]])
>>> bool(abs(mean[0, 0] - np.sin(3.0)) < 0.05)
True
```

#### `class GaussianEmulator(processes: list[GaussianProcess], names: list[str], space: ScenarioSpace | None = None)`

Independent Gaussian processes, one per output.

**Variables:**

- **processes** ([*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[*[*modelly.calibrate.gp.GaussianProcess*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/calibrate.html#modelly.calibrate.gp.GaussianProcess)*]*) – the fitted processes, one per output.
- **names** ([*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*]*) – the outputs.
- **space** ([*modelly.experiments.space.ScenarioSpace*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/experiments.html#modelly.experiments.space.ScenarioSpace)* | **None*) – the space whose unit cube the inputs are, if known.

#### `classmethod fit(units: ndarray, values: ndarray, names: Sequence[str] | None = None, *, space: ScenarioSpace | None = None, restarts: bool = True) → GaussianEmulator`

Fit one process per column of `values`; `restarts` as in `GaussianProcess.fit`.

#### `predict(units: ndarray) → tuple[ndarray, ndarray]`

The mean and standard deviation of the fitted functions, `[point, output]`.

#### `covariance(a: ndarray, b: ndarray) → ndarray`

The predictive covariance `[output, row of a, row of b]`.

#### `property noise_variance: ndarray`

The fitted noise variance of every output (run-to-run scatter).

#### `condition(units: ndarray) → GaussianEmulator`

The emulator as if `units` had been run and returned the predicted mean.

The hyperparameters are kept, so the standard deviations are those the emulator would have after the runs: how a batch is chosen.

A small neural emulator: an ensemble of multilayer perceptrons, numpy only.

Each member is a fully connected network (`tanh` hidden layers, a linear output per emulated output) trained on the standardised data by full-batch Adam on the mean squared error plus a weight penalty. The members differ only in their random initial weights; the ensemble’s mean is the prediction and the spread between members its standard deviation (a “deep ensemble”, Lakshminarayanan, Pritzel and Blundell 2017). It needs no deep-learning library and suits a few hundred to a few thousand runs, where a Gaussian process gets slow; with few runs the Gaussian process is usually more accurate.

Every weight is drawn from `settings.seed`: the same data and seed give the same emulator.

Example

```default
>>> import numpy as np
>>> units = np.linspace(0, 1, 40)[:, None]
>>> emulator = NeuralEmulator.fit(units, units[:, 0] ** 2)
>>> bool(abs(emulator.predict([[0.5]])[0][0, 0] - 0.25) < 0.05)
True
```

#### `class NeuralSettings(hidden: tuple[int, ...] = (32, 32), members: int = 5, epochs: int = 2000, learning_rate: float = 0.01, penalty: float = 1e-05, seed: int = 0)`

How the ensemble is built and trained.

**Parameters:**

- **hidden** – the width of each hidden layer.
- **members** – the number of networks in the ensemble.
- **epochs** – full-batch Adam steps per network.
- **learning_rate** – Adam’s step size.
- **penalty** – the weight of the squared-weights penalty.
- **seed** – the root of every initial weight.

#### `class NeuralEmulator(members: list[list[tuple[ndarray, ndarray]]], names: list[str], center: ndarray, scale: ndarray, space: ScenarioSpace | None = None)`

An ensemble of small networks over the unit cube.

**Variables:**

- **members** ([*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[*[*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[*[*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)*[**numpy.ndarray**, **numpy.ndarray**]**]**]*) – every network’s layers.
- **names** ([*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*]*) – the outputs.
- **center** (*numpy.ndarray*) – the outputs’ training means.
- **scale** (*numpy.ndarray*) – the outputs’ training standard deviations.
- **space** ([*modelly.experiments.space.ScenarioSpace*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/experiments.html#modelly.experiments.space.ScenarioSpace)* | **None*) – the space whose unit cube the inputs are, if known.

#### `classmethod fit(units: ndarray, values: ndarray, names: Sequence[str] | None = None, *, space: ScenarioSpace | None = None, settings: NeuralSettings | None = None) → NeuralEmulator`

Train `settings.members` networks on `units` and the columns of `values`.

#### `predict(units: ndarray) → tuple[ndarray, ndarray]`

The ensemble’s mean and spread (standard deviation), `[point, output]`.

## Runs

What an emulator learns: the outputs of a model (or a function) at points of a space.

A [`Simulation`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.simulation.Simulation) turns rows of the unit cube of a `ScenarioSpace` into `values[point, output]`:

- a Model class (or `"module:Class"` reference) is run through the experiment executors ([`modelly.calibrate.simulator`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/calibrate.html#module-modelly.calibrate.simulator)), each batch of runs written to a Parquet store; every output is something the model records each step, reduced to one number per run by a statistic and averaged over replicates:

```default
Simulation(Epidemic, space, {"peak": ("infected", "max"), "size": "recovered"})
```

- a plain function is called with the parameters as keyword arguments and returns one number, a sequence, or a mapping `{output: value}`.

Run seeds follow the experiment discipline: a batch’s seeds depend only on the simulation’s `seed` and the batch key, never on the executor. With `common=True` every point runs with the same replicate seeds (common random numbers), which makes a stochastic model’s output a smoother function of its parameters.

#### `class Simulation(model: Any, space: ScenarioSpace, outputs: Mapping[str, ~typing.Any] | ~collections.abc.Sequence[str] | None=None, seed: int = 0, steps: int = 100, replicates: int = 1, common: bool = False, store: str | Path | None = None, executor: Any = 'serial', max_parallel: int | None = None, options: Mapping[str, ~typing.Any]=<factory>)`

A model or function and the outputs an emulator learns.

**Parameters:**

- **model** – a Model class or reference, or a function of the parameters.
- **space** – the parameter space; its ranges and choices are the inputs.
- **outputs** – for a model, a list of recorded outputs (each run’s last value) or `{name: output}` / `{name: (output, statistic)}`, the statistic one of `"last"`, `"max"`, `"min"`, `"mean"`, `"sum"` or a function of the series; for a function, its outputs’ names (one output named `"output"` by default).
- **seed** – the root of every run’s seed.
- **steps** – steps per run (models only).
- **replicates** – runs per point, averaged (models only).
- **common** – run every point with the same replicate seeds (models only).
- **store** – the folder of the runs (a temporary one by default).
- **executor** – where the runs execute (any experiment executor).
- **max_parallel** – the most runs at once.
- **options** – the executor’s options.

`with simulation:` keeps one pool of workers for every batch run inside the block (`"processes"` otherwise starts one per batch).

#### `property names: list[str]`

The outputs, in column order.

#### `evaluate(units: ndarray, key: Sequence[int]) → ndarray`

`values[point, output]` at the rows of `units`; `key` names the batch.

## Active learning

Active learning: choose the next runs where the emulator is least certain.

An [`ActiveLearning`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.active.ActiveLearning) design starts from a small Latin hypercube, fits an emulator, and then, batch after batch, runs the candidate points the emulator would learn most from, refitting after every batch:

- `criterion="ivr"` (the default): the largest integrated variance reduction, the drop in predictive variance averaged over the whole space that running the point would bring (Cohn 1996’s ALC; Sacks, Welch, Mitchell and Wynn 1989), the error measure an emulator is judged by;
- `criterion="variance"`: the largest predictive variance (MacKay 1992’s ALM): cheaper, but it favours the edges of the space, more so in more dimensions.

A batch of several runs is chosen greedily: after each pick the emulator is conditioned on it (its variance becomes what it would be after the run, the “kriging believer”), so the batch spreads out instead of piling up where the variance was largest. The batch then runs at once on the simulation’s executor. With several outputs, the criteria add the outputs’ variances, each relative to its spread in the runs so far.

Every random draw (the first design, the candidates, the reference points) comes from the simulation’s seed: the same seed chooses the same runs.

Example

```default
>>> import math
>>> from modelly.experiments import ScenarioSpace
>>> space = ScenarioSpace(x=(0.0, 1.0), y=(0.0, 1.0))
>>> simulation = Simulation(lambda x, y: math.sin(6 * x) + y, space, seed=1)
>>> design = ActiveLearning(simulation, ActiveSettings(batch=2)).run(runs=14)
>>> len(design.units)
14
```

#### `class ActiveSettings(initial: int | None = None, batch: int = 1, criterion: str = 'ivr', candidates: int = 1000, references: int = 300, emulator: type[Emulator] = <class 'modelly.emulate.gaussian.GaussianEmulator'>, options: Mapping[str, ~typing.Any]=<factory>)`

How an active-learning design chooses its runs.

**Parameters:**

- **initial** – runs of the first Latin hypercube (`2 * dimensions + 2` by default).
- **batch** – runs chosen and run together at each iteration.
- **criterion** – `"ivr"` (integrated variance reduction) or `"variance"`.
- **candidates** – random points scored at each iteration.
- **references** – points the integrated variance is averaged over (`"ivr"`).
- **emulator** – the emulator class (a batch needs `condition`, as [`GaussianEmulator`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.gaussian.GaussianEmulator) has).
- **options** – keyword arguments of the emulator’s `fit`.

#### `emulator`

alias of [`GaussianEmulator`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.gaussian.GaussianEmulator)

#### `class ActiveDesign(simulation: Simulation, units: ndarray, values: ndarray, iterations: ndarray, emulator: Emulator)`

The runs an active-learning design chose, and the emulator fitted to them.

**Variables:**

- **simulation** ([*modelly.emulate.simulation.Simulation*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.simulation.Simulation)) – what was run.
- **units** (*numpy.ndarray*) – the runs’ points of the unit cube, in the order they ran.
- **values** (*numpy.ndarray*) – their outputs `[run, output]`.
- **iterations** (*numpy.ndarray*) – the iteration of each run (0 for the first design).
- **emulator** ([*modelly.emulate.base.Emulator*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.base.Emulator)) – the emulator fitted to every run.

#### `points() → list[dict[str, Any]]`

The parameters of every run, in the order they ran.

#### `design() → Custom`

The runs as a custom design, to rerun them in an `Experiment`.

#### `frame() → DataFrame`

One row per run: the iteration, the parameters and the outputs.

#### `class ActiveLearning(simulation: Simulation, settings: ActiveSettings | None = None)`

An active-learning design over a simulation (see the module docstring).

`run(runs)` can be called again with a larger `runs` to go on.

Nothing runs before `run`.

#### `run(runs: int) → ActiveDesign`

Run until `runs` runs are done; the design and its emulator.

#### `fit() → Emulator`

The emulator fitted to every run so far.

## History matching

History matching: rule out, wave by wave, the parameters that cannot match the data.

For an observed value `z` of an output, the implausibility of a point `x` of the parameter space is:

```default
I(x) = |z - E[f(x)]| / sqrt(Var[f(x)] + Var_obs + Var_discrepancy)
```

where `E[f(x)]` and `Var[f(x)]` are an emulator’s prediction of the model’s output, `Var_obs` the observation error and `Var_discrepancy` the model discrepancy (what even the best parameters miss, the run-to-run scatter of a stochastic model included). With several outputs a point’s implausibility is the largest of theirs (or, with `rank=2`, the second largest). A point with `I(x) > cutoff` (3, by Pukelsheim’s three-sigma rule) is implausible.

A [`HistoryMatch`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.history.HistoryMatch) runs waves (Vernon, Goldstein and Bower 2010; Andrianakis et al. 2015). Wave 1 spreads `runs` runs over the whole space, fits an emulator and rules out the implausible part. Each later wave spreads its runs over the space not yet ruled out, refits the emulators on the runs inside it (more accurate there, as the region is smaller) and rules out more. The space not ruled out yet, NROY, is tracked on a fixed random sample of `candidates` points of the space, so its volume is the share of the sample left.

Example

```default
>>> from modelly.experiments import ScenarioSpace
>>> space = ScenarioSpace(a=(0.0, 1.0), b=(0.0, 1.0))
>>> simulation = Simulation(lambda a, b: [a + b, a - b], space, ["sum", "diff"])
>>> observed = [Observation("sum", 1.0, 1e-4), Observation("diff", 0.2, 1e-4)]
>>> result = HistoryMatch(simulation, observed).run(waves=2, runs=12)
>>> bool(result.volumes[-1] < 0.1 and result.contains({"a": 0.6, "b": 0.4}))
True
```

#### `class Observation(name: str, value: float, variance: float, discrepancy: float = 0.0)`

One observed output and its uncertainty.

**Parameters:**

- **name** – the simulation output it observes.
- **value** – the observed value `z`.
- **variance** – the observation error variance.
- **discrepancy** – the model discrepancy variance.

#### `implausibility(mean: ndarray, sd: ndarray, observations: Sequence[Observation]) → ndarray`

`I[point, output]` from an emulator’s `mean` and `sd` (columns as observations).

#### `class MatchSettings(cutoff: float = 3.0, rank: int = 1, candidates: int = 20000, emulator: type[Emulator] = <class 'modelly.emulate.gaussian.GaussianEmulator'>, options: Mapping[str, ~typing.Any]=<factory>)`

How the waves rule out space.

**Parameters:**

- **cutoff** – the implausibility above which a point is ruled out.
- **rank** – combine the outputs by their largest implausibility (1) or the `rank`-th largest (2 tolerates one badly matched output).
- **candidates** – the random points of the space NROY is tracked on.
- **emulator** – the emulator class refitted at every wave.
- **options** – keyword arguments of the emulator’s `fit`.

#### `emulator`

alias of [`GaussianEmulator`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.gaussian.GaussianEmulator)

#### `class Wave(number: int, units: ndarray, values: ndarray, training: int, emulator: Emulator, volume: float)`

One wave: its runs, the emulator fitted to the runs inside its region, and NROY.

**Variables:**

- **number** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – 1 for the first wave.
- **units** (*numpy.ndarray*) – the wave’s runs, as points of the unit cube.
- **values** (*numpy.ndarray*) – their outputs `[run, output]`.
- **training** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – how many runs (this wave’s and earlier ones in its region) fitted the emulator.
- **emulator** ([*modelly.emulate.base.Emulator*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.base.Emulator)) – the wave’s emulator of the observed outputs.
- **volume** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – the share of the space not ruled out after this wave.

#### `class MatchResult(simulation: Simulation, observations: list[Observation], settings: MatchSettings, waves: list[Wave], candidates: ndarray, alive: ndarray)`

The waves of a history match and the space they did not rule out.

**Variables:**

- **simulation** ([*modelly.emulate.simulation.Simulation*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.simulation.Simulation)) – what was run.
- **observations** ([*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[*[*modelly.emulate.history.Observation*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.history.Observation)*]*) – what was matched.
- **settings** ([*modelly.emulate.history.MatchSettings*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.history.MatchSettings)) – how.
- **waves** ([*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[*[*modelly.emulate.history.Wave*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/emulate.html#modelly.emulate.history.Wave)*]*) – every wave, the first first.
- **candidates** (*numpy.ndarray*) – the sample of the space NROY is tracked on.
- **alive** (*numpy.ndarray*) – which candidates are not ruled out.

#### `property volumes: list[float]`

The share of the space not ruled out after each wave.

#### `implausibility(units: ndarray) → ndarray`

The combined implausibility `[wave, point]` of each wave’s emulator.

#### `wave_implausibility(wave: Wave, units: ndarray) → ndarray`

One wave’s combined implausibility at `units`: the `rank`-th largest output’s.

#### `nonimplausible(units: ndarray) → ndarray`

Whether each point is below the cutoff under every wave.

#### `contains(params: Mapping[str, Any]) → bool`

Whether the parameters `params` are not ruled out.

#### `samples() → DataFrame`

The candidates not ruled out, as parameters: a sample of NROY.

#### `table() → DataFrame`

One row per wave: its runs, its training runs and the volume left.

#### `maximin(region: ndarray, count: int, rng: Generator) → ndarray`

`count` points of `region` chosen greedily far from each other (all if fewer).

#### `class HistoryMatch(simulation: Simulation, observations: Sequence[Observation], settings: MatchSettings | None = None)`

History matching of a simulation to observations (see the module docstring).

`run(waves)` can be called again with more waves to go on.

Check the observations name outputs; nothing runs before `run`.

#### `run(waves: int, runs: int = 40) → MatchResult`

Run `waves` more waves of `runs` runs each; stop early if NROY is empty.

# Batch

`modelly.batch` runs many independent model runs and holds counted populations.

Module

Contents

modelly.batch.runs

run_batch, run_grid

modelly.batch.cohorts

CohortTable

## Parallel runs

Run independent model runs over processes with the results in a deterministic order: `run_batch` for any list of tasks, `run_grid` for a factorial design with one seed per run. The output is the same as the sequential loop’s, whatever the number of workers.

Run many independent model runs in parallel, results in a deterministic order.

An experiment is usually a loop over parameter combinations and replicates, each run depending only on its own parameters and seed. `run_batch` spreads those calls over processes and returns the results in task order, so the output (a CSV, a DataFrame) is identical to the sequential loop’s, row for row. `run_grid` builds the factorial design, gives every run its own seed and returns a DataFrame.

A function defined at module level in an importable file runs in workers that start clean (`forkserver`, or `spawn`). A function defined in a notebook, a lambda or a closure cannot be imported by a fresh process; on Linux its workers are forked instead and inherit it. Forking a process with threads (numpy’s BLAS pool, for one) can deadlock the child; it is rare in practice, so the warning Python raises for it is silenced for these forks, and an importable function avoids it. As with any multiprocessing code on macOS and Windows, a script that calls `run_batch` needs the usual `if __name__ == "__main__":` guard, because the workers re-import it.

#### `default_workers() → int`

`MODELLY_WORKERS` if set, else the number of CPUs, at most eight.

#### `run_batch(run: Callable[[Any], Any], tasks: Iterable[Any], workers: int | None = None) → list[Any]`

Call `run(task)` for every task; return the results in task order.

**Parameters:**

- **run** – the function computing one run’s result.
- **tasks** – one argument per run (parameters, seed, …).
- **workers** – processes to use; `None` means `default_workers()`, 1 runs inline in this process. At most one worker starts per task.

An exception raised by a run propagates, as in the sequential loop.

#### `grid_tasks(grid: Mapping[str, Sequence[Any]], replicates: int = 1, seed: int = 0) → list[dict[str, Any]]`

Every combination of `grid` times `replicates`, each with its own seed.

Seeds come from `numpy.random.SeedSequence(seed).spawn`: independent streams, the same for a given design whatever the number of workers.

#### `run_grid(run: Callable[[dict[str, Any]], Mapping[str, Any]], grid: Mapping[str, Sequence[Any]], replicates: int = 1, seed: int = 0, workers: int | None = None) → DataFrame`

Run a factorial design in parallel; one DataFrame row per run.

`run` receives a dict with the grid’s parameters, `replicate` and `seed`, and returns a mapping of outcome names to values. The row is the task followed by the outcomes, in design order.

## Cohorts

A counted population: one row per state (stage, age, sex…) with a `count`, and every per-individual draw replaced by one binomial draw per row with exactly the same law. See [Vectorised step phases](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/vectorised_phases.html) for the argument.

Counted populations: one row stands for every individual in the same state.

When individuals that share a state (stage, age, sex, patch…) also share every probability they face, the model does not need one object per individual. A `CohortTable` keeps one row per state with a `count`, and the per-individual draws become one binomial draw per row:

- survival with probability `s`: `Binomial(count, s)` survivors (`thin`);
- a two-way outcome with probability `p` (sex, mating, emergence): `Binomial(count, p)` rows move to the new state (`split`);
- an event each member triggers with probability `p`: `Binomial(count, p)` events (`draw`).

Each has exactly the law of the independent per-individual draws (a sum of `count` independent Bernoulli(p) variables is Binomial(count, p)), so the counts per state have the same distribution as in the individual model; see `docs/vectorised_phases.md`. The table grows by doubling and `compact` / `merge` keep it small: it holds as many rows as there are distinct states.

eggs = CohortTable(rng, stage=np.int8, age=np.int16) eggs.add(500, stage=EGG, age=0) eggs.thin(survival[eggs[“stage”]]) eggs[“age”] += 1

#### `class CohortTable(rng: Generator, *, storage: InMemory = InMemory(), **columns: Any)`

Rows of (state columns, count); every operation is one numpy call per column.

Create an empty table with an int64 `count` and the given state columns.

**Parameters:**

- **rng** – the model’s seeded numpy generator (`model.rng`).
- **storage** – where the columns live (`modelly.core.storage`); a `MemoryMapped` keeps them in files, for more rows than memory.
- **columns** – state column names and their numpy dtypes.

#### `property columns: list[str]`

`count` then the state columns.

#### `total(where: ndarray | None = None) → int`

Individuals in the table, or in the rows selected by the mask `where`.

#### `totals_by(column: str, minlength: int = 0) → ndarray`

Individuals per value of an integer state column (a weighted bincount).

#### `add(count: Any, **values: Any) → ndarray`

Append cohorts; scalars or equal-length arrays. Returns their row indices.

Unset state columns are zero. Cohorts of size zero are kept until `compact`.

#### `thin(survival: Any) → ndarray`

Each count becomes Binomial(count, survival); returns the new counts.

#### `draw(p: Any, where: ndarray | None = None) → ndarray`

Binomial(count, p) events per row (or per selected row); counts are unchanged.

#### `split(p: Any, where: ndarray | None = None, **changes: Any) → ndarray`

Move Binomial(count, p) individuals of each selected row to a new row.

The new rows copy the state of their source row, then apply `changes` (scalars or one value per selected row). The source rows keep the rest. Returns the new rows’ indices.

#### `compact() → int`

Drop the empty cohorts, keeping row order; returns how many were dropped.

#### `merge() → int`

Combine rows with identical state into one, summing counts; drops empties.

Rows come out sorted by state. Returns how many rows were removed.

#### `to_dataframe() → DataFrame`

A copy of the live rows.

#### `from_counts(rng: Generator, counts: Mapping[tuple[Any, ...], int], **columns: Any) → CohortTable`

A table from `{(state values...): count}`, the state in `columns` order.

# GPU

`modelly.gpu` runs column phases, cohort tables and cell-space operators on numpy, CuPy or JAX, with counter-based random numbers that are the same on every backend. How to use it is in [GPU arrays](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/gpu.html).

## Backends

Array backends: numpy on the CPU, CuPy on CUDA GPUs, JAX on CPU, CUDA or Metal.

A [`Backend`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/gpu.html#modelly.gpu.backend.Backend) wraps one array library (`backend.xp`, used like numpy) and adds the handful of operations whose spelling differs between them: a functional scatter (JAX arrays are immutable), per-bin sums, the Philox rounds, device synchronisation and free memory. Everything in `modelly.gpu` is written against it, so one setting moves a model between devices:

```default
backend = get_backend("cupy")      # or "jax", "numpy", "auto"
MODELLY_BACKEND=cupy python run.py # the same, for get_backend()
```

A backend that cannot be loaded falls back to numpy with a [`BackendFallbackWarning`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/gpu.html#modelly.gpu.backend.BackendFallbackWarning) (`strict=True` raises instead), so a model written for the GPU always runs. CuPy and JAX are imported only when their backend is requested: `import modelly` and the numpy backend never load them.

#### `exception BackendUnavailableError`

The requested array backend cannot be loaded on this machine.

#### `exception BackendFallbackWarning`

A GPU backend was requested but numpy runs instead.

#### `class Backend`

The numpy backend, and the interface the GPU backends implement.

**Variables:**

- **name** – `"numpy"`, `"cupy"` or `"jax"`.
- **xp** – the array namespace.
- **gpu** – whether arrays live on an accelerator.

Bind numpy as the array namespace.

#### `property float_dtype: Any`

The widest float the backend computes in (float64, or float32 on 32-bit JAX).

#### `property int_dtype: Any`

The widest integer the backend stores (int64, or int32 on 32-bit JAX).

#### `property device: str`

A short description of where the arrays live.

#### `asarray(values: Any, dtype: Any = None) → Any`

`values` as an array of this backend (copied to the device if needed).

#### `to_numpy(array: Any) → ndarray`

A numpy copy (or view) of `array` on the host.

#### `put(array: Any, index: Any, values: Any) → Any`

A copy of `array` with `array[index] = values`; `array` is unchanged.

#### `segment_add(index: Any, weights: Any, n: int) → Any`

`out[b]` = sum of `weights` where `index == b`, for `b < n`.

Integer and boolean weights give exact integer sums (below 2**53); float sums may differ in the last bits between devices, which add in a different order.

#### `bincount(index: Any, n: int) → Any`

How many times each bin `b < n` occurs in `index`.

#### `argsort_stable(values: Any) → Any`

Indices that sort `values`, equal values keeping their order.

#### `philox(block: Any, words: tuple[int, int, int], key: tuple[int, int])`

Philox4x32-10 at counters `(block, *words)`: four uint32 arrays.

#### `synchronize(array: Any = None) → None`

Wait for the device to finish (for timing); numpy is always finished.

#### `free_bytes() → int`

Bytes available for new arrays: available host memory for numpy (0 if unknown).

#### `get_backend(name: str | Backend | None = None, strict: bool = False) → Backend`

The array backend `name`: `"numpy"`, `"cupy"`, `"jax"` or `"auto"`.

**Parameters:**

- **name** – a backend name, a Backend (returned as is), or None for the `MODELLY_BACKEND` environment variable (numpy when unset).
- **strict** – raise BackendUnavailableError instead of falling back to numpy.

#### `available_backends() → list[str]`

The backends that load on this machine, numpy first.

The CuPy backend: arrays on an NVIDIA GPU through CUDA (Linux and Windows).

`pip install "modelly-abm[gpu]"` installs `cupy-cuda13x`, whose wheels carry the CUDA runtime and NVRTC: no CUDA toolkit is needed, only the NVIDIA driver. The Philox rounds run in compiled elementwise kernels, one per kind of draw (words, uniforms, bounded integers), each computing an element’s block and converting it in registers; everything else is CuPy’s numpy-compatible API. CuPy is imported when the backend is created, never by `import modelly`.

The kernels follow the numpy code of `modelly.gpu.philox` and `modelly.gpu.streams` operation for operation (integer arithmetic, and float conversions that are exact), so they give numpy’s numbers bit for bit.

#### `class CupyBackend`

Arrays on the current CUDA device, through CuPy.

Import CuPy, check a device answers and declare the Philox kernels.

#### `property device: str`

The CUDA device’s name.

#### `to_numpy(array: Any) → ndarray`

Copy `array` from the device to a numpy array.

#### `argsort_stable(values: Any) → Any`

CuPy’s argsort is a stable radix sort.

#### `philox(block: Any, words: tuple[int, int, int], key: tuple[int, int])`

The Philox rounds at every block, one kernel launch: four word arrays.

#### `bits_at(positions: Any, words: tuple, key: tuple) → Any`

The uint32 word of the elements at `positions` (four per block).

#### `bounded_at(positions: Any, high: Any, words: tuple, key: tuple) → Any`

`high * word >> 32` for the elements at `positions`.

#### `uniform_at(positions: Any, words: tuple, key: tuple, single: bool) → Any`

Uniforms of the elements at `positions`: float32 (24 bits) or float64 (53).

#### `neighbor_at(rows: Any, csr: tuple, words: tuple, key: tuple) → Any`

`random_neighbor` in one kernel: the uniform pick and the gather, per row.

`csr` is `(indptr, indices)` as int64 device arrays; element `i` draws the bounded integer at position `i`, as the generic path does.

#### `synchronize(array: Any = None) → None`

Wait for every kernel queued on the current device.

#### `free_bytes() → int`

Free device memory plus what CuPy’s pool holds and can reuse.

The JAX backend: CPU everywhere, CUDA on Linux and Windows, Metal on macOS.

JAX runs on whatever device its installed plugins provide: `pip install "jax[cuda13]"` for NVIDIA GPUs, `jax-metal` for Apple GPUs (where available; untested in Modelly’s own runs), the CPU otherwise. JAX arrays are immutable, so every update in `modelly.gpu` is functional (`put` returns a new array).

Without `jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True)` JAX has no 64-bit types: floats are float32, integers int32, and the Philox products go through 16-bit halves. The integers drawn are the same either way; uniforms are float32 with 24 random bits, the same values numpy gives for `random(n, dtype=float32)`.

#### `class JaxBackend`

Arrays on JAX’s default device.

Import JAX, find its default device and jit the Philox rounds.

#### `property float_dtype: Any`

float64 with `jax_enable_x64`, else float32.

#### `property int_dtype: Any`

int64 with `jax_enable_x64`, else int32.

#### `property device: str`

The platform and kind of JAX’s default device (`cuda`, `METAL`, `cpu`).

#### `to_numpy(array: Any) → ndarray`

Copy `array` to the host.

#### `put(array: Any, index: Any, values: Any) → Any`

`array` with `array[index] = values`, as a new array.

#### `segment_add(index: Any, weights: Any, n: int) → Any`

Per-bin sums by a scatter-add; integer weights stay integers (exact).

#### `bincount(index: Any, n: int) → Any`

Occurrences of each bin by a scatter-add of ones.

#### `argsort_stable(values: Any) → Any`

A stable argsort (JAX’s keyword differs from numpy’s).

#### `philox(block: Any, words: tuple[int, int, int], key: tuple[int, int])`

The jitted Philox rounds (compiled once per shape; any key, no recompiling).

#### `synchronize(array: Any = None) → None`

Block until `array` (or every pending computation) is ready.

#### `free_bytes() → int`

Free memory of the device; available host memory on the CPU.

## Random streams

Philox4x32-10: the counter-based generator every Modelly backend draws from.

A counter-based generator maps a 128-bit counter and a 64-bit key to 128 random bits with no state in between (Salmon, Moraes, Dror and Shaw, “Parallel random numbers: as easy as 1, 2, 3”, SC 2011). Any element of any stream can therefore be computed on its own, on any device, in any order: the numbers a GPU draws for agent `i` are the numbers the CPU draws for agent `i`.

`philox4x32` here is written once against the array API (`xp` is numpy, CuPy or `jax.numpy`) and checked against the published known-answer vectors of the Random123 library. Numpy’s own `numpy.random.Philox` is the 4x64 variant, so its streams are not these. The CuPy backend runs the same rounds as CUDA kernels (`CUDA_PHILOX`), checked bit for bit against this one.

Two ways to compute the high half of a 32 x 32-bit product: in 64-bit integers (numpy, CuPy, JAX with `jax_enable_x64`), or from 16-bit halves in 32-bit integers (JAX without 64-bit types). Both give the same bits.

#### `mulhilo_wide(a: Any, b: Any, xp: Any) → tuple[Any, Any]`

High and low words of `a * b` for uint32 arrays, through 64-bit integers.

#### `mulhilo_narrow(a: Any, b: Any, xp: Any) → tuple[Any, Any]`

High and low words of `a * b` for uint32 arrays, from 16-bit halves only.

#### `philox4x32(counter: tuple[Any, Any, Any, Any], key: tuple[int, int], xp: Any, wide: bool = True) → tuple[Any, Any, Any, Any]`

The four output words of Philox4x32-10 for every counter.

**Parameters:**

- **counter** – four uint32 words; arrays broadcast against each other.
- **key** – two 32-bit integers (or two uint32 arrays, such as a traced JAX key).
- **xp** – the array namespace (numpy, CuPy or `jax.numpy`).
- **wide** – multiply through 64-bit integers; `False` for 32-bit-only JAX.

**Returns:**

Four uint32 arrays of the broadcast shape of `counter`.

#### `philox4x32_reference(counter: tuple[int, ...], key: tuple[int, int]) → tuple`

Philox4x32-10 for one counter in Python integers: the reference of the others.

Random streams keyed by (seed, stream) that give the same numbers on every backend.

A [`PhiloxStream`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/gpu.html#modelly.gpu.streams.PhiloxStream) holds no generator state, only a count of the draws made so far. Draw number `call` of stream `stream` gives element `i` the Philox4x32-10 block at counter `(i // k, sub, call, stream)` and key `seed`, where `k` elements share one 128-bit block. So the numbers depend on the element’s position only, not on the device, the batch it is drawn in or the order of evaluation:

```default
stream = PhiloxStream(seed=42, stream=0, backend="cupy")
alive = stream.bernoulli(survival)              # one draw per element
draws = stream.draws()                          # one draw, in batches
first, rest = draws.random(1000), draws.random(500, start=1000)
```

Uniforms are float64 with 53 random bits (two words, as numpy builds them) or float32 with 24 (one word); bounded integers are `high * word >> 32`, which is exact and the same on every backend, with a bias below `high / 2**32`. Limits per draw: `2**32` blocks, so about 8.6 billion float64 uniforms.

#### `class PhiloxDraw(stream: PhiloxStream, call: int)`

One draw of a stream: elements addressed by position, drawable in batches.

Bind the stream and this draw’s number.

#### `property backend: Backend`

The stream’s backend.

#### `words(n: int, start: int = 0, per_element: int = 1, sub: int = 0)`

`per_element` uint32 words for each of `n` elements from `start`: (n, k).

#### `words_at(positions: Any, per_element: int = 1, sub: int = 0)`

The words `words` gives the elements at `positions` (any order): (n, k).

#### `bits(n: int, start: int = 0, sub: int = 0)`

`n` uniform uint32 words.

#### `random(n: int, start: int = 0, dtype: Any = None, sub: int = 0)`

`n` uniforms in [0, 1); float64 unless `dtype` or the backend says float32.

#### `random_at(positions: Any, dtype: Any = None, sub: int = 0)`

The uniforms `random` gives the elements at `positions`.

#### `integers(high: Any, n: int | None = None, start: int = 0, sub: int = 0)`

Integers in `[0, high)`, `high` a scalar or one bound per element (< 2**32).

#### `binomial(count: Any, p: Any, start: int = 0)`

One Binomial(count, p) variate per element (see `modelly.gpu.binomial`).

#### `class PhiloxStream(seed: int, stream: int = 0, backend: Any = None)`

Counter-based random numbers for one (seed, stream) pair, on one backend.

**Parameters:**

- **seed** – a non-negative integer below 2**64, the Philox key.
- **stream** – the stream number below 2**32; streams of one seed are independent.
- **backend** – a backend or backend name (see `get_backend`).

Key the stream; no number is drawn yet.

#### `draws() → PhiloxDraw`

The next draw, for drawing one quantity in batches or by position.

#### `random(n: int, dtype: Any = None)`

`n` uniforms in [0, 1).

#### `integers(high: Any, n: int | None = None)`

Integers in `[0, high)`, one per element of `high` (or `n` of them).

#### `bernoulli(p: Any, n: int | None = None)`

`n` (or one per element of `p`) booleans, True with probability `p`.

#### `binomial(count: Any, p: Any)`

One Binomial(count, p) variate per element of `count`.

#### `spawn(stream: int) → PhiloxStream`

Stream `stream` of the same seed and backend, at its first draw.

Binomial variates from a Philox draw, the same on every backend for the same draw.

Two exact samplers, chosen per element by the mean `m = count * min(p, 1 - p)`:

- `m < 10`: inversion. One uniform `u`; walk the cumulative probabilities from `P(0) = (1 - p) ** count` (by repeated squaring, multiplications only) with the ratio `P(k) / P(k - 1)` until they pass `u`. The walk stops at `m + 10 * sqrt(m (1 - p) + 1)`, beyond which the remaining mass is below 1e-20 (the bound numpy uses before it restarts).
- `m >= 10`: BTRS, the transformed rejection with squeeze of Hörmann (1993, “The generation of binomial random variates”, J. Stat. Comput. Simul. 46), the algorithm of `jax.random.binomial` and TensorFlow. Rounds draw two uniforms for every element still pending; about nine in ten accept at each.

`p > 1/2` draws `count - Binomial(count, 1 - p)`. Element `i` uses the uniforms at position `start + i` of sub-streams `0` (inversion) and `2r + 1`, `2r + 2` (round `r` of BTRS), so a batch, a subset or another device gets the same variates. Only IEEE-exact operations (`+ - * /`, `sqrt`, comparisons) decide the inversion; BTRS takes logarithms, whose last bit may differ between numpy, CUDA and XLA. A different last bit changes an outcome only when a uniform falls within one rounding error of the acceptance bound, so the results are the same in practice and the same law always.

#### `binomial(draw: PhiloxDraw, count: Any, p: Any, start: int = 0) → Any`

One Binomial(count[i], p[i]) variate per element; `p` may be a scalar.

## Tables and cell spaces

Agent columns on a device: the array side of a `ColumnTable`, on a GPU.

A [`DeviceTable`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/gpu.html#modelly.gpu.table.DeviceTable) holds one device array per column and a [`PhiloxStream`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/gpu.html#modelly.gpu.streams.PhiloxStream). A step phase reads columns as arrays and assigns new ones; assignment replaces the column (JAX arrays cannot be written in place), so a phase is written functionally:

```default
people = DeviceTable.from_columns(model.columns[Person], stream)
infected = people.state == I
exposure = index.counts(people.row, infected)[people.row]
catches = (people.state == S) & people.draw(escape_probability[exposure])
people.state = xp.where(catches, I, people.state)
people.write_to(model.columns[Person])   # back to the agents, when needed
```

The same code runs on numpy, CuPy and JAX; with the same seed and stream it draws the same numbers on each. The population is fixed while the columns are on the device: add and remove agents on the host table, then copy again.

#### `class DeviceTable(stream: PhiloxStream, **columns: Any)`

Equal-length device columns and the stream their phases draw from.

**Parameters:**

- **stream** – the PhiloxStream of the table; its backend holds the columns.
- **columns** – column names and their initial values (host or device arrays).

Copy every column to the stream’s backend; they must have one length.

#### `classmethod from_columns(table: ColumnTable, stream: PhiloxStream, names: list[str] | None = None) → DeviceTable`

The live rows of a host `ColumnTable` (every column, or `names`).

#### `property backend: Backend`

The backend the columns live on.

#### `property xp: Any`

The backend’s array namespace.

#### `property columns: list[str]`

The column names.

#### `draw(p: Any) → Any`

One Bernoulli(p) per row, `p` a probability or one per row.

#### `set_where(name: str, mask: Any, value: Any) → None`

`column[mask] = value`, functionally.

#### `thin(name: str, survival: Any) → Any`

Replace the counts in `name` by Binomial(count, survival); returns them.

#### `to_numpy(name: str) → Any`

A host copy of column `name`.

#### `to_dataframe() → DataFrame`

A host copy of every column, indexed by `unique_id` when it is one.

#### `write_to(table: ColumnTable, names: list[str] | None = None) → None`

Copy columns back into the live rows of a host `ColumnTable` (same rows).

`CohortTable` on a device: binomial thinning, splits and merges as array programs.

[`DeviceCohortTable`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/gpu.html#modelly.gpu.cohorts.DeviceCohortTable) has the operations of [`CohortTable`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/batch.html#modelly.batch.cohorts.CohortTable) (`add`, `thin`, `draw`, `split`, `compact`, `merge`, `total`, `totals_by`) with the columns on a backend and the binomial draws from a [`PhiloxStream`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/gpu.html#modelly.gpu.streams.PhiloxStream), so the same seed gives the same counts on numpy, CuPy and JAX. Updates are functional: `table["age"] = ...` replaces the column, and `table["stage"][rows] = x` (which works on the host table) is written `table.set_where("stage", mask, x)`.

The law of every operation is the host table’s (`docs/vectorised_phases.md`, cohort compression); the numbers differ from the host table’s, which draws from `model.rng`.

#### `class DeviceCohortTable(stream: PhiloxStream, **columns: Any)`

Rows of (state columns, count) on a device.

**Parameters:**

- **stream** – the PhiloxStream the binomial draws come from; its backend holds the rows.
- **columns** – state column names and their dtypes.

An empty table with an integer `count` and the given state columns.

#### `classmethod from_table(table: CohortTable, stream: PhiloxStream) → DeviceCohortTable`

A copy of the live rows of a host `CohortTable`.

#### `property backend: Backend`

The backend the rows live on.

#### `property columns: list[str]`

`count` then the state columns.

#### `set_where(name: str, mask: Any, value: Any) → None`

`column[mask] = value`, functionally.

#### `total(where: Any = None) → int`

Individuals in the table, or in the rows selected by the mask `where`.

#### `totals_by(column: str, minlength: int = 0) → Any`

Individuals per value of an integer state column (a device array).

#### `add(count: Any, **values: Any) → Any`

Append cohorts (scalars or equal-length arrays); returns their row indices.

#### `thin(survival: Any) → Any`

Each count becomes Binomial(count, survival); returns the new counts.

#### `draw(p: Any, where: Any = None) → Any`

Binomial(count, p) events per row (or per selected row); counts unchanged.

#### `split(p: Any, where: Any = None, **changes: Any) → Any`

Move Binomial(count, p) individuals of each selected row to a new row.

The new rows copy their source row’s state, then apply `changes`. Returns the new rows’ indices.

#### `compact() → int`

Drop the empty cohorts, keeping row order; returns how many were dropped.

#### `merge() → int`

Combine rows with identical state, summing counts; sorted by state, no empties.

#### `to_dataframe() → DataFrame`

A host copy of the rows.

A `CellIndex` on the device: per-cell counts, neighbour sums and random moves.

`DeviceCellIndex(index, backend)` copies the CSR adjacency of a [`CellIndex`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/space.html#modelly.space.cells.index.CellIndex) (the cells’ `connections`, in their order) to the device once. Its three operations answer the same questions as the host index, as array programs:

- `counts(rows, weights)`: agents (or a quantity) per cell, a scatter-add;
- `neighbor_sum(values)`: per cell, the sum over its neighbours, a gather and a segmented sum along the CSR rows;
- `random_neighbor(rows, stream)`: a uniformly chosen neighbour per agent, with a bounded integer from a [`PhiloxStream`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/gpu.html#modelly.gpu.streams.PhiloxStream).

Integer counts and sums are exact, so they are identical on every backend. Float sums are exact up to the order of additions: within a few ulps.

#### `class DeviceCellIndex(index: CellIndex, backend: Any = None)`

The adjacency of a cell space as device arrays.

**Parameters:**

- **index** – the host `CellIndex` whose adjacency is copied.
- **backend** – a backend or backend name (see `get_backend`).

Copy the CSR adjacency (row pointers and neighbour rows) to the device.

#### `classmethod from_csr(indptr: ndarray, indices: ndarray, backend: Any = None) → DeviceCellIndex`

An index from CSR arrays directly (row pointers, then neighbour rows).

#### `counts(rows: Any, weights: Any = None) → Any`

Per-cell total of `weights` (or of ones) over the agents in `rows`.

#### `neighbor_sum(values: Any) → Any`

For every cell, the sum of `values` over its neighbouring cells.

#### `random_neighbor(rows: Any, stream: PhiloxStream | PhiloxDraw) → Any`

One uniformly chosen neighbour row per entry of `rows` (from `stream`).

A row without neighbours is returned unchanged. `stream` is a `PhiloxStream` (its next draw is used) or one `PhiloxDraw`.

#### `to_layer(values: Any) → Any`

Reshape a per-cell vector to the grid’s dimensions.

## Memory

Populations larger than the GPU’s memory: plan batches and run a phase over them.

The columns stay on the host (numpy, or memory-mapped files); a phase runs on the device one batch of rows at a time. [`plan_memory()`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/gpu.html#modelly.gpu.memory.plan_memory) sizes the batches from the bytes a row needs on the device (its columns plus the temporaries the phase makes) and the device’s free memory; [`run_batched()`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/gpu.html#modelly.gpu.memory.run_batched) copies each batch in, runs the phase and copies its outputs back:

```default
plan = plan_memory(len(state), bytes_per_row=64, backend=backend)
draw = stream.draws()                       # one draw for the whole phase

def recover(batch, start):
    u = draw.random(len(batch["days"]), start=start)
    return {"state": xp.where(u < gamma, R, batch["state"])}

out = run_batched(plan, recover, {"state": state, "days": days}, backend)
```

A phase that draws by position (`start`) gives the same numbers whatever the batch size, so a batched run equals the run in one batch, bit for bit. Only phases whose rows do not read each other batch exactly; a reduction over rows (counts per cell) is a sum of per-batch reductions, which the caller adds.

#### `class MemoryPlan(rows: int, batch_rows: int, bytes_per_row: int, budget: int)`

How many rows go to the device at once.

**Variables:**

- **rows** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – rows of the population.
- **batch_rows** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – rows per batch (the last batch may be shorter).
- **bytes_per_row** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – device bytes one row needs during the phase.
- **budget** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – device bytes the plan allows.

#### `property batches: int`

The number of batches.

#### `slices() → Iterator[slice]`

The row range of each batch, in order.

#### `plan_memory(rows: int, bytes_per_row: int, backend: Any = None, budget: int | None = None) → MemoryPlan`

Batches of rows that fit in `budget` bytes (half the free device memory by default).

**Raises:**

[**ValueError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#ValueError) – when `bytes_per_row` is not positive.

#### `run_batched(plan: MemoryPlan, phase: Callable[[dict[str, Any], int], Mapping[str, Any]], columns: Mapping[str, ndarray], backend: Backend | str | None = None) → dict[str, ndarray]`

Run `phase(batch, start)` over the batches of `plan`; host outputs, joined.

`batch` maps each column name to the batch’s rows on the device, and `start` is the batch’s first row, for drawing by position. The phase returns device arrays, one value per row of the batch.

# Differentiable models

`modelly.diff` simulates models written as JAX phases and differentiates their outputs with respect to their parameters. How to use it, and when the gradients mean something, is in [Differentiable models](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/differentiable.html).

## Models and phases

A model as JAX column phases: traced, compiled and differentiated with respect to parameters.

A [`DiffModel`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/diff.html#modelly.diff.model.DiffModel) is the array side of a Modelly model written with columns: a state (a dict of column arrays and model-level values), an `init(params, rng)` that builds it, and step phases that each return the columns they change. JAX traces the phases once, runs the steps with `lax.scan` and differentiates the recorded outputs with respect to `params`:

```default
@phase
def returns(state, params, rng):
    w = state["wealth"] * jnp.exp(params["volatility"] * rng.normal(n))
    return {"wealth": w / w.mean()}

@phase(differentiable=False)
def census(state, params, rng):
    return {"rich": (state["wealth"] > 2).sum()}

model = DiffModel(init, [returns, census], outputs={"gini": gini})
series = model.simulate({"volatility": 0.4}, steps=100, seed=1)
grads = jax.grad(lambda p: model.simulate(p, 100, 1)["gini"][-1])(params)
```

`differentiable=False` stops gradients at the phase’s updates (bookkeeping, integer counters, a rule the gradient should not see) and makes its Bernoulli draws exact 0/1 draws. In a differentiable phase a Bernoulli draw goes through an estimator (`modelly.diff.estimators`), and warns that the gradient is an approximation; normal and uniform draws are pathwise and exact.

#### `class Phase(function: Callable[[dict[str, Any], Mapping[str, Any], DiffRandom], Mapping[str, Any]], differentiable: bool = True, name: str = '')`

One step phase: a function of (state, params, rng) returning updated entries.

**Variables:**

- **function** ([*collections.abc.Callable*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)*[**[*[*dict*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **Any**]**, *[*collections.abc.Mapping*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **Any**]**, *[*modelly.diff.estimators.DiffRandom*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/diff.html#modelly.diff.estimators.DiffRandom)*]**, *[*collections.abc.Mapping*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **Any**]**]*) – the phase; it returns a dict of the state entries it changes.
- **differentiable** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – whether gradients flow through its updates.
- **name** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the phase’s name (the function’s by default).

#### `phase(function: Callable[[dict[str, Any], Mapping[str, Any], DiffRandom], Mapping[str, Any]] | None = None, *, differentiable: bool = True) → Any`

Declare a step phase, as `@phase` or `@phase(differentiable=False)`.

#### `class Trace(outputs: dict[str, Any], log_prob: Any)`

One simulated run: the output series and the score-function log-probability.

**Variables:**

- **outputs** ([*dict*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **Any**]*) – `{name: array}`, one value per step, the initial state first.
- **log_prob** (*Any*) – sum of log P(draw) over score-function draws (0 without any).

#### `class DiffModel(init: Callable[[Mapping[str, Any], DiffRandom], dict[str, Any]], phases: Sequence[Phase | Callable[[dict[str, Any], Mapping[str, Any], DiffRandom], Mapping[str, Any]]], outputs: Mapping[str, Callable[[dict[str, Any], Mapping[str, Any]], Any]], estimator: str = 'straight_through')`

Column phases over a state of arrays, simulated and differentiated by JAX.

**Parameters:**

- **init** – `init(params, rng) -> state`, the initial state (a dict of arrays).
- **phases** – the step phases in order (`Phase` objects or plain functions).
- **outputs** – `{name: fn(state, params) -> scalar}`, recorded every step.
- **estimator** – the default estimator of Bernoulli draws (see `estimators`).

Check the phases and the estimator; nothing is traced yet.

#### `record(state: dict[str, Any], params: Mapping[str, Any]) → dict[str, Any]`

The outputs of `state`.

#### `trace(params: Mapping[str, Any], steps: int, key: Any) → Trace`

Simulate `steps` steps from `key` (traceable: use it inside jax.grad).

#### `simulate(params: Mapping[str, Any], steps: int, seed: int = 0) → dict`

The output series of one run seeded with `seed` (JAX arrays).

## Discrete choices

Gradients through discrete random choices: three estimators, all approximations.

An agent that adopts, dies or infects with probability `p` makes a 0/1 choice; the model’s output is a step function of `p` for fixed random numbers, whose derivative is zero almost everywhere. Three standard ways to get a usable gradient anyway, each with a cost:

- `"straight_through"` (Bengio, Leonard and Courville 2013): the forward pass draws the exact 0/1 Bernoulli; the backward pass treats the draw as if it were `p` (derivative one). Exact simulation, **biased** gradient.
- `"gumbel_softmax"` (Jang, Gu and Poole 2017; Maddison, Mnih and Teh 2017): the draw is replaced by the relaxed Bernoulli `sigmoid((logit p + logistic noise) / temperature)`, a smooth function of `p`. Exact gradient of a **relaxed model** that is not the original one; the lower the temperature, the closer the model and the noisier the gradient.
- `"score_function"` (REINFORCE, Williams 1992): the draw is exact and carries no gradient; the gradient of the expected output comes from `output * d log P(draw) / dp`. **Unbiased** for the expectation, with a variance that grows with the number of draws: average many replicates.

Every use warns once with [`GradientApproximationWarning`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/diff.html#modelly.diff.estimators.GradientApproximationWarning). A pathwise draw (`normal`, `uniform` through a smooth function) needs no estimator: its gradient is exact for the given random numbers.

#### `exception GradientApproximationWarning`

A gradient goes through a discrete random choice and is only an approximation.

#### `warn_approximation(estimator: str) → None`

Warn that gradients through `estimator` are approximate, and how.

#### `class DiffRandom(key: Any, estimator: str = 'straight_through', differentiable: bool = True, temperature: float = 0.5, log_prob: Any = 0.0)`

The random numbers of one phase in one step, and the log-probability of its draws.

**Variables:**

- **key** (*Any*) – the JAX key the draws are split from.
- **estimator** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – how `bernoulli` passes gradients (see the module docstring).
- **differentiable** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – False in a phase whose updates carry no gradient (exact draws).
- **temperature** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – the Gumbel-softmax temperature.
- **log_prob** (*Any*) – the sum of log P(draw) of score-function draws, for the surrogate.

#### `uniform(shape: tuple[int, ...]) → Any`

Uniforms in [0, 1): a pathwise draw, exact gradients through what uses them.

#### `normal(shape: tuple[int, ...]) → Any`

Standard normals: a pathwise draw (reparameterisation), exact gradients.

#### `bernoulli(p: Any, estimator: str | None = None) → Any`

0/1 draws with probability `p` (floats), differentiable by an estimator.

## Gradient checks

Gradient checks: automatic derivatives against central finite differences.

`check_gradients(f, params)` compares `jax.grad(f)` at `params` with `(f(p + h) - f(p - h)) / 2h` for each parameter, in float64 (inside `jax.enable_x64`), with `h` relative to the parameter’s size. They agree when `f` is smooth: a model whose randomness is pathwise (normals, uniforms through smooth functions) or relaxed (`gumbel_softmax`) with the random numbers fixed by a seed. They do not agree, and should not, through a straight-through or score-function estimator: there `f` is a step function for fixed random numbers and its finite differences are zero or huge.

#### `class GradientCheck(autodiff: dict[str, float], finite_difference: dict[str, float], relative_error: dict[str, float], tolerance: float)`

Automatic and finite-difference derivatives, parameter by parameter.

**Variables:**

- **autodiff** ([*dict*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*]*) – `{name: df/dname}` from `jax.grad`.
- **finite_difference** ([*dict*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*]*) – `{name: central difference}`.
- **relative_error** ([*dict*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*]*) – `{name: |a - f| / max(|a|, |f|)}` (0 when both are tiny).
- **tolerance** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – the largest relative error accepted.

#### `property ok: bool`

Whether every parameter’s relative error is within the tolerance.

#### `check_gradients(function: Callable[[Mapping[str, float]], float], params: Mapping[str, float], step: float = 1e-05, tolerance: float = 0.0001) → GradientCheck`

Compare `jax.grad(function)` with central differences at `params`, in float64.

## Gradient-based calibration

Gradient-based calibration of a [`DiffModel`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/diff.html#modelly.diff.model.DiffModel).

The parameters, the targets and the result read like the other methods of `modelly.calibrate`: priors give the search box (their support, log-scaled priors on a log scale), targets give the observed series or statistics:

```default
fit = GradientCalibration(
    model,
    priors={"innovation": Prior.uniform(0.001, 0.2), "imitation": Prior.uniform(0.05, 1)},
    targets=[Target("adoption", observed=curve)],
    options=GradientOptions(steps=100, iterations=300, seed=1),
).run()
fit.params, fit.gradient   # the estimate and the local sensitivities there
```

The optimiser is Adam on unconstrained coordinates (a logistic map onto the box), started at the prior medians. Every iteration runs the same replicate seeds (common random numbers), so the objective is a deterministic function of the parameters and the whole fit is the same for the same seed. Replicates are averaged before the distance, as in the other methods. Score-function draws add the surrogate `L + stop_gradient(L) * (log P - stop_gradient(log P))`, whose gradient is the score-function estimate and whose value is `L`.

#### `class GradientOptions(steps: int = 100, iterations: int = 200, learning_rate: float = 0.05, replicates: int = 1, seed: int = 0, fixed: Mapping[str, float]=<factory>)`

How the fit runs.

**Variables:**

- **steps** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – steps per simulated run.
- **iterations** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – optimiser iterations.
- **learning_rate** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – Adam’s step size, in unconstrained coordinates.
- **replicates** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – runs per evaluation, averaged before the distance.
- **seed** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – the root of every random number: same seed, same fit.
- **fixed** ([*collections.abc.Mapping*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*]*) – parameters every run takes, not fitted.

#### `class GradientFit(params: dict[str, float], loss: float, gradient: dict[str, float], history: DataFrame)`

The result: the estimate, its loss, the gradient there and the path to it.

**Variables:**

- **params** ([*dict*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*]*) – the parameters with the lowest loss seen.
- **loss** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – their loss.
- **gradient** ([*dict*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#dict)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*]*) – d loss / d parameter at `params` (local sensitivities).
- **history** (*pandas.DataFrame*) – one row per iteration: the parameters and the loss.

#### `class GradientCalibration(model: DiffModel, priors: Mapping[str, Prior], targets: Sequence[Target], options: GradientOptions | None = None)`

Fit the priors’ parameters of a DiffModel to targets by gradient descent.

**Parameters:**

- **model** – the differentiable model.
- **priors** – `{parameter: Prior}` (continuous priors) for every fitted parameter.
- **targets** – the observed quantities; distances are the built-in `rmse`, `mae` or `euclidean`, or any function written with `jax.numpy`.
- **options** – steps, iterations, learning rate, replicates and seed.

Check the definition; nothing runs before `run`.

#### `params(z: Any) → dict[str, Any]`

The parameters at unconstrained coordinates `z` (traceable).

#### `loss(params: Mapping[str, Any]) → Any`

The total distance at `params` over the replicates (traceable).

#### `run() → GradientFit`

Run Adam for `options.iterations` iterations; the best point seen.

## Zoo twins

The Bouchaud-Mezard model as a differentiable model (`modelly.diff`).

The same step as `model.py`: a multiplicative random return `W_i <- W_i exp(sigma sqrt(dt) xi_i - sigma^2 dt / 2)`, an exchange toward the mean at rate `J`, and a division by the mean, with the Gini coefficient recorded every step. The returns are pathwise (`xi_i` standard normal times a smooth function of `sigma`), so for fixed random numbers the Gini series is a smooth function of `volatility` and `exchange` and its gradient is exact: it agrees with finite differences, and gradient descent on it fits both parameters to a Gini series of the agent model.

model = differentiable_model(n=2000, dt=0.01) series = model.simulate({“volatility”: 1.0, “exchange”: 1.0}, steps=300, seed=1)

#### `gini(wealth: Any) → Any`

The Gini coefficient `sum_i (2 i - n - 1) x_(i) / (n sum x)`, in JAX.

#### `differentiable_model(n: int = 2000, dt: float = 0.01) → DiffModel`

`n` savers stepped by `dt`; parameters `volatility` and `exchange`.

The well-mixed Bass diffusion model as a differentiable model (`modelly.diff`).

The same step as `model.py` with `mixing="well-mixed"`: every household that has not adopted adopts with probability `(innovation + imitation * share) * dt`, `share` the adopted share of the population. Adoption is a 0/1 choice, so its gradient needs an estimator (`modelly.diff.estimators`):

- `"straight_through"` (the default): the run is the exact agent model; the gradient differentiates each draw as if it were its probability, which is biased but points the right way, enough to fit `innovation` and `imitation` to an adoption curve;
- `"gumbel_softmax"`: each household holds a relaxed adoption in (0, 1); the gradient is exact for that relaxed model (and agrees with finite differences), whose curve is close to, not equal to, the agent model’s;
- `"score_function"`: unbiased for the expected curve, very noisy with thousands of households.

Every use warns with `GradientApproximationWarning`.

#### `differentiable_model(households: int = 5000, dt: float = 0.1, estimator: str = 'straight_through') → DiffModel`

`households` well-mixed households; parameters `innovation` and `imitation`.

## ODEs in a differentiable model

ODEs in a differentiable model: gradients of ODE parameters, for gradient calibration.

`ode_phase(rhs, state)` is a `DiffModel` phase that integrates `dy/dt = rhs(t, y, params)` over one step for every agent, the state variables being columns of the model’s state, with the classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method on `substeps` equal steps, run by `lax.scan`. JAX differentiates through those steps, so the gradient is the exact gradient of the computed solution (discretise, then differentiate) and `check_gradients` and `GradientCalibration` work on ODE parameters as on any other: a viral clearance rate or a growth rate is fitted to observed curves by gradient descent. No package beyond JAX (the `diff` extra) is needed.

Why not an adaptive solver with an adjoint (`jax.experimental.ode.odeint`): its adjoint rebuilds the state by integrating backwards in time, which is unstable for any system that decays (a virus being cleared, a population dying out), and its gradients then blow up. A fixed step is stable both ways; check the accuracy by halving it (`substeps`), and use `modelly.couple.solve_batch` (adaptive, per agent, no gradients) in an ordinary model.

from modelly.diff import DiffModel from modelly.diff.ode import ode_phase

**def decay(t, y, params):**

return -params[“clearance”] * y

model = DiffModel(init, [ode_phase(decay, [“virus”])], outputs={“load”: mean_virus})

#### `integrate(rhs: Callable[[Any, Any, Mapping[str, Any]], Any], y0: Any, duration: float, params: Mapping[str, Any], substeps: int = 64, start: Any = 0.0) → Any`

The state after `duration` by RK4 on `substeps` steps (traceable, differentiable).

`start` is the time of the first step, as `rhs` sees it.

#### `ode_phase(rhs: Callable[[Any, Any, Mapping[str, Any]], Any], state: Sequence[str], duration: float = 1.0, *, substeps: int = 64, name: str | None = None) → Phase`

A differentiable phase integrating `rhs` over `duration` for the columns `state`.

`rhs(t, y, params)` receives `y` of shape `(len(state), agents)` and the model’s parameters; it is written with `jax.numpy`.

# Viz

`modelly.viz` draws models in the browser and in notebooks. The names most models need are exported by the package itself: `from modelly.viz import SolaraViz, SpaceRenderer`.

Module

Contents

modelly.viz.solara

SolaraViz, the model controller, parameter inputs and Slider

modelly.viz.components

make_space_component, make_plot_component

modelly.viz.render

SpaceRenderer, the portrayal styles, backends and space drawers

modelly.viz.mpl

matplotlib backend, draw_space and plot components

modelly.viz.altair

Altair backend and plot components

modelly.viz.console

CommandConsole

⚠️ **Important note for SolaraViz users**

When using **SolaraViz**, Modelly models must be instantiated **using keyword arguments only**. SolaraViz creates model instances internally via keyword-based parameters, and positional arguments are **not supported**.

**Not supported:**

```python
MyModel(10, 10)
```

**Supported:**

```python
MyModel(width=10, height=10)
```

To avoid errors, it is recommended to define your model constructor with keyword-only arguments, for example:

```python
class MyModel(Model):
    def __init__(self, *, width, height, rng=None): ...
```

For detailed tutorials, please refer to:

- [Basic Visualization](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/6_visualization_basic.html)
- [Dynamic Agent Visualization](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/7_visualization_dynamic_agents.html)
- [Custom Visualization Components](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/tutorials/10_visualization_custom.html)

## Solara app

Modelly visualization module for creating interactive model visualizations.

This module provides components to create browser- and Jupyter notebook-based visualizations of Modelly models, allowing users to watch models run step-by-step and interact with model parameters.

**Key features:**

- SolaraViz: Main component for creating visualizations, supporting grid displays and plots
- ModelController: Handles model execution controls (step, play, pause, reset)
- UserInputs: Generates UI elements for adjusting model parameters

The module uses Solara for rendering in Jupyter notebooks or as standalone web applications. It supports various types of visualizations including matplotlib plots, agent grids, and custom visualization components.

**Usage:**

1. Define an agent_portrayal function to specify how agents should be displayed
1. Set up model_params to define adjustable parameters
1. Create a SolaraViz instance with your model, parameters, and desired measures
1. Display the visualization in a Jupyter notebook or run as a Solara app

See the Visualization Tutorial and example models for more details.

- **kwargs** – additional keyword arguments passed to ax.scatter

**Returns:**

Returns the Axes object with the plot drawn onto it.

`agent_portrayal` is called with an agent and should return a AgentPortrayalStyle. Valid fields in this object are “color”, “size”, “marker”, “zorder”, alpha, linewidths, and edgecolors. Other field are ignored and will result in a user warning.
