# Lint

The static checks behind `python -m modelly.lint`. The rules, with examples, are in [Lint](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/lint.html).

Static checks for Modelly models: bugs that break reproducibility and loops that scale badly.

Run as `python -m modelly.lint PATH [PATH ...]`. Nothing is imported or executed: the source is parsed and walked. A finding on a line ending in `# noqa` (or `# noqa: MDL101`) is skipped, and `[tool.modelly.lint]` in pyproject.toml selects and ignores rules (see `modelly.lint.config`). The rules, with examples, are in `docs/lint.md`; `--explain CODE` prints one of them.

#### `class Finding(path: str, line: int, column: int, rule: Rule)`

One rule hit at a place in a file.

#### `location() → str`

`path:line:col: CODE message`, the format editors jump to.

#### `class Rule(code: str, severity: str, message: str, hint: str)`

One check: its code, how serious it is, what it found and what to do instead.

#### `lint_paths(paths: Iterable[str | Path]) → list[Finding]`

Return the findings for every Python file in `paths`.

**Raises:**

[**SyntaxError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#SyntaxError) – when a file is not valid Python.

#### `lint_source(source: str, path: str = '<string>', siblings: SiblingColumns | None = None) → list[Finding]`

Return the findings for one module’s source, sorted by position.

`siblings` resolves the agent classes the module imports from other files of the project, so MDL107 knows their Column attributes; without it only this source counts.

**Raises:**

[**SyntaxError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#SyntaxError) – when `source` is not valid Python.

The rules of `modelly.lint` and the AST helpers they share.

Codes below 100 are errors: the model runs but gives a wrong or unreproducible result. Codes from 100 are warnings: the model is right but its cost grows faster than it needs to.

#### `class Rule(code: str, severity: str, message: str, hint: str)`

One check: its code, how serious it is, what it found and what to do instead.

#### `dotted(node: AST | None) → list[str]`

Return the names along an attribute chain: `self.model.agents` -> self, model, agents.

#### `is_population(node: AST | None, in_model: bool) → bool`

Whether `node` is the model’s whole population or one type of it, not a cell’s agents.

#### `is_set_expr(node: AST) → bool`

Whether `node` builds a set, whose iteration order follows memory addresses.

#### `is_mutable_literal(node: AST | None) → bool`

Whether `node` is `[]`, `{}`, a set literal or an empty list/dict/set call.

#### `calls_super_init(func: FunctionDef | AsyncFunctionDef) → bool`

Whether `func` calls `super().__init__` or `<Base>.__init__(self, ...)`.

#### `branches(func: FunctionDef | AsyncFunctionDef) → int`

Count the decision points of `func`: its cyclomatic complexity minus one.

Lint rules from other packages: the `modelly.lint_rules` entry-point group.

An entry point names an object with two attributes: `rule`, a `Rule` whose code is not one of Modelly’s, and `check(tree)`, which takes the parsed module (`ast.Module`) and yields the `(line, column)` of every hit. `# noqa` and the `[tool.modelly.lint]` selection apply to plugin codes as to built-in ones.

A plugin that fails to load, lacks either attribute or reuses a built-in code is left out with a `RuntimeWarning` naming it; the other rules still run. Plugins are read once per process (`plugin_rules.cache_clear()` reads them again).

#### `plugin_rules() → dict[str, Any]`

The usable plugin rules, by code.

#### `all_rules() → dict[str, Rule]`

The built-in rules, then the plugin rules, by code.

#### `plugin_hits(tree: Module) → set[tuple[int, int, str]]`

`(line, column, code)` of every plugin rule’s hit in `tree`.

The `[tool.modelly.lint]` table of pyproject.toml: which findings to keep.

``toml [tool.modelly.lint] select = ["MDL0", "MDL101"]           # only these codes or prefixes (default: all) ignore = ["MDL105"]                   # drop these codes or prefixes per-file-ignores = { "tests/*" = ["MDL001"], "setup_*.py" = ["MDL1"] } ``

The file is the first `pyproject.toml` found from the working directory upwards; per-file patterns are globs on the path relative to that file’s folder, or on the bare file name. `--select` and `--ignore` on the command line replace the file’s values.

#### `exception ConfigError`

The `[tool.modelly.lint]` table has a key or value the linter does not know.

#### `prefixes(value: str | list[str]) → tuple[str, ...]`

Normalise `"MDL0, MDL101"` or `["MDL0", "MDL101"]` to upper-case prefixes.

#### `matches(code: str, codes: tuple[str, ...]) → bool`

Whether `code` starts with one of `codes`.

#### `class Config(select: tuple[str, ...] = (), ignore: tuple[str, ...] = (), per_file_ignores: tuple[tuple[str, tuple[str, ...]], ...] = (), root: Path = PosixPath('.'))`

Which findings to keep: the select, ignore and per-file-ignores settings.

#### `keeps(finding: lint.Finding) → bool`

Whether `finding` survives select, ignore and its file’s ignores.

#### `file_ignores(path: str) → tuple[str, ...]`

The codes ignored for `path` by the per-file-ignores patterns it matches.

#### `find_pyproject(start: Path) → Path | None`

The first `pyproject.toml` in `start` or one of its parents.

#### `load_config(start: Path | None = None) → Config`

Read `[tool.modelly.lint]` from the nearest pyproject.toml; empty when there is none.

**Raises:**

- [**ConfigError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/lint.html#modelly.lint.config.ConfigError) – on an unknown key or a value that is not a list of codes.
- [**tomllib.TOMLDecodeError**](https://docs.python.org/3/library/tomllib.html#tomllib.TOMLDecodeError) – when the file is not valid TOML.

# Profile

The runtime profiler behind `python -m modelly.profile`. How to read its report is in [Profiling a model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/profile.html).

Runtime profiling for Modelly models: where each step’s time goes, in Modelly terms.

The runtime companion of `python -m modelly.lint`. `Profiler` times each step, every `AgentSet.do` / `shuffle_do` / `map` call by agent class and method, `DataCollector.collect` and the scheduled-event callbacks, and counts births and deaths per step:

```default
from modelly.profile import Profiler

with Profiler(model) as prof:
    model.run_for(100)
print(prof.report())
```

From a shell: `python -m modelly.profile path/to/model.py:MyModel --steps 100`. `compare_sizes` builds the model at several population sizes and compares the cost per agent (`--sizes 1000,4000` on the command line). Nothing is patched outside the `with` block. The guide is `docs/profile.md`.

#### `class Profiler(model: Model[Any, Any], sample_every: int = 1)`

Record where each step of `model` spends its time.

Use it as a context manager around the run:

```default
with Profiler(model) as prof:
    model.run_for(100)
print(prof.report())
frame = prof.to_dataframe()
```

**Parameters:**

- **model** – the model to profile.
- **sample_every** – profile one step in `sample_every` (steps 1, 1 + N, …); the others run through the wrappers untimed.

Notes

The patched methods are class attributes, so while the block runs every agent set, collector and event in the process is timed, not only those of `model`. Only one profiler can be active at a time. Times of nested loops (an agent’s step calling `do` on another set) are inclusive.

Prepare a profiler; nothing is patched until the `with` block starts.

#### `report(top: int = 15) → str`

A text table of the `top` costliest operations, with hints.

#### `to_dict() → dict[str, Any]`

The summary, the per-step totals and the hints, JSON-ready.

#### `to_dataframe() → pd.DataFrame`

One row per step (kind `step`) and per operation within a step.

#### `class SizeComparison(model: str, runs: list[SizeRun])`

The profiles of one model built at several sizes, compared per agent.

`runs` are ordered by size, smallest first.

#### `growths() → list[Growth]`

The whole step, then each agent loop, costliest at the largest size first.

#### `hints() → list[str]`

A hint per notable operation whose cost per agent grows roughly with N.

#### `report(top: int = 15) → str`

The us-per-agent table, one column per size, then the growth and the hints.

#### `to_dict() → dict[str, Any]`

The sizes, each operation’s us per agent and growth, and the hints.

#### `to_dataframe() → DataFrame`

One row per operation and size: `operation`, `size`, `us_per_agent`.

#### `class StepRecord(step: int, time: float, agents: int, wall: float = 0.0, cpu: float = 0.0, births: int = 0, deaths: int = 0, ops: dict[tuple[str, str, str], list[~typing.Any]] = <factory>)`

What one profiled step cost.

`ops` maps `(kind, owner, name)` to `[calls, agents visited, wall s, CPU s]`. `kind` is an AgentSet method (`do`, `shuffle_do`, `map`), `collect` or `event`; `owner` is the agent class (`A|B` for a mixed set) or the collector class. Births and deaths count from this step’s start to the next one’s, so agents created by events in between are included.

#### `add(key: tuple[str, str, str] | None, agents: int, times: tuple[Any, ...]) → None`

Add one timed call; `key` None is the step itself.

#### `compare_sizes(factory: Callable[[int], Model[Any, Any]], sizes: Sequence[int], steps: int = 100, sample_every: int = 1) → SizeComparison`

Build the model with `factory(size)` at each size, profile `steps` steps of each.

**Raises:**

[**ValueError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#ValueError) – when there are fewer than two different positive sizes.

The profiler: time a running model’s steps, agent-set loops, data collection and events.

`Profiler` replaces a handful of framework methods while its `with` block runs and puts the originals back on exit, so a model that is not being profiled runs exactly the code it always does. The wrappers never draw a random number nor reorder a loop: a profiled run gives the same results as an unprofiled one.

#### `class StepRecord(step: int, time: float, agents: int, wall: float = 0.0, cpu: float = 0.0, births: int = 0, deaths: int = 0, ops: dict[tuple[str, str, str], list[~typing.Any]] = <factory>)`

What one profiled step cost.

`ops` maps `(kind, owner, name)` to `[calls, agents visited, wall s, CPU s]`. `kind` is an AgentSet method (`do`, `shuffle_do`, `map`), `collect` or `event`; `owner` is the agent class (`A|B` for a mixed set) or the collector class. Births and deaths count from this step’s start to the next one’s, so agents created by events in between are included.

#### `add(key: tuple[str, str, str] | None, agents: int, times: tuple[Any, ...]) → None`

Add one timed call; `key` None is the step itself.

#### `agent_classes(agentset: Any) → str`

The class names of the members of `agentset`, sorted and joined by `|`.

#### `callable_name(fn: Any) → str`

A readable name for a method name, a function or an event callback.

#### `class Profiler(model: Model[Any, Any], sample_every: int = 1)`

Record where each step of `model` spends its time.

Use it as a context manager around the run:

```default
with Profiler(model) as prof:
    model.run_for(100)
print(prof.report())
frame = prof.to_dataframe()
```

**Parameters:**

- **model** – the model to profile.
- **sample_every** – profile one step in `sample_every` (steps 1, 1 + N, …); the others run through the wrappers untimed.

Notes

The patched methods are class attributes, so while the block runs every agent set, collector and event in the process is timed, not only those of `model`. Only one profiler can be active at a time. Times of nested loops (an agent’s step calling `do` on another set) are inclusive.

Prepare a profiler; nothing is patched until the `with` block starts.

#### `report(top: int = 15) → str`

A text table of the `top` costliest operations, with hints.

#### `to_dict() → dict[str, Any]`

The summary, the per-step totals and the hints, JSON-ready.

#### `to_dataframe() → pd.DataFrame`

One row per step (kind `step`) and per operation within a step.

# Provenance

Manifests, verification, bundles and ODD skeletons behind `modelly run`, `modelly verify`, `modelly bundle` and `modelly odd`. How to use them to publish a study is in [Publishing a reproducible study](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/provenance.html).

Provenance and reproducible publication: manifests, verification, bundles and ODD.

`modelly run` runs a model once and writes its collected data and a manifest that records the code, environment, scenario, seeds, inputs, outputs and timing. `modelly verify` reruns a manifest and reports the first output that differs. `modelly bundle` packs a run into a deterministic zip for an archive such as Zenodo. `modelly odd` writes an ODD protocol skeleton from the model’s code.

The same steps from Python:

```default
from modelly.provenance import RunSpec, bundle, run_study, verify

run_study(RunSpec("model.py:Epidemic", out=Path("runs"), steps=100, seed=1))
assert verify(Path("runs/manifest.json")).matches
bundle(Path("runs"), Path("study.zip"))
```

The run manifest: a versioned JSON record of what produced a set of outputs.

`format` names the schema and its major version (`modelly-manifest/1`). A reader accepts any manifest of the same major version and refuses others, so fields can be added without breaking old readers. Paths are relative to the manifest’s folder and written with forward slashes; hashes are `sha256:<hex>` over bytes.

Top-level fields (all present in version 1):

```default
format       the schema name and version
target       {"kind": "file" | "module", "source", "class"}; a file source is
             relative to code.root
code         {"root", "files": {path: hash}, "hash", "git": {"commit", "dirty",
             "diff_hash"} | null}
environment  {"modelly": {"version", "build", "native"}, "python", "platform",
             "dependencies": {name: version}, "packages": {name: version}}
scenario     {"file", "hash", "parameters", "resolved"}
run          {"steps", "seed"}
seeds        {"seed", "entropy", "spawn_key", "stdlib_seed"}
inputs       [{"path", "hash"}]
outputs      [{"table", "path", "format", "hash", "rows", "columns"}]
timing       {"wall_seconds", "cpu_seconds"}
```

Optional fields (added within version 1, absent when they do not apply):

```default
llm_cache    {"path", "hash", "responses"}: the replies of the model's
             language-model clients, replayed by ``modelly verify``
```

#### `exception ManifestError`

A manifest that cannot be read, or one written in an unsupported format.

#### `json_safe(value: Any) → Any`

`value` if JSON can hold it, else its `repr` (documents, never re-reads).

#### `manifest_path(path: Path) → Path`

`path` itself, or the manifest inside it when `path` is a run folder.

#### `check_format(record: Any) → None`

Raise ManifestError unless `record` is a version-1 manifest with every field.

#### `read_manifest(path: Path) → dict[str, Any]`

The manifest at `path` (a file or a run folder), checked against the schema.

#### `write_manifest(folder: Path, record: dict[str, Any]) → Path`

Check and write `record` as `folder/manifest.json` atomically; its path.

Run a model once and record it: outputs on disk and a manifest next to them.

#### `class RunSpec(target: str, out: Path, steps: int, seed: int | None = None, scenario: Path | None = None, params: dict[str, ~typing.Any]=<factory>, inputs: tuple[~pathlib.Path, ...]=())`

What `modelly run` was asked to do.

#### `read_scenario(path: Path | None) → dict[str, Any]`

The parameters of a TOML scenario file (a flat table); `{}` for no file.

#### `run_study(spec: RunSpec) → dict[str, Any]`

Run the model `spec` names, write its outputs and manifest to `spec.out`.

Raises TargetError when the target, scenario or inputs cannot be used; anything the model raises propagates.

Rerun a recorded run from its manifest and compare the new outputs with the old.

The rerun uses the manifest’s target, parameters, seed and step count, writes its outputs to a temporary folder in the recorded formats, reads both sets back and reports the first table, column and row where they differ. A run whose model called a language model is rerun from the replies it recorded (`llm_cache`), offline. Changes that do not stop the rerun (code files, input files or the environment differ from the record) are notes.

#### `class Verification(difference: Difference | None, notes: list[str] = <factory>)`

The outcome of [`verify()`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/provenance.html#modelly.provenance.verify.verify): the first difference (None if all match) and notes.

#### `property matches: bool`

True when every recorded output was reproduced.

#### `verify(path: Path, tolerance: Tolerance | None = None) → Verification`

Rerun the manifest at `path` (a file or run folder) and compare outputs.

Raises ManifestError for an unreadable manifest and TargetError when the model cannot be loaded; anything the model raises propagates.

Find the first place where two runs’ output tables differ.

Numeric columns are compared with `numpy.isclose` under the given tolerances (both 0 by default: the values must be identical); other columns must be equal. Missing values match missing values.

#### `class Difference(table: str, message: str, column: str | None = None, row: int | None = None)`

Where an output differs: table, then column and row when the shapes agree.

#### `class Tolerance(rtol: float = 0.0, atol: float = 0.0)`

Relative and absolute tolerance for numeric columns.

#### `first_difference(table: str, expected: DataFrame, actual: DataFrame, tolerance: Tolerance = Tolerance(rtol=0.0, atol=0.0)) → Difference | None`

The first differing column, row and values of one table, or None if they match.

Columns are scanned in table order and rows top to bottom; the reported row is the row’s position (0-based) in the table.

Pack a recorded run into one deterministic zip a reviewer can verify.

The archive holds the manifest (its paths rewritten for the archive layout), the outputs, the language-model replies the run recorded (if any), the model’s source files under `code/`, the input files under `inputs/`, `requirements.lock`, `seeds.json`, Zenodo metadata (`.zenodo.json`) and a `CITATION.cff` stub. Entries are sorted, stored uncompressed and stamped with a fixed time and mode, so the same run gives the same bytes on every machine.

#### `exception BundleError`

The run folder does not hold what its manifest records.

#### `bundle_entries(folder: Path) → dict[str, bytes]`

Archive name to bytes for the run recorded in `folder`.

#### `bundle(folder: Path, out: Path) → Path`

Write the bundle of the run in `folder` (or of a manifest path) to `out`.

Raises ManifestError for an unreadable manifest and BundleError when outputs or code changed since the run.

The language-model replies of a recorded run, so a rerun needs no network.

`modelly run` exports the replies every [`modelly.llm.Client`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.Client) of the model holds (its attributes, `model.llm` by convention) to `llm-responses.jsonl.gz` next to the outputs, and records it in the manifest as `llm_cache` (`{"path", "hash", "responses"}`). `modelly bundle` packs that file, and `modelly verify` reruns the model inside `modelly.llm.replay.replaying` so every client answers from it, read-only: the study verifies offline, and a call the record does not hold stops the rerun with `CacheMiss`. A run without a client records nothing and its manifest has no `llm_cache`.

#### `model_clients(model: Any) → list[Client]`

The distinct clients among the model’s attributes, in attribute order.

#### `cache_record(model: Any, out: Path) → dict[str, Any] | None`

Export the replies of the model’s clients to `out`; the manifest entry.

**Returns:**

`{"path", "hash", "responses"}`, or None when the model has no client.

#### `cache_problem(manifest: dict[str, Any], folder: Path) → str | None`

Why the recorded cache cannot be used as recorded, or None if it can.

#### `replay_for(manifest: dict[str, Any], folder: Path) → AbstractContextManager[object]`

Replay the run’s recorded replies, or nothing when there are none to replay.

An ODD protocol skeleton (Grimm et al.’s Overview, Design concepts, Details) for a model.

The seven ODD elements are written from what `modelly.provenance.odd_facts` finds in the code; every place only the modeller can fill holds a `TODO` marker.

#### `odd_markdown(model: Model[Any, Any]) → str`

The ODD skeleton of a built model, as Markdown.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.md -->

# LLM

Language-model agents: the client, its cache, budgets, retries, providers and structured decisions. How to use them is in [Language-model agents](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/llm_agents.html).

Language-model agents with runs that replay and costs that stay bounded.

Every call goes through a [`Client`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.Client): it builds the request, answers from the [`ResponseCache`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.ResponseCache) when it can, holds the call against the [`Budget`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.Budget), sends it with retries and a concurrency limit, and caches the reply. Agents mix in [`LLMAgent`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.LLMAgent) and call `self.decide(prompt, schema)`; `decide_all` asks a whole population at once and returns the decisions in agent order.

Adapters: [`AnthropicProvider`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.AnthropicProvider) (Messages API), [`OpenAICompatibleProvider`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.OpenAICompatibleProvider) (OpenAI and local servers such as Ollama or llama.cpp) and [`FakeProvider`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.FakeProvider) (tests and teaching). They use the standard library only; no provider SDK is needed.

Example

```default
>>> from modelly import Agent, Model
>>> from modelly.llm import Client, FakeProvider, LLMAgent
>>> class Voter(LLMAgent, Agent):
...     persona = "You are a voter."
>>> model = Model(rng=7)
>>> model.llm = Client(FakeProvider(lambda r: '{"vote": "yes"}'))
>>> Voter(model).decide("Vote?", {"properties": {"vote": {"enum": ["yes", "no"]}}})
{'vote': 'yes'}
```

Agents with more: `MemoryAgent` (episodic memory, summarised), `plan`, `reflect` and `use_tools` (`modelly.llm.reasoning`), `converse` and `converse_many` (`modelly.llm.conversation`) and `evaluate`, a harness reporting behaviour, consistency and cost per provider (`modelly.llm.evaluate`). `modelly.llm.market` is a 500-trader conversational market that runs offline.

See `docs/llm_agents.md` for reproducibility, budgets, keys and limitations.

## Client and agents

#### `class Client(provider: Provider, *, model: str | None = None, cache: ResponseCache | None = None, budget: Budget | None = None, retry: RetryPolicy | None = None, max_concurrency: int = 4, system: str = '', seed: int | None = None, **params: Any)`

Language-model calls with a cache, a budget, retries and a concurrency limit.

**Parameters:**

- **provider** – The adapter: `AnthropicProvider`, `OpenAICompatibleProvider` or `FakeProvider`.
- **model** – The model name; the provider’s default when None.
- **cache** – Where replies are kept; a fresh in-memory cache when None. Inside `modelly.llm.replay.replaying`, the replayed cache instead.
- **budget** – Token and cost limits; no limit when None.
- **retry** – How failed calls are retried.
- **max_concurrency** – The most calls in flight at once.
- **system** – The system prompt used when a call sets none.
- **seed** – Part of every cache key; agents pass their model’s seed instead.
- ****params** – Default call parameters (`temperature`, `max_tokens`, …).

Example

```default
>>> from modelly.llm import FakeProvider
>>> client = Client(FakeProvider())
>>> client.complete("Hello").cached
False
>>> client.usage.calls
1
```

Set the provider and the defaults of every call.

#### `property usage: Usage`

Calls, cache hits, retries, tokens and cost so far.

#### `next_index(scope: str) → int`

The next call counter of `scope`, for calls not made by an `LLMAgent`.

#### `request(prompt: str | Sequence[Message], *, scope: str = 'model', call_index: int | None = None, system: str | None = None, seed: int | None = None, schema: dict[str, Any] | None = None, **params: Any) → Request`

Build a [`Request`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.Request); `prompt` is a user message or a list of messages.

#### `complete(prompt: str | Sequence[Message], **options: Any) → Response`

One call: options are those of [`request()`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.Client.request).

#### `complete_many(requests: Iterable[Request]) → list[Response]`

Replies to `requests`, in their order.

Cached replies come first and cost nothing. The calls left are held against the budget in order; up to the first that could pass it, they are sent concurrently, counted and cached, then [`BudgetExceeded`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.BudgetExceeded) is raised for the rest.

**Raises:**

- [**CacheMiss**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.CacheMiss) – In replay mode, for the first call the cache does not hold.
- [**BudgetExceeded**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.BudgetExceeded) – Before the first call that could pass the budget.
- [**ProviderError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.ProviderError) – The first call (in order) that failed after its retries.

#### `lookup(request: Request) → Response | None`

The cached reply of `request`; a miss in replay mode raises.

#### `lookup_many(batch: Sequence[Request]) → list[Response | None]`

The cached reply of each request (one query); a miss in replay mode raises.

Hits are counted in order up to the first miss in replay mode, as one [`lookup()`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.Client.lookup) per request would.

#### `reserve(batch: list[Request], pending: list[int]) → tuple[list[int], BudgetExceeded | None]`

The pending calls the budget allows, and the refusal that stopped the rest.

#### `dispatch(batch: list[Request], replies: list[Response | None], allowed: list[int]) → None`

Send the `allowed` calls, then count and cache their replies in order.

#### `collect_all(batch: list[Request], replies: list[Response | None], allowed: list[int], futures: list[Future[Any]]) → list[ProviderError]`

Count every finished call in order; cache the replies in one transaction.

#### `executor() → ThreadPoolExecutor`

The client’s thread pool, made on first use and kept for later batches.

Its threads stop when the client is collected; a pickle leaves it out.

#### `send_here(request: Request) → Future[Any]`

Send `request` in this thread; its outcome as a finished future.

#### `collect(request: Request, future: Future[Any], replies: list[Response | None], index: int, stored: list[tuple[Request, Response]]) → ProviderError | None`

Count one finished call and queue it in `stored` to cache, or return its error.

#### `class LLMAgent`

Mix into an `Agent` (`class Voter(LLMAgent, Agent)`) to ask `model.llm`.

**Variables:**

- **persona** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – The system prompt of this agent’s calls; the client’s when empty.
- **llm_calls** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – How many calls this agent made (including repairs).

Example

```default
>>> from modelly import Agent, Model
>>> from modelly.llm import Client, FakeProvider
>>> class Voter(LLMAgent, Agent):
...     persona = "You are a careful voter."
>>> model = Model(rng=1)
>>> model.llm = Client(FakeProvider())
>>> Voter(model).ask("Vote?").startswith("fake reply")
True
```

#### `property llm: Client`

The client of this agent’s model.

#### `property llm_scope: str`

Who is asking, in cache keys and error messages.

#### `next_call_index() → int`

Take this agent’s next call index.

#### `llm_request(prompt: str, *, schema: dict[str, Any] | None = None, **params: Any) → Request`

A request from this agent; with a schema, the prompt asks for JSON.

#### `ask(prompt: str, **params: Any) → str`

The reply text to `prompt`.

#### `decide(prompt: str, schema: dict[str, Any], *, repairs: int = 1, **params: Any) → Any`

A decision matching `schema`, with up to `repairs` repair calls.

**Raises:**

[**DecisionError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.DecisionError) – When the reply is still invalid after the repairs.

#### `decide_all(agents: Sequence[LLMAgent], prompt: str | Callable[[Any], str], schema: dict[str, Any], *, repairs: int = 1, **params: Any) → list[Any]`

One decision per agent, sent concurrently, returned in the order of `agents`.

**Parameters:**

- **agents** – `LLMAgent` instances of one model.
- **prompt** – The same prompt for all, or a function of the agent.
- **schema** – What each decision must match.
- **repairs** – Repair rounds for invalid replies.
- ****params** – Call parameters for every request.

## Requests and replies

#### `class Request(provider: str, model: str, messages: tuple[Message, ...], system: str = '', params: tuple[tuple[str, Any], ...] = (), scope: str = 'model', call_index: int = 0, seed: int | None = None, schema: dict[str, Any] | None = None)`

Everything that decides a reply, and who asked.

`scope` and `call_index` say which caller made the call and how many it made before: an agent’s id and its own call counter. They are part of the cache key, so two agents asking the same question get their own replies, and the key of a call does not depend on which thread sent it.

Example

```default
>>> r = Request("fake", "m", (Message("user", "Hi"),), scope="a1", call_index=0)
>>> len(r.key())
64
```

#### `property max_tokens: int | None`

The `max_tokens` parameter, the most the reply may use.

#### `identity() → dict[str, Any]`

The fields the cache key hashes, as plain JSON values.

#### `key() → str`

SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of [`identity()`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.Request.identity): the cache key.

Computed once per request and kept outside the dataclass fields, so it takes no part in equality, hashing, `repr` or pickles.

#### `prompt_chars() → int`

Characters in the system prompt and every message.

#### `excerpt() → str`

The start of the last message, for error messages.

#### `follow_up(reply: str, prompt: str, call_index: int) → Request`

This conversation, the model’s `reply`, then a new user `prompt`.

#### `class Response(text: str, input_tokens: int = 0, output_tokens: int = 0, cached: bool = False, key: str = '')`

A reply: its text, the tokens it used, and whether it came from the cache.

#### `property tokens: int`

Input plus output tokens.

#### `class Message(role: str, content: str)`

One turn of a conversation: who spoke (`"user"` or `"assistant"`) and what.

## Cache

#### `class ResponseCache(path: str | Path | None = None, mode: str = 'read-write')`

Replies by cache key, in memory (`path=None`) or in a SQLite file.

**Parameters:**

- **path** – The SQLite file; created when missing. None keeps the cache in memory.
- **mode** – `"read-write"`, `"read-only"` or `"off"`.

Open (or create) the store.

#### `classmethod from_file(path: str | Path, mode: str = 'read-only') → ResponseCache`

An in-memory cache filled from an exported file (JSON lines or SQLite).

The file itself is never written, so a cache shipped with a study bundle or a package stays as it was.

#### `property reads: bool`

Whether lookups are made (every mode but `"off"`).

#### `property writes: bool`

Whether new replies are stored (`"read-write"` only).

#### `get(key: str) → Response | None`

The stored reply for `key`, marked `cached`, or None.

#### `get_many(keys: Sequence[str]) → dict[str, Response]`

The stored replies among `keys`, by key, marked `cached`.

One `SELECT ... IN` per `IN_CHUNK` keys rather than one per key.

#### `put(request: Request, response: Response) → None`

Store `response` under the key of `request`, in one transaction.

#### `put_many(pairs: Iterable[tuple[Request, Response]]) → None`

Store each `(request, response)` pair, all in one transaction.

#### `insert(rows: list[tuple[Any, ...]]) → None`

Write `rows` (in `COLUMNS` order) atomically.

#### `rows() → Iterator[tuple[Any, ...]]`

Every stored row, sorted by key.

#### `export(path: str | Path) → Path`

Write the cache to `path`: JSON lines for `.jsonl` (`.jsonl.gz`), else SQLite.

The file is written next to its target and renamed over it, so a reader never sees half a file.

#### `merge(path: str | Path) → int`

Add every row of an exported file; return how many rows it held.

#### `close() → None`

Close the connection.

Replay a recorded response cache for every client built inside a block.

`modelly verify` reruns a study whose model builds its own `Client`, often with a real provider and an empty cache. Inside `with replaying(path):` every client created takes the cache exported to `path` instead, in read-only mode: a recorded call is answered from it, an unrecorded one raises `CacheMiss`, and no call ever reaches the network.

Example

```default
>>> from modelly.llm import Client, FakeProvider, ResponseCache
>>> recorded = Client(FakeProvider(lambda request: "yes"))
>>> _ = recorded.complete("Vote?")
>>> path = recorded.cache.export("replies.jsonl")
>>> with replaying(path):
...     replay = Client(FakeProvider(lambda request: "no"))
>>> replay.complete("Vote?").text, replay.usage.calls
('yes', 0)
```

#### `active_replay() → ResponseCache | None`

The cache every new client replays from, or None outside `replaying`.

#### `replaying(path: str | Path) → Iterator[ResponseCache]`

Make every client created in the block answer only from the file at `path`.

The file (JSON lines or SQLite, as `ResponseCache.export` writes it) is read into memory and never written.

## Budgets and retries

#### `class Budget(max_tokens: int | None = None, max_cost: float | None = None, prices: Mapping[str, ~modelly.llm.budget.Price]=<factory>, usage: Usage = <factory>)`

Limits for one run and the usage counted against them.

**Parameters:**

- **max_tokens** – The most input plus output tokens the run may send for. None: no limit.
- **max_cost** – The most the run may cost. Needs a price for every model it calls.
- **prices** – Model name to [`Price`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.Price).

#### `estimate(request: Request) → tuple[int, int]`

Worst-case (input, output) tokens of `request`.

#### `price_of(model: str) → Price | None`

The price of `model`; required when a cost budget is set.

#### `reserve(request: Request) → None`

Hold the worst case of `request`, or raise [`BudgetExceeded`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.BudgetExceeded).

#### `refuse_over(tokens: int, cost: float, request: Request) → None`

Raise when `tokens` or `cost` passes its limit.

#### `release(request: Request) → None`

Give back the reservation of `request` once its reply is counted.

#### `record(request: Request, response: Response, retries: int) → None`

Count a reply from the provider.

#### `record_hit() → None`

Count a reply served from the cache.

#### `class Price(input_per_million: float, output_per_million: float)`

Price per million input tokens and per million output tokens, in any currency.

#### `cost(input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int) → float`

The price of one call.

#### `class Usage(calls: int = 0, cache_hits: int = 0, retries: int = 0, input_tokens: int = 0, output_tokens: int = 0, cost: float | None = 0.0)`

What a run used so far.

**Variables:**

- **calls** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – Calls sent to the provider (retries not included).
- **cache_hits** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – Replies served from the cache.
- **retries** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – Extra tries after a 429, a 5xx or a lost connection.
- **input_tokens** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – Prompt tokens of the calls sent.
- **output_tokens** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – Reply tokens of the calls sent.
- **cost** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)* | **None*) – The cost of the calls sent, or None when a model has no price.

#### `property tokens: int`

Input plus output tokens.

#### `class RetryPolicy(max_retries: int = 3, base_delay: float = 1.0, max_delay: float = 30.0, sleeper: ~collections.abc.Callable[[float], None] = <built-in function sleep>)`

How many times to retry a failed call and how long to wait in between.

**Parameters:**

- **max_retries** – Extra tries after the first; 0 never retries.
- **base_delay** – Seconds before the first retry; doubled each time after.
- **max_delay** – The longest wait, also capping a server’s `Retry-After`.
- **sleeper** – Called with the seconds to wait; `time.sleep` by default.

Example

```default
>>> RetryPolicy(base_delay=1.0).delay(2, None)
4.0
```

#### `sleeper()`

sleep(seconds)

Delay execution for a given number of seconds. The argument may be a floating-point number for subsecond precision.

#### `delay(attempt: int, retry_after: float | None) → float`

Seconds to wait before retry number `attempt` (counting from 0).

#### `run(send: Callable[[Request], Response], request: Request) → tuple[Response, int]`

`send(request)`, retried on a retryable error; return the reply and the retries.

## Providers

#### `class Provider(*, api_key: str | None = None, base_url: str | None = None, timeout: float = 120.0)`

The interface of every adapter: a `name` and [`complete()`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.Provider.complete).

Subclasses set `name` (part of every cache key), `default_model` and `key_variable`, the environment variable holding the API key.

Keep the endpoint; the key stays in memory only.

#### `static default_url() → str`

The endpoint used when `base_url` is None.

#### `api_key(required: bool = True) → str | None`

The explicit key, else the environment’s; raise when one is required.

#### `complete(request: Request) → Response`

Send `request` and return the reply.

#### `class AnthropicProvider(*, api_key: str | None = None, base_url: str | None = None, timeout: float = 120.0)`

The Anthropic Messages API (`POST /v1/messages`); key from `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`.

Example

```default
>>> AnthropicProvider(api_key="sk-...")
AnthropicProvider(base_url='https://api.anthropic.com')
```

Keep the endpoint; the key stays in memory only.

#### `static default_url() → str`

The endpoint used when `base_url` is None.

#### `complete(request: Request) → Response`

Call the Messages API and join the text blocks of the reply.

#### `class OpenAICompatibleProvider(*, name: str | None = None, **options: Any)`

Any `POST /chat/completions` endpoint: OpenAI, or a local Ollama or llama.cpp.

The key comes from `OPENAI_API_KEY` and is optional, since local servers need none. `name` is part of the cache key: give each endpoint its own when they serve different models under one name.

Example

```default
>>> OpenAICompatibleProvider(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1", name="ollama")
OpenAICompatibleProvider(base_url='http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1')
```

Set the endpoint, and a `name` for its cache keys.

#### `static default_url() → str`

The endpoint used when `base_url` is None.

#### `complete(request: Request) → Response`

Call chat completions; the system prompt is the first message.

#### `class FakeProvider(responder: ~collections.abc.Callable[[~modelly.llm.request.Request], str] = <function echo>, failures: ~collections.abc.Iterable[int] = ())`

Replies come from `responder(request) -> str`; tokens are counted from length.

**Parameters:**

- **responder** – A module-level function (so a model holding it can be saved).
- **failures** – HTTP statuses to raise, one per call, before answering normally: `failures=[429, 503]` fails twice, then replies.

Example

```default
>>> from modelly.llm import Client
>>> client = Client(FakeProvider(lambda request: "yes"))
>>> client.complete("Agree?").text
'yes'
```

Keep the responder and the failures to play back.

#### `complete(request: Request) → Response`

Fail with the next queued status, if any; otherwise call the responder.

## Schemas

#### `validate(value: Any, schema: dict[str, Any], path: str = '$') → Any`

Return `value` when it matches `schema`; raise [`SchemaError`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.SchemaError) otherwise.

**Parameters:**

- **value** – Parsed JSON.
- **schema** – A schema using the supported keywords.
- **path** – Where `value` sits, for the error message.

#### `parse_json(text: str) → Any`

The JSON value in a reply: plain, inside a code fence, or after some prose.

**Raises:**

[**SchemaError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.SchemaError) – When the reply holds no JSON value.

## Errors

#### `exception LLMError`

Base class of every error raised by `modelly.llm`.

#### `exception ProviderError(message: str, *, status: int | None = None, retry_after: float | None = None, retryable: bool | None = None)`

A provider refused or failed a call.

**Variables:**

- **status** – The HTTP status, or None when no response came back.
- **retryable** – Whether the same call may succeed later (429, 5xx, a lost connection).
- **retry_after** – Seconds the server asked to wait, when it said so.

Record the status and whether another try may succeed (from it, by default).

#### `exception CacheMiss(scope: str, call_index: int, key: str, excerpt: str)`

A replay (`mode="read-only"`) asked for a response the cache does not hold.

**Variables:**

- **scope** – Who made the call (an agent’s id, or the scope passed to the client).
- **call_index** – The caller’s call counter for this call.
- **key** – The cache key that was looked up.

Name the call, so the user can see which prompt was never recorded.

#### `exception BudgetExceeded`

The next call could take the run past its token or cost budget.

Raised before that call is sent, so the money is never spent. Responses already received in the same batch are cached and counted first.

#### `exception SchemaError(path: str, problem: str)`

A value does not match a schema; `path` points at the first mismatch.

Say where the value breaks the schema and how.

#### `exception DecisionError(scope: str, reply: str, reason: str)`

A model reply stayed invalid after every repair attempt.

**Variables:**

- **scope** – Who asked.
- **reply** – The last reply received.

Keep the reply so the prompt or the schema can be fixed.

## Memory, reasoning, conversations and evaluation

Memory for language-model agents: what happened to them, kept and summarised.

A `MemoryAgent` (mix it in instead of `LLMAgent`) keeps a `Memory`: episodes, each a time and a line of text, recorded with `remember`. Every call the agent makes starts with what it remembers, so its decisions can depend on what it saw, said and did. Past `capacity` episodes, the oldest are folded into a summary by one call to the model, and the newest `keep` stay verbatim: the prompt stays bounded however long the run.

The memory is an ordinary attribute of the agent, so it is saved in checkpoints with it. The summary call is cached like every other, so a replay summarises from the cache.

#### `class Memory(capacity: int = 20, keep: int = 10, episodes: list[tuple[float, str]]=<factory>, summary: str = '')`

Episodes `(time, text)` and a summary of the ones folded away.

**Variables:**

- **capacity** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – episodes kept verbatim before the oldest are summarised.
- **keep** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – episodes left verbatim after a summary.
- **episodes** ([*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[*[*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)*[*[*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)*, *[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*]**]*) – the verbatim episodes, oldest first.
- **summary** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the summary of everything older.

#### `add(time: float, text: str) → None`

Record one episode.

#### `property full: bool`

Whether the oldest episodes should be summarised.

#### `older() → str`

The current summary and the episodes the next summary folds away, as text.

#### `fold(summary: str) → None`

Replace the older episodes with `summary`; the newest `keep` stay.

#### `context() → str`

What the agent remembers, as the start of a prompt; empty when nothing.

#### `class MemoryAgent`

An `LLMAgent` whose calls start with its memory.

**Variables:**

**memory_keep** (*memory_capacity**,*) – the sizes of each agent’s `Memory`.

Example

```default
>>> from modelly import Agent, Model
>>> from modelly.llm import Client, FakeProvider
>>> class Trader(MemoryAgent, Agent):
...     persona = "You trade apples."
>>> model = Model(rng=1)
>>> model.llm = Client(FakeProvider(lambda r: r.messages[-1].content[:21]))
>>> trader = Trader(model)
>>> trader.remember("I sold 3 apples at 2.")
>>> trader.ask("Price?")
'What you remember:\n- '
```

#### `property memory: Memory`

This agent’s memory, made on first use.

#### `remember(text: str) → None`

Record an episode at the model’s time; summarise when the memory is full.

#### `summarise() → None`

Fold the older episodes into a summary written by the model.

#### `llm_request(prompt: str, *, schema: dict[str, Any] | None = None, **params: Any) → Request`

A request whose prompt starts with what the agent remembers.

Planning, reflection and tool use for language-model agents.

- `plan(agent, goal)`: the agent writes a plan of a few steps, as a JSON list, and remembers it when it has a memory.
- `reflect(agent)`: the agent reads its memory and writes what it has learned, which it remembers: the reflection loop of generative agents.
- `use_tools(agent, prompt, tools)`: the agent may call functions of the model (look up a price, check its stock) before it answers. Each round it replies with a tool and its arguments or with its answer; a tool’s result is sent back in the same conversation, and after `max_rounds` tool calls it must answer.

Every call goes through the agent’s client, cached and counted like any other, so a run with plans, reflections and tool calls replays from its cache.

**Reference:**

Park, J. S., O’Brien, J. C., Cai, C. J., Morris, M. R., Liang, P. and Bernstein, M. S. (2023). Generative agents: interactive simulacra of human behavior. UIST 2023.

#### `plan(agent: Any, goal: str, max_steps: int = 5) → list[str]`

The agent’s plan toward `goal`: at most `max_steps` steps.

#### `reflect(agent: Any, question: str = 'What have you learned so far?') → str`

The agent’s reflection on its memory, remembered.

#### `class Tool(name: str, description: str, function: ~collections.abc.Callable[[...], ~typing.Any], parameters: ~collections.abc.Mapping[str, str] = <factory>)`

A function the agent may call.

**Variables:**

- **name** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – how the agent calls it.
- **description** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – what it does, shown to the agent.
- **function** ([*collections.abc.Callable*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Callable)*[**[**...**]**, **Any**]*) – `function(**arguments)`; its result is shown to the agent as JSON.
- **parameters** ([*collections.abc.Mapping*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*]*) – the names of its arguments and what each is.

#### `line() → str`

One line describing the tool to the agent.

#### `class ToolUse(answer: ~typing.Any, calls: list[tuple[str, dict[str, ~typing.Any], ~typing.Any]] = <factory>)`

The answer, and every tool call made on the way: `(name, arguments, result)`.

#### `use_tools(agent: Any, prompt: str, tools: Sequence[Tool], max_rounds: int = 3, repairs: int = 1) → ToolUse`

Let `agent` call `tools` before answering `prompt`.

**Raises:**

[**DecisionError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/llm.html#modelly.llm.DecisionError) – when it still calls a tool after `max_rounds` calls.

Conversations between language-model agents, turn by turn, many at once.

`converse_many(groups, topic, turns)` runs one conversation per group of agents. In each turn every group’s next speaker is asked, with the transcript so far, and all groups’ calls of that turn are sent together, so 250 pairs of traders talk in `turns` rounds of concurrent calls rather than 500 one after another. Speakers take turns in order (`"round-robin"`) or are drawn from a generator (`order=rng`, never the same agent twice in a row), the model’s own, so a run is a function of its seed. After the conversation every participant that has a memory remembers it.

Each call carries the speaker’s scope and call counter, as every agent call does, so a conversation replays from the cache.

#### `class Turn(speaker: int, text: str, time: float)`

One utterance: who spoke (unique id), what, and the model’s time.

#### `converse_many(groups: Sequence[Sequence[Any]], topic: str, turns: int, *, order: Any = 'round-robin') → list[list[Turn]]`

One conversation per group; the transcripts, in the order of `groups`.

**Parameters:**

- **groups** – lists of `LLMAgent` instances of one model, two or more each.
- **topic** – what they talk about.
- **turns** – utterances per conversation.
- **order** – `"round-robin"`, or a `numpy` generator to draw each next speaker.

#### `converse(agents: Sequence[Any], topic: str, turns: int, *, order: Any = 'round-robin') → list[Turn]`

One conversation among `agents`: its transcript.

An evaluation harness for language-model agents: behaviour, consistency and cost.

`evaluate(build, clients, seeds=..., steps=..., metrics=...)` runs the same model with each client (a provider, a hosted model, a local one) on each seed, and records per run every behaviour metric (a function of the finished model), the calls sent and served from the cache, the tokens and the cost. `Evaluation.report()` gives per client the mean and spread of each metric over the seeds, how consistently its agents chose the same thing from one seed to the next (`choices`), and the totals of calls, tokens and cost: which model behaves as the study needs, how stably, and at what price.

#### `agreement(choices: Sequence[Sequence[Any]]) → float`

The share of positions where two seeds’ choices agree, over every pair of seeds.

#### `class Evaluation(runs: DataFrame, choices: Mapping[str, list[list[Any]]], metrics: tuple[str, ...])`

Every run’s metrics and usage, and the choices recorded for consistency.

**Variables:**

- **runs** (*pandas.DataFrame*) – one row per (client, seed).
- **choices** ([*collections.abc.Mapping*](https://docs.python.org/3/library/collections.abc.html#collections.abc.Mapping)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[*[*list*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#list)*[**Any**]**]**]*) – per client, one list of choices per seed (empty without `choices`).
- **metrics** ([*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **...**]*) – the names of the behaviour metrics.

#### `report() → DataFrame`

Per client: each metric’s mean and sd, the agreement, and the usage totals.

#### `evaluate(build: Callable[[int, Any], Any], clients: Mapping[str, Callable[[], Any]], *, seeds: Sequence[int], steps: int, metrics: Mapping[str, Callable[[Any], float]], choices: Callable[[Any], Sequence[Any]] | None = None) → Evaluation`

Run `build(seed, client)` for `steps` steps with every client on every seed.

`clients` maps a name to a function making a fresh `Client`, so runs share no cache unless the factory gives them one. `choices(model)` lists the agents’ decisions, in a fixed order, for the agreement between seeds.

A conversational market: traders who talk, ask a price, and buy or walk away.

Half the traders sell one crate a round at a cost of their own; the other half buy one if the price is below their value. Each round the model pairs every seller with a buyer, the pair talks for two turns (`converse_many`), the seller states an asking price and the buyer accepts or refuses (`decide_all`), and both remember the round (`MemoryAgent`). Every call goes through `model.llm`.

`local_trader` is an offline stand-in for a language model: it reads the trader’s value from its persona and answers in character (a seller asks a fifth above its cost, a buyer accepts a price at or below its value), so the market runs, caches and replays with no network and no key. Swap it for a real provider to study what a language model does.

#### `local_trader(request: Request) → str`

An offline trader: in character, from the value in its persona.

#### `class Trader(model: Market, value: float, seller: bool)`

A buyer or a seller of crates, with a value and a memory of its rounds.

A trader of value `value` (a seller’s cost, a buyer’s willingness to pay).

#### `property traded`

Column(int64, default=0)

#### `property value`

Column(float64, default=0.0)

#### `property seller`

Column(bool, default=False)

# Plugins

`modelly.plugins` finds third-party extensions through package entry points. The guide is [Plugins](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/plugins.html).

Third-party extensions found through package entry points.

A package extends Modelly by declaring entry points in one of the groups of `GROUPS`, for example in its `pyproject.toml`:

```default
[project.entry-points."modelly.spaces"]
hexworld = "hexworld.space:HexWorld"
```

`discover(group)` lists what is installed without importing anything; each `Plugin` is imported the first time it is loaded.

**Plugin API v1.** The groups, `Plugin`, `discover` and `load_all` are frozen for the 1.x line (`API_VERSION`). A plugin declares the Modelly versions it supports as an ordinary dependency, `"modelly-abm>=1.5,<2"`; `Plugin.compatible` checks it against the running Modelly (a pre-release or development build counts as its release), and loading a plugin whose declaration excludes it raises `PluginError` instead of importing code written for another version. A plugin that fails to import raises `PluginError` naming the plugin and its distribution, and never stops the others from being found or loaded: `load_all` returns the loaded objects and the errors apart.

from modelly.plugins import discover

spaces = discover(“modelly.spaces”) # {“hexworld”: Plugin(…)} HexWorld = spaces[“hexworld”].load()

#### `exception PluginError`

A plugin could not be loaded; `__cause__` is the original error.

#### `class Plugin(name: str, group: str, value: str, distribution: str | None, requires: str | None, _entry_point: EntryPoint, _loaded: Any = <object object>)`

One entry point: imported on the first `load` and cached.

**Variables:**

- **name** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the entry point’s name, the key in `discover`’s result.
- **group** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – its group, such as `"modelly.spaces"`.
- **value** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the `module:attribute` it points to.
- **distribution** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)* | **None*) – the installed distribution that declares it, if known.
- **requires** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)* | **None*) – the distribution’s version specifier on `modelly-abm` (`">=1.5,<2"`), `""` for any version, None when it does not declare Modelly at all.

#### `load() → Any`

Import and return the object the entry point names.

**Raises:**

[**PluginError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/plugins.html#modelly.plugins.PluginError) – if importing or resolving it fails, with the original error as its cause.

#### `property compatible: bool`

Whether the running Modelly meets the plugin’s declaration (true without one).

#### `clear_cache() → None`

Forget the scanned entry points: the next `discover` reads them again.

#### `discover(group: str) → dict[str, Plugin]`

The installed plugins of `group`, by name, sorted; nothing is imported.

Any group name works, so a feature may define its own; `GROUPS` lists Modelly’s. When two distributions declare the same name, the first distribution in alphabetical order wins and a `RuntimeWarning` names both.

Example

```default
>>> discover("modelly.no_such_group")
{}
```

#### `load_all(group: str) → tuple[dict[str, Any], dict[str, PluginError]]`

Load every plugin of `group`: `(objects by name, errors by name)`.

A plugin that fails is reported in the second dictionary; the others still load.

## The model builder

The model builder: a few choices in a form, one ordinary Modelly `model.py` out.

For teaching. A `ModelSpec` names one kind of agent, how many there are, the size of the grid they live on, and their behaviours, picked from `BEHAVIOURS` (walk to a random neighbouring cell, give wealth to a cellmate, catch an infection from cellmates, recover). `build_code(spec)` writes a single module with a `Scenario` holding every parameter, the agent class with its `Column` attributes and one method per behaviour, and the model with its grid and a `DataCollector`: code a student reads, runs and changes, which passes `modelly lint`. Studio’s Builder tab is a form over it.

#### `class Behaviour(summary: str, columns: tuple[tuple[str, str, str], ...], parameters: tuple[tuple[str, str, str], ...], body: tuple[str, ...], reporters: tuple[tuple[str, str], ...] = ())`

One behaviour: its columns, its parameters, its method body and its reporters.

#### `exception BuilderError`

A spec the builder cannot write a model from; the message says why.

#### `class ModelSpec(name: str = 'Classroom', agent: str = 'Student', count: int = 100, width: int = 20, height: int = 20, behaviours: tuple[str, ...]=('walk', ), initially_infected: int = 5, seed: int = 42, steps: int = 100, extra: dict[str, str]=<factory>)`

What the form chose.

**Variables:**

- **name** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the model class’s name (CapWords); the agent is `agent`.
- **agent** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the agent class’s name (CapWords).
- **count** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – how many agents.
- **width** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – the grid’s width, in cells.
- **height** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – the grid’s height, in cells.
- **behaviours** ([*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)*[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, **...**]*) – names of `BEHAVIOURS`, in the order the agent does them each step.
- **initially_infected** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – agents infected at the start (with `infect`).

#### `check() → None`

Refuse names that are not class names, unknown behaviours, bad sizes.

#### `build_code(spec: ModelSpec) → str`

**Raises:**

## Epidemiology

Age-structured SEIR epidemic with a contact matrix.

A population split into age groups, each person susceptible (S), exposed (E), infectious (I) or recovered (R). A susceptible of group `a` is infected in one step with probability `1 - exp(-beta * sum_b C[a, b] * I_b / N_b)`, where `C[a, b]` is the mean number of contacts a member of `a` has with members of `b` per step (a contact matrix, as measured by social-contact surveys or computed by `modelly.space.networks.contact_matrix`). Exposed people become infectious with probability `incubation` per step and infectious people recover with probability `recovery` per step.

Everybody in the same group and state faces the same probabilities, so the population is a `CohortTable` with one row per (group, state): every transition is one binomial draw per row, with exactly the law of the per-person draws (see `docs/vectorised_phases.md`). A million people cost the same as a hundred.

Validation: the final-size relation. Summing the force of infection over the epidemic, `log(s_a) = log(s0_a) - (beta / recovery) * sum_b C[a, b] * (1 - s_b)`, where `s_a` is the share of group `a` never infected; with one group this is the Kermack-McKendrick relation `s = s0 * exp(-R0 * (1 - s))`. `final_size()` solves it and the test compares it with the simulated epidemic. `r0()` is `beta / recovery` times the spectral radius of the next-generation matrix. People vaccinated at the start (`vaccinated`) are immune: the relation holds with their share `v_a` removed, `log(s_a) = log(s0_a) - (beta / recovery) * sum_b C[a, b] * (1 - v_b - s_b)`.

Starting from a synthetic population: `scenario_from_population(people, network, levels)` takes the group sizes from the people’s age levels and the contact matrix from their contact network (`modelly.population`: households, schools and workplaces), so the model runs on a population built from census tables instead of the illustrative default.

References

Kermack, W. O. and McKendrick, A. G. (1927). A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 115, 700-721.

Mossong, J. et al. (2008). Social contacts and mixing patterns relevant to the spread of infectious diseases. PLoS Medicine, 5(3), e74.

Andersson, H. and Britton, T. (2000). Stochastic Epidemic Models and Their Statistical Analysis. Lecture Notes in Statistics 151, Springer.

Parameters of the age-structured SEIR model.

The default contact matrix is illustrative (children, adults, seniors), not survey data; it is reciprocal, `N[a] * C[a, b] == N[b] * C[b, a]`.

**Variables:**

- **recovery** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – probability per step that an infectious person recovers.
- **initial_infected** ([*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)) – infectious people at the start, per group.

**Parameters:**

#### `scenario_from_population(people: Any, network: Any, levels: Sequence, **parameters: Any) → SEIRScenario`

**Parameters:**

- **network** – the people’s contact network, node `i` the `i`-th row (`modelly.population.contact_network`); its weights are contacts per step.
- **levels** – the age levels in group order, for example `("0-17", "18-64", "65+")`.
- ****parameters** – any other `SEIRScenario` field (`rng`, `beta`, …); `initial_infected` defaults to 10 per group, or the whole group if smaller.

**Returns:**

an `SEIRScenario` with `group_sizes` counted from `people` and `contacts` from `contact_matrix(network, groups)`.

**Raises:**

[**ValueError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#ValueError) – if an age level has nobody in it.

#### `count_in(model: AgeSEIR, state: State) → int`

The number of people in `state`, all groups together (a model reporter).

Vector-borne transmission on a landscape (Ross-Macdonald).

Hosts live on the cells of a landscape grid and move to a random neighbouring cell with probability `move` per step; each is susceptible, infectious or recovered. Mosquitoes live in the cells too, `m` per host on average (times a per-cell `habitat` suitability, a raster of values), each susceptible, exposed (the extrinsic incubation) or infectious. Every step a mosquito survives with probability `survival` and bites `a` times, each time a host of its cell chosen at random. A bite of an infectious mosquito infects a susceptible host with probability `b`; a bite on an infectious host infects a susceptible mosquito with probability `c`. Exposed mosquitoes become infectious with probability `incubation` per step, infectious hosts recover with probability `recovery`, and new susceptible mosquitoes emerge so as to keep the density at `m`.

Mosquitoes in the same cell and state are interchangeable, so they are a `CohortTable` with one row per (cell, state): survival, infection and incubation are binomial draws per row. Hosts are agents with `Column` arrays for their state and cell row.

Validation: the Ross-Macdonald reproduction number (host to host, over one full cycle), `R0 = m a^2 b c P / (recovery (1 - survival))`, where `P` is the probability that an infected mosquito survives the incubation, is linear in the vector density `m` (`r0()`). Outbreaks are small when `R0 < 1` and their size grows with `R0` above it, so the attack rates of three densities come out in the order of their `R0`.

References

Ross, R. (1911). The Prevention of Malaria, 2nd ed. John Murray.

Macdonald, G. (1957). The Epidemiology and Control of Malaria. Oxford University Press.

An epidemic among agents coupled to a hospital-capacity model.

People are agents, each susceptible (S), infectious (I) or recovered (R), mixing homogeneously. A susceptible is infected in a step with probability `1 - exp(-beta_eff * I / N)`, an infectious person recovers with probability `recovery` per step, and a share `severe` of the new infections need a hospital bed.

The hospital is a stock-flow model (`modelly.couple.StockFlow`) integrated with `solve_ivp`: the `occupied` beds fill with the admissions of the agents’ step and empty at rate `occupied / stay`; the `beds` open and close towards `base_beds + surge * occupied` with time constant `ramp`, as a hospital adds surge capacity. People respond to the hospital’s pressure: contacts fall with the share of beds occupied, `beta_eff = beta / (1 + response * occupied / beds)`. The agents’ phase reads `occupied` and `beds` and writes `admissions`; the hospital, one phase later, reads the admissions and writes the beds, so the feedback acts with a lag of one step.

Validation: three known answers. Without the response (`response = 0`) the epidemic is the stochastic general epidemic, whose attack rate solves the final-size relation `s = s0 exp(-R0 (1 - s))` with `R0 = beta / recovery`, within the central-limit bound (Andersson and Britton, 2000). The hospital equations are linear, so for the admissions of each step, held over the step, the exact solution is a matrix exponential; the integrated occupancy and beds match it to the solver’s tolerance. And the stock-flow keeps its mass balance: the admissions the agents wrote equal the patients in hospital plus those discharged, to round-off.

References

Kermack, W. O. and McKendrick, A. G. (1927). A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics. Proceedings of the Royal Society A, 115, 700-721.

Andersson, H. and Britton, T. (2000). Stochastic Epidemic Models and Their Statistical Analysis. Lecture Notes in Statistics 151, Springer.

Sterman, J. D. (2000). Business Dynamics: Systems Thinking and Modeling for a Complex World. Irwin/McGraw-Hill.

#### `class State(*values)`

Infection states.

#### `class Person(model: HospitalEpidemic, state: int)`

A person: their infection state.

Start in `state`.

#### `property state`

Column(int8, default=0)

#### `class HospitalScenario(*, rng: Generator | BitGenerator | int | integer | Sequence[int] | SeedSequence | None = None, scenario_id: int | None = None, replication_id: int = -1, **kwargs: Any)`

Parameters of the epidemic and of the hospital.

**Variables:**

- **population** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – number of people.
- **initial_infected** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – infectious people at the start.

## Ecology

Individual-based population with energy budgets.

Foragers walk a grid on which a resource flows in at a constant rate per cell. Every step each forager moves to a random neighbouring cell, the foragers in a cell share its resource equally and turn it into energy with an assimilation `efficiency`, and each pays a metabolic `cost`. A forager whose energy reaches `birth_threshold` splits it with an offspring in its cell; one whose energy falls below zero starves.

Validation: the energy balance. Energy is the only currency, so it regulates the population. The resource is never capped and is eaten whenever a forager visits, so in the long run all of it is eaten: intake equals inflow. At equilibrium the energy assimilated equals the energy spent, `efficiency * inflow * cells = cost * N`, which gives the carrying capacity `K = efficiency * inflow * cells / cost` (`carrying_capacity()`). The only energy leaving the balance otherwise is the deficit of starving foragers, at most one `cost` each, so the mean population sits at or slightly above `K`.

The foragers keep their energy and their cell row in `Column` arrays and are placed by row (`CellIndex.track`): moving, eating and starving are whole-population numpy operations; only births create objects.

**Reference:**

Grimm, V. and Railsback, S. F. (2005). Individual-based Modeling and Ecology. Princeton University Press.

Foragers on a diffusing nutrient field.

A nutrient enters a closed landscape along its western edge (a river bank, say) at `supply` per edge cell per step, diffuses with coefficient `diffusion` and decays at rate `decay`: a `modelly.couple.Field` on the grid’s `nutrient` layer, stepped on its own stable sub-steps. Foragers walk the grid at random. Every step each moves to a random neighbouring cell, the foragers in a cell share all of its nutrient and turn it into energy with an assimilation `efficiency`, and each pays a metabolic `cost`. A forager whose energy reaches `birth_threshold` splits it with an offspring; one whose energy falls below zero starves.

The two scales are coupled by a `Coupling`: the foragers’ phase reads the field and writes `nutrient_input` (the supply minus what was eaten, per cell), and the field, one phase later, adds that input and diffuses. Nothing else changes the field, so its budget closes exactly: the nutrient on the grid is the supply minus what was eaten and what decayed, to round-off.

Validation: the energy balance. At equilibrium the nutrient stock is stationary, so what the foragers eat equals what enters minus what decays, and what they assimilate equals what they spend: `efficiency * (supply_total - decayed) = cost * N`. Without decay this is the carrying capacity `K = efficiency * supply * height / cost` (`carrying_capacity()`) however far the nutrient has to diffuse; with decay the measured decay loss takes its share. The foragers’ density falls with the distance from the river, as the diffusing nutrient does.

References

Grimm, V. and Railsback, S. F. (2005). Individual-based Modeling and Ecology. Princeton University Press.

Okubo, A. and Levin, S. A. (2001). Diffusion and Ecological Problems: Modern Perspectives, 2nd ed. Springer.

Forest fire and succession on a raster.

A raster of cells, each empty, a tree, burning or burnt. At the start every cell holds a tree with probability `density` (or with its own probability, from a `cover` raster such as the values of a `modelly.space.geo.RasterLayer`), and the trees of the west edge are set alight. Every step a tree next to a burning cell (von Neumann neighbourhood) catches fire and a burning cell burns out. With `growth > 0` empty and burnt cells grow a tree with that probability per step and with `lightning > 0` a tree is struck with that probability per step: the Drossel-Schwabl forest-fire model of succession and disturbance.

The state is one integer per cell, a property layer of the grid (`model.layer`, shaped like the grid); the spread is one sparse product per step, `CellIndex.neighbor_sum`, over the grid’s adjacency.

Validation: without growth and lightning the fire burns exactly the clusters of trees that touch the west edge, so the model is site percolation on the square lattice. The share of trees burnt jumps, and the fire starts to reach the east edge, at the percolation threshold `p_c = 0.592746` (Newman and Ziff 2000): it stays small below and covers most trees above.

References

Drossel, B. and Schwabl, F. (1992). Self-organized critical forest-fire model. Physical Review Letters, 69(11), 1629-1632.

Newman, M. E. J. and Ziff, R. M. (2000). Efficient Monte Carlo algorithm and high-precision results for percolation. Physical Review Letters, 85(19), 4104-4107.

Stauffer, D. and Aharony, A. (1994). Introduction to Percolation Theory, 2nd ed. Taylor and Francis.

## Economics

Continuous double auction: a zero-intelligence limit order book.

Prices are integer ticks. The book keeps, for every tick, the number of resting buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks) of one unit each. Order flow is random, as in the zero-intelligence model of Farmer, Patelli and Zovko: each event is, with probabilities in proportion to its rate,

- a market buy or sell (rate `market_rate / 2` each): it takes one unit at the best opposite price;
- a limit buy or sell (rate `limit_rate / 2` each): it rests at a price drawn uniformly `1 .. window` ticks away from the opposite best quote, on its own side of it (a buy below the best ask, a sell above the best bid), so it never crosses;
- a cancellation (rate `cancel_rate` per resting order): a uniformly random resting order leaves the book.

A side is never emptied: an event that would remove its last order becomes a limit order on that side. A step is `events` events; the mid price is recorded after each step.

Validation: the stylised fact of fat tails (Cont, 2001). The excess kurtosis of mid-price returns is positive, far above the `sqrt(24 / n)` standard error it would have if returns were normal. The spread is at least one tick at all times.

References

Farmer, J. D., Patelli, P. and Zovko, I. I. (2005). The predictive power of zero intelligence in financial markets. PNAS, 102(6), 2254-2259.

Cont, R. (2001). Empirical properties of asset returns: stylized facts and statistical issues. Quantitative Finance, 1, 223-236.

Boltzmann wealth exchange: random pairs pass one unit of money.

`n` agents start with `money` units each. Every step the agents are split into random pairs (a uniformly random perfect matching; with an odd `n` one agent sits out), each pair picks a direction at random, and the giver passes one unit to the other if it has any. Money is conserved and never negative.

The Markov chain on configurations is symmetric: a transfer from `i` to `j` and its reverse have the same probability, one half of the probability of the matching. Its stationary law is therefore uniform over every way of sharing the `M = n * money` units among the `n` agents, and one agent’s wealth has the exact marginal `P(w = k) = C(M - k + n - 2, n - 2) / C(M + n - 1, n - 1)`, which tends to the geometric (discrete Boltzmann-Gibbs, exponential) law with mean `money` as `n` grows. Its Gini coefficient tends to one half.

Wealth is a `Column`, so a step is a handful of numpy operations on the whole table: no agent is visited in a Python loop.

Validation: the time-averaged Gini coefficient and the histogram of wealth after burn-in against `stationary_distribution()`, the exact marginal above.

References

Dragulescu, A. and Yakovenko, V. M. (2000). Statistical mechanics of money. European Physical Journal B, 17, 723-729.

#### `stationary_gini() → float`

Gini of the exact marginal: `E|X - Y| / (2 mean)`, `X, Y` independent.

For integer variables `E|X - Y| = 2 sum_k F(k) (1 - F(k))`.

#### `gini_of(model: KineticWealth) → float`

The Gini coefficient of the agents’ wealth (a model reporter).

Bouchaud-Mezard wealth condensation: random returns plus exchange.

Each agent’s wealth follows, in the mean-field version of the model, `dW_i = J (mean(W) - W_i) dt + sigma W_i dB_i` (Ito): an independent random return on what it holds, of variance `sigma^2` per unit time, and an exchange that pulls it toward the mean at rate `J`. A step of length `dt` applies the multiplicative part exactly, `W_i <- W_i exp(sigma sqrt(dt) xi_i - sigma^2 dt / 2)` with `xi_i` standard normal (mean preserving), then the exchange `W_i <- W_i + J dt (mean(W) - W_i)`, then divides by the mean, so `wealth` is relative wealth `w = W / mean(W)`.

The Fokker-Planck equation of `w` has the stationary density `P(w) ~ exp(-(alpha - 1) / w) / w^(1 + alpha)`, an inverse-gamma law with shape `alpha = 1 + 2 J / sigma^2` and scale `alpha - 1` (mean one): a Pareto tail of exponent `alpha`. Bouchaud and Mezard write the noise variance as `2 sigma^2`, hence their `mu = 1 + J / sigma^2`; with the convention here it is `1 + 2 J / sigma^2`. The larger `sigma^2 / J`, the fatter the tail and the more unequal the wealth.

Validation: the Gini coefficient of the simulated stationary wealth against the Gini of the inverse-gamma law (`stationary_shape()`), and its increase with `sigma^2 / J`.

References

Bouchaud, J.-P. and Mezard, M. (2000). Wealth condensation in a simple model of economy. Physica A, 282, 536-545.

## Sociology and political science

Deffuant bounded-confidence opinion dynamics.

Every agent holds an opinion in `[0, 1]`. Two agents who meet compromise only when their opinions differ by less than the confidence bound `epsilon`: each moves a fraction `mu` of the way towards the other. A wide bound ends in consensus; a narrow one freezes the population into several opinion clusters, about `floor(1 / (2 epsilon))` of them for opinions drawn uniformly.

The original model picks one random pair per time step. Here one step is a sweep: the agents are put into a uniformly random perfect matching (a permutation cut into consecutive pairs) and every pair interacts at once, from the start-of-step opinions. The pairs are disjoint, so the updates do not interfere, and every agent meets exactly one uniformly random partner per step; a step is about `n / 2` events of the original dynamics, with the same kind of absorbing states (clusters more than `epsilon` apart). Opinions are a `Column`, so the sweep is three numpy operations.

Validation: one cluster for `epsilon = 0.4`, several for `epsilon = 0.1` (around `1 / (2 epsilon) = 5`), and a cluster count that does not grow as `epsilon` grows.

References

Deffuant, G., Neau, D., Amblard, F. and Weisbuch, G. (2000). Mixing beliefs among interacting agents. Advances in Complex Systems, 3, 87-98.

#### `class DeffuantScenario(*, rng: Generator | BitGenerator | int | integer | Sequence[int] | SeedSequence | None = None, scenario_id: int | None = None, replication_id: int = -1, **kwargs: Any)`

- **mu** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – convergence parameter, the share of the difference each partner moves.
