Hegselmann-Krause bounded-confidence opinion dynamics.

Every agent holds an opinion in `[0, 1]`. At each step, all at once, every agent moves to the mean opinion of the agents within `epsilon` of its own (itself included). Agents further apart never influence each other, so the population splits into clusters that stop moving after a finite number of steps; a wide bound ends in consensus.

The confidence set of an agent is a contiguous range of the sorted opinions, found with two binary searches, and its mean comes from a running sum, so a step costs `O(n log n)` instead of the `O(n^2)` of comparing every pair. The run stops (`running` turns `False`) when no opinion moves by more than `tolerance`.

Validation: consensus for `epsilon = 0.3`, several clusters for narrow bounds, a cluster count that falls as `epsilon` grows, and identical steps to the plain `O(n^2)` definition.

References

Hegselmann, R. and Krause, U. (2002). Opinion dynamics and bounded confidence: models, analysis and simulation. Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation, 5(3).

Axelrod’s model of the dissemination of culture.

Every site of a square grid holds a culture: `features` features, each taking one of `traits` values. At each event a random site and a random neighbour interact with probability equal to their cultural overlap (the share of features on which they agree); when they interact, the site copies one of the features on which they differ. Similar neighbours become more similar, and neighbours with nothing in common never interact, so the grid freezes into regions of identical culture. Few traits per feature end in a single culture; many traits leave many regions (the transition studied by Castellano, Marsili and Vespignani).

The sites are the rows of a `CellIndex` over a von Neumann grid, the cultures one `(n_sites, features)` integer array. Events stay sequential, as in the original, but a step pre-draws `events_per_step` sites, neighbours (`CellIndex.random_neighbor`) and uniforms in three numpy calls and runs the events on plain lists. After each step the model checks, over every bond at once, whether a pair with partial overlap is left; when none is, the culture map is frozen and `running` turns `False`. Cultural regions are the connected components of the bonds with full overlap.

Validation: with five features on a 10 x 10 grid, two traits end in one region for most seeds and thirty traits in many; the mean number of regions grows with the traits.

References

Axelrod, R. (1997). The dissemination of culture: a model with local convergence and global polarization. Journal of Conflict Resolution, 41(2), 203-226.

Castellano, C., Marsili, M. and Vespignani, A. (2000). Nonequilibrium phase transition in a model for social influence. Physical Review Letters, 85(16), 3536-3539.

## Transport and energy

Nagel-Schreckenberg traffic on a ring road.

A single-lane ring road of `length` cells, each holding at most one car. Every step, all cars update in parallel:

1. accelerate: `v = min(v + 1, max_speed)`;
1. brake to the gap: `v = min(v, gap)`, the number of empty cells to the car ahead;
1. dawdle: with probability `dawdle`, `v = max(v - 1, 0)`;
1. move `v` cells forward.

Cars are `Car` agents whose `position` and `velocity` are `Column` attributes, so the whole road updates with a handful of numpy operations on the column table. Cars never overtake, so the rows stay in road order (cyclically) and the car ahead of row `i` is row `i + 1`.

Validation: the fundamental diagram, flow `J = density * mean speed` against density. Without dawdling the steady-state flow is exactly `min(density * max_speed, 1 - density)`: free flow below the critical density `1 / (max_speed + 1)`, a jam moving backwards above it. With dawdling the flow rises with density, peaks at an interior density and falls; at low density every car runs at `max_speed - 1` with probability `dawdle` and at `max_speed` otherwise, so `J = density * (max_speed - dawdle)`.

References

Nagel, K. and Schreckenberg, M. (1992). A cellular automaton model for freeway traffic. Journal de Physique I, 2(12), 2221-2229.

Bass diffusion of an innovation (rooftop solar, heat pumps) on a network.

Every household either has adopted the innovation or not. In each step of length `dt` (in years) a household that has not adopted does so with probability `(innovation + imitation * share) * dt`: `innovation` is the pull of advertising and `imitation` the pull of the households it knows, `share` being the share of its neighbours that have adopted. With `mixing="well-mixed"` the share is that of the whole population, as in Bass’s original model; with `mixing="network"` it is over the household’s neighbours in a random network of mean degree `degree` (a `MultilayerNetwork` with one layer), so the infection pressure is one sparse product per step.

Households are `Household` agents whose `adopted` flag is a `Column`; the whole population adopts in one `ColumnTable.draw`.

Validation: in the well-mixed limit the expected cumulative adoption follows the Bass equation `dF/dt = (innovation + imitation * F) * (1 - F)`, whose solution is `F(t) = (1 - exp(-(p + q) t)) / (1 + (q / p) exp(-(p + q) t))` with `p = innovation` and `q = imitation`; `bass_curve` evaluates it. On a dense random network the curve stays close to it; on a sparse one adoption is slower, because non-adopters cluster together and see fewer adopters than the population average.

References

Bass, F. M. (1969). A new product growth for model consumer durables. Management Science, 15(5), 215-227.

#### `class BassScenario(*, rng: Generator | BitGenerator | int | integer | Sequence[int] | SeedSequence | None = None, scenario_id: int | None = None, replication_id: int = -1, **kwargs: Any)`

- **imitation** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – Bass `q`, adoption rate per year when every neighbour has adopted.

- **degree** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – mean number of neighbours in the random network.

**Type:**

#### `bass_curve(t: ndarray, innovation: float, imitation: float) → ndarray`

The Bass solution `F(t)`: cumulative share adopted at time `t`, from `F(0) = 0`.

Example

```default
>>> float(bass_curve(np.array([0.0]), 0.03, 0.38)[0])
0.0
```

# Distributed

One model split across processes or machines (provisional, new in 1.4), with the same results as one process for the same seed. The guide is [From laptop to cluster](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/distributed.html); the per-agent random streams it relies on are in [Determinism](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/determinism.html).

`Cluster`: build a partitionable model split across workers, and run it.

```default
from modelly.distributed import Cluster, partition

with Cluster(backend="dask", workers=4) as cluster:
    model = cluster.build(Epidemic, scenario, partition=partition.grid_blocks(2, 2))
    model.run_for(365)
    cluster.collect().to_parquet("runs/epidemic.parquet")
```

Backends: `"local"` (every partition in this process, in turn), `"mpi"` (one partition per rank: run the script with `mpirun -n <partitions>`), `"dask"` and `"ray"` (one actor per partition). Under MPI every rank runs the same script and gets the same results; write files from `cluster.is_root` only.

What a model declares so that it can be split across processes.

A partitionable model sets `agent_streams = True` and a class attribute `partitionable = Partitionable(space=..., phases=..., reporters=...)`, and its `step` runs the declared phases (`self.partitionable.step(self)`). Each phase is one method that every agent (of the phase’s types) runs, and the contract is what makes a split run draw and compute what one process does:

- a phase reads other agents only within its `radius` (cells, network hops or distance in a continuous space) and writes only the agent running it;
- the outcome of a phase does not depend on the order agents run in, nor on the order neighbours are listed (sort them by `stream_key()` if it must);
- every draw in a phase comes from the agent’s own streams (`self.random`, `self.rng`), never from the model’s generators;
- agents move only in phases declared with `moves=True`, and they migrate to the partition that owns their new location after the phase;
- agent attributes hold plain data, not references to agents, cells or the model.

`plan_of` and the checks of the distributed build refuse a model that breaks a part of the contract they can see; `check_independence` compares a split run with a single process for whatever they cannot.

#### `exception PartitionError`

A model cannot be split across processes, or a split run broke the contract.

#### `class Phase(method: str, radius: float = 0, moves: bool = False, types: tuple[type, ...] | None = None)`

One phase of a step: every agent (of `types`) calls `method`.

**Variables:**

- **method** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the agent method the phase calls.
- **radius** ([*float*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#float)) – how far the method reads other agents (Chebyshev cells on a grid, hops on a network, distance in a continuous space); 0 reads only the agent itself and the agents in its own cell.
- **moves** ([*bool*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#bool)) – whether the method may change the agent’s location.
- **types** ([*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)*[*[*type*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#type)*, **...**] **| **None*) – the agent classes that run the phase (exact classes); all agents when `None`.

#### `run_phase(model: Model, phase: Phase) → None`

Call `phase.method` on the model’s agents (of `phase.types`).

#### `class Partitionable(space: str, phases: tuple[Phase, ...], reporters: Mapping[str, Reducer] = <factory>)`

The declaration that lets a model be split across processes.

**Variables:**

- **space** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)) – the name of the model attribute holding the space to split (a grid, a `Network` or a `ContinuousSpace`).
- **phases** ([*tuple*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#tuple)*[*[*Phase*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/distributed.html#modelly.distributed.contract.Phase)*, **...**]*) – the phases of one step, in order.
- **reporters** (*Mapping**[*[*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)*, *[*Reducer*](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/distributed.html#modelly.distributed.reduce.Reducer)*]*) – name to reducer (`Sum`, `Min`, `Max`); each reducer’s function computes a partition’s part of the value from its model.

#### `step(model: Model) → None`

Run every phase once, in order: the model’s `step` on one process.

#### `report(model: Model) → dict[str, Any]`

The reporters’ values for one whole model (a single-process run).

#### `plan_of(model_class: type) → Partitionable`

The `Partitionable` of `model_class`, after the checks of its class.

**Raises:**

[**PartitionError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/distributed.html#modelly.distributed.contract.PartitionError) – when the class declares none, or does not use agent streams.

Reporters that reduce across partitions, and agent snapshots in key order.

A reducer wraps a function of a (partition’s) model: `Sum(count_infected)` calls `count_infected` on every partition and adds the parts, `Min` and `Max` keep the smallest and largest. Integer sums, minima and maxima equal the single-process value exactly; a float sum is added with `math.fsum`, so it does not depend on the order of the parts, but each part is rounded before the parts are added: use integer reporters when byte identity matters.

`snapshot` lists agents by stream key with their location and attributes; the same call on a single-process model and on a split run gives equal frames.

#### `plain(value: Any) → Any`

`value` as a Python scalar when it is a numpy one (for JSON and equality).

#### `class Reducer(function: Callable[[Model], Any])`

A reporter: `function(model)` gives a partition’s part of the value.

#### `combine(parts: Sequence[Any]) → Any`

The whole value from the parts of every partition.

#### `class Sum(function: Callable[[Model], Any])`

The sum of the parts (`math.fsum` when any part is a float).

#### `combine(parts: Sequence[Any]) → Any`

Add the parts: exactly for integers, with `math.fsum` for floats.

#### `class Min(function: Callable[[Model], Any])`

The smallest part.

#### `combine(parts: Sequence[Any]) → Any`

The smallest part.

#### `class Max(function: Callable[[Model], Any])`

The largest part.

#### `combine(parts: Sequence[Any]) → Any`

The largest part.

#### `location_of(agent: Agent) → Any`

The agent’s place: its cell coordinate, or its position as a tuple of floats.

#### `records(agents: Iterable[Agent], attributes: Sequence[str]) → list[tuple]`

`(stream key, location, *attributes)` of each agent.

#### `states(agents: Iterable[Agent]) → list[tuple]`

`(stream key, location, pickled attributes and streams)` of each agent.

Two runs agree on an agent when these tuples are equal: every attribute and the state of its random streams, byte for byte.

#### `frame_of(rows: Iterable[tuple], attributes: Sequence[str]) → DataFrame`

The records as a frame indexed by stream key, in key order.

#### `snapshot(model: Model, attributes: Sequence[str] = ()) → pd.DataFrame`

The agents of a single-process model by stream key, with location and attributes.

Example

```default
>>> snapshot(model, ["state"])
```

Build only a partition’s agents: `owns(model, location)` in a model’s `__init__`.

By default every worker builds the whole initial population and then keeps its part, which costs the memory of the whole model in every worker while it builds. A model can build only what its partition owns instead:

```default
for key, cell in enumerate(cells):
    if owns(self, cell.coordinate):
        Person(self, cell, key=key)  # stream_key() returns key
```

`owns` is always `True` in a single process, so the model builds the same agents there. Agents built this way must override `stream_key()` with a key that does not depend on how many agents the process built (here the index in the single-process creation order); the build refuses a split model whose workers built different populations with the default keys. Grid blocks and graph parts can be asked during the build, as they depend on the space only; k-d boxes are computed from the built positions, so a `kd` split needs the whole population built.

#### `class Build(spec: Any, index: int, layout: Any = None)`

The partition a worker is building, and its layout once asked for.

#### `building(spec: Any, index: int) → Iterator[Build]`

Make `owns` answer for partition `index` of `spec` inside the block.

#### `owns(model: Any, location: Hashable) → bool`

Whether this process builds the agent at `location` (always, on one process).

**Raises:**

[**PartitionError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/distributed.html#modelly.distributed.contract.PartitionError) – for a `kd` split, whose boxes need the built positions.

Check that a split run gives what one process gives, byte for byte.

`single_process` runs the model as anyone would, `model.step()` after `model.step()` in one process, and records its reporters and the full state of every agent. `check_independence` runs the same scenario split by each partition given, on the `local` backend, and raises at the first reporter value or agent state that differs, naming it. The partition-independence test suite is this check on reference models; run it on your own model before a long split run, since it catches what the build checks cannot see (a phase that reads past its radius, depends on the order of neighbours, or writes to another agent).

#### `class Run(rows: DataFrame, states: list[tuple])`

The outputs of a run: reporter rows and the state of every agent.

#### `single_process(model_class: type, scenario: Any, steps: int) → Run`

Run `model_class` in one process for `steps` steps from a copy of `scenario`.

#### `split_run(model_class: type, scenario: Any, partition: Any, steps: int) → Run`

Run `model_class` split by `partition` on the local backend.

#### `first_difference(reference: Run, other: Run) → str | None`

A description of the first output that differs, or `None`.

#### `check_independence(model_class: type, scenario: Any, partitions: Sequence[Any], steps: int) → Run`

Run one process and every split in `partitions`; raise if any output differs.

**Returns:**

The single-process run.

**Raises:**

[**PartitionError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/distributed.html#modelly.distributed.contract.PartitionError) – naming the partition and the first differing output.

Split a space into partitions, one per worker, with their halos.

`grid_blocks` cuts a grid into rectangles (below), `graph` a network into parts with few edges between them (`modelly.distributed.graphs`) and `kd` a continuous space into boxes (`modelly.distributed.kdtree`). Each gives a layout that names the owner of a location and the halo of a partition.

Grid blocks, one per worker, with their halos.

`grid_blocks(rows, cols)` describes the split; `.layout(grid)` applies it to a grid’s dimensions and torus setting. A layout says which block owns a cell (`owner`, `owners`, `owner_map`) and which cells of other blocks lie within a radius of a block (`halo`): the ghost cells a worker must receive from its neighbours before a step that looks that far.

Each axis is cut into nearly equal runs, the larger runs first, so the same grid and split always give the same blocks, whichever process asks.

#### `class Block(index: int, lower: tuple[int, int], upper: tuple[int, int])`

One block: cells with `lower <= coordinate < upper` on every axis.

#### `property shape: tuple[int, int]`

Cells along each axis.

#### `cells() → Iterator[tuple[int, int]]`

The block’s coordinates, row by row.

#### `class GridBlocks(rows: int, cols: int)`

A split of a 2-D grid into `rows` by `cols` blocks.

#### `property partitions: int`

Number of blocks.

#### `layout(grid: Any = None, *, dimensions=None, torus=None) → BlockLayout`

The blocks of `grid` (or of explicit `dimensions` and `torus`).

#### `grid_blocks(rows: int, cols: int) → GridBlocks`

Split a 2-D grid into `rows` by `cols` rectangular blocks.

#### `class BlockLayout(dimensions, torus: bool, x_cuts, y_cuts)`

The blocks of one grid: who owns each cell, and each block’s halo.

Blocks bounded by `x_cuts` and `y_cuts`, numbered row-major.

#### `owners(coordinates: Iterable) → ndarray`

The index of the block owning each coordinate (an (n, 2) array or pairs).

#### `owner(coordinate: tuple[int, int]) → int`

The index of the block owning `coordinate`.

#### `property owner_map: ndarray`

Block index of every cell, shaped like the grid (read-only).

#### `halo(index: int, radius: int = 1) → frozenset[tuple[int, int]]`

Cells of other blocks within `radius` steps (Chebyshev) of block `index`.

#### `neighbours(index: int, radius: int = 1) → frozenset[int]`

Blocks owning a cell of block `index`’s halo.

Split a network into balanced parts with few edges between them.

`graph(parts)` describes the split; `.layout(network)` applies it to a `Network` (or a networkx graph). The method is deterministic: nodes are ordered by breadth-first search from a pseudo-peripheral node of each component (the banding order of Cuthill and McKee), the order is cut into `parts` runs of nearly equal size, the larger first, and a few passes of greedy boundary refinement (the k-way form of Fiduccia and Mattheyses) move a border node to the neighbouring part it has most edges to, while every part stays within `imbalance` of its target size. The same graph and node order give the same parts in every process.

A `GraphLayout` answers the questions of a `BlockLayout`: who owns a node (`owner`, `owners`) and which nodes of other parts lie within `radius` hops of a part (`halo`).

#### `neighbours_of(indptr: ndarray, indices: ndarray, nodes: ndarray)`

The neighbours of every node in `nodes`, concatenated (with repeats).

#### `banded_order(indptr: ndarray, indices: ndarray) → list[int]`

All nodes, component by component, each in BFS order from a far node.

#### `class GraphPartition(parts: int, imbalance: float = 0.03, passes: int = 4)`

A split of a network into `parts` parts (see the module docstring).

#### `property partitions: int`

Number of parts.

#### `layout(network: Any) → GraphLayout`

The parts of `network` (a `Network` or a networkx graph).

#### `graph(parts: int, imbalance: float = 0.03) → GraphPartition`

Split a network into `parts` balanced parts with few edges between them.

#### `class GraphLayout(nodes: list, assignment: ndarray, indptr, indices)`

The parts of one network: who owns each node, and each part’s halo.

Parts given by `assignment[i]` for `nodes[i]`, over CSR adjacency.

#### `owners(nodes: Iterable[Hashable]) → ndarray`

The part owning each node.

#### `owner(node: Hashable) → int`

The part owning `node`.

#### `sizes() → ndarray`

Nodes in each part.

#### `cut() → int`

Edges whose ends lie in different parts.

#### `halo(index: int, radius: int = 1) → frozenset`

Nodes of other parts within `radius` hops of part `index`.

#### `neighbours(index: int, radius: int = 1) → frozenset[int]`

Parts owning a node of part `index`’s halo.

Split a continuous space into boxes holding nearly equal numbers of agents.

`kd(parts)` describes the split; `.layout(space)` applies it to a `ContinuousSpace` from the positions of its agents. The domain is cut in two along its longest side (the lowest axis on ties) at the position that leaves `ceil(parts / 2) / parts` of the points on the low side, halfway between the two points either side of the cut; each side is cut again until there are `parts` boxes (recursive coordinate bisection, a k-d tree). The boxes cover the whole domain, so a point that moves anywhere has an owner.

A `KDLayout` says which box owns a point (`owner`, `owners`) and which points lie within a distance of a box (`near`, wrapping on a torus): the ghosts a worker sends before a phase that looks that far.

#### `class Box(index: int, lower: tuple[float, ...], upper: tuple[float, ...])`

One box: points with `lower <= x < upper` on every axis.

#### `class KDPartition(parts: int)`

A split of a continuous space into `parts` boxes (see the module docstring).

#### `property partitions: int`

Number of boxes.

#### `layout(space: Any = None, *, points=None, bounds=None) → KDLayout`

The boxes of `space` (or of explicit `points` and `bounds`).

#### `kd(parts: int) → KDPartition`

Split a continuous space into `parts` boxes of nearly equal population.

#### `class KDLayout(boxes: list[Box], torus: bool = False)`

The boxes of one continuous space: who owns a point, and who is near a box.

Boxes covering the domain, numbered in bisection order.

#### `owners(points: Any) → ndarray`

The box owning each point (an (n, d) array); the domain’s top edge included.

#### `owner(point: Any) → int`

The box owning `point`.

#### `distances(index: int, points: Any) → ndarray`

Euclidean distance from each point to box `index` (wrapping on a torus).

#### `reaches(index: int, lower: Any, upper: Any, radius: float) → bool`

Whether some point of the box `lower`..``upper`` may lie within `radius`.

False only when none can: rounding is monotone, so no point of the box is nearer box `index` than `distances` finds for the box itself (NaN bounds: True).

#### `near(index: int, points: Any, radius: float) → ndarray`

Whether each point lies within `radius` of box `index`.

Checkpoints of a split run: one file per partition plus an index.

`part-00003.ckpt` holds partition 3: a short header line and a pickle of its index, its layout and its model as a core checkpoint (`checkpoint_bytes`, so the Modelly and Python versions are checked the same way). `index.json` names the model class, the number of partitions, the time, the reporter rows so far and each file with its SHA-256; a restore checks every file against it.

Security: the files are pickles; only restore checkpoints you wrote or trust.

#### `digest(path: Path) → str`

The SHA-256 of a file, in hex.

#### `write_part(directory: Path, index: int, model: Any, layout: Any) → dict`

Write partition `index`; its entry for the index.

#### `read_part(path: Path, expected: str | None) → tuple[int, Any, Any]`

`(index, layout, model)` of a partition file, checked against its digest.

**Raises:**

[**CheckpointError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.exceptions.CheckpointError) – when the file is not a partition checkpoint or has changed.

#### `class_path(model_class: type) → str`

`module:QualName` of a class.

#### `load_class(path: str) → type`

The class named by `class_path`.

#### `write_index(directory: Path, model_class: type, rows: list, files: list) → Path`

Write `index.json` for the partition files `files`.

#### `read_index(directory: str | Path) → dict`

The index of a split-run checkpoint.

**Raises:**

[**CheckpointError**](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/core.html#modelly.core.exceptions.CheckpointError) – when there is no index, or one of another format.

The workers of a split run and the way bytes travel between them.

A group calls the same worker method on every partition (`invoke` with the same arguments, `deliver` with one payload each), routes the outboxes the workers return to the inboxes of their receivers (`exchange`), and gives every process all the workers’ values in partition order (`gather`).

`LocalGroup` keeps every partition in this process and runs them one after the other: no parallelism, the reference for the other backends and the easiest to debug. `MPIGroup` is one partition per MPI rank (run the script under `mpirun -n <partitions>`); routing is one `alltoall` and an error on any rank is raised on every rank instead of leaving the others waiting.

#### `transpose(outboxes: dict[int, dict[int, bytes]]) → dict[int, dict[int, bytes]]`

Turn `{sender: {receiver: data}}` into `{receiver: {sender: data}}`.

#### `class LocalGroup(requests: Sequence[BuildRequest])`

Every partition in this process, run in turn.

Build one worker per request.

#### `invoke(method: str, *args: Any) → dict[int, Any]`

Call `method(*args)` on every worker.

#### `deliver(method: str, payloads: dict[int, Any]) → dict[int, Any]`

Call `method(payloads[i])` on worker `i`.

#### `static exchange(outboxes: dict[int, dict[int, bytes]]) → dict[int, dict[int, bytes]]`

Route every outbox to its receivers.

#### `gather(values: dict[int, Any]) → list[Any]`

The values in partition order.

#### `invoke_exchange(method: str, *args: Any) → dict[int, dict[int, bytes]]`

`exchange(invoke(method, *args))`: call, then route the outboxes.

#### `invoke_gather(method: str, *args: Any) → list[Any]`

`gather(invoke(method, *args))`: call, then the values in partition order.

#### `close() → None`

Drop the workers.

#### `class MPIGroup(requests: Sequence[BuildRequest], comm: Any = None)`

One partition per MPI rank of `comm` (`COMM_WORLD` by default).

Build this rank’s worker; the number of ranks must equal the partitions.

#### `invoke(method: str, *args: Any) → dict[int, Any]`

Call `method(*args)` on this rank’s worker.

#### `deliver(method: str, payloads: dict[int, Any]) → dict[int, Any]`

Call `method` on this rank’s worker with its payload.

#### `exchange(outboxes: dict[int, dict[int, bytes]]) → dict[int, dict[int, bytes]]`

Send each rank its part of this rank’s outbox; receive everyone’s.

#### `gather(values: dict[int, Any]) → list[Any]`

Every rank’s value, in rank order, on every rank.

#### `invoke_exchange(method: str, *args: Any) → dict[int, dict[int, bytes]]`

Call `method` and route its outbox in one `alltoall`, the status inside.

Each part carries the sender’s failure, if any, so every rank still learns of a failure on any rank and raises it, without a collective of its own.

#### `invoke_gather(method: str, *args: Any) → list[Any]`

Call `method` and gather every rank’s value in one `allgather`, as above.

#### `close() → None`

Drop this rank’s worker (MPI itself stays initialised for the script).

Split runs on Dask or Ray: each partition is an actor on a worker process.

The process that builds the model is the coordinator: it calls every actor in parallel and passes the ghosts and migrants between them, so the bytes of an exchange travel through it. That keeps the protocol identical to the MPI one, at the price of a round trip per exchange; for many partitions on a cluster prefer MPI, where neighbours talk directly.

`DaskGroup` starts a local cluster of one-thread worker processes (bound to 127.0.0.1, no dashboard) unless given an `address` or a `client`, and places one actor on each worker. `RayGroup` calls `ray.init` when Ray is not running yet and shuts it down afterwards. Both import their library only when used: `pip install "modelly-abm[dask]"` or `"modelly-abm[ray]"`.

#### `class DaskGroup(requests: Sequence[BuildRequest], **options: Any)`

One Dask actor per partition, each on a worker process of its own.

Connect (or start a local cluster) and start one actor per request.

#### `close() → None`

Drop the actors and close the client and cluster this group started.

#### `class RayGroup(requests: Sequence[BuildRequest], **options: Any)`

One Ray actor per partition.

Start Ray if needed, then one actor per request.

#### `close() → None`

Drop the actors, and shut Ray down when this group started it.

One partition of a split run: a model holding the agents of its part of space.

Every worker builds the model from the same scenario, so agents get the `unique_id` (and so the default stream key) of the single-process build, then keeps the agents its partition owns; a model that asks `owns()` builds only those in the first place. A step is the declared phases; around a phase that looks `radius` away, the worker sends copies of its border agents (ghosts) to its neighbours and receives theirs, and after a phase that moves agents it sends away those now standing on another partition’s ground (migrants, with their streams). Ghosts exist only during their phase.

The backends call these methods in the same order on every worker, and pass the bytes between them (`modelly.distributed.groups`).

#### `class BuildRequest(model_class: type | None, scenario: bytes | None, partition: Any, index: int, checkpoint: str | None = None, digest: str | None = None)`

What a worker needs to start: a model to build, or a checkpoint to load.

**Variables:**

- **model_class** ([*type*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#type)* | **None*) – the partitionable model class.
- **scenario** ([*bytes*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#bytes)* | **None*) – the scenario, pickled (every worker starts from the same bytes).
- **partition** (*Any*) – the partition spec (`grid_blocks`, `graph`, `kd`).
- **index** ([*int*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/functions.html#int)) – the partition this worker runs.
- **checkpoint** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)* | **None*) – a partition file to restore instead of building.
- **digest** ([*str*](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/stdtypes.html#str)* | **None*) – the SHA-256 the checkpoint file must have.

#### `class PartitionWorker(request: BuildRequest)`

The model of one partition and the steps of the exchange protocol.

Build (or restore) the model, check it, and keep this partition’s agents.

#### `info() → tuple[int, int, int, bool]`

Agents built, agents kept, id counter after the build, own stream keys.

#### `begin_step() → None`

Advance the model’s time by one step, as its default schedule does.

#### `ghosts_for(phase: int) → dict[int, bytes]`

The ghosts each neighbour needs before `phase`.

#### `accept_ghosts(inbox: dict[int, bytes]) → None`

Place the neighbours’ ghosts, by sender then in the sender’s order.

#### `act(phase: int) → dict[int, bytes]`

Run `phase` on the local agents; the migrants, for a moving phase.

#### `accept_migrants(inbox: dict[int, bytes]) → None`

Register the arriving agents, by sender then in the sender’s order.

#### `report() → tuple[float, dict[str, Any]]`

The model’s time and this partition’s part of every reporter.

#### `snapshot(attributes: tuple[str, ...]) → list[tuple]`

`(stream key, location, *attributes)` of the local agents.

#### `states() → list[tuple]`

The full state of every local agent (see `reduce.states`).

#### `save(directory: str) → dict`

Write this partition’s checkpoint file; its entry for the index.

Per-agent random streams: each agent draws from generators of its own.

A model opts in with `agent_streams = True` on its class. `agent.random` and `agent.rng` then come from a seed derived from the model’s seed and the agent’s stream key (its `unique_id` unless `stream_key` is overridden), so an agent’s draws do not depend on how many draws other agents made or on the order in which agents step. This is what lets a population split across processes give the same results as one process: an agent takes its stream with it. Without the flag, every agent shares `model.random` and `model.rng` as before.

The seed of key `k` is `SeedSequence(entropy, spawn_key=(*root, DOMAIN, k))` where `entropy` and `root` are the scenario’s seed sequence: replicates of a scenario get different streams, and no stream equals one that `SeedSequence.spawn` hands out, since spawned keys never reach `DOMAIN`. The generators are created on an agent’s first draw and travel with it in checkpoints and pickles.

#### `stream_seed(agent: Agent) → np.random.SeedSequence`

The seed sequence of `agent`’s own streams.

#### `own_random(agent: Agent) → Random`

`agent`’s stdlib-compatible generator, created on first use.

#### `own_rng(agent: Agent) → np.random.Generator`

`agent`’s numpy generator, of the scenario’s bit generator, created on first use.


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/stream.md -->

# Stream

Live observations for running models (provisional, new in 1.4): sources that hand out observations as they arrive, observation operators that read the same quantities from a model, ensembles of replicates advanced in lock step, and the filters that keep an ensemble close to the observations. The [data assimilation tutorial](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/assimilation.html) walks through all of them on a synthetic truth.

Module

Contents

modelly.stream.sources

Observation, ReplaySource, CSVSource, HTTPSource, due

modelly.stream.connectors

MQTTSource (extra mqtt), KafkaSource (extra kafka)

modelly.stream.operators

ObservationOperator

modelly.stream.ensemble

Ensemble, derived_seed, replicate_scenarios

modelly.stream.particle

ParticleFilter, FilterStep, systematic_resample, effective_sample_size

modelly.stream.kalman

EnsembleKalmanFilter, enkf_update

modelly.stream.bands

forecast_band, weighted_quantiles, quantile_column

Methods: the bootstrap particle filter of Gordon, Salmond & Smith (1993) with systematic resampling (Douc & Cappé 2005); the stochastic ensemble Kalman filter of Evensen (1994, 2003) with perturbed observations (Burgers, van Leeuwen & Evensen 1998). Full references are in the tutorial.

Bands (`Ensemble.band`, `Ensemble.forecast`, `ParticleFilter.band`, `ParticleFilter.forecast`) are long-format DataFrames with the columns `time`, `quantity`, `mean` and one `q<level>` per quantile (`q0.05`, `q0.5`, `q0.95` by default): plain data for plots and live views.

Where observations come from: a replayed table, a growing CSV file, an HTTP endpoint.

Every source has `poll(until=None)`: the observations it has not handed out yet, in time order, up to `until` when given (later ones wait for a later poll). A source never hands out an observation twice, so a loop that polls before each model step sees each data point exactly once. An observation that arrives after a later one was handed out is dropped: a run cannot go back to use it.

#### `class Observation(time: float, values: Mapping[str, float])`

Values observed at one time; `values` maps a quantity to a number.

#### `class ReplaySource(records: Any, *, time: str = 'time')`

Observations from memory: a list of records, or a pandas DataFrame.

Replay `records` (mappings with a `time` field, or a DataFrame).

#### `poll(until: float | None = None) → list[Observation]`

The observations not handed out yet, up to `until`.

#### `class CSVSource(path: str | Path, *, time: str = 'time')`

A CSV file that grows: each poll reads the rows appended since the last one.

Follow `path`; its first line is the header.

#### `poll(until: float | None = None) → list[Observation]`

Read complete new lines, then hand out what is due.

#### `class HTTPSource(url: str, *, time: str = 'time', fetch: ~collections.abc.Callable[[str], bytes] = <function _get>, parse: ~collections.abc.Callable[[bytes], ~collections.abc.Iterable[~collections.abc.Mapping[str, ~typing.Any]]] = <function loads>)`

An endpoint returning a JSON list of records; each poll fetches it again.

Poll `url`; `fetch` and `parse` replace the HTTP call and the JSON decoding.

#### `poll(until: float | None = None) → list[Observation]`

Fetch, keep records not seen before, then hand out what is due.

#### `due(source: Any | Iterable[Observation], until: float | None = None) → list[Observation]`

The observations of `source` up to `until`, in the order it gives them.

`source` is a stream source (anything with `poll(until)`) or an iterable of observations, such as a list.

Message-broker sources: MQTT topics and Kafka topics (optional extras).

Both behave like the other stream sources: `poll(until=None)` hands out the observations received since the last poll, in time order, each once. A message’s payload is a JSON record with a `time` field (or a list of them); `parse` replaces the decoding.

The client libraries are optional and imported only when a source builds its own client:

```default
pip install "modelly-abm[mqtt]"    # paho-mqtt
pip install "modelly-abm[kafka]"   # confluent-kafka
```

Pass `client=` (MQTT) or `consumer=` (Kafka) to use one you configured yourself, with authentication, TLS and so on, or a stand-in in tests.

#### `class MQTTSource(topic: str, *, host: str = 'localhost', port: int = 1883, client: ~typing.Any = None, time: str = 'time', parse: ~collections.abc.Callable[[bytes], ~typing.Any] = <function loads>)`

Observations published to an MQTT topic (paho-mqtt).

Subscribe to `topic` on the broker at `host:port`, or through `client`.

A `client` needs `subscribe(topic)` and an `on_message` attribute, as a paho `Client` has; it is used as given (connected, its loop running). Messages arrive on the client’s thread and wait in a queue for the next `poll`.

#### `poll(until: float | None = None) → list[Observation]`

Decode the messages received since the last poll, then hand out what is due.

#### `close() → None`

Stop and disconnect the client when this source created it.

#### `class KafkaSource(topic: str, *, config: ~collections.abc.Mapping[str, ~typing.Any] | None = None, consumer: ~typing.Any = None, time: str = 'time', parse: ~collections.abc.Callable[[bytes], ~typing.Any] = <function loads>, timeout: float = 1.0)`

Observations from a Kafka topic (confluent-kafka).

Consume `topic` with a consumer built from `config`, or with `consumer`.

`config` is the confluent-kafka configuration, for example `{"bootstrap.servers": "broker:9092", "group.id": "twin"}`. A `consumer` needs `subscribe([topic])`, `consume(num_messages, timeout)` and `close()`. Each poll waits at most `timeout` seconds.

#### `poll(until: float | None = None) → list[Observation]`

Read the messages waiting on the topic, then hand out what is due.

Messages that carry an error (such as the end of a partition) are kept in `errors` instead of being decoded.

#### `close() → None`

Leave the consumer group and close the consumer.

Observation operators: what a model would report if it were observed like the world.

An operator names each observed quantity and how to read it from a model:

```default
observe = ObservationOperator(
    cases=lambda m: m.new_cases,
    hospital=lambda m: m.count("hospitalised"),
)
observe(model)                      # {"cases": 41.0, "hospital": 7.0}
observe.residuals(model, obs)       # observed minus modelled, for the quantities obs has
```

`log_likelihood` scores a model against an observation under independent Gaussian errors; the particle filter weights replicates with it.

#### `class ObservationOperator(**quantities: Callable[[Any], float])`

Maps a model to the quantities an observation reports.

One callable per observed quantity, taking the model.

#### `property names: tuple[str, ...]`

The observed quantities, in declaration order.

#### `residuals(model: Any, observation: Observation) → dict[str, float]`

Observed minus modelled, for the quantities both the operator and `observation` have.

#### `log_likelihood(model: Any, observation: Observation, sd: float | Mapping[str, float]) → float`

Log density of `observation` given `model` under independent Gaussian errors.

`sd` is one standard deviation for every quantity, or one per quantity. Quantities the observation lacks do not count.

Ensembles: replicates of one scenario advanced in lock step.

An [`Ensemble`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/stream.html#modelly.stream.ensemble.Ensemble) builds `n` models from one scenario, each with a seed spawned from the scenario’s seed sequence, so replicate `i` gets the seed `Scenario.spawn_replications(n)[i]` gets on a fresh scenario:

```default
ensemble = Ensemble(Epidemic, EpidemicScenario(rng=7), 40)
ensemble.advance(10)                      # every replicate to time 10
ensemble.band(observe)                    # quantiles across replicates, a DataFrame
```

Replicates run one after the other in this process, in index order: the ensemble is deterministic for a seed. The assimilation filters ([`modelly.stream.particle`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/stream.html#module-modelly.stream.particle), [`modelly.stream.kalman`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/stream.html#module-modelly.stream.kalman)) work on an ensemble: they weight, duplicate and adjust its replicates between advances.

Every random draw the ensemble or a filter makes outside the models comes from a seed sequence derived from the scenario’s with a domain of its own (`derived_seed`), so no derived stream equals a replicate’s or an agent’s.

#### `derived_seed(root: SeedSequence, domain: int, *key: int) → SeedSequence`

The seed sequence of `key` in `domain`, below `root`.

`SeedSequence.spawn` hands out keys `(*root.spawn_key, i)`; these keys are one level deeper and start with `domain`, a number far above any replicate count, so they never collide with a spawned seed.

#### `replicate_scenarios(scenario: Scenario, n: int) → list[Scenario]`

`n` replicates of `scenario`, as `spawn_replications(n)` on a fresh one.

The scenario’s seed sequence is left as it was, so building a second ensemble from the same scenario gives the same replicates.

#### `class Ensemble(factory: Callable[..., Model], scenario: Scenario, n: int, *, prior: Prior | None = None)`

`n` replicates of a model, built from one scenario with spawned seeds.

Build `factory(scenario=replicate)` for each of `n` replicate scenarios.

A model class is a factory. `prior` maps a model attribute to a callable drawing its starting value from a numpy generator: each replicate gets its own draw, set after the model is built and before it runs, from a generator derived from the scenario’s seed.

#### `seed(domain: int, *key: int) → SeedSequence`

A seed sequence derived from the scenario’s (see `derived_seed`).

#### `property time: float`

The time every replicate has reached.

#### `advance(until: float) → None`

Run every replicate to time `until`, one after the other.

Nothing happens when the replicates are already at `until`.

**Raises:**

[**ValueError**](https://docs.python.org/3/builtins/exceptions.html#ValueError) – If `until` is before the current time.

#### `values(operator: ObservationOperator) → np.ndarray`

`operator` read from every replicate: one row per replicate, one column per quantity.

#### `resample(indices: Sequence[int], reseed: Callable[[int], SeedSequence]) → None`

Replace the replicates by `models[i] for i in indices`, copying duplicates.

The first slot that takes a replicate keeps the model itself; every other slot gets a checkpoint copy (`modelly.core.checkpoint.checkpoint_bytes()`) reseeded in place from `reseed(slot)`, so duplicates diverge from their next draw on. A copy is a full checkpoint, so it holds every agent, space, column and scheduled event of the original.

Note

Per-agent streams (`agent_streams = True`) are copied, not reseeded: only `model.random` and `model.rng` are.

#### `band(operator: ObservationOperator, quantiles: Sequence[float] = (0.05, 0.5, 0.95), weights: Sequence[float] | None = None) → pd.DataFrame`

Mean and quantiles of `operator` across replicates, at the current time.

One row per quantity, with columns `time`, `quantity`, `mean` and one `q<level>` per quantile (`q0.05`, `q0.5`, …): plain data for a plot or a live view. `weights` weight the replicates (equal by default).

#### `forecast(operator: ObservationOperator, until: float, *, every: float = 1.0, quantiles: Sequence[float] = (0.05, 0.5, 0.95), weights: Sequence[float] | None = None) → pd.DataFrame`

The band of `operator` from now to `until`, every `every` time units.

The forecast runs checkpoint copies of the replicates: the ensemble itself stays where it is. The frame has the columns of `band`, one row per time and quantity, the current time first.

Particle filter: keep an ensemble of runs close to the observations.

The bootstrap filter of Gordon, Salmond & Smith (1993), also called sequential importance resampling. Each replicate of an [`Ensemble`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/stream.html#modelly.stream.ensemble.Ensemble) is a particle. At each observation the replicates run to its time (the model itself is the proposal), each is weighted by [`ObservationOperator.log_likelihood`](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/apis/stream.html#modelly.stream.operators.ObservationOperator.log_likelihood), and when the effective sample size falls below `threshold * n` the ensemble is resampled with systematic resampling (Douc & Cappé 2005; Kitagawa 1996): a replicate drawn more than once is duplicated through a checkpoint and the duplicates are reseeded so they diverge:

```default
pf = ParticleFilter(ensemble, observe, sd=5.0)
pf.run(source)                       # assimilate every observation
pf.estimate()                        # weighted mean of each quantity now
pf.forecast(until=60)                # quantile bands ahead, a DataFrame
```

For a seed the filter is deterministic: the uniform of each systematic resampling comes from a generator derived from the scenario’s seed, and duplicate `slot` of resampling `g` is reseeded from the derived key `(RESAMPLE_DOMAIN, g, slot)`. Two runs give bit-identical weights and replicates, with the compiled core or the pure-Python one.

References

Gordon, N. J., Salmond, D. J. & Smith, A. F. M. (1993). Novel approach to nonlinear/non-Gaussian Bayesian state estimation. IEE Proceedings F, 140(2), 107-113. Douc, R. & Cappé, O. (2005). Comparison of resampling schemes for particle filtering. ISPA 2005, 64-69.

#### `effective_sample_size(weights: Sequence[float]) → float`

Kish’s effective sample size of `weights`: `1 / sum(w**2)` once they sum to one.

#### `systematic_resample(weights: Sequence[float], uniform: float) → ndarray`

The replicates systematic resampling keeps, one index per slot, in order.

Slot `k` takes the replicate whose cumulative weight first exceeds `(uniform + k) / n`; one uniform in `[0, 1)` decides every slot, which gives the lowest resampling variance of the usual schemes (Douc & Cappé 2005).

#### `class FilterStep(time: float, ess: float, resampled: bool, log_evidence: float)`

What one assimilated observation did to the ensemble.

`log_evidence` is the log of the observation’s likelihood averaged over the weighted replicates before it, an estimate of `log p(y_t | y_<t)`; the sum over steps estimates the log marginal likelihood of the data.

#### `class ParticleFilter(ensemble: Ensemble, operator: ObservationOperator, sd: float | Mapping[str, float], *, threshold: float = 0.5)`

Bootstrap particle filter over an ensemble (Gordon et al. 1993).

Weight `ensemble` against observations read through `operator`.

`sd` is the observation error, one standard deviation for every quantity or one per quantity. `threshold` is the fraction of the ensemble size under which the effective sample size triggers a resampling: `1.0` resamples at every observation.

#### `property weights: ndarray`

The normalised weight of each replicate.

#### `property ess: float`

The effective sample size of the current weights.

#### `property resamplings: int`

How many times the ensemble has been resampled.

#### `assimilate(observation: Observation) → FilterStep`

Run the ensemble to `observation`, weight it, resample when the ESS is low.

#### `run(source: object | Iterable[Observation], until: float | None = None) → list[FilterStep]`

Assimilate every observation `source` has, up to `until`.

`source` is a stream source (anything with `poll(until)`) or an iterable of observations in time order (see `sources.due`).

#### `estimate(operator: ObservationOperator | None = None) → dict[str, float]`

The weighted mean of each quantity of `operator` (the filter’s own by default).

#### `band(operator: ObservationOperator | None = None, quantiles: Sequence[float] = (0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) → pd.DataFrame`

The weighted band of `operator` now (see `Ensemble.band()`).

#### `forecast(until: float, operator: ObservationOperator | None = None, *, every: float = 1.0, quantiles: Sequence[float] = (0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) → pd.DataFrame`

The weighted band ahead to `until` (see `Ensemble.forecast()`).

#### `property history: DataFrame`

time, ESS, resampled, log evidence.

**Type:**

One row per assimilated observation

Ensemble Kalman filter for continuous parameters (state/parameter augmentation).

The stochastic ensemble Kalman filter of Evensen (1994, 2003) with perturbed observations (Burgers, van Leeuwen & Evensen 1998). The quantities it adjusts are named model attributes: parameters such as a contact rate, or any continuous state the model reads back. At each observation the replicates run to its time; with `X` the attributes (one row per replicate), `Y` what the operator reads from each and `R` the observation error variance:

```default
K   = cov(X, Y) (cov(Y, Y) + R)^-1
X_i = X_i + K (y + e_i - Y_i),      e_i ~ N(0, R)
```

Agent-level state is left alone: an agent-based model is rarely a vector the filter could shift, so the attributes are where it learns. Parameters can be kept in a range with `bounds`, clipping after each update:

```default
enkf = EnsembleKalmanFilter(ensemble, observe, sd=4.0, parameters=["beta"],
                            bounds={"beta": (0.0, 2.0)})
enkf.run(source)
enkf.estimate()                      # {"beta": 0.31}, the ensemble mean
```

The perturbations come from a generator derived from the scenario’s seed, so the filter is deterministic for a seed.

References

Evensen, G. (1994). Sequential data assimilation with a nonlinear quasi-geostrophic model using Monte Carlo methods to forecast error statistics. Journal of Geophysical Research, 99(C5), 10143-10162. Burgers, G., van Leeuwen, P. J. & Evensen, G. (1998). Analysis scheme in the ensemble Kalman filter. Monthly Weather Review, 126(6), 1719-1724. Evensen, G. (2003). The Ensemble Kalman Filter: theoretical formulation and practical implementation. Ocean Dynamics, 53(4), 343-367.

#### `enkf_update(states: ndarray, predicted: ndarray, observed: ndarray, variance: ndarray) → ndarray`

The EnKF analysis of `states` (replicates by attributes).

`predicted` holds what each replicate would observe (replicates by quantities), `observed` one perturbed observation per replicate (same shape) and `variance` the observation error variance of each quantity.

#### `class EnsembleKalmanFilter(ensemble: Ensemble, operator: ObservationOperator, sd: float | Mapping[str, float], parameters: Sequence[str], *, bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None)`

Stochastic EnKF with perturbed observations (Evensen 1994, 2003).

Adjust the `parameters` attributes of `ensemble` to fit the observations.

`sd` is the observation error, one standard deviation for every quantity or one per quantity. `bounds` maps a parameter to the `(low, high)` range it is clipped to after each update.

#### `states() → ndarray`

The adjusted attributes: one row per replicate, one column per parameter.

#### `assimilate(observation: Observation) → dict[str, float]`

Run the ensemble to `observation` and update the parameters.

Returns the ensemble mean of each parameter after the update; an observation with none of the operator’s quantities changes nothing.

#### `run(source: object | Iterable[Observation], until: float | None = None) → list[dict[str, float]]`

Assimilate every observation `source` has, up to `until`.

`source` is a stream source (anything with `poll(until)`) or an iterable of observations in time order (see `sources.due`).

#### `estimate() → dict[str, float]`

The ensemble mean of each parameter.

#### `property history: DataFrame`

time, then each parameter’s mean and `<name>_sd`.

**Type:**

One row per observation

Quantile bands across an ensemble, as plain DataFrames.

A band is the spread of the observed quantities across replicates at a time: the (weighted) mean and a few quantiles. Rows are long-format, one per time and quantity, so a plot, a table or a live view (Studio) reads them without knowing anything about ensembles:

```default
time  quantity  mean   q0.05  q0.5   q0.95
12.0  cases     41.3   30.0   40.5   55.2
```

Weighted quantiles put each replicate’s weight at the midpoint of its step in the cumulative weights and interpolate linearly between them; with equal weights this is the Hazen definition (Hyndman & Fan 1996, definition 5).

#### `quantile_column(level: float) → str`

The column of quantile `level`: `q0.05`, `q0.5`, …

#### `weighted_quantiles(values: Sequence[float], weights: Sequence[float] | None, quantiles: Sequence[float]) → ndarray`

Quantiles of `values` weighted by `weights` (equal when `None`).

#### `forecast_band(models: Sequence[Model], operator: ObservationOperator, until: float, *, every: float = 1.0, quantiles: Sequence[float] = (0.05, 0.5, 0.95), weights: Sequence[float] | None = None) → pd.DataFrame`

Run checkpoint copies of `models` to `until`, a band at every forecast time.

The times are the models’ current time, then every `every` time units, ending exactly at `until`; `models` themselves do not move.

# What’s new

What each release lets you do, in a few lines per feature, newest first. Every feature links to its guide. The [changelog](https://github.com/RemiPelloux/Modelly/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) has the full detail of every change, and [Deprecations](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/deprecations.html) what is going away and when.

Each release adds its section here before it is tagged: the release script refuses a release whose notes are missing (see “Release notes” in [CONTRIBUTING](https://github.com/RemiPelloux/Modelly/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)).

## Unreleased

### Changed

- **A clearer home page**: the headline spans the page, the six example models run as large live sketches, the guides are grouped by goal in rows, and the benchmark chart shows each Modelly time leaving Mesa’s when it scrolls into view. [Home](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/index.html)
- **An interactive home page hero**: a model runs across the whole top of the page. Pick an epidemic, a flock or Schelling’s segregation, move its parameter and watch the line of Python that parameter lives in change; click, drag or move the pointer to disturb it. The guide finder moved to “Start from what you need”. [Home](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/index.html)
- **The version menu shows the full release**: “1.5.1 (stable)” rather than “1.5”, and each older version by its last patch.

## 1.5.1 - 2026-11-07

### New

- **Docs for AI assistants**: every page of this documentation is also plain Markdown. The *Copy page* button under each title puts it on your clipboard for a chat; replace `.html` with `.md` in any address to read it; [llms.txt](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/llms.txt) lists every page and [llms-full.txt](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/llms-full.txt) holds them all in one file.
- **A home page that finds the guide**: type a task (calibrate, GPU, from R) and the matching guides are listed; the benchmark against Mesa 3.5 is drawn model by model. [Home](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/index.html)

### Faster

Every result is unchanged: the golden digests are identical, compiled and pure Python.

- **Each step costs less**: the schedule’s event is reused, the time signal is skipped when nothing listens, and `do`, `shuffle_do` and `map` run in C on every agent set: scheduling an event and running it takes 0.62 times as long as in 1.5.0, `do` 0.81 times.
- **Random draws**: `select_random`, `random.sample(..., k=)` and `random.choices(..., k=)` take the compiled path, up to ten times faster.
- **`import modelly`** no longer loads pandas, and `modelly.viz` loads each backend only when used; the Studio starts in a third of the time and redraws only what moves.
- **Data collection** takes 0.58 times as long per step, and creating and removing an agent with Column attributes 0.66 times; continuous state reads, neighbour queries, occupancy claims and network collectors are faster too.
- **Studies**: sweeps hand runs to workers in chunks, priors and type hints are cached, an active-learning or history-matching study keeps one pool, and the JAX backend no longer recompiles for each new seed. `decide.compare`, `decide.robust`, `decide.optimise`, `treatment_effect` and `attribute` take `workers=` to run in parallel.
- **LLM agents** hash each request once and write a batch of replies in one transaction.

### Changed

- `ContinuousSpace.dimensions` is read-only in place; assigning a new array still works.
- `get_neighbors_in_radius` returns no neighbours, instead of an IndexError, when nothing is in range.

### Fixed

- Matplotlib draws agents in the same order whatever `PYTHONHASHSEED` is.
- `python -m modelly.dev perf --against v1.5.0` accepts the tag name as well as `1.5.0`.
- The browser runner’s plots no longer fail on runs longer than about 100,000 values.
- **Causes and explanations** gives the variance reduction of common random numbers as its spread over ten seeds (24 to 62 times on the Bass example, median 42) instead of one seed’s value. [Causes and explanations](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/explain.html)

## 1.5.0 - 2026-11-03

**Ecosystem and collaboration.** Publish a model on the hub with its card, decide and explain with intervals, give agents memories and inner dynamics, and work from R, Julia, a classroom or another language. The last release before 2.0: everything 2.0 changes now warns or changes no call, and `modelly migrate --check-2.0` lists what a project must change.

### New

- **Decisions**: compare strategies on the same chance events, so their differences come with tight intervals; see which are cost-effective and at what price; check which hold up across many possible futures; and search a policy’s parameters. A worked study asks which age group should get 10,000 vaccine doses. [Decisions](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/decide.html)
- **Accessible, and in five languages**: Studio and the docs pass the automated WCAG 2.2 AA checks; Studio can be zoomed, works with screen readers and the keyboard, and speaks French, Spanish, Portuguese and Chinese (`--language fr`), right to left where the language is. The getting-started page is translated too. [Accessibility and languages](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/accessibility.html)
- **For classes**: a twelve-session course with instructor notes and assessments, a track for instructors coming from NetLogo, and a classroom mode in Studio where the instructor shares parameters and every student’s run lands in one table. [Course](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/course/index.html)
- **Studio for everyone**: open a hub model by name with no code tabs (`modelly studio --hub age_seir --no-code`), compare scenarios with intervals, read the model card, build a teaching model from a form and download its code, and export a report (HTML or PDF) with the figures, the card and how to rerun the run. [Studio](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html#studio-for-everyone)
- **Language-model agents that remember, plan and talk**: agents keep a memory that is summarised as it grows, write plans, reflect, call functions of the model before answering, and hold conversations with each other, many at once. A 500-trader market runs offline and replays from its cache, and an evaluation harness compares providers on behaviour, consistency and cost. [Language-model agents](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/llm_agents.html#memory)
- **Modelly from Julia**: `Modelly.jl` runs and calibrates models from Julia, returns DataFrames and hands over agent columns without copying them. [From R and Julia](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/r_and_julia.html#the-julia-package)
- **Modelly from R**: the `modelly` R package runs and calibrates models from R and returns data frames, with no Python to write: `modelly_calibrate(...)` fits the SIR tutorial and prints its posterior. [From R and Julia](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/r_and_julia.html#the-r-package)
- **Causes and explanations**: the effect of an intervention with an interval, and how much running both arms on the same chance events tightened it; the agents an outcome depended on (it finds an outbreak’s index case); what a recorded run would have done with one change; and how much each parameter moved an emulator’s prediction. [Causes and explanations](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/explain.html)
- **The model hub**: `modelly hub search malaria` finds published models, `modelly hub info` shows what each is for and how to cite it, and `modelly hub install` gets one, checking its hash and signature first. `modelly hub publish` prepares your model’s entry, with a DOI from Zenodo and a Sigstore signature when you ask. All eighteen zoo models are on it. [The model hub](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/hub.html)
- **Inputs that change inside a step**: `Forcing(function)` and `Series(times, values)` drive an `AgentODE` or `solve_batch` at the times each system’s own steps land on (daylight, a dosing schedule, a measured series), instead of holding the value over the model’s step. [ODEs in every agent](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/agent_odes.html#inputs-that-change-inside-the-step)
- **The state inside a step**: with `dense_output=True`, `ode.at(t)` reads every agent’s state at any time of the last step on the solver’s interpolant, so an agent acting at 14:00 sees the value at 14:00. [ODEs in every agent](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/agent_odes.html#reading-the-state-inside-the-step)
- **Delays, noise and the mean-field limit**: an agent’s equation can read its own state some time ago (`Delay`), carry noise drawn from the model’s seed (`AgentSDE`, Euler-Maruyama or Milstein), and run next to its ODE limit to show how far the agents stray from it (`Companion`). [ODEs in every agent](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/agent_odes.html#delay-equations)
- **ODE parameters by gradient**: `ode_phase` puts an ODE into a differentiable model, so a clearance or growth rate is fitted to data by gradient descent. [Differentiable models](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/differentiable.html#odes-in-a-differentiable-model)
- **A zoo model with an ODE in every host**: `within_host`, an outbreak whose hosts each carry a viral-load ODE and become infectious the instant their load crosses a threshold. A hundred thousand hosts run sixty days in about fourteen seconds. [Within-host epidemic](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/within_host.html)
- **Model cards**: a short `card.toml` beside a model says what it is for, what it must not be used for, its data, how it was validated, its limits and who decisions taken with it could affect. `modelly card stamp` runs the validation tests and records the source they passed on, and `modelly card check` fails once the model has changed since. All eighteen zoo models have one, at the end of their page. [Model cards](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/model_cards.html)
- **Plugin API v1**: the way packages extend Modelly is now stable and frozen for 1.x. A plugin says which Modelly it supports with its usual `modelly-abm>=1.5,<2` dependency, and a plugin built for another version is skipped instead of breaking the run. `modelly new --template plugin` starts one, and `modelly plugins --check` shows what is installed. [Plugins](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/plugins.html)

### Deprecated

- **Typed scenarios**: in 2.0 a `Scenario` subclass is typed and validated. An attribute without an annotation, a parameter the scenario does not declare, or a value of another type than its annotation now warns and says what to write. `modelly migrate --check-2.0 src/` lists everything a project must change before 2.0. [Deprecations](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/deprecations.html)

### Fixed

- **Pages made by `modelly export-web`** keep small parameters as they are: a tolerance of one in a billion used to be rounded to zero by its slider.

## 1.4.3 - 2026-11-02

**An ODE in every agent.** Continuous dynamics inside each agent (the virus in a host, the energy budget of an animal, the potential of a neuron), integrated for the whole population at once.

### New

- **`solve_batch`**: `solve_ivp` for many independent systems. Each system takes exactly the steps its own `solve_ivp` call would take and ends at the same values, while the right-hand side is evaluated once per stage for all of them: 100 to 300 times faster than a loop of `solve_ivp` calls from a thousand systems up. A system’s result is the same, bit for bit, alone or among a hundred thousand others. [ODEs in every agent](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/agent_odes.html)
- **`ODEEvent`**: the moment a quantity crosses a threshold, located per system on the step’s interpolant, as `solve_ivp`’s `events=` does; terminal (stop there) or recorded, upward, downward or both.
- **`AgentODE`**: an ODE per agent inside a model. The state lives in the agents’ columns, events call back into the model (a host becomes infectious the instant its virus passes a level), and terminal events resume within the step (a neuron fires and resets). Stiff systems run through `solve_ivp`’s implicit methods with a block-diagonal Jacobian pattern.

The new names are provisional (`docs/api_stability.toml`). Nothing else changed: every playbook gives 1.4.2’s results.

## 1.4.2 - 2026-10-29

A fix for numpy datasets.

### Fixed

- **Two models of the same agent class** with a numpy dataset (`DataRegistry.track_agents_numpy`) no longer read each other’s values, a model restored by `Model.load` reads its own, and a checkpoint loads in a fresh process. Checkpoints written by 1.4.0 and 1.4.1 load as before.
- The SQL recorder stores `agent_id` as an integer, as the other recorders do.

## 1.4.1 - 2026-10-29

Three operations that grew quadratically with the size of a run now grow linearly. Results are unchanged.

### Faster

- **Parquet recording** of long runs: 2,000 agents for 200 steps in 1.0 s instead of 7.9 s, and twice the steps take twice the time.
- **Removing cells** from a discrete space or a network: half of a 32,000-node network in 0.14 s instead of 7.9 s.
- **Batches of many short runs** (`run_batch`, `run_grid`): workers take tasks in chunks, so 20,000 short tasks spend 0.01 s in hand-offs instead of 0.49 s.

### Fixed

- The JSON recorder returns one row per agent for a numpy dataset, as the others do.
- A network cell replaced at the same coordinate can no longer be returned by `find_nearest_cell`.

### Documentation

- The site’s header has six sections, each with its own sidebar, instead of a menu that ran off the screen.

## 1.4.0 - 2026-10-29

**Scale out and connect.** One model split across processes, on a GPU, differentiated, corrected by live data, coupled to fields and ODEs, started from a synthetic population, and shared as a web page. No playbook is slower than 1.3.3 and every output is identical.

### New

- **Split runs** (`modelly.distributed`): one model divided between processes or machines (local, MPI, Dask or Ray), with ghost agents at the borders and agents migrating with their own random streams. The result equals the single-process run, byte for byte, which the tests check at 1 to 16 partitions. [From laptop to cluster](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/distributed.html)
- **Per-agent random streams**: with `agent_streams = True`, each agent draws its own numbers, whatever the activation order or the population. [Determinism](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/determinism.html)
- **GPU backend** (`modelly.gpu`): column phases, cohorts and cell operators on CuPy or JAX, with a random stream that draws the same numbers on every backend. The grid epidemic at ten million agents runs 34 times faster than on one CPU core, bit for bit. [GPU](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/gpu.html)
- **Differentiable models** (`modelly.diff`): gradients of a model’s outputs with respect to its parameters through JAX, checked against finite differences, and gradient-based calibration. [Differentiable models](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/differentiable.html)
- **Live data and assimilation** (`modelly.stream`): sources reading files, HTTP, MQTT or Kafka; ensembles; particle filters and ensemble Kalman filters that correct a running model as data arrives, and forecast from it. [Live data and assimilation](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/assimilation.html)
- **Coupling** (`modelly.couple`): grid fields that diffuse, drift and decay, ODEs and stock-flow models, run with the agents on their own clocks, with a schedule checked before the first step. [Coupling fields and ODEs](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/coupling.html)
- **Emulators, active learning and history matching** (`modelly.emulate`): fast statistical stand-ins for a slow model, designs chosen where the emulator is least sure, and the plausible parameter space narrowed in waves. [Emulators](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/emulators.html)
- **Synthetic populations** (`modelly.population`): people and households drawn from census tables, assigned to homes, schools and workplaces, with their contact network. [Synthetic populations](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/population.html)
- **Modelly in the browser**: `modelly export-web` writes a static site that runs the model in any browser, no installation. [In the browser](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/browser.html)
- **Studio II**: ensemble bands, assimilation, an experiment browser, calibration and sensitivity results, a WebGL map for 100,000 agents, and export of a session as a script or a verifiable bundle. [Studio](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html)
- **More tools**: a NetLogo translator ([From NetLogo](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/netlogo.html)), `modelly lint` as a language server and a pre-commit hook ([Checking a model](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/lint.html)), xarray export, results read from R and Julia ([From R and Julia](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/r_and_julia.html)), memory-mapped columns for populations larger than memory, `modelly bench --against` a release, and five new zoo models on real maps and coupled processes ([Model zoo](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/zoo/index.html)).

### Changed

- The event heap is compiled: event-heavy models run faster with the same ordering.
- Data collection reads column attributes in C: 0.47 of 1.3.3’s time.

### Deprecated

- `modelly.space.geo.ipf` and `synthesize_population`: import them from `modelly.population`; they go in 2.0.

**Answers and trust.** Calibrate, explain and publish a model, on Windows, macOS and Linux.

### New

# Deprecations

Modelly changes its public API only in a way you can see coming. This page is the policy, the list of what is deprecated now, and how to find and silence the warnings.

## The policy

1. **Nothing is removed without a warning first.** A deprecated name keeps working and raises a warning for at least one minor release before it can go.
1. **The warning tells you what to do.** Every message names the replacement and the release that removes the old name:

```text
make_space_altair() is deprecated and will be removed in Modelly 2.0; use make_altair_space() instead.
```

1. **Removals happen only in a major release.** Everything deprecated during 1.x is removed in 2.0, not before. Minor releases add and deprecate; they never remove.
1. **One mechanism.** Every deprecation goes through `modelly._deprecation.deprecated(name, replacement, removal="2.0")`, which refuses to warn without a replacement or with a removal before 2.0. A test fails if any module in `modelly/` raises a deprecation warning itself.

The warning class is `ModellyDeprecationWarning`. It is a `DeprecationWarning`, so the standard Python tools find it, and also a `FutureWarning`, so filters written for the warnings Modelly 1.2 raised keep matching.

## Finding them in your code

Python shows a `DeprecationWarning` when the deprecated call is in the script you run, in a notebook, or under pytest. To find every one, including those raised from your own modules, turn them into errors and run your model or its tests:

```bash
python -W error::DeprecationWarning my_model.py
python -W error::DeprecationWarning -m pytest
```

In PowerShell the commands are the same. To see them without stopping at the first:

```bash
python -W always::DeprecationWarning my_model.py
```

## Silencing them

Fix the call: the message says what to write instead. When you cannot change the code yet, silence Modelly’s deprecations only, so that warnings from other libraries still show:

```python
import warnings
from modelly._deprecation import ModellyDeprecationWarning

warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", category=ModellyDeprecationWarning)
```

In a pytest configuration (`pyproject.toml`):

```toml
[tool.pytest.ini_options]
filterwarnings = ["ignore::modelly._deprecation.ModellyDeprecationWarning"]
```

## Announced for 2.0

2.0 is the one release allowed to break things ([its roadmap](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/2.0.0.html)). Everything it removes warns in a 1.x release first, naming the replacement. As of 1.5 every 2.0 change either warns or changes no call (the last column says which), and `modelly migrate --check-2.0` reports what a project must change. `modelly migrate --to 2.0` will rewrite what can be rewritten.

To see what your project must change, without running it:

```bash
modelly migrate --check-2.0 src/        # exit 1 when there is something to change
```

It reads every Python file and reports, with the line, each deprecated call and each Scenario attribute without an annotation, and as notes what changes without a warning: models without `agent_streams = True` (their numbers change in 2.0) and a `requires-python` below 3.13. To see what warns at run time, run the project with `python -W error::DeprecationWarning` (above).

## Deprecating something (for contributors)

```python
from modelly._deprecation import deprecated

def old_name(*args, **kwargs):
    deprecated("old_name()", "new_name()")
    return new_name(*args, **kwargs)
```

`stacklevel` counts from the caller of `deprecated`, like `warnings.warn` counts from its caller: the default (2) points the warning at whoever called `old_name`. In the same change, add the row to the table above, the entry to `modelly/_inventory.py` (the 2.0 inventory that `modelly migrate --check-2.0` reads, with the identifiers that find the old use in a project) and a changelog entry under “Deprecated”. `tests/test_inventory.py` fails when a `deprecated()` call, a table row and an inventory entry disagree.

The stability level of every public name (stable or provisional) is in [`docs/api_stability.toml`](https://github.com/RemiPelloux/Modelly/blob/main/docs/api_stability.toml): a stable name follows this policy; a provisional one (new in 1.3) may still change in a minor release, with a changelog entry.
