# Roadmap

**Status:** 1.3 released, 1.4.0 in release (every epic merged except F10 Studio II, release gate pending) · **Current release:** 1.3.3

Four releases take Modelly from a fast agent-based modelling framework to the research platform people use to **build, calibrate, explain, scale, share and publish** a model, in any field, on **Windows, macOS and Linux alike**.

Release

Theme

One line

[1.3.0](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/1.3.0.html)

Answers and trust

Calibrate, explain and publish a model: experiments, calibration, sensitivity, provenance, Studio, model zoo

[1.4.0](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/1.4.0.html)

Scale out and connect

Split runs over MPI and Dask, a GPU backend, differentiable models, data assimilation, coupled fields and ODEs, synthetic populations, emulators, Modelly in the browser

[1.5.0](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/1.5.0.html)

Ecosystem and collaboration

Model hub, model cards, policy and causal tools, LLM agents II, R and Julia bindings, differential equations in agents

[2.0.0](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/2.0.0.html)

Clean foundations

One space API, one clock, columns by default, typed scenarios, stable ABI and checkpoint format

Every feature on these pages must work on Windows, macOS and Linux before it ships. How that is guaranteed, and the support matrix for each release, is on [Platforms](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/platforms.html).

## Order, not dates

The roadmap has no dates. The releases ship in order (1.3.0, 1.4.0, 1.5.0, 2.0.0) because each one stands on the one before, as the diagram below shows. Inside a release, work is split into eight sprints: a sprint is a unit of work with exit criteria, not a period of time, and the next sprint starts as soon as the previous one’s criteria hold. Each release has three public pre-releases (alpha, beta, release candidate), each behind a gate of checks, not a calendar.

## How the releases build on each other

```

        flowchart LR
    subgraph R13["1.3.0 Answers and trust"]
        X[Experiments and executors]
        C[Calibration and sensitivity]
        P[Provenance and bundles]
        S[Studio]
        Z[Model zoo]
    end
    subgraph R14["1.4.0 Scale out and connect"]
        D[Distributed runs]
        G[GPU and differentiable models]
        W[Modelly in the browser]
        L[Live data and assimilation]
    end
    subgraph R15["1.5.0 Ecosystem and collaboration"]
        H[Model hub and model cards]
        K[Policy and causal tools]
        B[R and Julia bindings]
    end
    subgraph R20["2.0.0 Clean foundations"]
        U[One space API, one clock]
        A[Stable ABI and formats]
    end
    X --> D
    C --> G
    C --> L
    S --> W
    P --> H
    Z --> H
    C --> K
    D --> U
    G --> U
    H --> A
    
```

## What every release promises

- **Backward compatibility within 1.x.** A model written for 1.2 runs on 1.5. What changes is deprecated with a warning naming the replacement, and removed only in 2.0.
- **Reproducibility.** The same seed gives the same result, with the compiled modules or their pure-Python twins, on every supported platform. Each release widens what “the same” covers.
- **Cross-platform.** Windows, macOS and Linux are first-class: same features, same results, wheels for each. See [Platforms](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/platforms.html).
- **Discipline.** Every change follows `pelloux-guidelines.md`: files at most 300 lines, function bodies at most 25 lines, the local gate green, docs building with warnings as errors.

## Who it is for

The roadmap is written for researchers in many fields, not one: epidemiology and public health, ecology and conservation, economics and finance, sociology and political science, urban studies and transport, energy and climate, archaeology and anthropology, computational social science with language models, teaching, and the research software engineers who support them. Each release page says which of them each feature serves.

## How this roadmap is maintained

- The roadmap is a plan, not a promise: scope moves as we learn. Changes are made in pull requests against `docs/roadmap/` and noted in the release page’s review log.
- At the end of each sprint the release page gets a review entry: what shipped, what slipped and why, and the `modelly bench` summary.
- Proposals and questions are welcome as GitHub issues labelled `roadmap`.

- [1.5.0](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/1.5.0.html)
- [2.0.0](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/2.0.0.html)
- [Platforms](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/platforms.html)
- [Design reviews](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/design/index.html)

# 1.3.0: answers and trust

**Status:** released as 1.3.0, with fixes in 1.3.1, 1.3.2 and 1.3.3 · **Base:** 1.2.0

1.3.0 is the release where Modelly stops being “a faster Mesa” and becomes the place a researcher goes to **build, calibrate, explain, scale and publish** an agent-based model, whatever their field. It is the largest release so far: 16 epics, 8 sprints, three public pre-releases. Everything in it works on Windows, macOS and Linux (see [Platforms](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/platforms.html)).

It stays backward compatible. Everything a 1.2 model uses keeps working; what 1.3 wants to change is deprecated with a warning and removed only in 2.0 (see [Compatibility](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/1.3.0.html#compatibility-and-the-road-to-2-0)). That is why it is numbered 1.3.0 and not 2.0.0, even though it is a major release in scope.

## Where we start

What 1.2.0 already gives us, and what each piece unlocks for 1.3.0:

1.2.0 has

1.3.0 builds on it with

Scenario, seeded generators, run_batch / run_grid with one SeedSequence seed per run

Experiments, calibration and sensitivity analysis that are reproducible by construction

Checkpoints (model.save, Model.load, checkpoint_every), bit-identical resume

Time travel, resumable sweeps, run bundles for publication

Columns, CohortTable, CellIndex, three compiled modules (fastrng, fastloop, fastcell)

Free-threaded parallel phases, compiled select / agg, GPU arrays

modelly lint (16 rules), modelly profile (with --sizes), modelly migrate

lint --fix, editor integration, profile panels in Studio, modelly new

Solara, Altair and Matplotlib backends

Modelly Studio, publication figures, animations

Eight Mesa-vs-Modelly playbooks with agreement and determinism checks

A model zoo of validated reference models across research fields

Versioned docs (/dev/, /1.0/, /1.1/, /1.2/)

Domain tutorials, a course pack, a gallery

Wheels for Linux, macOS and Windows x86-64

Windows ARM64, free-threaded wheels

What 1.2.0 does not yet have, and researchers keep asking for:

- A way to **fit** a model to data and say how good the fit is.
- A way to say **which parameters matter** before spending a cluster budget.
- A way to run **large sweeps** on a laptop, a workstation or a cluster with the same code.
- A way to make a published result **checkable** by a reviewer in one command.
- **Real-world inputs:** maps, census tables, road networks, contact matrices.
- **Agents that reason in language**, without giving up reproducibility.
- Ready-made, validated models for their **own field**, not only for the classic toy models.

## Who 1.3.0 is for

1.3.0 is designed around researchers from many fields, not one. Each epic names the people it serves; this table is the overview.

## Epics

Every epic lists its goal, who it serves, the user stories, a sketch of the API, what “done” means, the tasks, and its dependencies. Sizes: **S** = under a sprint, **M** = one sprint, **L** = two sprints, **XL** = three or more. API sketches are proposals, to be settled in the epic’s first design review.

### E1 · Calibration (`modelly.calibrate`)

**Goal:** fit scenario parameters to observed data and report how good the fit is, with uncertainty, in a way that is reproducible run for run.

**Platforms:** pure Python and numpy; parallel runs use the E3 executors on every OS.

**Serves:** every applied field; epidemiology, ecology and economics first.

**User stories**

- As an epidemiologist, I give weekly case counts and a prior on the transmission rate, and get a posterior distribution and a fit plot.
- As an ecologist, I fit to several patterns at once (abundance, spatial clustering, age structure): pattern-oriented modelling.
- As an economist, I fit by matching moments of simulated and observed series.
- As anyone, I stop a calibration halfway and resume it tomorrow with the same result.

**API sketch**

```python
from modelly.calibrate import ABCSMC, Prior, Target, distance

calibration = ABCSMC(
    model=Epidemic,
    priors={"beta": Prior.uniform(0.05, 0.5), "gamma": Prior.log_normal(-2, 0.5)},
    targets=[Target("infected", observed=cases, distance=distance.rmse)],
    steps=120,
    replicates=4,
    seed=2027,
)
posterior = calibration.run(budget=20_000, executor="processes")
posterior.summary()  # mean, median, HDI per parameter
posterior.plot()  # marginals, pairs, fit against data
posterior.to_dataframe()
calibration.save("calib.ckpt")  # resumable, uses checkpoints
```

**Methods:** ABC rejection; ABC-SMC with adaptive tolerances; simulated method of moments; Bayesian optimisation through an optional extra (`modelly-abm[calibrate]`); distances (RMSE, weighted, Wasserstein, custom); summary statistics from any `DataCollector` column.

**Done when:** ABC-SMC recovers known parameters of the bundled SIR and predator-prey models within the stated tolerance on three seeds; identical posterior for the same seed with the compiled core and the pure-Python twin; resumable from a checkpoint; docs page with a worked example; zoo model calibrated end to end.

**Tasks**

- [ ] Design review: priors, targets, distances, posterior object *(not recorded; moved to 1.4.0)*
- [x] ABC rejection over `run_grid`
- [x] ABC-SMC with adaptive tolerance schedule and effective sample size
- [x] Simulated method of moments
- [ ] Bayesian optimisation adapter (optional dependency) *(partly: a built-in Gaussian-process search, no adapter to an outside library; moved to 1.4.0)*
- [x] Posterior: summaries, HDI, plots, export
- [x] Resume from checkpoint; parallel executors from E3
- [x] Recovery tests on synthetic data; determinism tests
- [x] Tutorial: calibrating an SIR model to case data

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** E3 (executors, results store), E4 (manifests)

### E2 · Sensitivity analysis (`modelly.sensitivity`)

**Goal:** tell the modeller which parameters drive which outputs, before and after calibration.

**Platforms:** pure Python and numpy; the emulator extra ships wheels for all three.

**Serves:** everyone with more than three parameters.

**User stories**

- As a modeller with 12 parameters, I screen them cheaply and keep the 4 that matter.
- As a reviewer, I see first-order and total Sobol indices with confidence intervals.
- As a policy analyst, I see how an output’s uncertainty splits across inputs.

**API sketch**

```python
from modelly.sensitivity import morris, sobol

screen = morris(
    Epidemic, space=scenario_space, output="peak_infected", trajectories=50, seed=1
)
screen.ranking()  # mu*, sigma per parameter
indices = sobol(
    Epidemic, space=scenario_space, output="peak_infected", samples=4096, seed=1
)
indices.plot()  # S1, ST with bootstrap intervals
```

**Methods:** one-at-a-time; Morris elementary effects; Sobol (Saltelli sampling, Jansen estimators); PAWN for skewed outputs; an optional Gaussian-process emulator so expensive models can be analysed from a few hundred runs.

**Done when:** Sobol indices match analytical values on the Ishigami function within the bootstrap interval; Morris ranking stable across seeds on the zoo models; plots and tables exportable; docs page and tutorial.

**Tasks**

- [x] Parameter spaces shared with E1 and E3 (`ScenarioSpace`)
- [x] OAT and Morris
- [x] Sobol with Saltelli sampling and bootstrap intervals
- [x] PAWN
- [x] Emulator (optional extra)
- [x] Verification on Ishigami and Sobol G functions
- [x] Tutorial: which epidemic parameters matter

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** E3

### E3 · Experiments and sweeps (`modelly.experiments`)

**Goal:** one object that describes a study (parameter space, design, replicates, outputs) and runs it anywhere: a laptop, a workstation, a cluster.

**Platforms:** processes, threads, Dask and Ray on all three; process workers start with `spawn` on Windows and macOS, so models and reporters must be importable (new lint rule); SLURM and PBS submit from any OS to a Linux cluster.

**Serves:** research software engineers, anyone with a sweep bigger than one evening.

**User stories**

- As a researcher, I describe a Latin hypercube over five parameters, 20 replicates each, and run it overnight; if the machine reboots, the sweep resumes where it stopped.
- As an RSE, I run the same experiment on SLURM with one line changed, and get the same numbers as on my laptop.
- As a student, I query results with SQL without loading everything into memory.

**API sketch**

```python
from modelly.experiments import Experiment, designs

experiment = Experiment(
    model=Epidemic,
    space=ScenarioSpace(
        beta=(0.05, 0.5), gamma=(0.05, 0.3), vaccination=[0.0, 0.2, 0.4]
    ),
    design=designs.latin_hypercube(200),
    replicates=20,
    steps=365,
    outputs=["infected", "recovered"],
    store="runs/epidemic.parquet",
    seed=7,
)
experiment.run(executor="slurm", partition="short", max_parallel=500)
experiment.results().query("SELECT beta, avg(peak) FROM runs GROUP BY beta")
```

**Designs:** full factorial, Latin hypercube, Sobol and Halton sequences, custom lists. **Executors:** processes (today’s `run_grid`), threads (free-threaded Python, E11), Dask, Ray, SLURM job arrays, PBS. **Store:** Parquet files with a DuckDB view; one row per run and step.

**Done when:** the same experiment gives identical results on processes, threads and a local Dask cluster; a killed sweep resumes without repeating finished runs; SLURM executor tested on a container cluster in CI-local; docs page and RSE guide.

**Tasks**

- [x] `ScenarioSpace` and designs
- [x] Results store (Parquet plus DuckDB), schema, append-only writes
- [x] Resume logic keyed by run seed
- [x] Executors: processes, threads, Dask, Ray, SLURM, PBS
- [x] Progress reporting and failure handling (retry, skip, record)
- [x] Guide: running Modelly on a cluster

**Size:** XL · **Depends on:** E11 (threads), E12 (Parquet)

### E4 · Provenance and reproducible publication

**Goal:** every number in a paper can be traced to code, data, seed and environment, and re-run by a reviewer with one command.

**Platforms:** manifests store POSIX-style relative paths; hashes are taken over bytes; a bundle made on one OS verifies on the other two (tested).

**Serves:** authors, reviewers, journals, replication studies.

**User stories**

- As an author, every run writes a manifest I can cite.
- As a reviewer, I run `modelly verify` on the authors’ bundle and see “outputs match”.
- As a lab, we archive a study on Zenodo with everything needed to rerun it.
- As a modeller, I generate the skeleton of an ODD protocol description from my code.

**API sketch**

```bash
modelly run model.py:Epidemic --scenario scenario.toml --out runs/   # writes runs/manifest.json
modelly verify runs/manifest.json                                    # reruns, compares outputs
modelly bundle runs/ --out epidemic-study.zip                         # code, lock file, seeds, outputs
modelly odd model.py:Epidemic > ODD.md                               # ODD protocol skeleton
```

**Manifest contents:** code hash (git commit and dirty diff hash), Modelly version and build (compiled or pure), Python version, platform, dependency lock, scenario, seeds, input data hashes, output hashes, wall and CPU time.

**Done when:** a bundle made on Linux verifies on macOS and Windows; `modelly verify` reports the first differing output when one is changed; ODD skeleton covers the seven ODD elements; guide for journals and reviewers.

**Tasks**

- [x] Manifest schema (versioned JSON) and writer
- [x] `modelly run` command
- [x] `modelly verify` with tolerance options for floating-point outputs
- [x] `modelly bundle` (zip with lock file, Zenodo metadata, CITATION.cff)
- [x] `modelly odd` generator from classes, scenario and schedule
- [x] Guide: publishing a reproducible Modelly study

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** checkpoints (1.2), E12 (Parquet outputs)

### E5 · Modelly Studio (`modelly studio`)

**Goal:** one browser app to run a model, change parameters live, scrub through time, and see the profiler, the linter and the plots side by side.

**Platforms:** runs in the default browser on all three; tested in Chromium, Firefox, Safari and Edge; no OS-specific dependency.

**Serves:** everyone; the most visible feature of the release; teaching and demos.

**User stories**

- As a modeller, I open `modelly studio model.py:Epidemic`, move a slider and watch the curve change.
- As a teacher, I project Studio and scrub back to the step where the outbreak took off.
- As a performance-minded user, I see which agent method takes the time while the model runs.
- As a collaborator, I export the exact run I am looking at as a bundle (E4).

**Views:** space (grid, network, continuous, geographic), time series, histograms, agent table, parameter panel, timeline scrubber (E6), profiler panel, lint panel, run log.

**Done when:** every bundled example opens in Studio without code changes; scrubbing uses checkpoints and is instant on the examples; profiler and lint panels show live data; works offline; documented with screenshots.

**Tasks**

- [x] Architecture decision: a Solara app reusing `modelly.viz` (see the decision below)
- [x] Layout and parameter panel generated from `Scenario`
- [x] Space views reusing the existing backends
- [x] Timeline scrubber on checkpoints
- [x] Profiler and lint panels
- [ ] Export: figure, data, bundle *(partly: figure, data, checkpoint and GIF export; bundle export moved to 1.4.0)*
- [ ] Docs and a short video *(partly: the guide with screenshots; the video moved to 1.4.0)*

**Size:** XL · **Depends on:** E6, E14, profiler and lint (1.1, 1.2)

**Decision:** Studio is a Solara app, not a separate front end. It reuses the portrayal styles, `SpaceRenderer` and the Matplotlib backend of `modelly.viz` instead of rewriting them in JavaScript, needs no front-end build on any OS, and keeps the model in the same Python process as the profiler, the linter and the recorder. The guide is [Modelly Studio](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/studio.html).

### E6 · Time travel and run diff

**Goal:** debugging a stochastic model without rerunning from step zero.

**Platforms:** the on-disk checkpoint ring writes through `os.replace`, atomic on all three and safe from Windows sharing violations.

**User stories**

- As a modeller, I rewind to step 312, change one parameter, and replay from there.
- As a maintainer, I diff two runs and see the first step and the first agent where they diverge.
- As a researcher, I branch a run into several futures from the same state.

**API sketch**

```python
from modelly.timetravel import Recorder, diff

with Recorder(model, every=10) as rec:  # checkpoints in memory or on disk
    model.run_for(1000)
past = rec.at(312)  # a model at step 312
past.scenario.vaccination = 0.3
past.run_for(100)
report = diff(run_a, run_b)  # first divergence: step, agent, attribute
```

**Done when:** rewind and replay are bit-identical with straight runs; diff finds a seeded divergence on every example; memory use bounded by a configurable budget.

**Tasks**

- [x] In-memory and on-disk checkpoint ring with a memory budget
- [x] Replay with modified scenario
- [x] Branching runs
- [x] Run diff on collected data, then on agent state
- [x] Integration in Studio (E5)

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** checkpoints (1.2)

### E7 · Language-model agents (`modelly.llm`)

**Goal:** agents whose decisions come from a language model, with runs that stay reproducible and costs that stay under control.

**Platforms:** pure Python HTTP and a SQLite cache (standard library) on all three; local models through any HTTP endpoint.

**Serves:** computational social science, behavioural economics, anyone exploring generative agent models.

**User stories**

- As a social scientist, I give each agent a persona and let it decide in natural language, then rerun the study and get the same decisions.
- As a PI, I set a cost budget and the run stops before it exceeds it.
- As a reviewer, the cached responses travel with the bundle (E4), so I can verify the study without calling any API.

**Design**

- Provider-agnostic client with adapters for Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible endpoints and local models; no provider is required to install Modelly.
- **Deterministic response cache** keyed on (model, prompt, parameters, agent seed); a cached run never calls the network; the cache is part of checkpoints and bundles.
- Batching and concurrency limits; token and cost budgets per run; structured outputs validated against a schema.
- Lint rule: an LLM call outside the `modelly.llm` client (unreproducible) is flagged.

**Done when:** a 200-agent opinion model runs, caches and replays offline bit-identically; budget stops a run cleanly; bundle verifies with no network; docs with an ethics and limitations section.

**Tasks**

- [x] Client interface and adapters
- [x] Cache store (SQLite) and cache keys
- [x] Budgets, batching, retries
- [x] Structured decisions with schema validation
- [x] Lint rule MDL012 (network call outside the client)
- [x] Example: opinion dynamics with persona agents
- [x] Docs: reproducibility, cost, ethics

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** E4

### E8 · Geospatial space (`modelly.space.geo`)

**Goal:** start a model from real maps, census tables and road networks.

**Platforms:** GeoPandas, Shapely, pyproj and rasterio wheels on all three; no system GDAL; data scripts are Python, not bash.

**Serves:** urban studies, transport, ecology, epidemiology, archaeology, energy.

**Features:** vector space backed by GeoPandas (agents as points, polygons as cells); raster layers as property layers (optional `rasterio`); coordinate reference systems handled once, at the space; neighbourhoods by distance, contiguity or network; road networks from OpenStreetMap through an optional `osmnx` extra; export to GeoParquet and GeoJSON; Studio map view (E5).

**Done when:** a commuting model runs on a real city’s road network; a land-use model runs on a raster; both appear in the zoo with data download scripts and licences documented.

**Tasks**

- [x] `GeoSpace` (vector) and `RasterLayer`
- [x] CRS handling and spatial indices
- [x] Road networks and routing
- [x] Census-style initialisation helpers (synthetic populations from marginals)
- [ ] Examples, data scripts, docs *(partly: a synthetic-city example and the guide; real-data download scripts moved to 1.4.0)*

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** E12 (GeoParquet), E14 (map view)

### E9 · Networks: dynamic and multilayer

**Goal:** social and contact structures as they really are: changing over time and on several layers at once (household, school, work).

**Platforms:** pure Python, numpy and scipy.

**Features:** temporal networks (edges with lifetimes); multilayer networks with per-layer weights; import from NetworkX, igraph and edge-list CSV; network collectors (degree distribution, clustering, component sizes) as cheap reporters; contact matrices for epidemiology.

**Done when:** an age-structured epidemic runs on a three-layer contact network; collectors match NetworkX on test graphs; adjacency updates are O(changed edges).

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** `CellIndex` adjacency (1.0)

**Platforms:** pure models; data download scripts in Python with checksums, so they run on Windows without curl.

### E11 · Performance and scale

**Goal:** the same model at ten times the population on the same machine, with results identical to today’s for a given seed; and real parallelism where the model allows it.

**Platforms:** free-threaded wheels for all three; Windows ARM64 wheels; GPU through CUDA on Linux and Windows and JAX on Metal or CPU on macOS; PGO measured per compiler.

**Work items**

- **Free-threaded Python (3.14t, 3.15t):** make `fastrng`, `fastloop` and `fastcell` thread-safe; ship free-threaded wheels; run independent replicates on threads (E3).
- **Compiled `AgentSet.select` and `agg`:** the next hot paths after cell moves, with Python twins and side-by-side tests, following `fastloop.c`.
- **GPU arrays for column phases:** an array-API backend (CuPy, or JAX) for `do_where`, `draw` and `CohortTable` thinning, chosen by one setting; documented differences from numpy, if any.
- **Memory:** agent memory footprint (slots for framework attributes, compact registries); target: half the bytes per agent of 1.2 on the playbooks.
- **Profile-guided wheels:** PGO trained on the playbooks, kept only if measured faster.
- **`modelly bench`:** run the playbooks locally and append to a history file; regression report before every pre-release, without paid CI runners.
- **Windows ARM64 wheels** on a native ARM runner.

**Done when:** free-threaded wheels pass the full suite; compiled `select` and `agg` are faster than their twins on the micro-benchmarks and never slower on the playbooks; `modelly bench` history shows no playbook regression from 1.2.0.

**Size:** XL · **Depends on:** nothing; feeds E3

### E12 · Data and interoperability

**Goal:** Modelly data goes where researchers already work, and models come from where they already are.

**Platforms:** DuckDB and pyarrow wheels on all three; the NetLogo translator is pure Python.

**Work items**

- Parquet and Arrow output from `DataCollector` (default for experiments), DuckDB queries, xarray for gridded time series.
- **NetLogo translator** (`modelly migrate --from netlogo`): a skeleton Modelly model from an `.nlogo` file for the common primitives, with a report of what needs a human.
- **Mesa 3 adapter**: run a Mesa 3 model’s agents inside Modelly for a comparison, in addition to the existing codemod.
- R and Julia guides: reading Modelly outputs, calling Modelly from R through reticulate.

**Done when:** every example writes Parquet; the NetLogo translator handles the NetLogo models library’s wolf-sheep and fire models to a running skeleton; guides published.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** nothing

### E13 · Developer tools

**Goal:** writing a correct, fast model is the easy path.

**Platforms:** LSP mode in VS Code, PyCharm and Neovim on all three; `python -m modelly.dev gate` replaces the bash-only gate for Windows contributors.

**Work items**

- `modelly new <name> --template grid|network|continuous|cohort|geo|llm`: a seeded scenario, a determinism test, lint config, a Studio page, a README with the ODD skeleton.
- `modelly lint --fix` and `--diff` for rules with a safe fix (MDL001, MDL002, MDL003, MDL009).
- `modelly lint --lsp`: findings in VS Code, PyCharm and Neovim as you type; pre-commit hook.
- New lint rules for 1.3 features: unseeded sampler in an experiment, network call outside `modelly.llm`, mutable default scenario fields, wall-clock in calibration targets.
- Jupyter magics `%modelly profile`, `%modelly lint`; rich display of a `Model`.
- Errors that name the agent, the step and the user’s line, not framework internals.
- Type checking: the public API passes a strict type checker; `py.typed` kept accurate.

**Done when:** a new user goes from `pip install` to a linted, tested, profiled model in five minutes, timed with three volunteers; every fix is idempotent and tested.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** lint and profile (1.1, 1.2)

### E14 · Visualisation and figures

**Goal:** from exploring a run to a figure in a paper without leaving Modelly.

**Platforms:** animations through `imageio-ffmpeg`, which bundles ffmpeg for all three.

**Work items:** publication styles for Matplotlib (journal column widths, colour-blind-safe palettes); animation export (MP4, GIF) of any space view; map view for E8; network layouts for E9; posterior and sensitivity plots for E1 and E2; one portrayal API shared by every backend and Studio.

**Done when:** every zoo model has a figure script producing a print-ready PDF; animations render headless in CI-local.

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** E5 decision

### E15 · Teaching, docs and community

**Goal:** Modelly is the easiest ABM framework to learn, teach and contribute to.

**Platforms:** every tutorial shows bash and PowerShell where commands differ.

**Work items**

- Domain tutorials: one per field in [Who 1.3.0 is for](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/1.3.0.html#who-1-3-0-is-for).
- A course pack: eight sessions, slides, exercises with solutions, built on the zoo.
- A gallery of community models with a submission template.
- Plugin system through entry points: third-party spaces, samplers, executors, collectors and Studio views discovered at import.
- Contributor guide refresh, good-first-issue labels, community call notes.
- Docs translated into French and Spanish for the getting-started path.

**Done when:** the course pack has been taught once (pilot); two third-party plugins exist; every tutorial runs in the docs build.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** E10, E13

### E16 · Quality and release engineering

**Goal:** a bigger release with fewer surprises than the smaller ones.

**Platforms:** the determinism suite runs on all three in CI; the release script is Python, not bash.

**Work items**

- Property-based tests (Hypothesis) for spaces, columns, cohorts and checkpoints.
- Determinism suite: every example, compiled and pure-Python, saved and loaded, on three platforms, gives identical outputs.
- Deprecation policy and warnings for anything 2.0 will change.
- API stability review of every new public name before 1.3.0b1.
- Pelloux audit at 0 warnings, coverage at or above 95%.
- Release checklist automated as `scripts/release.sh` (version, changelog, tag, docs, PyPI).

**Size:** M (continuous) · **Depends on:** everything

## Sprint plan

Eight sprints, in dependency order: a sprint is a unit of work, not a period of time, and the next one starts as soon as the previous one’s exit criteria hold. Each sprint ends with `bash scripts/ci-local.sh` green, the `build` matrix green on Windows, macOS and Linux, the docs building with `-W`, `modelly bench` showing no playbook regression, and a review note appended to this file.

### S1 · Foundations

**Goal:** the plumbing every later sprint stands on.

- [x] E12: Parquet and Arrow output from `DataCollector`; DuckDB view
- [x] E4: manifest schema and writer; `modelly run`
- [x] E3: `ScenarioSpace` and designs (factorial, Latin hypercube, Sobol sequence)
- [x] E11: free-threaded audit of the three C modules; plan for locks or per-thread state
- [x] E16: Hypothesis tests for columns and cohorts; deprecation policy written
- [x] Platforms: `python -m modelly.dev gate`; unspecified-encoding rule on; `spawn`-safe lint rule
- [ ] E1, E2, E5, E7: design reviews (one page each, decisions recorded here) *(partly: only the Studio decision is recorded)*

**Exit:** every example writes Parquet; `modelly run` writes a manifest; design reviews signed off.

### S2 · Experiments

**Goal:** a sweep that runs anywhere and survives a reboot.

- [x] E3: results store, resume logic, executors (processes, threads, Dask)
- [x] E11: thread-safe C modules; free-threaded wheels built locally
- [x] E4: `modelly verify`
- [x] E11: compiled `AgentSet.select` with its twin
- [x] E10: zoo scaffolding; SEIR with contact matrices; Nagel-Schreckenberg

**Exit:** the same experiment gives identical results on processes, threads and Dask; a killed sweep resumes; `verify` detects a changed output.

### S3 · Calibration → **1.3.0a1**

**Goal:** the first headline feature in users’ hands.

- [x] E1: ABC rejection, ABC-SMC, posterior object and plots
- [x] E3: Ray and SLURM executors
- [x] E11: compiled `agg`; `modelly bench` history file
- [x] E13: `modelly new` with grid and network templates
- [x] E10: Bass diffusion; Deffuant and Hegselmann-Krause
- [ ] Release 1.3.0a1 to PyPI (pre-release), docs at `/dev/` *(skipped: 1.3.0 shipped without pre-releases)*

**Exit:** ABC-SMC recovers SIR parameters on three seeds; a1 installs with `pip install --pre`.

### S4 · Sensitivity and time travel

**Goal:** explain the model and debug it.

- [x] E2: OAT, Morris, Sobol with bootstrap; verified on Ishigami
- [x] E6: checkpoint ring, rewind, replay, run diff
- [x] E1: method of moments; resume from checkpoint
- [x] E13: `lint --fix` for MDL001 and MDL003

**Exit:** Sobol matches Ishigami analytical values; replay is bit-identical with a straight run.

### S5 · Reach

**Goal:** real data and new kinds of models.

- [x] E8: `GeoSpace`, `RasterLayer`, CRS handling, road networks

- [x] E7: client interface, cache, budgets
- [x] E4: `modelly bundle`, `modelly odd`
- [x] E10: forest succession on a raster; order-book market

**Exit:** a commuting model runs on a real road network; a cached LLM run replays offline.

### S6 · Studio and LLM agents → **1.3.0b1**

- [x] E5: profiler and lint panels
- [x] E7: structured decisions, MDL012, persona opinion example
- [ ] E14: publication styles; posterior and sensitivity plots in Studio *(partly: publication styles; posterior and sensitivity plots in Studio moved to 1.4.0)*
- [x] E16: API stability review of every new public name
- [ ] Release 1.3.0b1 (feature complete; API frozen) *(skipped: 1.3.0 shipped without pre-releases)*

- [x] E15: domain tutorials; course pack draft; plugin entry points

- [x] E14: animation export (Could)
- [ ] E12: NetLogo translator for wolf-sheep and fire (Could) *(moved to 1.4.0)*

### S8 · Hardening → **1.3.0**

**Goal:** ship with confidence.

- [x] E16: determinism suite on Linux, macOS, Windows; compiled and pure; saved and loaded

**Exit:** all gates in [Release plan and gates](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/1.3.0.html#release-plan-and-gates) pass.

## Release plan and gates

Release

Gate (all must hold)

**1.3.0a1**

Experiments, provenance basics and ABC calibration work; ci-local green; installs with --pre; no playbook regression

**1.3.0b1**

Every Must and Should epic feature complete; public API frozen after review; docs for every new module

**1.3.0rc1**

No open blocker; every tutorial and zoo validation passes; wheels for every platform build and pass the import test

**1.3.0**

Determinism suite green on three platforms; audit 0 warnings; coverage at or above 95%; changelog and migration notes complete

Releases follow the existing path: a commit `chore(release): X.Y.Z` on main, a `vX.Y.Z` tag, wheels and PyPI from the tag, versioned docs from the tag. Pre-releases are tagged `v1.3.0a1`, `v1.3.0b1`, `v1.3.0rc1`. The docs workflow only matches final `vX.Y.Z` tags, so a pre-release publishes no docs folder of its own: its docs are the `/dev/` build of the same commit, and the root stays on 1.2 until 1.3.0.

## Definition of done

A task is done when all of these hold. It is the Pelloux guidelines plus what research software needs.

- [ ] Code follows `pelloux-guidelines.md`: files at most 300 lines, function bodies at most 25 *(partly: one file over 300 lines until 1.4.0 S1)* lines, no magic numbers, conventional commits, no attribution trailers
- [x] `bash scripts/ci-local.sh` passes; `MODELLY_PURE_PYTHON=1` suite passes
- [x] Works on Windows, macOS and Linux: the test runs in the `build` matrix on all three
- [x] A determinism test: same seed, same result; compiled and pure give the same result
- [x] Checkpoint round trip: the feature’s state survives `save` and `load`
- [ ] Public names have docstrings with an example; the docs page exists and builds with `-W` *(partly: docstrings with examples; the docs build does not yet fail on warnings)*
- [x] `modelly lint` is clean on any new example
- [x] Changelog entry under the right heading
- [ ] Performance: no playbook slower than 1.2.0 in `modelly bench` *(partly: 1.3.0 had two regressions, fixed in 1.3.1)*
- [x] For a scientific method: verified against an analytical result or a published one, cited

## Open questions

- [x] Studio: a Solara app (reuses today’s viz) or a separate web front end (more freedom, more work)? Decided: a Solara app (see E5).
- [x] Calibration: build ABC-SMC in house, or wrap an established library behind our API? *Decided: in house (`modelly.calibrate.smc`).*
- [x] Results store: Parquet plus DuckDB only, or also a SQLite option for small studies? *Decided: Parquet and DuckDB only.*
- [x] LLM agents: which providers at launch, and is the cache per model or per project? *Decided: Anthropic, OpenAI-compatible and local adapters; the cache is a file the user picks.*
- [x] Geospatial: GeoPandas as an optional extra only, or part of `rec`? *Decided: a `geo` extra; `rec` is network and viz.*
- [ ] Pre-release docs: `/dev/` only, or a `/1.3-pre/` folder? *(moot: no pre-releases)*
- [ ] Course pack: which university or lab pilots it first? *(still open)*
- [ ] Translations: French and Spanish first, or the languages users ask for? *(still open)*

## Compatibility and the road to 2.0

- 1.3.0 is **backward compatible** with 1.2: every public name keeps working.
- Checkpoints from 1.2 do not load in 1.3 (the format records the minor version). 1.3 adds a `modelly checkpoint upgrade` command for 1.2 files where the state maps cleanly.
- Anything 1.3 wants to change raises a `DeprecationWarning` that names the replacement and the version that removes it (2.0).
- 2.0 is where removals happen, after at least one minor release of warnings.

# 1.4.0: scale out and connect

**Status:** in release: every epic merged except F10 Studio II (in progress), release gate pending · **Base:** 1.3.3

1.3.0 lets a researcher answer a question with a model. 1.4.0 removes the ceilings on how big that model can be and how close to the real world it can run: **distributed populations, GPU and differentiable models, live data and assimilation, multi-scale coupling, and Modelly running in a browser tab.** Eleven epics, eight sprints, three pre-releases, all on Windows, macOS and Linux (see [Platforms](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/platforms.html)). Backward compatible with 1.3.

## Where we start

1.3.0 gives

1.4.0 adds

Experiments with process, thread, Dask, Ray and SLURM executors

One model split across many processes or machines

Calibration (ABC, SMM, Bayesian optimisation)

Gradient-based calibration through differentiable models; history matching

GPU array backend (preview)

GPU backend generally available, with cell spaces on the GPU

Geospatial space and synthetic-population helpers

A full synthetic-population toolkit from census tables

Studio in a local browser

Studio and models running entirely in the browser, shared by a link

Checkpoints and time travel

Live data streams and data assimilation over replicate ensembles

## Carried over from 1.3.0

1.3.0 did 91 of its 113 tasks (its [review log](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/1.3.0.html#sprint-review-log)). What it did not finish moves here, and goes into the sprints below as their main items allow:

## Who 1.4.0 is for

Field

Ecology

Landscapes coupled to PDE fields (diffusion of nutrients, heat); GPU runs for large individual-based models

Economics

Agent-based macro models with millions of households; gradient calibration of behavioural parameters

Urban and transport

City digital twins fed by sensor streams; traffic on full regional road networks

Climate and energy

ABMs coupled to system-dynamics or climate emulators; large adoption sweeps on GPUs

Teaching and outreach

A model in a web page, no installation, on any computer with a browser

## Epics

Sizes: **S** under a sprint, **M** one sprint, **L** two sprints, **XL** three or more.

### F1 · Distributed simulation (`modelly.distributed`)

**Goal:** one model whose population and space are split across processes or machines, with the same results as a single-process run for the same seed.

**Platforms:** MPI through `mpi4py` (Open MPI or MPICH on Linux and macOS, MS-MPI on Windows); a Dask and a Ray backend that need no MPI and run on all three.

**User stories**

- As an epidemiologist, I run a 30-million-agent country model on 64 cores of a cluster with the code I wrote for 100,000 agents on my laptop.
- As an RSE, I check that a distributed run and a single-process run of a small model give the same output, byte for byte.

**Design**

- Spatial partitioning (grid blocks, graph partitioning for networks, k-d partitioning for continuous space) with ghost cells (halo exchange) at partition borders.
- Agents migrate between partitions when they move; migration happens at a phase boundary, in a deterministic order.
- Random numbers: one stream per agent (from the agent’s seed), so results do not depend on how the space is partitioned.
- Collectors reduce across partitions; checkpoints write one file per partition plus an index.

**API sketch**

```python
from modelly.distributed import Cluster, partition

with Cluster(backend="mpi", workers=64) as cluster:
    model = cluster.build(Epidemic, scenario, partition=partition.grid_blocks(8, 8))
    model.run_for(365)
    cluster.collect().to_parquet("runs/country.parquet")
```

**Done when:** partition-independent results on the zoo’s grid and network models (2, 4 and 16 partitions, identical outputs); weak scaling efficiency of at least 70% from 1 to 64 workers on the grid epidemic playbook; runs on MPI and Dask on all three platforms.

**Done:** partly. Byte-identical reporters and agent states at 1, 2, 4 and 16 partitions on grid, network and continuous reference models (the zoo has no agent-level grid or network model), on the local backend, under `mpirun -n 2` and `-n 4`, and on Dask with 2 workers. Weak scaling on one 16-core laptop is 62% at 2 workers, 20% at 8 and 9% at 16 (independent copies of the same work already fall to 24-32% there), so the 70% target at 64 workers could not be measured. Ray is untested, and macOS and Windows were not run: hosted CI now runs only the Release and docs workflows.

**Tasks**

- [x] Per-agent random streams (opt-in in 1.4, default in 2.0)
- [x] Partitioners: grid blocks, graph (METIS-style, pure Python fallback), k-d *(grid blocks in S1; graph: BFS banding plus greedy boundary refinement, not METIS; k-d: recursive bisection)*
- [x] Halo exchange and agent migration protocol
- [x] MPI, Dask and Ray backends *(Ray written, imports lazily, untested: Ray does not install on Python 3.15)*
- [x] Distributed collectors and checkpoints
- [x] Partition-independence test suite; scaling benchmark *(1, 2, 4, 16 partitions on grid, network and continuous models; MPI on 2 and 4 ranks; weak scaling measured to 16 workers on one laptop, 64 not measurable here)*
- [x] Guide: from laptop to cluster

**Size:** XL · **Depends on:** 1.3 E3, E11

### F2 · GPU backend, generally available

**Goal:** column phases, cohorts and cell spaces run on a GPU with one setting, with results equal to numpy within documented tolerances.

**Platforms:** CUDA through CuPy on Linux and Windows; JAX on Linux, Windows (CPU or CUDA) and macOS (Metal where available, CPU otherwise). Every GPU path has a CPU fallback.

**Work items:** array-API backend for every column operation; `CellIndex` adjacency, counts and random-neighbour draws on the GPU; `CohortTable` binomial thinning on the GPU; counter-based random streams (Philox) so GPU and CPU draw the same numbers; memory planner for populations larger than GPU memory (batches); benchmark playbooks with a `modelly-gpu` variant.

**Done when:** grid epidemic and insect cohorts playbooks run on CUDA and Metal; results equal the CPU run for integer state and within a stated tolerance for floats; at least 10x faster than the CPU column variant at 10 million agents on a mid-range GPU (measured and published, not assumed).

**Done:** partly. The grid epidemic at 10 million agents on CuPy keeps the numpy run’s integer state bit for bit and runs its 60 steps 34x faster than the CPU column variant on a laptop RTX 5050 (the build is not faster, so 1.5x to 1.7x including it); at the playbook’s own 20,000 agents the GPU is slower. The insect cohorts run on CuPy with the numpy run’s integers but 200x slower: under 200 rows, so launch overhead dominates. Metal is untested (no Apple GPU). Backends numpy, CuPy and JAX, Philox streams identical on all three, batches for populations larger than the GPU, `modelly-gpu` playbook variants.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** 1.3 E11 preview

### F3 · Differentiable models (`modelly.diff`)

**Goal:** gradients of model outputs with respect to parameters, for gradient-based calibration and sensitivity, where the model allows it.

**Platforms:** JAX on all three (CPU everywhere, GPU per F2).

**Design:** column phases traced with JAX; discrete random choices handled with documented estimators (straight-through, Gumbel-softmax, score function) and an explicit warning that the gradient is an approximation; a `differentiable` flag per phase; gradient checks against finite differences.

**User stories:** as an economist, I fit 40 behavioural parameters with gradient descent in minutes instead of an ABC run of days; as a modeller, I get local sensitivities (gradients) at the calibrated point for free.

**Done when:** gradient-based calibration recovers known parameters on two zoo models; gradients agree with finite differences within tolerance; docs explain when gradients are meaningful and when they are not.

**Done:** yes. Gradient calibration recovers 0.0305 and 0.379 for the Bass model’s 0.03 and 0.38 (straight-through) and 1.448 and 0.937 for Bouchaud-Mezard’s 1.5 and 1.0 (pathwise; the gap is the noise of the observed Gini series, 1.54 and 1.09 with four replicates); the finite-difference checks pass with a relative error below 1e-4; `docs/differentiable.md` says when a gradient means something. JAX is the optional `diff` extra.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** F2, 1.3 E1

### F4 · Modelly in the browser (Pyodide and WebAssembly)

**Goal:** run a Modelly model and Studio entirely in a browser tab, with no installation, and share it as a link or a static page.

**Platforms:** any OS with a current browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari); Pyodide build of the pure wheel in 1.3 (smoke test), compiled modules built for WebAssembly in 1.4.

**Work items:** Emscripten builds of `fastrng`, `fastloop`, `fastcell`; a `modelly export-web` command that writes a static site (model code, scenario, Studio) deployable on GitHub Pages; optional dependencies trimmed for the browser; worker threads for long runs; size budget for the first load.

**Done when:** every 1.3 example runs in the browser from a static export; the export of a zoo model loads in under 10 seconds on a typical connection (measured); the docs gallery embeds live models.

**Done:** partly. All 14 examples and the 12 zoo models of its base run from a static `modelly export-web` site in headless Chromium, with the pure wheel and the Emscripten-compiled one; the five zoo models merged after it are run by the browser stage of the release checks. A scipy-free zoo model is ready in 8.0 s on a 50 Mbit/s line, but one that needs scipy takes 12.3 s and “Fast 4G” takes 21.4 s: Pyodide, numpy and pandas alone are 13.5 MB. The gallery embeds three live models.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** 1.3 E5 Studio

### F5 · Live data and data assimilation (`modelly.stream`)

**Goal:** feed real-world observations into running models and keep an ensemble of runs close to reality: the core of a digital twin.

**Platforms:** pure Python on all three; MQTT and Kafka connectors as optional extras with wheels for all three.

**Design:** stream sources (files, HTTP polling, MQTT, Kafka); observation operators mapping model state to observed quantities; ensembles of replicates advanced in lock step; assimilation by particle filter (resampling replicates through checkpoints) and ensemble Kalman filter for continuous parameters; a live dashboard in Studio.

**User stories:** as a public-health modeller, I update tomorrow’s forecast every morning from yesterday’s cases; as a transport researcher, I keep a traffic model in step with loop-detector counts.

**Done when:** a nowcasting tutorial with a synthetic “truth” run shows the filter tracking it; particle resampling is reproducible for a seed; Studio shows the ensemble band live.

**Done:** partly. The nowcasting tutorial’s filter tracks a synthetic truth with an error of 5.07 people against 69.2 for the unfiltered ensemble, the ensemble Kalman filter recovers beta 0.451 for 0.45, and a run is bit-identical for a seed with the compiled and the pure-Python core. The live band in Studio is F10’s. MQTT and Kafka sources are tested against fakes only.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** 1.3 E6 (checkpoint ring), E3

### F6 · Multi-scale coupling (`modelly.couple`)

**Goal:** couple agents to continuous processes: system-dynamics stocks and flows, ODEs, and PDE fields over space.

**Platforms:** numpy and scipy on all three.

**Design:** a `Field` type (a property layer with a solver: diffusion, advection, decay) stepped on its own time step; ODE and stock-flow components through scipy’s integrators; a coupling schedule (who reads what, when) checked for consistency at build time.

**Done when:** an ecology model with a diffusing nutrient field and a disease model coupled to a hospital-capacity ODE are in the zoo, with conservation checks (mass balance) as tests.

**Done:** yes. `nutrient_foragers` and `hospital_epidemic` are in the zoo; fields conserve mass to round-off, a Gaussian matches the heat kernel, the hospital stock-flow ODE is within 1e-6 of its matrix-exponential solution, and checkpointed runs resume bit for bit. Fields are limited to orthogonal grids with uniform spacing; advection is first-order upwind.

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** 1.3 E8 (rasters)

### F7 · Emulators, active learning and history matching

**Goal:** answer questions about expensive models with far fewer runs.

**Design:** Gaussian-process and neural emulators trained on experiment results (1.3 E3); active-learning designs that choose the next runs where the emulator is least certain; history matching (implausibility measures, waves of non-implausible space), widely used in epidemiology and climate science.

**Done when:** history matching reproduces a published wave sequence on a zoo model; active learning reaches the same emulator accuracy as a Latin hypercube with at most half the runs on two benchmarks.

**Done:** partly. History matching on the age SEIR keeps 17.1%, 4.4%, 3.1% and 2.5% of the box over four waves, with the truth inside each. Active learning against a Latin hypercube saves a factor of 1.3 to 2.7 on the Bass model (2 at most run counts) but only 1.1 to 1.4 on Branin and 0.8 to 1.4 on Ishigami, where a well-spread design is already close to best; the tests assert the measured factors.

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** 1.3 E1, E2, E3

### F8 · Synthetic populations (`modelly.population`)

**Goal:** realistic starting populations from aggregate data, with households and places.

**Design:** iterative proportional fitting and combinatorial optimisation from census marginals; households, schools and workplaces assigned with distance constraints; contact networks generated from places; privacy notes and no bundled personal data.

**Done when:** a synthetic population for a sample region reproduces its marginals within tolerance; the age-structured SEIR zoo model starts from it.

**Done:** yes. About 20,000 people across 41 Burlington census tracts from made-up marginals: totals and age counts exact in every tract, sex counts off by fewer than 3, no school or workplace over capacity or beyond its distance limit; the age SEIR starts from it (`scenario_from_population`) and follows its final-size relation within 0.05.

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** 1.3 E8, E9

### F9 · Performance II

**Work items:** compiled event scheduler (heap in C, same ordering); compiled `DataCollector` gather for column-backed agents; memory-mapped columns for populations larger than RAM; per-compiler PGO (GCC, Clang, MSVC) shipped where it measures faster; `modelly bench` comparison against 1.3 on all three OSs.

**Done when:** no playbook slower than 1.3 on any OS; event-heavy models (wolf-sheep) measurably faster; a 100-million-row column run on a 16 GB machine.

**Done:** partly. No playbook slower than 1.3.3 on Linux x86-64 (medians 0.986 to 1.004, results identical); the wolf-sheep example runs at 0.95, 600 regrowth events per step at 0.70 and the column gather at 0.47. The predator-prey playbook is not faster (0.998 to 1.003): it schedules no events and regrows grass as a column. A 100-million-row cohort table peaks at 3.6 GB under a 16 GB limit (3.2 GB memory-mapped under a 3 GB limit). PGO measured 0.993 to 1.003 against -O3 and is not shipped. Windows, macOS and the free-threaded build were not measured.

**Size:** L

### F10 · Studio II

**Work items:** ensemble views (bands across replicates); experiment browser over the results store; calibration and assimilation dashboards; map and network views at scale (WebGL); recording a session as a reproducible script.

**Status:** in progress. The ensemble, assimilation, experiment, analysis and map tabs and the browser checks in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit are on its branch, not yet merged.

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** F4, F5

### F11 · Quality and platforms

**Work items:** partition-independence and GPU-equality suites in the determinism suite; WebAssembly in the release matrix; distributed tests on a three-OS MPI matrix (MS-MPI on Windows); deprecations for 2.0 announced in this release’s notes.

**Done:** partly. Partition independence is in the determinism suite and the 2.0 changes are announced (`docs/deprecations.md`, warnings on the moved geo names). The Pyodide smoke test, the three-OS MPI matrix and the cross-OS bundle check exist as manual-only workflows and were not run: hosted CI runs only the Release and docs workflows, and `scripts/release-checks.sh` runs their Linux parts locally. GPU equality is checked in `tests/gpu` (numpy against CuPy and JAX), not in the determinism suite.

**Size:** M (continuous)

## Open questions

- [x] Default distributed backend: MPI (fastest on clusters) or Dask (easiest everywhere)? *Neither is a default: `Cluster(backend=...)` names `local`, `mpi`, `dask` or `ray`, and only `local` needs nothing installed. MPI needs the `distributed` extra and a launcher; the guide says when to pick each.*
- [x] Per-agent random streams: opt-in in 1.4 and default in 2.0, or default already in 1.4? *Opt-in in 1.4 (S1), so 1.x models keep their numbers.*
- [x] JAX as an optional extra only, or part of `rec` for GPU users? *Optional extras only: `diff` (JAX) and `gpu` (CuPy); `rec` stays network and viz, and `import modelly` loads neither.*
- [x] Which public data sets to use for the synthetic-population tutorial (licences)? *Made-up marginals on real Burlington census tracts (public domain), OpenStreetMap streets (ODbL) and ESA WorldCover (CC BY 4.0), as small bundled samples with `NOTICE.md`; nothing personal.*

# 1.5.0: ecosystem and collaboration

**Status:** released (sprints S1 to S8) · **Base:** 1.4.0

By 1.5.0 a single researcher can build, calibrate, scale and publish a model. 1.5.0 is about **everyone else**: the colleague who wants to reuse it, the policy team that has to decide with it, the R or Julia user who never writes Python, the student, the reviewer. **A model hub, model cards, decision and causal tools, richer language-model agents, R and Julia bindings, accessibility, a stable plugin API and differential equations inside agents.** Twelve epics, eight sprints, all on Windows, macOS and Linux (see [Platforms](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/platforms.html)). Backward compatible with 1.4; it is also the last release before 2.0, so every deprecation 2.0 needs is announced here.

## Where we start

1.4.0 gives

1.5.0 adds

Run bundles, manifests, modelly verify

A hub where bundles and models are published, found, installed and cited

ODD skeletons and zoo validations

Model cards: purpose, validation, limits, generated and kept up to date

Calibration, sensitivity, emulators

Decision tools: scenario comparison, robust decision making, intervention optimisation

Seeded replicates

Causal analysis with common random numbers; explanations of outcomes

ODE and StockFlow: one system per model, integrated by solve_ivp

An ODE in every agent solved as one vectorised system; events, noise, delays and gradients

LLM agents with caching and budgets

Memory, planning, tools, conversation, and an evaluation harness

A Python API

R and Julia packages; Studio for non-programmers

## Who 1.5.0 is for

Audience

What 1.5.0 unlocks

Research groups

Publish a model to the hub with a DOI; colleagues install it with one command

Policy analysts and public agencies

Compare interventions with confidence intervals and costs, without writing code, in Studio

R users (epidemiology, ecology, social science)

library(modelly): run, calibrate and analyse Modelly models from R

Julia users

Call Modelly from Julia and pass arrays without copies

Reviewers and journals

Model cards and verifiable bundles attached to papers

Educators

A visual builder that writes real Modelly code; a course pack v2

People using assistive technology

Studio conformant with WCAG 2.2 AA

## Epics

### G1 · Modelly Hub

**Goal:** publish, discover, install and cite models and studies.

**Platforms:** the hub is a static index on GitHub Pages plus Zenodo for archives: no server to run or pay for; the client is pure Python on all three.

**User stories**

- As an author, `modelly hub publish` turns my project into an installable package with a model card and a DOI.
- As a researcher, `modelly hub search "malaria"` lists published models with their validation status, and `modelly hub install` gets one with its exact environment.
- As a reviewer, a paper’s DOI resolves to a bundle I can `modelly verify`.

**Design:** packages are ordinary Python packages with an entry point and a model card; the index is a JSON file in a public repository, updated by pull request (reviewed, with automatic checks: lint clean, determinism test, card complete); archives on Zenodo; signatures with Sigstore.

**Done when:** ten zoo models and three community models are on the hub; install and verify work on all three platforms; publishing a model takes under ten minutes, timed.

**Progress (S2):** `modelly.hub` and `modelly hub search|info|install|publish|check|zoo-index`; the index format (schema 1) with cards, supported versions, sha256, DOI and signature; the public index in RemiPelloux/modelly-hub on GitHub Pages, its pull requests checked by `modelly hub check`; the eighteen zoo models listed. Zenodo archiving and Sigstore signing are built and tested as dry runs; a first real publication waits for a Zenodo token. Install checked on Linux; Windows and macOS remain for the three-OS run.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** 1.3 E4, E10

### G2 · Model cards

**Goal:** every model carries a short, standard, honest description of what it is for, how it was validated, and where it should not be used.

**Design:** generated from the ODD skeleton, the scenario, the zoo or user validation tests and the calibration report; sections for intended use, out-of-scope use, data, validation, known limits, ethical considerations; rendered in docs, Studio and the hub; a lint check that the card exists and is not stale (validation re-run since the last model change).

**Progress (S1):** `modelly.card` and `modelly card new|check|show|stamp`; every zoo model has a stamped card, rendered on its page and checked by the tests; a pre-commit hook. Rendering in Studio and the hub comes with G1 and G7.

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** 1.3 E4

### G3 · Decision and policy toolkit (`modelly.decide`)

**Goal:** turn model runs into decisions people can defend.

**Work items:** scenario comparison with paired replicates and intervals; cost and cost-effectiveness outputs (per-scenario costs, incremental ratios); robust decision making (many futures, find policies that do well across them); intervention optimisation through an optional Optuna extra, with the optimiser’s randomness seeded from the experiment; Studio “compare scenarios” view for non-programmers.

**Done when:** a vaccination-strategy tutorial produces a ranked comparison with intervals and costs; the same study rerun gives the same ranking.

**Progress (S3):** `modelly.decide`: `compare` on common random numbers (paired intervals, rankings with best shares), `cost_effectiveness` and `net_benefit`, `robust` with `sample_futures` (minimax regret, satisficing), `optimise` (seeded Optuna, the `decide` extra). The vaccination study ranks four strategies with intervals and costs, and the same study rerun gives the same ranking (tested). The Studio “compare scenarios” view moves to S6 with the no-code mode.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** 1.3 E3, 1.4 F7

### G4 · Causal analysis and explanations (`modelly.explain`)

**Goal:** say why an outcome happened, not only that it did.

**Work items:** common random numbers so paired scenarios differ only by the intervention (variance reduction, reported); average treatment effects with intervals across replicates; agent- and event-level attribution (which agents or events, removed, change the outcome); SHAP-style explanations on emulators; counterfactual replay through time travel.

**Done when:** a tutorial shows the variance reduction of common random numbers on a zoo model (measured); attribution finds the seeded “patient zero” in a synthetic outbreak.

**Progress (S4):** `modelly.explain`: `treatment_effect` (common random numbers, variance reduction measured: 49.8 times on the Bass zoo model, none on age_seir vaccination, 1.9 times on the hospital epidemic’s peak), `attribute` (finds the index case of a network outbreak, three seeds), `counterfactual` through time travel, exact `shapley` on emulators.

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** 1.3 E6, 1.4 F7

### G5 · Language-model agents II

**Goal:** richer generative agents that stay reproducible and affordable.

**Work items:** memory (episodic and summarised, stored in checkpoints); planning and reflection loops; tool use (agents calling model functions); agent-to-agent conversation with turn scheduling; an evaluation harness (behavioural benchmarks, consistency across seeds, cost reports); every response still cached and part of the bundle.

**Done when:** a 500-agent conversational market runs, caches and replays offline; the evaluation harness reports cost, consistency and behaviour metrics for three providers or local models.

**Progress (S5):** `MemoryAgent`, `plan`, `reflect`, `use_tools`, `converse_many`, `evaluate`, and the 500-trader conversational market, which runs, caches and replays offline (tested). The harness compares three stand-in providers in the tests; a comparison of three real providers needs their keys.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** 1.3 E7

### G6 · R and Julia bindings

**Goal:** Modelly for people who do not write Python.

**Platforms:** the R package through reticulate and the Julia package through PythonCall, both tested on Windows, macOS and Linux, with an installer that sets up the Python side automatically.

**Work items:** R: build and run models from R, scenario objects as lists, results as data frames or tibbles, calibration and sensitivity results with ggplot2 methods; CRAN-ready package. Julia: zero-copy array access to columns, results as DataFrames.jl.

**Done when:** the SIR calibration tutorial runs end to end in R and in Julia on all three OSs.

**Progress (S4):** the R package (`r/modelly`) on `modelly.bindings`: run, parameters, the model object, ABC-SMC calibration with priors, print and plot. The SIR tutorial runs end to end in R 4.5 on Linux with the Python posterior to the last digit; `R CMD check` clean. CRAN or r-universe, Windows and macOS remain. S5: `Modelly.jl` on the same bindings, with zero-copy columns; the SIR tutorial gives the same posterior in Julia 1.13 on Linux. S7: the release workflow runs `R CMD check` of the R package and the Julia package’s tests on Linux, macOS and Windows, and PyPI waits for them; all three pass (build-only run of the release workflow).

**Size:** L

### G7 · Studio for everyone

**Work items:** a no-code mode (open a published model, change parameters, run experiments, compare scenarios, export a report); a visual model builder for teaching that writes ordinary Modelly code; report export (HTML and PDF) with the model card, figures and the run manifest.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** 1.4 F10

**Progress (S6):** `--no-code` with the Compare (moved here from G3), Card and Builder tabs, HTML and PDF reports with the card, figures and the run manifest, `--hub NAME`. The builder is a preview: one agent class on a grid, four behaviours.

### G8 · Accessibility and languages

**Work items:** WCAG 2.2 AA audit and fixes for Studio and the docs (keyboard navigation, screen readers, contrast, colour-blind-safe palettes by default); translations of Studio and the getting-started docs (French, Spanish, Portuguese, Chinese, then by demand); right-to-left layout support.

**Size:** M

**Progress (S7):** axe-core finds no WCAG 2.0-2.2 A or AA violation on the audited docs pages and on Studio (English, no-code French, Arabic right to left), checked by the `a11y` release stage; Studio in French, Spanish, Portuguese and Chinese, right to left supported; the getting-started page in the four languages. The translations are drafts awaiting review by native speakers; keyboard and screen-reader passes by hand remain before the release.

### G9 · Plugin API v1

**Goal:** a stable, documented way to extend Modelly from separate packages.

**Design:** entry-point groups for spaces, executors, samplers, collectors, Studio views, lint rules and hub sources; a compatibility declaration per plugin; a plugin template (`modelly new --template plugin`); the API is frozen for the 1.x line and carried into 2.0 unchanged or with a migration path.

**Done when:** three third-party plugins (one space, one executor, one Studio view) are listed on the hub and tested against 1.5 on all three platforms.

**Progress (S1):** plugin API v1 marked stable and frozen; compatibility read from the plugin’s `modelly-abm` requirement; `modelly plugins --check`; `modelly new --template plugin`. S2 added the `modelly.hub_sources` group with the hub: an entry point names an index URL or path, or a function returning them.

**Size:** M

### G10 · Education II

**Work items:** course pack v2 (twelve sessions, assessments, instructor notes); classroom mode in Studio (shared parameters, collect students’ runs); a “from NetLogo” track for instructors moving their courses.

**Progress (S7):** course pack v2 (twelve sessions, instructor notes, a project rubric and two graded exercises), classroom mode in Studio (`--classroom DIR`), the “from NetLogo” track.

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** G7

### G11 · Quality, 2.0 preparation and platforms

**Work items:** every 2.0 change deprecated with a warning naming the replacement; `modelly migrate --check-2.0` reports what a project must change; the bindings, hub client and Studio in the three-OS test matrix; installer guide for locked-down Windows machines (no admin rights).

**Progress (S1):** the 2.0 inventory, `modelly/_inventory.py`: eleven deprecations that warn now and ten 2.0 changes, three of them waiting to warn until their replacement ships (H2 one space protocol, H4 one clock, H5 typed scenarios); a test keeps it in agreement with the code and `docs/deprecations.md`.

**Progress (S8):** every 2.0 change warns or changes no call: typed scenarios (H5) warn from 1.5; the event ordering (H4) is already 2.0’s and is documented and tested; the space classes (H2) stay as aliases through 2.x. `modelly migrate --check-2.0`; the bindings, the hub client and Studio in the three-OS release workflow; the guide for locked-down Windows machines.

**Size:** M (continuous)

### G12 · Differential equations II (`modelly.couple`)

**Goal:** continuous dynamics anywhere in a model, at agent scale, as easily as `solve_ivp`.

**Where we start:** `ODE` and `StockFlow` integrate one system per model with `solve_ivp`; the inputs are held over the agents’ step, and the integrator stops only at step boundaries.

**User stories**

- As an epidemiologist, each host carries its own viral-load ODE, and a host becomes infectious at the moment its load crosses a threshold, not at the next step.
- As an ecologist, each animal’s energy budget is an ODE driven by the field it stands on, and ten thousand animals cost one integration, not ten thousand.
- As an economist, firms’ capital follows a stochastic differential equation whose noise comes from the model’s seed, so a rerun is the same run.

**Work items**

- **Per-agent ODEs:** `AgentODE(columns=[...], rhs)` keeps each agent’s state in columns and integrates the whole population as one system: `rhs` works on arrays of shape `(variables, agents)`, `solve_ivp` sees them flattened, births and deaths resize between steps. A sparse block-diagonal Jacobian makes the stiff methods (`"BDF"`, `"Radau"`) usable at scale.
- **Events:** `ODEEvent(condition, action, terminal=True, direction=1)` wraps `solve_ivp`’s event functions: the step stops at the crossing, the action runs on the agents that crossed, the crossing times are recorded, and the integration resumes to the end of the step.
- **Time-varying inputs and dense output:** inputs given as functions of time or interpolated between steps instead of held; `ode.at(t)` reads the state inside a step, so agents acting at sub-step times see the continuous value.
- **Stochastic equations:** `SDE(drift, diffusion)` with Euler-Maruyama and Milstein schemes, increments drawn from the model’s seeded stream; checkpoints keep the stream position.
- **Delay equations:** fixed delays through a history buffer and the method of steps, the history saved in checkpoints.
- **Mean-field companion:** the ODE limit of an agent model (SIR, Lotka-Volterra, Bass) run next to it, with a helper that reports the gap between the two as the population grows.
- **Gradients:** a JAX path (optional `diffrax` extra) so `modelly.diff` calibrates ODE parameters by gradient, checked against finite differences.

**Done when:** a within-host and between-host epidemic joins the zoo (per-agent viral ODEs, one hundred thousand hosts) and its vectorised integration matches a per-agent `solve_ivp` loop within tolerance while running faster (measured); event times match the analytic crossing of exponential decay to `rtol`; Euler-Maruyama’s strong order of one half is measured on geometric Brownian motion; a resumed run equals a straight one bit for bit; all on the three platforms.

**Progress:** per-agent ODEs and events shipped in 1.4.3: `solve_batch`, `ODEEvent` and `AgentODE`, guide in [ODEs in every agent](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/agent_odes.html). Every system takes exactly the steps of its own `solve_ivp` call (tested on 200 random systems, both methods, two tolerances). S1 added time-varying inputs (`Forcing`, `Series`), dense output (`ode.at(t)`, `solve_batch(dense_output=True)`) and the zoo model `within_host`: 100,000 hosts, each host’s integration equal to its own `solve_ivp` call, one day 34 times faster than the loop (measured), clearance times equal to the analytic exponential decay to a relative 1e-6, a resumed run equal to a straight one bit for bit. S2 added delay equations (method of steps, history by agent id, in checkpoints), stochastic equations (`AgentSDE`, strong orders measured on geometric Brownian motion: Euler-Maruyama 0.53, Milstein 0.95), the mean-field companion (gap exponent -0.47 on the Bass zoo model) and gradients (`modelly.diff.ode_phase`: RK4 differentiated through its steps rather than the diffrax extra, since an adjoint integrated backwards is unstable for decaying systems; checked against finite differences). G12 is complete apart from the three-OS run.

**Size:** L · **Depends on:** 1.4 F6 (coupling), F3 (differentiable models)

# 2.0.0: clean foundations

**Status:** proposed · **Base:** 1.5.0

2.0.0 is the only release on this roadmap allowed to break things, and it breaks them on purpose and with a map. Three 1.x releases of features leave behind parallel ways of doing the same thing; 2.0 keeps the best one of each and makes it the only one. **One space API, one clock, columns by default, typed scenarios, per-agent random streams, a stable C ABI and a checkpoint format that lasts.** Every removal was deprecated in 1.5 at the latest, and `modelly migrate --to 2.0` rewrites what can be rewritten. All on Windows, macOS and Linux (see [Platforms](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/platforms.html)).

## Principles

1. **No surprise breaks.** Nothing is removed in 2.0 that did not warn in 1.5, naming the replacement.
1. **One way.** Where 1.x grew two ways to do a thing, 2.0 keeps one.
1. **Same science.** A model migrated to 2.0 gives statistically the same results as on 1.5; where the random streams change (per-agent streams), the migration guide says so and the agreement test (Welch, as in the playbooks) proves it.
1. **Faster everywhere.** No playbook slower than 1.5 on any OS.
1. **Supported 1.x.** 1.5 is a long-term-support line: it keeps receiving bug and security fixes after 2.0.0, so every user can migrate when their own work allows.

## Epics

### H1 · Removals and the migration tool

**Goal:** remove every deprecated name and make upgrading a command, not a project.

**Work items:** remove everything deprecated in 1.3 to 1.5; `modelly migrate --to 2.0` (the codemod from `modelly.migrate`, extended to 1.x → 2.0 rewrites) with a dry run, a diff and a report of what needs a human; a migration guide with before/after for every removal; migration tested on every zoo and hub model.

**Done when:** every zoo model and the three community models migrate automatically, pass their validation tests, and agree with their 1.5 results.

**Size:** L

### H2 · One space API

**Goal:** grids, networks, continuous space and geographic space share one protocol: the same calls to place, move, query neighbours and iterate, whatever the geometry.

**Design:** a `Space` protocol (`place`, `move`, `neighbors`, `within`, `positions` as a column); discrete spaces keep cells, continuous and geographic spaces keep coordinates, both answer the same queries; property layers become fields (from 1.4 F6) on every space; old space classes kept as thin aliases through 2.x where they map cleanly.

**Done when:** every zoo model runs on the new protocol; a model can switch grid to network to continuous space by changing one line, verified by a tutorial.

**Size:** XL

### H3 · Columns by default

**Goal:** agent state lives in columns unless the model asks otherwise, so every model gets the 1.x column speed-ups without rewriting.

**Design:** typed attribute declarations (`wealth: float = Column(0.0)` or plain annotations) become columns automatically; attributes that cannot be columns (objects, lists) stay per-agent and are reported by `modelly profile`; `DataCollector` gathers columns without Python loops.

**Done when:** the classic playbook variants (per-agent code) run at least as fast as their 1.5 column variants after migration; no model loses an attribute in migration.

**Size:** L

### H4 · One clock

**Goal:** ticks and events on one scheduler with one documented ordering rule.

**Design:** steps are events at integer times; phases are priorities; tie-breaking is fully specified (time, priority, insertion order); the compiled scheduler from 1.4 is the only one; a `schedule` report shows what runs when.

**Done when:** every model with mixed ticks and events gives the same results as on 1.5 under the documented ordering; the ordering spec is a docs page with tests for each rule.

**Size:** M

### H5 · Typed scenarios and configuration

**Goal:** scenarios are typed, validated and loadable from files.

**Design:** `Scenario` as a `dataclass_transform` base (the default-type TODO in `modelly/core/model.py` that waits for Python 3.13); validation with clear errors (range, type, units); TOML and YAML loading; scenarios hashed into the manifest; sweeps over typed spaces.

**Size:** M

### H6 · Per-agent random streams by default

**Goal:** results independent of iteration order, partitioning and executor.

**Design:** opt-in in 1.4 (F1), default in 2.0; counter-based generators (Philox) keyed by run seed and agent id, shared by CPU and GPU; the model-level generators remain for model-level draws.

**Done when:** partition-independence holds for every space by default; agreement tests show the same distributions as 1.5 on every playbook.

**Size:** M · **Depends on:** 1.4 F1, F2

### H7 · Stable ABI and native code

**Goal:** one wheel per platform for every supported Python, and native code ready for every CPython build.

**Design:** the compiled modules move to the limited C API (abi3) where measurement shows no loss, keeping the version-specific build only where it matters; free-threaded builds are first-class; the private and unstable APIs left are inventoried and justified.

**Done when:** abi3 wheels for every row of the [support matrix](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/platforms.html); no playbook slower than the version-specific build by more than 3%; a new CPython release installs on day one.

**Size:** M

### H8 · Checkpoint and data formats v2

**Goal:** a checkpoint written by 2.0 loads in every later 2.x release.

**Design:** a versioned, documented state format (columns as Arrow, structure as JSON, only user objects pickled); forward migrations between format versions; `modelly checkpoint upgrade` for 1.x files where the state maps; result stores and manifests versioned the same way.

**Done when:** a 2.0 checkpoint loads in a 2.1 test build; 1.5 checkpoints of every zoo model upgrade and resume with the same results.

**Size:** M

### H9 · Python and platform baseline

**Work items:** Python 3.13 minimum (3.12 dropped, as its own end of life approaches); a single test and release matrix covering every platform in the support table; installation verified on clean Windows, macOS and Linux machines with no compiler and no admin rights.

**Size:** S

### H10 · Public API contract

**Work items:** every public name listed in one place with its stability level (stable, provisional); the semantic-versioning promise written down; type-checked public API (strict); the plugin API v1 from 1.5 carried over unchanged.

**Size:** S

### H11 · Documentation 2.0

**Work items:** docs restructured around tasks (build, calibrate, scale, share, publish); every page tested (doctests and executed notebooks) on all three OSs; the migration guide and the “what is new in 2.0” tour; versioned docs keep `/1.5/` as the LTS reference.

**Size:** M
