# Platforms: Windows, macOS and Linux

**Rule:** a feature ships only when it works on Windows, macOS and Linux, with the same results for the same seed. A feature that cannot (for example, a SLURM executor, which needs a Linux cluster) must still be usable from all three: you submit from your Windows or macOS laptop, the cluster runs Linux.

## Support matrix

Wheels carry the compiled modules; every other platform installs the pure-Python wheel, which gives the same results, more slowly.

## Engineering rules that keep it true

1. **CI tests on all three.** The `build` workflow already runs the suite on Ubuntu, macOS and Windows; every new test runs there. The release workflow builds and import-tests wheels for each platform before anything is published.
1. **A local gate that runs everywhere.** `scripts/ci-local.sh` is bash. 1.3.0 adds `python -m modelly.dev gate`, the same stages in Python, so contributors on Windows run the same gate without WSL or Git Bash.
1. **No Unix tools in library code.** No calls to `sh`, `taskset`, `curl` or `sed` from `modelly/`. Scripts that users run (data downloads, benchmarks) are Python, not bash. `modelly bench` pins CPUs with `psutil` where the OS allows it (Linux, Windows) and says so where it does not (macOS).
1. **Paths and text.** `pathlib` everywhere; every `open()` of a text file names `encoding="utf-8"` (Windows defaults to a legacy code page); manifests store paths relative and in POSIX form; hashes are taken over bytes, never over text with platform line endings. The ruff rule for unspecified encodings is turned on in 1.3.
1. **Files that are written while read.** Checkpoints and result stores are written to a temporary file and moved into place with `os.replace`, which is atomic on all three and avoids Windows sharing violations.
1. **Native code for three compilers.** Every C module builds with GCC, Clang and MSVC, at warning level `-Wall` / `/W4`, with no compiler extensions outside an `#ifdef`. Thread safety is checked with ThreadSanitizer on Linux and macOS and by the free-threaded test suite on all three.
1. **Optional dependencies must have wheels for all three.** A library that needs a system install on one OS is not accepted as a dependency of a shipped feature.
1. **Determinism across platforms.** The determinism suite (1.3) runs every example, compiled and pure, saved and loaded, on all three and compares the outputs byte for byte; floating-point outputs that legitimately differ (for example a GPU reduction) are listed with their tolerance.
1. **Docs for both shells.** Where a command differs between bash and PowerShell, the docs show both.

## Per-release platform work

Release

Platform work

# Design reviews

A design review records, for one epic, what was decided, what else was considered and why the choice was made. The 1.3.0 roadmap asked for one page each for calibration (E1), sensitivity analysis (E2), Studio (E5) and language-model agents (E7); the Studio decision is in the [1.3.0 roadmap](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/roadmap/1.3.0.html) (E5), the other three are written here, after the fact, against the code as shipped in 1.3 and extended in 1.4.

- [Calibration (E1)](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/design/calibration.html)
- [Sensitivity analysis (E2)](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/design/sensitivity.html)
- [Language-model agents (E7)](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/design/llm-agents.html)


<!-- https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/design/calibration.md -->

# Design review: calibration (E1)

**Scope:** priors, targets, distances, the posterior object, the methods and how they run. **Code:** `modelly.calibrate`. **Guide:** [Calibration](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/calibration.html).

## Decisions

Question

Decision

Alternatives considered

Why

What is calibrated

Scenario parameters, named as in the model’s Scenario; other parameters fixed with fixed=

Free-form parameter functions; attributes set after construction

A scenario is already typed and validated, and it is what modelly run, experiments and manifests record, so a fitted point can be rerun and cited as is

Priors

One Prior class with named constructors (uniform, log_uniform, normal, log_normal, truncated_normal, choice) evaluated through scipy.stats

Accept any scipy.stats frozen distribution; a probabilistic-programming library

A closed set has known bounds (for the optimisers’ box and the plots) and pickles in checkpoints; scipy is already a dependency, a PPL is not

Targets

Target(name, observed, distance, weight, summary, output): an output the model records every step, the observed series or statistics, and how far apart they are

Distances on whole DataCollector frames; one global summary function

Reading outputs exactly as experiments do reuses the executors and the results store; per-target summaries and weights express pattern-oriented modelling (several patterns at once)

Distances

A function (simulated, observed) -> float; built-ins rmse, mae, euclidean, wasserstein, weighted(...)

Only RMSE; a distance object hierarchy

A plain function is the smallest contract; replicates are averaged before the distance so stochastic noise does not inflate it

Posterior

Weighted samples (Posterior): summary (mean, median, sd, HDI), to_dataframe, best, predict, plot

Return raw arrays; return ArviZ InferenceData

One small object covers every method (ABC returns many weighted samples, optimisers one); ArviZ would be a heavy dependency for a table and a plot

Methods

ABC rejection, ABC-SMC with an adaptive tolerance (quantile of the last distances), simulated method of moments, a built-in Gaussian-process Bayesian optimiser, and from 1.4 an adapter to outside optimisers (ExternalBayesOpt, optuna built in)

pyABC or ELFI as the engine; only one method

ABC needs no likelihood, which ABMs rarely have; SMC is the standard efficient variant; moments suit economists’ practice; a GP search covers expensive models without an extra install, and the adapter covers the cases where a dedicated library does better

Reproducibility

Every random draw comes from a named stream of the seed (Stream.PROPOSAL, DESIGN, …); a batch’s runs use the seeds of the batch

One generator advanced through the run

Named streams make the posterior identical on every executor, with the compiled or the pure-Python core, and after a resume

Running

Batches of runs through the experiment executors, written to a Parquet store; a rerun into the same store reads finished runs

Calling the model in a loop in-process

Parallel and cluster execution, failure handling and resumption come for free, and the same store answers later questions

Checkpoints

save / load pickle the whole calibration with a magic header

A JSON state file

The state includes priors, kernels and generations; pickling is the only complete form, and the header refuses foreign files

## What 1.4 added

- `ExternalBayesOpt` (optional `calibrate` extra): an outside optimiser behind `ask()` and `tell(point, value)` over the same unit box and common random numbers as `BayesOpt`. optuna is the built-in backend because it installs from pure-Python wheels on all three platforms and has a stable ask-and-tell API; scikit-optimize fits the same interface but is no longer actively released, so it is documented as a user-supplied factory instead of a built-in.
- A zoo model calibrated end to end: ABC-SMC recovers both Bass diffusion parameters inside their 95 % intervals on three seeds (`tests/calibrate/test_zoo_end_to_end.py`).

## Known limits

- ABC’s posterior is approximate: its width depends on the final tolerance, which the trace reports; it is not a likelihood-based posterior.
- The optimisers return the best point, not an uncertainty.
- Gradient-based calibration needs differentiable models (1.4 F3, not part of this review).

# Design review: sensitivity analysis (E2)

**Scope:** what is analysed, the parameter space, the methods, their estimators and results. **Code:** `modelly.sensitivity`. **Guide:** [Sensitivity analysis](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/sensitivity.html).

## Decisions

Question

Decision

Alternatives considered

Why

What is analysed

A Study: a Model class run through the experiment executors (an output reduced by a statistic, averaged over replicates), a plain function, or an emulator

Models only; wrap SALib

One interface lets the same call verify a method on an analytical function (Ishigami, Sobol G) and then run it on a model or its emulator

Parameter space

ScenarioSpace, shared with experiments and calibration; methods work in the unit cube and map points back

A space of the method’s own

A study, an experiment and a calibration of the same model describe their parameters once, and integer and choice dimensions behave the same everywhere

Screening

One-at-a-time sweeps and Morris elementary effects (mu*, sigma) on a grid of levels

Only Sobol

Morris ranks a dozen parameters for a few hundred runs, which is what a modeller needs before spending thousands on variance-based indices

Variance-based indices

Saltelli sampling from one scrambled Sobol sequence; Jansen estimators by default (Saltelli’s as an option); bootstrap confidence intervals

Monte Carlo sampling; FAST

Saltelli’s design gives S1 and ST from samples * (parameters + 2) runs; Jansen’s estimators have the lowest variance in Saltelli et al. (2010); the bootstrap needs no extra runs

Skewed outputs

PAWN, moment-independent, from output distributions

Only variance-based indices

Variance misleads for heavy-tailed or multimodal outputs, common in ABMs

Expensive models

An optional Gaussian-process emulator in place of the model (and, in 1.4, the modelly.emulate emulators)

Always run the model

A few hundred runs can stand for the tens of thousands Sobol needs

Seeds

The design, the bootstrap and the runs draw from named streams of seed

Global state

The same seed gives the same indices on every executor

Results

Result objects (MorrisResult, SobolResult, …) with tables (ranking(), indices()), plots and export

Plain dicts

Tables export to papers; plots follow the publication styles

## What 1.4 added

- Morris stability across seeds on zoo models: the ranking of the top parameters is the same for every seed on the Bass diffusion and the age-structured SEIR models (`tests/sensitivity/test_morris_stability.py`), the “done when” left open in 1.3.

## Known limits

- Morris with few trajectories ranks parameters whose effects are close in an order that can change with the seed; only clearly separated parameters are stable, which is what the test checks.
- Indices of a stochastic model mix parametric and run-to-run variance unless replicates are averaged; the guide says how many to use.

# Design review: language-model agents (E7)

**Scope:** the client, providers, the response cache, budgets, structured decisions and how LLM runs stay reproducible. **Code:** `modelly.llm`. **Guide:** [Language-model agents](https://remipelloux.github.io/Modelly/dev/llm_agents.html).

## Decisions

Question

Decision

Alternatives considered

Why

How agents call a model

Every call goes through one Client (model.llm by convention); agents mix in LLMAgent and call decide(prompt, schema)

Agents call provider SDKs directly; a framework such as LangChain

One choke point is where caching, budgets, retries, concurrency and the ordering of replies are enforced; lint rule MDL012 flags network calls that bypass it

Providers

Adapters over the standard library’s HTTP: Anthropic’s Messages API, OpenAI-compatible endpoints (OpenAI, Ollama, llama.cpp), and a FakeProvider for tests and teaching

Depend on each vendor’s SDK

No provider is needed to install Modelly, the same code reaches local models, and the adapters are small enough to audit

Reproducibility

A deterministic response cache keyed on the SHA-256 of provider, model, prompts, parameters, the model’s seed, the calling agent and its own call counter

Rely on temperature 0; seed the provider

Hosted models are not deterministic and may be retired; recording what was said is the only way to replay a run, and per-agent counters make keys independent of thread timing

The store

SQLite from the standard library, rollback journal, one transaction per reply; exports as sorted JSON lines (plain or gzip with a zero timestamp) or SQLite

A JSON file; a key-value server

Crash-safe and dependency-free; the sorted text export is diffable and gives the same bytes for the same calls

Modes

read-write (record what is missing), read-only (replay: a miss raises CacheMiss, nothing is sent), off

Always read-write

A reviewer must be able to prove that a replay made no call

Budgets

Token and cost budgets reserved before each call (prompt estimate plus max_tokens); no bundled prices

Count after the fact; ship a price table

A budget must stop a run before it overspends; prices change and a stale one is worse than none

Structured decisions

JSON Schema validation of replies, with a bounded number of repair calls

Free text parsed by the model code

Decisions that feed a model’s state must be typed; repairs are calls too, so they are cached and counted

Checkpoints and bundles

The client, its cache and counters are part of the model’s checkpoint; from 1.4 modelly run exports the replies next to the outputs and modelly bundle packs them, and modelly verify replays them

Leave the cache to the user

“The bundle verifies with no network” was a done-when of E7 that 1.3 left to the user; 1.4 closes it

## What 1.4 added

- `modelly.llm.replay.replaying(path)`: inside the block every `Client` created answers only from the recorded replies, read-only, whatever provider and cache the model builds. `modelly verify` reruns under it, so a study that called a hosted model verifies offline and without an API key (`tests/provenance/test_provenance_llm.py` refuses every socket while it checks).

## Known limits

- A replay reproduces a run only when the run asks the same questions in the same order; a changed prompt changes its key and stops the replay at the first unrecorded call.
- The cache records a model’s answers, not the model: a replay cannot say what a newer model would have answered.
